runs: the loose steep rib that divides two prominent drainages
hits.text: Walk the East Eagle Trail up the valley for about 1.5 mi, then leave it and head right into the steep basin on Krag Peak's west side. The line climbs the loose, steep rib that divides two prominent drainages; stay on the crest of the rib rather than in the gullies either side. Expect sections of exposure with big loose blocks, and test every hold. The rib tops out on the west (northwest) summit. From there, traverse the crest to the slightly higher east summit, then continue along the ridge crest before descending the rubbly slopes toward Crater Lake. From the lake, pick up the Little Kettle Creek Trail and follow its many switchbacks back down to the East Eagle Trailhead.

The Middle Point Ridge Trailhead sits on the river at about 3,373 feet, with a vault toilet and no water. The road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter; snow on the crags and approach slopes is what limits climbing, to roughly May through October, sometimes from April. hits.text: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike North: park 1.1 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, where a dirt road intersects the paved road on the left (SE side), or continue to 1.2 miles and use the large pull-off. Cross the main road and pick up the approach trail between the two parking spots, marked by a short steep drainage topped with a downed tree.

hits.text: This is the side every recorded ascent of the north ridge has come from. Maps show an old trail running west from Gardner Meadows toward a mine at a small tarn on the peak's northeast side, but there is very little evidence of it leaving the meadows and it is effectively abandoned: parties bushwhack along its rough line, picking up occasional cairns and cut logs, and the tread only firms up nearer the tarn. Expect the trail to peter out past the campsites and the going to become a matter of climbing over, around and under downed timber. Keep above the lake below the ridge rather than dropping to it. The north side can also be entered from the North Creek valley on the far side of the range, but that way is undescribed, so the marks below are written for this approach rather than that one.

runs: to the mouth of a steep snow gully
hits.text: Follow a faint climbers' path along the crest for about two hundred yards, then traverse right onto slabby red ledges near a rock rib. A cleft just left of the rib and more slabby ledges gain a flat step on top of it; a down-sloping bench then crosses to the mouth of a steep snow gully, where a tall snow fin splits the gully and you take a moat on either side or the hole through the fin itself. From the notch above, two pitches of the Great Chimney lead to the top — a 5.3 entry, then a smooth 5.4 face move over a large chockstone and a squeeze so tight that packs have to be pushed through ahead of the climber. Above the chimney a dirty slabby trough, a row of horns and gaps, and one dramatically exposed step-across finish the climb.

runs: the high pass trail at a quarter mile
hits.text:
Contamination warning before anything else: this is American Border Peak, 7,998 ft, in Washington. Canadian Border Peak is about a kilometre north across the international line and is a different mountain with its own routes, reached from British Columbia. Beta for the two is routinely mixed up because both are called 'Border Peak'. Everything here is the Washington approach from Twin Lakes.

From the Twin Lakes trailhead at about 5,200 ft, take the High Pass Trail; at a quarter mile it splits from the short spur up Winchester Mountain — stay left, north. The trail contours the west side of Winchester, dips across Low Pass, and climbs to High Pass near 5,960 ft, about two miles and 750 ft of gain, where Mount Baker comes into view south.

At High Pass leave the maintained tread and follow the climbers' path north and west down to the old Gargett Mine workings around 5,400 ft. The mine creek is the last reliable water until lingering snow high on the peak.

From the mine, traverse north and contour onto Mount Larrabee's southwest and west flanks. This is a long, unmarked, exposed sidehill of well over a mile across steep talus, scree, heather and brush.

Most parties camp at Gargett Basin or in the moraine bowl and climb from there rather than pushing summit day from the car.

runs: up and across a series of steep gullies and ribs
hits.text:
The 6,200-6,300 ft notch on Larrabee's northwest rib is the first gate, and the South Ambo Saddle at about 6,840 ft is the second. Those two are the whole navigation of this approach and both are cols — places where the ridge is low and you can stand on the crest with ground falling away on the far side. In cloud you are counting cols, not looking at the peak.

Between them is a red talus and moraine bowl. From the notch you drop slightly into it and then climb north out of it, up and across a series of steep gullies and ribs, to the saddle. Red rock underfoot after the first col is the confirmation you are in the right bowl.

Arrival at the saddle: it is on the ridge crest directly south of the summit. Standing there, the peak is north of you and Larrabee is behind you to the south. That bearing is the check — this is not a saddle you reach with the mountain to one side.

Where the climbing actually starts is 200 yards above the saddle, not at it. From the saddle, go up the ridge crest on a faint climbers' path for roughly 200 yards, then start traversing rightward on slabby red ledges. The rock scrambling begins where the angle steepens noticeably at a distinctive rock rib: the first real move is up a small Class 3.5 cleft closely left of that rib.

De Gaulle's Nose is the aiming mark on the far side of the red face, at about 7,300 ft. The rising traverse across the red slopes goes toward it and the crossing feels very exposed. Beyond it come two 60-metre gullies with a sand-covered ledge traverse between them, and a chimney at the top of the second reached by a very airy ledge. If your route has no red traverse and no pair of long gullies, it is not this one.

And the hard condition rule: do not attempt the Larrabee sidehill on wet grass or wet rock. Parties flag that as a genuine no-go rather than a discomfort.

runs: friction moves crossing the top of the block to
hits.text: The count is the test. Middle Finger Buttress is the biggest feature on the wall, and Ka'aba — where this route is — sits two buttresses to its left. So find the biggest one first, then count two left. Ka'aba itself is blocky and stepped, described as looking like stepping stones, which is quite unlike the clean sweep of Middle Finger. Be aware that the two buttresses between them are unnamed, so the count is the only handle you have — there is no known left-to-right inventory of this wall. Arrival is a large block at the base that you scramble onto for the first pitch, and getting onto it has a known seasonal trap. Approaching from the left side of the block runs into a large snow moat that stopped one party in early July. The right side goes, though it needs some care on friction moves crossing the top of the block to reach the wall. Walk-off, and there are two. The short one is a gully on the north side about a thousand feet east of Ka'aba, roughly thirty-five to forty degrees, giving a half-mile return to the lake — but it can hold firm snow through July. The longer one circles south around Amphitheater's western arm on sand and then meadows with a decent trail, rejoining the Boundary Trail and returning to the lake in about two miles and fifty minutes of easy walking.

hits.text: From the Dosewallips Ranger Station (the road-walk/bike-in described separately covers reaching this point, since the Dosewallips River Road washout has closed vehicle access since 2002), pick up the Dosewallips River Trail and go about 1.4 miles to the signed junction with the West Fork Dosewallips Trail. Turn up the West Fork Trail and follow the river valley through old-growth forest roughly 8 miles to Honeymoon Meadows (3,527 ft) — this is the last reliable flat camping and dependable water before the climb, though the West Fork ford here (and a second crossing near Diamond Meadow lower down) can run thigh-deep and swift in early season or after rain, and the trail has substantial blowdown because NPS maintenance has lagged since the road closure. From Honeymoon Meadows continue up switchbacks about 1.2 more miles to Anderson Pass (4,464 ft), the Dosewallips/Quinault divide and junction with the Enchanted Valley trail — roughly 16 miles and the end of maintained tread. At the pass, leave the trail and follow a climbers' boot path north over talus and heather benches about a mile and 700+ ft of gain to the Anderson Glacier moraine (~5,200 ft), passing a small tarn; this is the customary high camp. From the moraine, ascend along the glacier margin/moraine crest toward Flypaper Pass (6,500 ft), the notch between Mount Anderson to the east and 7,033-ft Echo Rock to the west — historically a steep snow finger, now increasingly bare scree and, late season, exposed ice as the finger has receded, making an ice axe/crampons and careful footing important; this section is best done in spring or early summer before it melts out. Anderson's Thumb is the prominent sandstone pinnacle in this Flypaper Pass/Echo Rock vicinity (visible from the Anderson Glacier basin around 5,250 ft); below the pass, bear west under Echo Rock and scramble talus and ledges to its base. No water is reliably available above the Anderson Glacier moraine besides snowmelt, so fill up at camp.

Cross the moat and rappel 75 ft to the Klawatti Glacier from an old anchor. Getting back up on the return is a short belayed pitch graded 5.5–5.6 (stay left in the gully), so carry a small rack and retrievable cord.

hits.text: Leave packs and crampons at the rock. One line climbs a few hundred feet of 4th class, traverses left on a broken ridge, and finishes with about 30 ft of low 5th around to the right on the northeast face, which can be soloed or simul-climbed. An easier class 3 line on the southeast ridge also reaches this sub-summit, where most parties stop.

runs: around to the right on the northeast face
hits.text:
The base is a break in the ridge at about 7,900 ft that you rappel into, not walk through. That is the single most useful thing to know here: the correct notch takes about 75 ft of rope to get down onto the Klawatti Glacier, and on the way back it is roughly 75 ft of well-protected 5.5 to climb out. A gap you strolled through is Klawatti Col, one col short, at about 7,800 ft.

Get there by counting, not by sighting Austera. Cross the Inspiration to Klawatti Col; pass Klawatti Peak on your left through that col; follow the ridge along the upper McAllister Glacier about 0.4 mile to the second break. Austera is the high point of a whole arête of towers and picking it out from below is not a reliable way to navigate.

Above the glacier traverse the climbing is short and countable: a few hundred feet of 4th class gains a sub-summit, and a further short pitch — about 30 to 50 ft of low fifth, taken around to the right on the northeast face — reaches the true top.

The false summit is the real hazard on this peak, and it is the test that matters. Parties top out a few feet short of the true summit again and again. The true summit is reached only after crossing a narrow, often snowy ridge between two blocks and climbing a short chimney or a few feet of low fifth beyond it. If you got to where you are standing without a rope-worthy move and without crossing that ridge, you are on the false summit and the mountain is not finished with you.

The moat beside the rappel point is the thing most likely to change year to year; check it on the way in, because it has to work in the other direction at the end of the day.

runs: a small notch at the base of klawatti's north ridge
hits.text: The traverse ends at a small notch at the base of Klawatti's north ridge, and getting down from it onto the Klawatti Glacier is the crux of the whole traverse. Early in the season it downclimbs; as the moat opens through the summer it needs a rappel of roughly 75 ft, and the lowest notch can push into class 5 with class 4 ground to its southeast. Old rappel anchors turn up here — treat any in-place tat as suspect and carry cord to back it up or replace it. On the way back, some parties climb well-protected rock out of the glacier rather than rig a rappel.

hits.text: Marked as Horse Heaven Camp on the USGS topo, a meadow site about 2 miles south of the Brush Creek PCT junction; the unsigned Mill Creek/Azurite Pass path leaves the PCT roughly 120 yards east of Jet Creek, flagged by a small rock cairn.

runs: traverse across a series of ribs gullies and sandy slopes
hits.text: From the West Fork Methow River Trailhead (River Bend Campground, ~2,700 ft, at the end of Lost River Road/FR 5400), follow the West Fork Methow River Trail roughly 8 miles up-valley to its junction with the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT) at Brush Creek. Turn left (south/west) on the PCT and follow it about 1.5-2 miles, crossing Jet Creek, to Horse Heaven Camp (~4,350 ft) — the last reliable, easy water before the climb (treat before drinking; flows can drop significantly by late season). From camp, pick up the old, unsigned Azurite Pass (Mill Creek) trail, which departs the PCT roughly 120 yards east of the Jet Creek crossing at a small rock cairn — easy to miss, and parties note the tread is faint/braided enough that a GPS track is genuinely useful here. The path switchbacks up through slide-alder brush, firms up into a real trail around 5,000 ft, re-crosses Jet Creek at about 5,300 ft (a rock-hop ford, can run high with snowmelt in June/early July), then climbs through eroded, brushy benches before breaking out into open heather meadows and granite slabs just below Azurite Pass (6,700 ft) — roughly 3-3.5 hours from Horse Heaven Camp. From the pass, leave the trail and work northeast/east up a mix of krummholz, sand, scree, and talus to a broad shoulder around 7,400 ft, then follow a gently rising, ducked/cairned traverse across a series of ribs, gullies, and sandy slopes toward the base of the summit tower. The final push climbs a prominent south/southwest-facing gully — loose underfoot (watch for rockfall onto party members below) but no harder than Class 3 in dry conditions; it can hold firm snow well into summer, in which case an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) is worth carrying. Total one-way distance from the trailhead is on the order of 12-13 miles with about 6,700 ft of gain, so most parties backpack in to Horse Heaven Camp and climb from there rather than doing it car-to-car.

hits.text: From Azurite Pass leave the trail and work northeast and east up krummholz, sand, scree and talus to a flat shoulder at about 7,400 ft — flat enough that parties cache overnight gear on it, and easy to relocate on the way down. Continue up the crest to roughly 7,600 ft, where a lower south summit obstructs the ridge and the well-cairned climbers' route drops off westward. From there a gently rising traverse crosses a series of ribs, gullies and sandy slopes, well marked with ducks and cairns, staying below the cliffs rather than in them, and crossing two or three short snow runnels that an ice axe handles. The traverse runs toward the peak's prominent west rib.

runs: to the last gully to the south and
hits.text: Turn up too late and you meet the southwest face — that is the error to watch for. The correct gully is narrow at its base and cannot be seen from the ridge, so parties keep traversing hoping for something obvious, run out onto the imposing southwest face, and find it goes Class 4 in a hurry. The stated fix from those who have made that mistake is to retreat to the last gully to the south and go up that. The right line stays loose and never harder than short steps of Class 3 for roughly the last 200 ft to the top: if you are climbing more than short sections of Class 4, you are off route, and if you have drifted onto cleaner, more solid rock high on the gully's climber's-left wall you have left the gully floor for steeper and more exposed ground. One gully on this line pinches to about three feet, tight enough to touch both walls with your arms out — that constriction is a confirmation you are in a real line, not a warning.

hits.text: From Dayton, follow North Touchet Road up the East Fork Touchet River valley toward Ski Bluewood; it stays paved for roughly the first 15 to 16 miles, then turns to gravel as Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary. The Middle Point Ridge Trailhead sits on the river at about 3,373 feet, with a vault toilet and no water. The road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter; snow on the crags and approach slopes is what limits climbing, to roughly May through October, sometimes from April. The Dikes lie farther on, upstream and south toward Bluewood.

hits.text: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike North: park 1.1 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, where a dirt road intersects the paved road on the left (SE side), or continue to 1.2 miles and use the large pull-off. Cross the main road and pick up the approach trail between the two parking spots, marked by a short steep drainage topped with a downed tree.

hits.text: The standard descent reverses the ascent line: down the summit snow slopes and col, back onto and down the Diobsud Creek Glacier (roped, same crevasse caution as the approach), down through the steep loose gully/south-ridge terrain to Diobsud Lakes, then back over the Mt. Watson sidehill, saddle, and Anderson Lakes ridge path to the Watson Lakes Trailhead. This is a walk-off/glacier-descent — no rappels are used on the standard round trip; the technical difficulty is glacier travel and loose, steep downclimbing rather than anything requiring rope-anchored lowering. Parties continuing north as part of a longer Bacon-Hagan-Blum (or Watson-Bacon-Hagan-Blum) traverse instead descend from the summit down quick snow slopes to the "Bacon Tarns" (small glacial-melt ponds on a rock bench below the Green Lake Glacier), then follow heather and meadow along Bacon's north ridge, passing high above Green Lake toward Hidden Lake, continuing the traverse rather than returning to the Watson Lakes trailhead. Either way, expect the same loose-rock and brush hazards on the south-ridge gully in reverse, and re-assess glacier conditions/crevasse bridges on the return trip since afternoon snow softening changes the picture from the morning ascent.

A recreation pass must be displayed at the trailhead, and between December and April a state Sno-Park permit is required at the Anderson Creek Sno-Park instead. hits.text: The climber/hiker trailhead is at the end of FR 2870 (signed Baldy/Tyler Peak trailhead, ~12-car gravel pullout, roughly 47.883, -123.143) in the Upper Dungeness drainage of the Hood Canal Ranger District. From the trailhead, follow the old roadbed a short distance; at about 0.3 mile the Baldy climber's path (Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816) splits off to the right and begins climbing in earnest. At roughly 0.5 mile (~3,600 ft) the trail crosses a decommissioned logging road. Mueller Creek parallels the route through these early switchbacks and is the last reliable water low on the mountain — top off here, especially in late summer. The only water higher up is a small meadow stream reached by a short, steep side path just below where the trail gains the ridge crest, and nothing flows above that. Around 1.3 miles the path crosses the old Maynard Burn track near a brief junction with the Upper Dungeness Trail (#833.2) before continuing up as the Upper Maynard Burn Trail (#816.2). Hikers describe this middle section as a relentless, eroded 'staircase' — expect a narrow tread (in spots barely a foot wide) sidehilling an eroding slope, crumbly footing crossing a rocky ravine, and faint, muddy tread through boggy meadow benches where flagging/cairns can be sparse. By about 2 miles the forest thins and Tyler Peak comes into view; by 2.7 miles (~6,200 ft) the trail gains the open ridge crest/saddle east of Baldy, with the first views north to the Strait of Juan de Fuca and Vancouver Island — this is also where the route leaves the trees for good, an important landmark for the return. From the saddle, a boot path continues west along the exposed ridge, over a false summit (roughly 6,500 ft, frequently mistaken for the true top and a common confusion point in poor visibility) to the actual summit at 3.6 miles / 6,808 ft, which has an old campsite. Total is about 7.2 miles and 3,800 ft round trip. The ridge is fully exposed to wind and cloud, and lingering snow can bury the boot path into June; carry a map/GPS track for the upper mountain.

Do not plan on reversing the wall — the accepted way down is the non-technical walk-off on the far side of the mountain, and no fixed rappel stations should be assumed anywhere on the face.

From the Salmon La Sac trailhead, hike the Waptus River Trail about nine miles to Waptus Lake. The hiker bridge over Spinola Creek near the lake has washed out, so cross at the nearby horse ford, reached from the Waptus Pass Trail. Where the trail joins the PCT, head southbound (west).

Shortly before the PCT crosses the Waptus River, leave the trail and head northwest toward a faint shoulder and bench through flat, easy forest. Pick up a fisherman's trail on the southwest side of that bench and follow it toward Shovel Creek, then up and over the bench past an informal campsite with a giant cairn, where it starts to climb the shoulder on the east side of Shovel Creek.

Before long the trail leaves the forest straight onto talus. Easy talus walking brings you to Shovel Creek; cross where convenient.

Roughly 13 miles to the base, five to six hours. Most parties camp near the Waptus River PCT bridge.

hits.text:
Crossing Shovel Creek off the talus puts you at the foot of the Mega Slab — that is the arrival, and it is a creek crossing rather than a judgement. The slab drops from the peak's southeast shoulder at about 6,700 ft all the way to Shovel Creek at about 3,700 ft, so there is no ambiguity about which piece of rock it is: it is the enormous unbroken sheet above you, one of the longest continuous sandstone slabs in North America.

Which line on the slab is the real question here, and for this route the answer is a single word: lowest. Infinite Beauty begins at the lowest part of the slab, on a shallow rib. Walk the base downhill until it stops going down, and start on the rib there.

How that distinguishes it from its neighbour: Timeless Treasure climbs the middle of the slab. So if you have walked out along the base looking for a nicer-looking start, you are on Timeless Treasure. The lowest point is the whole distinction and it is decidable by walking downhill rather than by looking.

What the rock should feel like, as confirmation: clean, solid, grippy low-angle stone with minimal breaks, and roughly 2,000 ft of sustained fourth class. Approach shoes or trail runners friction well on it and most of the slab is climbed unroped. If you are pulling into cracks or dodging vegetation, you are off the clean sheet.

And where the route ends its own identity: after about 2,000 ft the line naturally angles right and joins Timeless Treasure for brief, unexposed low-fifth moves up overlaps trending up and right to the southeast shoulder. runs: move left and climb up on knobs to a belay
hits.text:
Look for two large Vs and start in the chimney to their left. That is the whole identification, it is published in exactly those terms, and the accompanying note is that you cannot miss it. Two prominent V-shaped features on the south face; the route's first pitch takes the chimney immediately left of them.

Confirm with the first pitch itself: from the chimney you move left and climb up on knobs to a belay, at about 5.7. Knobs after a leftward move out of a chimney is the signature. If you are pulling straight up out of the chimney with no traverse, look again.

Position relative to its neighbour, which is the check that catches the common error: this route is to the climber's right of the classic south-face line. So if you are at the middle of the base of the face, you are one route too far left. Walk right until the two Vs are on your right-hand side and you are at a chimney.

And a distance check on the route as a whole: seven pitches, about 650 ft, running 5.5 to 5.9, with a long chimney-gully crossing to a big ledge partway up and a forced rightward dihedral as the crux. A four- or five-pitch route ending on the West Ridge is one of the shorter lines on the left flank, not this.

In cloud, when you cannot see the Vs from a distance, walk the foot of the face and count chimneys rather than guessing: the Vs are large features and they are visible from close under them even when the summit is not.

hits.text: The route follows a ledge system extending from the center of the south face rightward into a series of chimneys and wide cracks. Lower pitches (roughly pitches 2-4) involve scrambling and chimney climbing from 5.6-5.7 up to 5.8+ on somewhat loose rock. The crux, pitch 5, is a pleasant finger-and-hands crack with good protection, finishing with a fist jam through a small overhang. Some parties continue up the final West Face 5.6 slab pitch to reach the true summit rather than stopping at the top of pitch 6.

Turn left (east) and climb broad scree to the low point on the ridge between Big Kangaroo and Half Moon, aiming for the col midway between them rather than the steeper notch nearer Half Moon, and cross into the basin under Big Kangaroo's south wall. Start up the obvious central ramp and climb six pitches of ramps, chimneys and cracks, 5.4 to 5.9+. To tag it, drop about 150 ft of scree on the far side, cross north into the West Route gully and climb its short pitches to the unprotected 5.6 summit slab (protected by a single old bolt), which is downclimbed or top-roped; then descend the shared gully: two slung-block anchors get you down with one or two single-rope rappels (a 60m rope is sufficient either way) through the steep/loose upper gully, after which it's a scree-and-snow walk/glissade down the gully back to the approach basin, across Early Winters Creek, and out the climbers' trail to the Hairpin Turn. runs: between the south face and the true summit
hits.text:
Cut left, east, toward the low point on the ridge between Big Kangaroo and Half Moon. That col drops and traverses you into the south-facing basin directly below Big Kangaroo's south wall.

Arrival at the route itself is visual and unambiguous when you can see the wall: the Beckey-Tate's obvious central ramp-and-ledge system splits the face. A single ramp system running up the middle of a south wall, splitting it, is the line.

So the order of finds is: stay west of the creek, reach the head of the basin, cut east to the Half Moon col, drop into the south basin, then look for the ramp splitting the middle of the wall.

The negative test against the west face, which is the commonest error from this car: the west face route crosses Early Winters Creek after only half a mile, at the edge of the talus field, and takes a broad shallow west-facing gully with a chockstone in it. If you crossed the creek early and are looking at a chockstone, you are on the west side of the mountain.

And against the other south-face lines, which share this basin: Kearney-Thomas crosses the creek and ascends the prominent gully system taking the left fork at the high Y-junction. Going down under starts at the Beckey-Tate base and then traverses right across overlaps to its own start ledge. Skinny Start is about 30 metres right of the Kearney-Thomas start. So on this wall: the central ramp is Beckey-Tate, and everything else is measured from either it or Kearney-Thomas.

Descent is not down this route, and the reason matters: rappelling the Beckey-Tate is technically possible with two ropes, roughly five to six rappels off slings and trees, but the route wanders and holds a lot of large loose rock, so rope-stuck and rockfall risk is high and most parties explicitly avoid it. Instead scramble about 20 ft up and left to the notch between the south face and the true summit, which is a few hundred feet higher, and descend the gully from there.

hits.text: Drive to the Sunrise Mine trailhead (Mountain Loop Highway, Forest Road 4065) and start up the Sunrise Mine Trail. Follow it about 2.5 miles, gaining to roughly 4,300 ft, to the last major switchback before the trail begins its final zigzag up toward Headlee Pass — this is the turnoff point, not the pass itself. Leave the maintained trail here and pick up a cairned traverse heading northeast across open talus toward Vega North Tower (also called Eros Tower). The line of cairns crosses two separate talus fields separated by strips of subalpine trees, passing just above a large flat-topped boulder near the first stand of trees. This talus traverse is the shared approach for Mile High Club, Marvin's Ear, and Beyond Redlining, so cairns and a boot path are well established in season, but talus can be loose and slow going with a pack. A reliable fresh-water seep is at a red-rock outcrop in the Mile High gully, roughly at the base of the formation — worth topping off here since there's no water higher on the wall. Beyond Redlining's start is on the dark gray face directly above the two largest boulders at the base of the tower, just left of (west of) Mile High Club's start. Expect lingering steep snow against the base in early season, which can make the last stretch of the talus approach and the transition onto rock its own small crux.

There is more than one gully in the headwall and the choice matters. The northernmost gully is the winter line. In dry conditions take the one trending west toward the upper basin, gained by a series of class 3-4 ledges and ramps rather than by a snow chute; in snow conditions the hidden chute goes instead.

From the upper basin, walk south across several gullies before you commit. The correct main couloir is the one that is noticeably narrower than the ones you crossed to get there, and it is the point where crampons go on. A gully you can stroll into without committing is not it — the right one is steep and offers no reprieve from the first steps. runs: onto the open granite slab of the north slope
hits.text:
The trail departure is marked by a fallen log across the road from it, and it is half a mile short of the Horse Camp. Those two facts together are what make it findable, because the boot path itself is unmarked. If you have reached the old Hardscrabble Horse Camp, you have gone about half a mile too far.

The rule that keeps you alive on the way to the lakes: climbing past the lower and upper Hardscrabble Lakes, stay close to the inlet. Straying left leads into cliff bands, and the east face and buttress above the lower lake drop directly into the water in steep walls. Inlet on your side, cliffs away to the left.

From upper Hardscrabble Lake, the sequence is short and countable: climb a gully to a col, drop onto the open granite slab of the north slope, then follow the east ridge to the summit. Gully, col, granite slab, ridge. If you top the gully and are not looking at an open slab of granite, you are at the wrong col.

What this route is not: the East buttress is a ten-pitch technical line on the same side of the mountain, reached from the lower lake rather than the upper one. If you are roping up, you are on the buttress and not on this route.

Where it sits relative to the peak: it is an isolated crag, separate from the rest of Guye, low down and near the base of the South Rib. If you are looking at the large west face, this cliff is just around the corner to the right of it and well below. So: west face on your left shoulder, corner, small isolated cliff low on the right.

The move off the ground is the proof, and it is unmistakable. The pitch starts steeply off a left-hand side-pull, and the first piece is a #1 Camalot plugged into a pod, before you clip the first bolt. If there is no pod at head height taking a #1 and no bolt above it, you are at the wrong bit of rock.

And the shape of the whole thing, as a final check: 50 ft, a rest ledge partway up, then a pumpy sequence moving left to a two-bolt chain anchor. It does not top out. Any line here that continues into the mountain above is not this route.

Honest caveat: this is a 2014 line with almost no recorded traffic, so the fixed gear is aging and seldom inspected.

hits.text:
The first pitch begins at a small caret-shaped snowpatch, and you start just right of it. That patch is the marker the first-ascent party chose to record, and it is the only thing at the base of this wall that is a shape rather than a description. Walk the talus until you find it.

The positive test is a colour change, and it is excellent in bad light: pitch one is a 220 ft scramble at about 5.4 up white slabs to a stance below a large, steeper band of darker rock. White below, dark above, easy climbing. If your first pitch is hard, or if the rock is uniform, you are somewhere else.

The second confirmation is above the first: from that stance you are aiming for an obvious, large open book, which takes the second pitch at 5.8. A big open corner directly above easy white slabs is the pair of features that identifies this route. One without the other is not enough.

Left to right across this wall, facing it from the west: Oregonian, Soviet, Cascadian. This is the right-hand one — looker's right of both older routes, which are on the north-west buttress and are out of view at the far left margin of the wall from here. If you can see two other lines to your left and none to your right, you are in the correct place.

The negative marker is the strongest on this page, and it is about what lies further right: the part of the wall to the right of this route, above the long snowfield, is unclimbed, and the party who looked hardest at it described it as atrocious. This route begins just right of a tiny snowpatch, not above a long one. If you are standing under a big snowfield, keep walking back left.

Where it eases: difficulties relent only on reaching the ridge just south of the true summit, sixteen pitches up. There is no midway escape.

hits.text: Bonanza Peak (9,516') is the highest non-volcanic summit in Washington and the highpoint of Chelan County. The Mary Green Glacier route — first climbed in 1937 by Curtis Ijames, Barrie James, and Joe Leuthold (Mazamas) — is the peak's classic standard line, ascending its eastern side. Reached only via the Lady of the Lake ferry up Lake Chelan and the remote trail-and-boat village of Holden, the climb combines glacier travel and a moat crossing with a short, exposed Class 3-4 rock finish to a summit deep in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. From the Holden Campground trailhead it's roughly 14 miles round trip with about 6,300 ft of elevation gain to the summit, on top of the multi-day boat-and-trail approach just to reach that trailhead.

A multi-day backpack toward Park Creek Pass and the head of Park Creek — from the Thunder Creek trail out of Colonial Creek Campground, or as part of a Buckner-area traverse — then camp near the base of the face for an alpine start.

From camp the sequence is: climb easier cliffs to a small glacier at the base of the face, ascend left up that glacier to an icefall, then traverse right through the icefall to reach the main rock wall. The first-ascent party described that crossing as genuinely exposed and frightening.

The face averages about 70 degrees and is over 3,000 ft high, on generally sound Cascade granodiorite and orthogneiss, apart from one band that is not. The first ascent was made in August 1964.

The descent is not the face: from the summit, take the ordinary route down to the Booker-Buckner col and back toward a Park Creek camp — which is what the first-ascent party did, reaching their camp just before dark.

runs: the first three pitches of the southwest rib
hits.text:
This route has no ground start, and that is the most important fact about finding it. You reach it by climbing the first three pitches of the southwest rib, or alternatively by the Northwest Face Boving-Pollock line, and then going left at a ledge where the two roofs come into view.

So the base of the day is the base of the southwest rib, and that has a landmark you can stand under: the Y-shaped larch tree at the base of the southwest rib, left of the southwest couloir. A larch with a forked trunk, at the foot of a rib, with a couloir to its right. That is the aiming point from the basin.

The in-route test is visual and binary: go left at the ledge where the two roofs come into view. Two roofs, stacked. If you can see only one overhang, or none, you have not reached the ledge. If you have climbed more than three pitches of the rib you have gone past it.

A hazard right at the start of the pitch, recorded because it is exactly where a party is committing: there is a loose block right at the start of the roof pitch.

What nobody does here, which answers the obvious question: parties do not reverse this pitch. Rappelling back through an overhanging roof is awkward and is not the documented practice. Most continue up the remaining Southwest Rib pitches to the true summit and take the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete to the rabbit ears then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted stations climber's right of the gully, which land at the foot of the South Arete rather than back at the larch.

hits.text: From I-90 Exit 47, take Denny Creek Road (FR 58) about 3 miles, past Denny Creek Campground, then turn left onto FR 5830 to the Denny Creek trailhead (~2,300 ft). Follow the Denny Creek Trail (#1014, the Melakwa Lake trail) up the valley past waterfalls, then up steeper switchbacks to Hemlock Pass, about 4 miles and roughly 2,300 ft above the car. At the crest of the pass turn right and follow the ridge on a bearing of about 33°, skirting cliff bands mainly on the left, to a plateau and meadow on the ridge. Early in the season, while snow still covers the brush, a brushy notch behind trees on the right leads about 170 ft up and then northeast to a meadow at the foot of the talus field that wraps about three-quarters of the peak's base; later in the season that line is choked with brush, so stay on the ridge and go straight up it to the summit block. The final scramble is loose rock on the left, or when snow-free around the exposed north side; helmets are recommended. The round trip is about 9 miles with roughly 3,600 ft of gain for Bryant alone; adding nearby Hemlock Peak makes it about 9.5 miles and 3,900 ft.

hits.text:
Start at Trinity at the end of the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, at about 2,800 ft. Take the Buck Creek trail #1513, which splits off the Chiwawa River trail within the first mile and climbs steadily to Buck Creek Pass — roughly six hours and about 3,100 ft of gain.

Why this way round at all is worth understanding before you commit: Buck sits only about three miles from Trinity as the crow flies and is Class 2-3 from the south-west, but a long rugged ridge runs north and south of it and there is no road or trail up the Napeequa on the west, so the normal route is a very long way round. The two documented ways to reach that west side are the high route north from Buck Creek Pass and Little Giant Pass from the south.

At the pass there is a large established camp with toilets just before the switchbacks up toward Liberty Cap. Fill up with water there — there is none for the next four miles and the ridge walk is fully sun-exposed.

Follow the old High Pass trail as it winds high around the side of Liberty Cap, then south for several miles until the tread dies out in talus and hard snowfields at High Pass; crampons are worth having for that. Contour through the pass and under Mount Berge, then angle up to the ridge crest just south of Point 7839. A short section of Class 3 reaches a faint saddle from which there is an easy walk-off down into Louis Creek Basin.

hits.text: Start from the Boston Basin Trailhead (~3,200 ft), about 21.7 miles up Cascade River Road from Marblemount (a separate, shorter-drive trailhead than the Cascade Pass TH used for the SW route). The unmaintained climbers' path follows an old, overgrown mining road for about 1 mile to a former mine site, then becomes a steep boot-path through old-growth forest with roughly four creek/stream crossings, emerging above treeline around 5,300 ft into Boston Basin — about 2.5 miles and 3,100 ft of gain, typically 3-4 hours. Boston Basin has two designated backcountry camps used as base for this route: low camp (~5,300 ft) and high camp (~6,300-6,400 ft); an NPS permit is required and camping is restricted to these established sites. From high camp, follow the Quien Sabe Glacier route, roping up for crevasses, and climb toward Sharkfin Col (rather than the loose class 3-4 scramble around Boston Peak). Many parties gain the ridge just east of Sharkfin Col, where a natural/fixed sling anchor is commonly used to make a short rappel — or, in leaner conditions, a steep no-fall-zone downclimb on crumbly mixed rock — down onto the Boston Glacier; multiple trip reports flag this as the technical crux of the approach, sometimes harder than the climbing above. Once on the Boston Glacier (one of the largest glaciers in the lower 48), rope up and traverse south toward the base of Buckner's north face, zig-zagging around a bergschrund and large crevasses near the toe of the face, with some rock scrambling to bypass the 'schrund. Many parties bivy on the glacier itself (~7,800 ft) to shorten summit day. From the base, the North Face climbs about 1,300 ft of 40-50 degree snow/ice: work left of the bergschrund, then back right to the center of the lower face and straight up until upper rock cliffs force a rising traverse leftward; within about 200 ft of the summit, go left around a craggy rock outcrop, then back right to the top. Competent parties in good nick conditions often solo this face; less experienced or larger parties belay it with pickets/ice screws. Glacier travel, the Sharkfin Col rappel/downclimb, and typical alpine hazards (rockfall, afternoon softening, weather) are the main approach concerns.

runs: up and left on slabs and snow above
hits.text: The standard descent does not reverse the North Face — parties continue over the summit and go down Buckner's southwest slopes. From the top, descend gullies, scree, and snow on the fall line to about 7,200 ft, then traverse down and right across Horseshoe Basin on a broad ledge system at 6,200-6,400 ft (passing near the old Davenport Mine) to a snow finger; ascend the snow finger about 100 ft to regain the rounded ridge above the toe of Sahale's south ridge. Scramble roughly 40 ft up short rock steps, then follow paths through heather and rock for about 300 ft along the ridge crest (with the Davenport Glacier in view), before traversing up and left on slabs and snow above the glacier debris to the moraine flats beneath Sahale. From here, parties who arranged a car shuttle can continue over Sahale Arm and out Cascade Pass; most parties who started at Boston Basin instead re-climb Sahale's south ridge back toward Sharkfin Col and reverse the Quien Sabe Glacier approach to Boston Basin and the trailhead — some elect to 'carry over' with full packs and skip returning to a Boston Basin camp entirely. The southwest-slopes portion of the descent itself is a scree/snow walk-off with no rappelling (0 rappels). However, on the return leg back through Sharkfin Col, expect the same technical step encountered on approach: many parties make one short rappel (a single rope length off the natural/fixed sling anchor at the col is sufficient — no multi-pitch rappelling reported) to get back down onto or off the glacier side, while others downclimb it unroped depending on conditions and party comfort; in bad weather/whiteout, at least one party describes rappelling a steep ice gully near a nearby col with pickets as an alternate exit. Treat this Sharkfin Col step, not the summit slopes, as the route's real technical/rappel hazard.

runs: the third highest peak in north cascades national park the
hits.text: Buckner Mountain is the third-highest peak in North Cascades National Park, the 14th-highest summit in Washington, and 11th on the state's Bulger list of 100 highest peaks — one of only about ten non-volcanic Washington summits above 9,000 ft. The mountain has two summits of nearly equal height a short distance apart along the summit ridge; nearly all parties top out on the southwest (true) summit reached by this route. It crowns the ridge between Sahale Arm and Horseshoe Basin and is a coveted objective on multi-day Cascade Pass carryovers with Sahale and Boston Peak. The southwest side gives the standard non-technical line — long, but largely third- and fourth-class scrambling — most commonly reached from a high camp on Sahale Arm.

at a notch between two points on the crest
hits.text: Huge pale talus in a northwest-facing couloir, then two points at a notch — the right-hand one is the top. From the basin, hike around Upper Chain Lake and climb the couloir above it. Low down the slope is a deceptively complex mix of steep heather, mossy slabs, bushes and short cliffs; the clean, huge, whitish talus higher up is what tells you that you are into the correct couloir rather than picking your way up the general hillside. It tops out at a notch between two points on the crest, and from that notch it is genuinely not obvious which is higher — take the right-hand, southern one. That is the summit, and the last stretch to it turns looser and sandier. The negative marker is a different summit sharing this name: a lower, fang-shaped tower southeast of the trail pass between the Chain and Doelle basins, shaped like a giant cuspid, which takes Class 4 and 5 climbing and rappels to get off. If you are standing under a spire that plainly needs a rope, you are beneath that one. The high point described here is bulky, and nothing about it is tooth-like.

hits.text: Burnt Boot Peak (P 6480) sits across the Middle Fork of the Snoqualmie River, about two miles southeast of Big Snow Mountain. From the base of the steepest part of the north ridge, three leads of fifth class on granite, the last along a very sharp crest, reach easier ground; three more leads of class 3 and 4 gain the summit. The peak's first ascent, by a 1963 survey party, came by an easier scramble line. No repeat ascents of the ridge are recorded, so expect little to no modern traffic.

hits.text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the exposed friction-slab ramp off the summit block (often the psychological crux of the day, since downclimbing low-angle slab is harder to read than ascending it), cross back over the Druid Plateau, and pick your way back down the talus/scree slopes to the rib at ~7,900-8,000 ft. From there reverse the contouring traverse at 7,300-7,400 ft past the Lorelei Lakelets to Prusik Pass, then drop back down the scrambler's path to Perfection Lake and rejoin the maintained Snow Lakes Trail for the long hike out past Sprite, Leprechaun, and Viviane Lakes, Snow Lakes, and down to the trailhead. This is a pure scramble/downclimb with no fixed rappel anchors on the standard South Slopes line — no rope or rappel gear is needed for typical summer conditions, though some parties carry a short rope/sling for confidence on the summit block slab. The main descent hazards are the same as the approach in reverse: losing the faint route back to Prusik Pass in whiteout or dusk, loose talus on the plateau slopes, and lingering snow/verglass on the slab or upper gullies in early season, which has turned some ascents into technical downclimbs requiring crampons and careful footwork on rock. A minority of strong parties link Cannon into a longer Enchantments traverse (continuing on to McClellan Peak or exiting via Aasgard Pass to Colchuck Lake) rather than reversing to Snow Lakes, but that is a route variation, not the standard descent.

runs: to a junction with the pyramid mountain trail
hits.text: From the end of FR-5606 (the North Fork Entiat Trailhead, ~3,940 ft), pick up the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437. This lower section sits outside wilderness, so mountain bikes are legal and commonly used to knock out easy miles. The first ~6 miles follow the North Fork Entiat River on a gentle, mostly forested grade, with the river itself as a reliable water source the whole way — top off here, since the route runs dry above. Some post-wildfire sections have significant blowdown; a few parties describe losing the tread briefly among downed timber and having to scramble back onto it. At about mile 6.1 a signed spur splits off to Fern Lake (Trail #1436) — stay on #1437. Around mile 7, at roughly 5,800 ft, the main trail bends sharply east and climbs switchbacks for about a half mile to a junction with the Pyramid Mountain Trail #1433 at about 6,600 ft, roughly a mile southwest of Cardinal's summit and a useful timing landmark. The final approach mile above this junction is noted as steep and loose underfoot. From the open meadow/basin past the junction, leave the trail and hike east through sparse forest, then talus, toward Cardinal's west/southwest flank. For the Southeast Slopes line specifically, contour or drop onto the peak's western slopes and work south below the summit ridge across steep talus and scree to reach the gully leading to the notch between the north and middle (traditionally climbed) summits — the same scree-gully notch most parties use regardless of which flank they approach from. Loose rock is constant in the upper basin and gully, so a helmet is worthwhile and parties should avoid stacking up directly below one another. Round trip to the summit runs roughly 20-21 miles with about 4,700 ft of gain, so most parties do it as a long single day or a one-night backpack with camp in the meadows/basin below the peak. The trail crosses Grouse Creek on a log partway up, within one of the fire-damaged sections that has blowdown.

runs: steep red heather talus and scree to a notch
hits.text: This route starts with a boat crossing of Ross Lake (Ross Lake Resort water taxi, or a private/inflatable boat carried in via the 0.6-mile portage trail from the SR-20 pullout), landing at the Lightning Creek Trailhead near the head of the lake at roughly 1,500 ft. From the shoreline, follow the Lightning Creek Trail north; parties with their own boat commonly start pre-dawn (around 4am) to leave enough daylight for the long day above, while the water taxi runs only from 8am to 5pm. After about 2 hours of hiking, watch for the junction with the old, no-longer-maintained Freezeout Creek Trail. The first stretch above the junction is the trickiest routefinding on the whole approach: steep rock-and-alder slopes that require a rising, diagonal ascent line before you regain proper forest and trail tread — recent parties note intermittent orange flagging tape marking this stretch, which is worth watching for. Once back in the trees, tread on the Freezeout Creek Trail improves to 'decent shape' as you climb to the Freezeout Cabin at about 3,600 ft, sited immediately after a creek crossing; the cabin (maintained bunks, wood stove, logbook) is a good psychological waypoint and emergency shelter. About a quarter mile past the cabin, cross Freezeout Creek again and pass through an old burn. Trail tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft, but the bushwhacking through here is described as minimal. From there, stay on the west side of Freezeout Creek, hiking roughly 50-100 ft above the waterline, which gives the most open going through 5,000 ft. At 5,000 ft, cross to the south/east side of the drainage, where the terrain opens into meadow and talus. Above this, climb steep red heather, talus, and scree to a notch on the peak's southwest ridge at about 7,600 ft. From the notch, the final roughly 700-750 vertical feet to the 8,300+ ft summit is class 2 with short class 3 sections. Total one-way distance from the lakeshore to the summit is on the order of 16-17 miles with close to 7,000 ft of gain from the boat landing alone (the 8,500 ft gain figure reflects the day's cumulative up-and-down, not just net elevation). Freezeout Creek is the reliable water source for essentially the entire approach up to about 5,000-5,500 ft; carry water above that, since there is no dependable source on the upper heather/talus/scree slopes or the summit ridge. Because of the remoteness and boat-access logistics, this is realistically a long single push (18+ hours car-to-car including the taxi) or a one-night backpack, not a casual day hike.

hits.text: Despite the north face already hosting several routes since its 1979 first ascent, the central buttress directly below the summit remained untouched until Morgan Zentler and Jason Schilling's 2017 ascent. They started with easy 5th-class climbing to escape the rockfall line, then hit a crux pitch (pitch 2) of mid-5.10/5.11-ish face climbing requiring a short aid move. Subsequent pitches traverse out of a dihedral on a tricky flake and surmount a roof on the left via fun but hard cracks and stemming; the middle section demanded extensive cleaning of dirt- and moss-covered slabs. After about five pitches the route gains the ridge proper, where the rock quality improves and climbing becomes more moderate, aside from one short, harder hand-and-fist crack. The final technical pitch dances delicately around teetering blocks before moderate snow slopes lead the last 400 ft to the summit.

hits.text: The lawful approach is from the US side: cross Ross Lake by boat, follow the Lightning Creek trail and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail, then work round to the glacier below the north face. The first-ascent party instead came in from Canada — from Lightning Lake in Manning Provincial Park, BC, up and over Frosty Mountain, into Princess Creek basin, across the Princess/Crow Creek divide and down into the Crow Creek drainage — but walking into the US away from a port of entry is not a lawful crossing. runs: one short harder hand and fist crack the
hits.text:
The north face is a wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs about fourteen hundred feet high, holding ice or the remnants of it, with a glacier at its foot. It carries several routes and they are not marked, so identification is by position against the summit and nothing else.

The test is simple and it is the whole identification: this route takes the central buttress, and that buttress sits directly below the summit. Stand back on the glacier, find the summit on the skyline, and drop a plumb line from it. The buttress under that line is this route. If the summit is off to one side from where you are standing, you are under a different climb.

Getting onto it is the second problem. Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock, and start with easy fifth-class ground whose purpose is to get out of the rockfall line rather than to climb anything — that first pitch is a position move, not a feature.

Confirm on pitch two, because it arrives fast and it is unmistakable: the crux comes almost immediately, mid-fifth-class face climbing hard enough that the first ascent used a short aid move to pass it. A wall this size whose hardest pitch is the second one is unusual, and it is the strongest evidence you are on line.

The middle of the route then traverses out of a dihedral on a tricky flake and takes a roof on the left via cracks and stemming, over slabs that needed heavy cleaning of dirt and moss. After about five pitches the route gains the ridge proper and the rock quality improves markedly, with one short harder hand-and-fist crack. The final technical pitch picks its way around teetering blocks, and then moderate snow slopes run the last four hundred feet to the top.

Negative marker: if your line starts in a blocky set of face holds beside a gully or chimney at the left edge of the buttress, you are on the neighbouring route at the buttress's left margin, and higher up it follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke that this route does not touch.

Descent is not the climb reversed. Walk off the south side and the east ridge back toward camp.

runs: on the only dry spot on the ridge
hits.text:
Read the legal point first. This line walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and then crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it requires prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is the first-ascent line, not a recommendation.

It starts from the lake in the provincial park, climbs up and over Frosty Mountain, descends into the next creek basin to the south, traverses to the divide, and drops into the Crow Creek drainage below the peak's north face. The first ascent camped on the only dry spot on the ridge, roughly two-thirds of the way down toward the glacier.

The wholly lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west.

runs: on the lower right side of the south face
hits.text: There is no climbers' trail to the base. A party who got there reported finding none and navigating purely off photographs, so stop looking for tread and navigate by the landform. The landform is the deep gully that separates Cathedral Peak from The Monk, the semi-detached tower on the lower right side of the south face. One published account leaves the maintained trail at the first switchback after Cathedral Pass and heads for the gully from there; others come across the parkland between Upper Cathedral Lake and the pass. Both end up in the same place, thirty to sixty minutes from camp. Go up into the gully — do not stop at its mouth. Three accounts put the start of the first pitch about 150 feet up the Cathedral–Monk gully, on the left wall, which is the Cathedral side. Scramble onto a tall pedestal there; it gives a decent belay stance to start from. Pedestal, left wall, about 150 feet in: that is the whole identification. How to tell this from the South Face routes, and it is a simple physical test: is there a semi-detached tower standing between you and the wall? If yes, you are at the SE Buttress, which follows the ridge behind The Monk on the right-hand edge of the south face. If you are walking up to an open face with nothing in front of it, that is the South Face route, a different and much harder climb. A related trap in the naming rather than on the ground: The Monk has its own south face with its own routes on it. Beta headed South Face may be describing the tower, not the mountain. Coming down, the descent is the walk-off to the west and then south-west back toward Upper Cathedral Lake, and its crux is a gap the route description tells you to hop across. It can be avoided by downclimbing the exposed nose beside it and stepping over — easy when dry, but no-fall ground.

runs: from upper cathedral lake 7 380 ft take the trail
hits.text: Also referred to as the West Ridge or the southwest slope, and universally described as the easy way up and the route of choice for descending after climbing the Southeast or North faces. From Upper Cathedral Lake (7,380 ft) take the trail 0.6 miles nearly to Cathedral Pass (7,600 ft), leave it, and climb easy sandy terrain for several hundred vertical feet. Ducks and cairns then lead over Class 2-3 granite outcrops, blocks and slabs — solid, coarsely crystalline rock with occasional spots where a friction hoist gets you over a block — to a hidden cleft running parallel to and just below the west ridge crest. There are two minor Class 3+ steps, and the summit chasm is crossed twice; the harder of the two step-acrosses is the Class 4 move. The chasm that cleaves the summit rocks into north and south sections is the crux: step onto a large chockstone jammed in the slot and mantle onto a bulge on the far side. The climbing is easy; the exposure is dramatic, and most parties carry a rope and harnesses for it, often rigging a handline with prusiks for the return. In early season the chasm is filled with snow, which makes the first of the two step-acrosses easy or trivial; the second never has snow in the hole. Overall the route is Class 3, with that one Class 4 move at the chasm and exposure well beyond the grade.

runs: exit back left into the moat at the top of the snow
hits.text:
The route starts at the top of a short, steep snowfield, and that snowfield is the arrival test. Crossing the loose talus under the east face you come to it; it is short but steep enough that parties in approach shoes have picked their way up it holding stones for security. Reaching the top of that snow patch is reaching the start of the climbing.

And here is the mistake parties actually make at that point, which is the most useful thing to know about this route: at the top of the snow it is natural to exit right onto ledges and start up from there. That is wrong. A party that does it finds the ground harder than the fourth class the description promises, wanders left, right and up, and comes back down. The correct start is to exit back left into the moat at the top of the snow, where the terrain is much easier.

So the test is a difficulty test: if your first moves off the snow feel harder than fourth class, you are on the wrong side of the snowfield. Go back and take the moat on the left.

What should follow: easy ground you can simul-climb, then a ledge system that traverses rightward toward the crest of the buttress. The buttress runs about seven pitches and 900 ft, 5.7, grade III. A route that is sustained from the first pitch is not it.

And one thing to settle before you leave the trees: this peak is descended by the south side, not by reversing the buttress. Note where you came up.

hits.text:
Drive the Cle Elum River Road, SR 903, to Salmon La Sac, then keep right just past the ranger station onto the rough Forest Road 4330 and follow it about twelve miles to the road end at roughly 3,350 ft.

There are two trailheads within a few yards of each other at the road end and this is the first place to go wrong. The Hyas Lake and Deception Pass trail heads north. You want the Cathedral Rock trail, #1345, heading west, and it may be signed slightly before the road actually ends. Vehicle break-ins have been a recurring problem at this trailhead, which is a pattern rather than a one-off.

The trail reaches Squaw Lake at about two and a half miles and continues to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, roughly four miles in with about 3,400 ft of gain. Turn left, west, onto the Pacific Crest Trail. In less than half a mile you reach the junction with Trail #1375 to Peggy's Pond.

At that junction two climbers' paths head toward the peak, and the counter-intuitive one is the right choice: the left path looks from a distance like the wrong way, but it avoids a scree slope and gives some scrambling instead. Either goes, but do not talk yourself out of the left one on appearances.

runs: gully on the south side of the east face
hits.text: From the summit, most parties reverse toward the notch/col below the summit block and descend the gully on the south side of the east face (sometimes described as the same gully used by the Northeast Buttress descent). Expect a mix of downclimbing and rappelling: parties commonly do two double-rope (60m) rappels — the first from trees/rock anchors near the head of the gully with some downclimbing to reach the next station, and a second double-rope rappel that reaches easier snow near the gully's base — though some parties describe reaching the base with a single 60m rappel plus downclimbing depending on snow coverage. Anchors are a mix of natural gear (trees, rock horns/slings) rather than bolts; bring cord/webbing to back up or replace tattered slings. From the base of the gully, downclimb snow/talus east back into the Chair Peak basin and pick up the approach trail to Source Lake and out. Watch for cornices at the gully lip early season, loose rock in the gully when snow-free, and wet-slide hazard on the descent slopes during warm spring conditions.

runs: gully on the south side of the east face
hits.text: The two counts on this page are the same descent with a different rope setup, not a disagreement. The gully on the south side of the east face goes in one 60 m double-rope rappel, or in the two ~30 m single-rope rappels listed here. How much you rappel at all depends on conditions: with good steep snow much of it is downclimbed, and parties describe reaching the base on a single rappel plus downclimbing. Two rappel stations were added in early summer 2023 so that a 60 m rope makes every rappel on the route - several leave under 5 ft of rope spare, so knot the ends.

hits.text: From the upper Alpental parking lot (I-90 Exit 52, end of Alpental Road), follow the Alpental Valley/Source Lake trail: the first 0.5 mile follows the old ski-area cat track, then it becomes a standard trail climbing gently through forest for about 0.75 mile to Source Lake (roughly 1.25-1.75 miles and a few hundred feet of gain from the car). From Source Lake, leave the maintained trail and head cross-country/up boot path toward the basin below Chair Peak's east face (~4200 ft), a further 0.5-1 mile with steeper talus, heather, and (early/mid season) snow slopes. From the basin, climb a short snow gully for approximately 300 ft to gain the crest of the ridge that forms the Northeast Buttress, then follow the ridge to the start of the technical climbing. Total approach is on the order of 2-2.5 miles and 1,700-2,000 ft of gain one-way to the base of the buttress. Thumbtack Rock is the decision point, and the turn is right and up a grassy gully. Everything else on this side of the mountain continues straight on up the basin to the foot of the east face. This route is the one that leaves at the Thumbtack and crosses the divide. A published fix for the Thumbtack is 10T 0616013E 5257415N. If you are still walking up the basin under a big east face, you have gone past the turn.

The start itself is a saddle with trees on it, and the first pitch goes up the gully to the left of that saddle. Trees on a saddle, gully immediately left — that pairing is the arrival test, and both halves are visible from below in poor light.

Confirmation one pitch up, which is the strongest signal on the route: pitch one runs about 200 ft to the crest and you belay off trees on the south side of the ridge. From those trees you scramble down and left to a chimney-shaped feature with a chockstone jammed at its top. You cannot see that chockstone from the trees; it becomes obvious as soon as you scramble across. A chockstone-capped chimney at the end of a short downward scramble means you are on the northwest ridge and nothing else.

Negative tests: if your first pitch is bolted, you are on Voie de Chaise on the east face. If you are looking up at a big buttress from the head of the basin, you never made the Thumbtack turn.

The line of bolts is the test, and it is the only one you need in cloud. This is a fully bolted alpine sport line. Every other route that starts on this side of Chair Peak is climbed on gear. If you cannot see a bolt from the ground, you are not at the start of this route, whatever the terrain looks like.

What pitch one feels like, as confirmation: a few tricky moves straight off the ground at about 5.7, and then it eases into sustained, clean 5.6 slab for roughly 120 ft. Hard slab on clean rock with bolts is right. Broken blocky ground, or a chimney, is not.

hits.text: Park at Trinity Trailhead (~2,800 ft), at the end of Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 by the old Trinity mine site. From the trailhead, hike the Buck Creek Trail #1513 up the valley; at roughly 1.4–1.5 miles, bear right (northeast) at the junction onto the Chiwawa River Trail #1550, an old mining-road grade that continues up-valley along the river (reliable water the whole way here). Follow the Chiwawa River Trail about 3.7 more miles to the signed Red Mountain Trail junction at Chiwawa Mountain's southeastern foot — roughly 5 miles and the last easy, obvious water before the basin. Most parties bear left here into Chiwawa Basin rather than taking the right-hand switchbacks up Red Mountain. The tread beyond the junction is rougher and sometimes braided; it climbs about a mile-plus through forest and then subalpine meadow toward the ~5,500 ft basin below the Fortress-Chiwawa col. Expect a shallow ford of the Chiwawa River/headwater creek in this stretch, and favor the more open, less-timbered ground along the east side of the basin to avoid brush-whacking. Above the basin, gain the ~6,300 ft bench via talus/scree gullies or vegetated slopes just left of them — early-season parties will find snow gullies here (ice axe/crampons recommended) that are faster than the loose summer scree. From the bench, the standard finish is a class 2 scramble up slabs and gullies on the southwest face; the short section gaining the summit ridge is the route's crux — loose, exposed class 2–3 rock — after which an easy ~100 ft rightward (west) traverse leads to the summit. One-way distance from Trinity is roughly 7–8 miles with about 5,700 ft of gain; most parties camp in Chiwawa Basin or on the 6,300 ft bench and treat it as an overnight, though fit parties do it car-to-car in a long day. A less-traveled alternate approach starts at the Phelps Creek Trailhead, bushwhacking to about 5,500 ft and following a gully right of Point 5971 up to the col west of the summit, then easy Class 2 along the west ridge.

Park at Trinity Trailhead near 2,800 ft at the end of Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 by the old mine site. Start up-valley on Buck Creek Trail #1513 for about a mile and a half and bear right at the fork onto Chiwawa River Trail #1550, which takes over an old mining-road grade close to the river — water is reliable along all of this.

About 3.7 more miles brings the signed Red Mountain Trail junction near 4,000 ft. This is the last water that is both obvious and easy to reach before the basin, so fill here. Bear left into Chiwawa Basin rather than taking the right-hand switchbacks up Red Mountain.

Beyond the junction the tread deteriorates, braids and climbs through forest toward the basin, with an unbridged ford of the Chiwawa headwater around 4,400 ft — manageable at summer flow, higher and pushier early. Above the ford the brush thickens and the tread fades: favour the more open, less-timbered ground along the east side of the basin, because drifting into the timber turns this into a bushwhack.

Camp is on benches around 6,300 ft. Several lines reach them: the left-trending gully is the most direct and easiest going though it is wet, and the vegetated slopes beside the talus gullies are the better choice coming down.

FR-6200 has been closed to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat since May 20, 2026 under storm-damage order 06-17-07-2026-11 (through December 31, 2027), so Trinity is not reachable by vehicle. The Little Giant Fire closure (order 06-17-07-2026-40) also closes the Chiwawa River Road and the trails from Trinity through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner.

The route opens with a short step of low-fifth-class slab and layback moves, and then it is walking up the gully bed; if you are pulling on anything hard in the first rope length you are on one of the face routes to either side, not in the gully. runs: south twin jaws tooth skookum little sister and cinderella
hits.text: Cinderella Peak (roughly 6,400-6,500 ft) is a minor summit on the south side of the Green Creek cirque in the Twin Sisters Range, immediately west of Mount Baker and within/adjacent to the Mount Baker Wilderness (Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest). The Twin Sisters massif is the largest exposed body of dunite/olivine rock in the Western Hemisphere, giving Cinderella and its neighbors (Little Sister, South Twin, Skookum, Jaws' Tooth) their signature reddish, ultra-grippy slabs. The standard route is a long approach via the Elbow Lake Trail and the unmaintained, blue-flagged Green Creek climbers' trail, gaining a saddle near Little Sister and following the connecting ridge onto Cinderella's west ridge for a final Class 3-4 scramble to the summit. Technical alternatives exist for parties wanting a real climb: a North Face route (5.2, Grade II, ~8 pitches) and an East Buttress line have both been climbed and reported. Cinderella is also a common link-up on the 'Green Creek Circuit,' which strings together South Twin, Jaws' Tooth, Skookum, Little Sister and Cinderella into a long (~11-13 mile, ~8,000 ft gain) day.

runs: the middle fork nooksack river there is no bridge
hits.text: Start at the Elbow Lake Trailhead (USFS Trail #697), at the end of FS Road 38 (the Mosquito Lake Road / FS-38 drive from Deming/Acme). The trail immediately meets the Middle Fork Nooksack River — there is no bridge at the marked crossing, and fording can be dangerous or outright impassable during high water; many parties instead use an unofficial log crossing roughly 1/4 mile downstream from the official ford, made of logs lashed between two boulders. Once across, pick up the Elbow Lake Trail proper and climb through forest for about 1.5 miles to a switchback near Hildebrand Creek, where an unmaintained but well-trodden, blue-blazed 'Green Creek Climber's Trail' splits off to the left into the Green Creek cirque (look closely for the small blue markers — it's easy to walk past). Follow this climber's trail up into the basin; Green Creek itself runs clear and is a reliable water source along this stretch. Above treeline the trail gives way to talus and boulder fields and then loose, unstable scree, with class 3 rock steps required to reach the toe of the Green Creek (Sisters) Glacier — route-finding through this section is the crux of the approach, and parties should expect to hunt for the least-loose line. Cross the low-angle glacier (crevasse hazard is generally low here but rises later season; carry basic glacier gear) up to the low notch on the ridge between Cinderella and Little Sister, which is the jumping-off point for Cinderella's west ridge/north face. Elevation gain from the river crossing to this notch is substantial — roughly 4,000 ft over about five miles — and fit parties often go car-to-car in one long day, while others split it with a camp in the Green Creek basin.

hits.text: Everything turns on one feature and it is misdescribed by its own name. Published descriptions call it the one and only easy gully breaching the ridge — the way down off the spur into Clark's south basin — and it leaves the crest at about 7,200 to 7,300 ft. The correction, from a climber who found it: it is Class 2, and it feels more like a sloping ledge than a gully. Parties hunting for a defined cleft walk past it and get cliffed out. Two accounts both put it at 7,200 ft and both anchor it to the south spur of Point 8373, so the elevation is the reliable half of the identification and the word gully is the unreliable half. The positional cue that puts you in the right place to look: there is a flattish section of the spur at 7,200 ft that is reached easily on scree and grass. Stand on that flat and you can see the south slope of Clark, which looks easy — and it is. The difficulty is purely in getting down to it, which is what the ledge is for. Drop a couple of hundred feet down that ledge, then contour the upper south basin on broken rock and patches of permanent snow to the final south ridge and a short Class 3 scramble to the top. A note on names before you cross-reference anything: the Walrus Glacier is shown as the Clark Glacier on maps. They are one feature with two names.

hits.text:
You cannot see the Walrus Glacier until you are committed to it. From the 6,700 ft bench you wrap around Clark's eastern arm, and only then does the glacier come into view for the first time. That is why the bench is the roping-up point rather than the glacier's edge — there is no convenient stopping place once you are round the corner.

The entry is specific and it is not the middle of the toe: go up a moderately steep chute on the left, southern margin of the glacier. Expect to step over several narrow crevasses and, in at least one recorded year, to cross a snowbridge over a large one.

Once on the gentle upper glacier the summit wedge is visible in the distance and the navigation problem is over. The finish skirts the upper south face of that wedge on a steep snowfield and ends with a short scramble onto the summit rocks — about six hours from camp.

Negative marker, and this one matters because it would send you to the wrong landmark entirely: the famous one-and-only-easy-gully at 7,200 ft belongs to the south basin route, not to this one. If you are on the Walrus you never touch it. A published page titled for the Walrus Glacier in fact describes the south-basin line in its turn-by-turn, so read carefully which route a description is actually walking.

In a heavy year the gully holds snow well into early summer and an axe or light traction is worth having.
