hits.text: The Colchuck Glacier (Beckey's 'East Route') is the classic, most-climbed line on Colchuck Peak: an easy-angled snow/glacier ascent up the peak's northeast side to the Colchuck-Dragontail col, then a short 3rd-class scramble to the summit. From the north shore of Colchuck Lake, climbers gain the crest of the lateral moraine early to avoid loose scree, then move onto the glacier's left (east) lobe, passing below Dragontail's Serpentine and Backbone Ridge. The glacier steepens to roughly 100 ft of 40-degree snow just below the Colchuck-Dragontail saddle; above the col, sandy 3rd-class steps lead to a broad summit plateau around 8,500 ft, and the true summit (8,705 ft) is a short walk west/north from there.

hits.text: Beckey's 'East Route,' almost universally known today as the Colchuck Glacier Route. From the base of the glacier, ascend easy snow on the left (east) lobe past the base of Dragontail's Serpentine and Backbone Ridge routes. The angle increases near the Colchuck-Dragontail saddle to roughly 100 ft of 40-degree snow, then eases into 3rd-class sandy scrambling to the 8,500 ft summit plateau and on to the true 8,705 ft summit. With good snow cover it's an easy 3-4 hour climb from a camp at Colchuck Lake, or is readily done car-to-car in a long day.

hits.text:
Stuart Lake Trail #1599 from the FR 7601 road end for about 2.5 miles to the signed fork, then right onto the Colchuck Lake Trail for another 1.6 miles of steep switchbacks through boulders to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Call it four miles and 2,200 ft. This is the last reliable water.

Follow the boot path along the east shore to the inlet at the south end, then leave the trail. Gain the crest of the lateral moraine as early as you can — the alternative is a long session in genuinely loose scree and talus, and parties consistently report an hour of boulder-hopping through it when they stay low.

With good snow cover much of this basin, and later much of the glacier, can be glissaded on the way out, which is why parties favour the early window. Aim to be off the glacier before early afternoon: it softens badly and post-holing plus wet-slide potential make a late descent both slow and unpleasant.

runs: up and left from the base of the hidden couloir
hits.text:
The Hidden Couloir is the marker and the route starts underneath it. This is the cleanest base identification on the whole face: find the Hidden Couloir, and the start is immediately below it — two 60 m pitches of good ice leading up to its base.

Position on the glacier, which is how you find the couloir in the first place: this line sits between the North Buttress Couloir and the Northeast Couloir. So walking up the glacier you pass the North Buttress Couloir first; the next thing is this. If you have already passed a second deep slot you have gone too high and are under the Northeast Couloir.

The positive test is the ice itself. This is the only line on the face that begins with two full rope-lengths of continuous ice off the deck. If the ground in front of you is snow, or mixed, or rock, it is not the start — whatever else it might be.

And the divergence above, because it is decided a couple of pitches up and not at the bottom: from the top of the ice this route goes up and left from the base of the Hidden Couloir onto difficult mixed ground. The variation instead climbs into the Hidden Couloir. Both start on the same ice. One is M6; the other is sustained moderate. Know which you have come for before you leave the second belay.

If you cannot find a couloir above your ice, you are not below the Hidden Couloir and should not assume the ice is the right ice.

runs: introduction to steep snow and easy mixed climbing
hits.text: The most direct couloir rising out of the Colchuck Glacier's moraine on Colchuck Peak's north side — a popular introduction to steep snow and easy mixed climbing, with conditions ranging from a straightforward snow slog to thin mixed rock-and-ice.

hits.text: From the far side of Colchuck Lake, hike uphill to gain the moraine, follow it to the right, and drop into the large couloir at the edge of the Colchuck Glacier. In winter and early season it is continuous snow the entire way; later in summer, Class 4 rock can be exposed in a few short steps. The route can be climbed minimalist and fast, or fully protected with rock gear, pickets, and screws. Descent is via the Colchuck Glacier route on the peak's far side.

hits.text:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FR 7601 to Colchuck Lake — roughly four to four and a half miles and 2,200 ft, commonly two and a half hours. Before the road opens, add about four miles of Eightmile Road each way on foot or ski, which is the single biggest variable in the day.

When the lake is frozen (typically until around mid-May) parties ski or walk straight across it. Otherwise take the boot path around to the far, south side; the large flat boulder there is the usual gear-up and pack-stash spot.

From the south side, climb up and gain the lateral moraine. In spring there is often a boot pack this far and nothing beyond it. Follow the moraine crest right (west, toward the glacier) and then drop into the couloir. From the flat boulder to the couloir entrance is about an hour when trail-breaking is easy.

Overnight parties camp at the south end of the lake.

hits.text: Follow the couloir off the Colchuck Glacier as it winds upward and steepens; the gully hits a steep wall, so continue along the base of this wall to climber's left to find the exit, finishing on steep snow/ice to 60+ degrees that gains the summit ridge. Protection is a mix of snow gear and a small alpine rock rack including pitons. It is usually rated roughly Grade II with an elevation gain of about 1,500 ft from the glacier to the ridge; some grade it up to Grade III depending on conditions.

hits.text:
Critical avalanche terrain: Slope angle of 35-45 degrees with extensive vertical relief and frequent terrain traps—couloir is prime avalanche slope with multiple fatal accidents (3 deaths in Feb 2023); only climb in ideal snow conditions with confirmed low/minimal avalanche hazard
Entry and exit of steep couloir can be technical with snow or ice up to 60 degrees—difficult down-climbing if route-finding error occurs; requires excellent snow/ice judgment
Rock and ice fall from walls above couloir—stay alert and compact party; position out of direct fall line; watch for ice/rock loosening due to solar warming
Bergschrund crossing at glacier base—may be significant obstacle early/mid-season with potential fall hazard; probe and belay crossing if uncertain
Late-season glacier becomes bare ice (July+)—surface becomes extremely difficult and icy; crampons and ice tools essential; increased rockfall risk from warming
Crevasses on the Colchuck Glacier approach are few, but they open as the season goes on—rope up and probe if any are showing
Limited escape options once committed to upper couloir—retreat can be hazardous in poor conditions; plan to turn back early if conditions deteriorate
Navigation difficulty in whiteout conditions—few visual landmarks; GPS/map essential; descending in low visibility is particularly risky

runs: higher up the glacier than the north buttress
hits.text: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FS Road 7601 (Eightmile Road), elevation ~3,400 ft — in early season when Eightmile Road is gated/snowed in, tack on roughly 4 additional miles of road walking/skiing from the Bridge Creek Campground area on Icicle Road. From the trailhead, follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 south along Mountaineer Creek about 2.5 miles and 1,100 ft of gain to the signed junction where the Colchuck Lake Trail forks left; the Stuart Lake Trail continues straight to Stuart Lake/Colchuck Pass and is not your route. Climb the steep, rooty switchbacks of the Colchuck Lake Trail through boulder fields for another 1.6 miles and 1,100 ft to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4 miles and 2,200 ft from the car) — this is the only reliable water source below the basin, and it's your last easy resupply. Follow the trail and boot path along the lake's west shore to the inlet at the south end (~5 miles in). Leave the maintained trail here and ascend talus, heather benches, or lingering snow (highly season-dependent) up the basin toward the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600–6,800 ft. Rather than heading up-glacier toward Colchuck/Banshee Col (that's the Colchuck Glacier route), traverse along the glacier's true-right (climber's right) margin toward Colchuck Peak's north side, staying well right of the main fall line under the north face and Northeast Buttress to limit rockfall and icefall exposure. The Northeast Couloir's entrance is the obvious narrow slot higher up the glacier than the North Buttress Couloir, directly below the Northeast Buttress; gaining it typically requires crossing a moat at the glacier's edge, which varies from a simple step-across in early season to an awkward downclimb by mid-to-late summer. Expect avalanche-prone slopes above the lake in spring/early-summer conditions, and increasing rockfall down the couloir itself as the day warms.

hits.text: Colfax Peak is one of the Black Buttes, eroded remnants of an older Mount Baker volcanic cone on Baker's northwest shoulder above the Coleman Glacier. The Cosley-Houston is the easiest of Colfax's steep north-face ice lines: a meandering ~600 ft, 4-pitch WI4 route that starts just above the bergschrund with a low-angle ice ramp to a short, near-vertical crux pillar, then follows a gully system up and right through mixed ground to the summit ridge. It's a popular cold-weather testpiece, often in condition from late October into May.

hits.text: Approach via the Coleman Glacier to the base of Colfax Peak's north face. Start just above the bergschrund with a low-angle ice ramp trending up to the base of the crux pillar. The crux pillar is short and steep, slightly overhung, with approximately 30-40 feet of dead vertical or slightly overhanging water ice. After the crux, continue up a steep snow gully trending right, then simul-climb upper snow slopes to the summit ridge. A working knowledge of ice screw placement and anchor construction is essential.

runs: most of the route is hidden during the standard approach to the north face
in a cleft around the right side of a buttress the
hits.text:
If you can see your route from the bench, it is not Ford's Theatre. That is the single most useful fact about this climb and it is the one the first-ascent party chose to record: most of the route is hidden during the standard approach to the north face, because it sits in a cleft around the right side of a buttress. The other three lines are all visible from the approach. This one is not.

So the procedure is: walk right along the base of the face, past the Cosley-Houston line, until a buttress cuts the face off from view — then go around the right side of that buttress. The route is in the cleft behind it. A climber who stops at the first steep ice they can see has stopped on Cosley-Houston.

Left to right, the four lines are: Kimchi, Polish, Cosley-Houston, Ford's Theatre. This is the far right end of that list, which is why the instruction is always 'keep going'.

Confirm on the climb: a steep ice step of three pitches, roughly one 70 m rope-length, then the angle eases into snow gullies; the whole line is roughly 500 ft. Belays are hard to find after the first pitch. If you get a comfortable stance every rope length, or if the route stays steep for far more than 500 ft, you are on something else.

What being short looks like: Cosley-Houston starts with a low-angle ice ramp above the schrund leading to a crux pillar. If you are walking up a ramp, you are one line to the left of where you meant to be — which is a fine route and a different one.

runs: an independent line to the left of the polish route
hits.text: Climbs an independent line to the left of the Polish Route on Colfax's north face, following steep ice interspersed with rock steps that offer plentiful face holds, though protection isn't always straightforward. Regarded by its first ascensionists as one of the highest-quality alpine climbs they'd done in the Cascades, alongside the Cosley-Houston and Polish Route.

runs: more of a mixed climb than a pure ice climb
hits.text:
Same approach as its three neighbours: Glacier Creek Road (FS-39) to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, Trail #677 through forest to the Coleman Glacier moraine, the Coleman-Deming boot track onto the ice, and climber's right to the bench beneath Colfax's north face. Rope up on the glacier.

The route itself is about 300 m at AI4+ M5 R. Its first-ascent party described it as more of a mixed climb than a pure ice climb, on rock that is well featured with plenty of face holds — which is what the M5 and the R are about.

runs: takes an independent line to the left of the polish route
hits.text:
This is the leftmost line on the face, and the test is whether you are climbing rock. Left to right the four lines are Kimchi, Polish, Cosley-Houston, Ford's Theatre. Kimchi takes an independent line to the left of the Polish Route, so from the bench you walk left, past the obvious continuous ice line up the middle of the face, and keep going.

The character of the ground is the confirmation, and it discriminates cleanly against the route next door. The Polish Route is continuous ice — that is its whole identity, and it is graded WI6 for it. This route is mixed: the first-ascent account is explicit that it is more mixed than pure ice, and that the rock is well featured with plenty of face holds. So the question to ask at the schrund is not 'which line is this' but 'am I about to use my hands on rock'. If the answer is no, you are on the Polish and on a much harder ice grade than you came for.

The R in the grade is part of the base finding. This is AI4+ M5 R, and R means the protection is poor enough that a fall has consequences beyond the fall. Being one line right of here — on continuous well-protected ice — is a materially different commitment. Confirm which you are on before the leader is 30 m up.

What being too far right looks like, all the way across the face: a low-angle ice ramp to a crux pillar is Cosley-Houston, the easiest line here. A route you cannot see at all from the bench, tucked behind a buttress, is Ford's Theatre at the far right end.

runs: long pitch of wi4+ to a snow slope
hits.text: Approach via Coleman Glacier to the base of Colfax Peak's north face, directly below the middle of the face. Ascend the initial bergschrund crossing (may require traversal from the right if overhanging). Pitch 1: Long pitch of WI4+ to a snow slope. Pitch 2 (crux): Steep ice for approximately 30 feet, easing briefly, then rising to a free-hanging ice dagger grading WI6. This is the technical and psychological crux requiring bold movement and precise tool placement. Above the dagger: additional steep ice steps in a right-side gully. Final pitches: Upper snowfield with occasional blue ice patches, traversing between rock buttresses to gain the summit snowfield.

hits.text: Colonial Peak is one of the steepest-rising summits in the North Cascades, gaining roughly 6,500+ ft above Diablo Lake's Thunder Arm in under 2.5 horizontal miles. It lies in the North Unit of North Cascades National Park, accessed through the Ross Lake National Recreation Area corridor along SR 20, and shares its glaciated basin with Snowfield Peak, Neve Peak, and Paul Bunyan's Stump — a popular multi-summit basin for Mountaineers-style basic glacier climbs. The standard route (sometimes called the West Ridge) climbs the Colonial Glacier on the northeast side to the Colonial-Snowfield col, then follows the ridge over talus and firn to a short, exposed class 3-4 summit block. First climbed July 31, 1931 by William Degenhardt and Herbert Strandberg.

hits.text: From Dayton, follow North Touchet Road up the East Fork Touchet River valley toward Ski Bluewood; it stays paved for roughly the first 15 to 16 miles, then turns to gravel as Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary. The Middle Point Ridge Trailhead sits on the river at about 3,373 feet, with a vault toilet and no water. The road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter; snow on the crags and approach slopes is what limits climbing, to roughly May through October, sometimes from April. The Dikes lie farther on, upstream and south toward Bluewood.

hits.text: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike North: park 1.1 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, where a dirt road intersects the paved road on the left (SE side), or continue to 1.2 miles and use the large pull-off. Cross the main road and pick up the approach trail between the two parking spots, marked by a short steep drainage topped with a downed tree.

runs: forest service road 64 at the forest boundary
hits.text: Paved North Touchet Road out of Dayton becomes gravel-to-dirt Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary as it climbs toward the Bluewood ski area; the climbing dikes sit right along this road roughly 18 miles in (about 1-2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, which is 16-17 miles from Dayton). Approach paths to individual crags (Megadike, Minidike, Weeping Wall, Joe's Rock) are unofficial, brushy, and easy to lose.

runs: the eastern boundary of north cascades national park
hits.text: Corteo Peak (8,107 ft) is a double-summited peak on the eastern boundary of North Cascades National Park, 1.7 mi southeast of Black Peak (8,970 ft), rising above the Heather-Maple Pass trail corridor near Rainy Pass. It was first climbed in July 1935 by John Lehmann and Hermann Ulrichs. Two routes are documented: the Southwest Ridge (the standard/easiest line, Class 3-4 scrambling reached via the Lewis Glacier basin) and a shorter but harder East Face. Corteo is frequently combined with Black Peak in the same trip since both share the Lewis Glacier approach.

runs: class 3 with a few class 4 moves
hits.text: Cross the cirque and climb the southwest ridge to the top on blocky Class 3 with a few Class 4 moves and real exposure in places; some parties put the rope on for the last section. Fix the notch you came down in your mind before you start up — the descent reverses this line and the notch is easy to lose from above.

runs: exposed class 3 with a few class 4 moves
hits.text: From the paved pullout at Rainy Pass (4,855 ft) on SR-20 — signed 'Rainy Pass Trailhead,' 52 miles east of Marblemount, right where the PCT crosses the highway — start on the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail (well-graded, heavily used). At roughly 1.25 miles, stay right at the Lake Ann junction (the lake itself, just below the junction, is the last reliable on-trail water source) and continue climbing switchbacks through heather meadows to Heather Pass (~6,080 ft, about 2 miles in), Leave the maintained trail here and head west across talus, keeping south of Lewis Lake (~5,700 ft), to the crest of the Lewis Glacier's east lateral moraine near 6,400 ft. Follow the moraine onto the glacier remnant and climb southeast, bearing left near the top, to a notch in the ridge at about 7,500 ft. Work west along the ridge to a second notch, downclimb roughly 400 ft of dirt or snow into the cirque under the west face, then take an easy gully up to a large notch on the Southwest Ridge and follow the crest (exposed class 3 with a few class 4 moves) to the 8,107 ft summit. Loose talus and scree cover much of the off-trail travel, and the downclimb sheds rock onto anyone below, so a helmet is worth carrying. Snow lingers on the glacier and on the traverse out of Heather Pass well into July, so bring an axe and crampons for early-season attempts.

runs: exposed class 3 with a few class 4 moves
hits.text: The standard descent reverses the same Southwest Ridge line used on ascent, down into the west-face cirque. From the summit, downclimb blocky, exposed class 3 (with a few class 4 moves) south/southwest along the ridge crest to a large notch roughly a third of the way down (approximately 7,600-7,700 ft), reached through an easy connecting gully. That gully has one distinctly steeper step, which is the crux of the way down: most parties downclimb it as class 4 on solid holds, but it is commonly protected with a single-strand rappel (one 30 m rope is sufficient) off natural gear — horns, chockstones, or a sling around a block; no fixed or bolted anchor has been reported here, so carry a few slings/cord. Treat this as optional but be ready for it, especially if the rock is wet or the party is not comfortable down-climbing exposed class 4. Below the step, follow the gully and talus down into the west-face cirque near the Lewis Glacier's east moraine (~6,400 ft), then pick up talus and intermittent boot path south past Lewis Lake to rejoin the trail near Heather Pass. From Heather Pass it's about 2 miles of maintained trail back down to the Rainy Pass Trailhead. This line involves glacier/snowfield travel past the Lewis Glacier remnant — rope up or use an axe/crampons if it's icy — and lingering snow on these slopes can be avalanche-prone in early summer. Total descent is roughly 5-6 miles with about 3,250 ft of net loss back to the car.

runs: the eastern boundary of north cascades national park
hits.text: The trail corridor and the usual camps at Lewis and Wing Lakes are Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District); the summit sits on the eastern boundary of North Cascades National Park. No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.

runs: exposed class 3 with a few class 4 moves
hits.text:
The route is a chain of notches, and the first one decides the day. From Heather Pass, head west across talus, passing south of Lewis Lake (about 5,700 ft), to the crest of the Lewis Glacier's east lateral moraine near 6,400 ft. Follow the moraine onto the glacier remnant and climb southeast, bearing left near the top, to a notch in the ridge at about 7,500 ft. Bearing right instead puts a party on narrow, sand-covered ledges and a steep, constricted snow gully — a much harder line.

From the first notch, follow the ridge west to a second notch, then downclimb roughly 400 ft of dirt or snow into the cirque under the west face. The ground is loose; space the party out.

From the cirque, an easy gully leads to a large notch on the Southwest Ridge, and the ridge crest — exposed class 3 with a few class 4 moves — goes to the 8,107 ft summit.

So the sequence of heights is 6,400, 7,500, the cirque below it, the ridge notch, 8,107: moraine, first notch, downclimb, ridge gained, summit.

The descent reverses the same line, including the climb back out of the cirque to the 7,500 ft notch. Fix the notches in your mind on the way up; they are easy to lose from above.

runs: 7 500 ft follow the ridge west to a
hits.text: From the Lewis Glacier's east moraine near 6,400 ft, climb the glacier remnant southeast, bearing left near the top, to a ridge notch at about 7,500 ft. Follow the ridge west to a second notch, downclimb roughly 400 ft of dirt or snow into the west-face cirque, and take an easy gully up to a large notch on the southwest ridge. Crampons and an axe are needed while snow lingers, and the downclimb is loose, so space the party out.

runs: trail along the north side of the creek
hits.text: Drop off the north side of the pass on roughly thirty switchbacks, losing nearly 1,400 ft into the Fisher Creek valley, then turn west and downstream on the Fisher Creek Trail along the north side of the creek. About three miles of valley walking brings you to this crossing.

runs: steep talus grass and some solid rock for
hits.text: Start at the Easy Pass Trailhead on the south side of SR 20 (Easy Pass Trail, North Cascades National Park, backcountry permit required for camping). The trail climbs steadily through forest, crossing Easy Pass Creek three times, and breaks out into subalpine meadows and heather benches before the final push to Easy Pass at about 6,550 ft — roughly 3.5-3.6 miles and 2,700-2,800 ft of gain, typically 2-3 hours. Steep snow can linger on this stretch well into July, and an ice axe is recommended; the tread can be hard to follow across snowfields, and the meadows are fragile, so stay on trail/rock where possible. From the pass, leave the high traverse and descend the Fisher Creek side: the trail switchbacks roughly 30 times, losing nearly 1,400 ft, into the Fisher Creek valley. Follow the Fisher Creek Trail west/downstream along the north side of the creek for about 3 miles (the creek itself is a reliable water source) to Cosho Camp (~3,900-4,200 ft, creekside, a designated NPS camping zone and the logical base camp for this peak). From Cosho Camp continue west on the trail roughly another mile until due south of the Cosho/Kimtah saddle, then leave the trail and begin climbing one of the gullies leading north, starting around 3,800 ft. This off-trail leg is the crux of the approach: steep talus, grass, and some solid rock for about 4,000 ft of gain to a saddle at roughly 7,830 ft, with sustained bushwhacking through trees and brush in the first thousand feet and loose, tedious scree higher up. Alternatively, some parties camp higher, in a basin south of Mesahchie Peak (~6,600 ft) reached by traversing south of the Easy Pass ridge at 6,600-6,700 ft across numerous small gullies and buttresses (~1 mile, ~5 hours from the trailhead), then climb about 800 ft to a 7,400 ft bench and traverse west to the Cosho/Kimtah col — a shorter final push at the cost of a longer, more exposed high traverse to reach camp. Expect this to be a full, long trekking day regardless of which camp is used; this is a remote, seldom-visited corner of the park and route-finding care is needed in poor visibility.

runs: at one of the gullies due south of the
hits.text: From Cosho Camp continue west down the Fisher Creek Trail about a mile and leave it at one of the gullies due south of the Cosho-Kimtah saddle, starting around 3,800 ft. The climb up is the crux of the day: sustained bushwhacking through trees and brush for the first thousand feet, then loose, tedious scree and steep grass with occasional solid rock, roughly 4,000 ft of gain to the saddle at about 7,830 ft.

runs: onto the snowfield on the north side and
hits.text: At the saddle, cross to the north side and climb snow until it runs out. From the 7,830 ft saddle the route does not follow the crest: step over onto the snowfield on the north side and climb moderate snow northwest to roughly 8,100 ft. Where the snow ends is the base of the climbing — a couple of hundred feet of third-class rock on the upper east face, reported mostly solid, with cairns marking the stretches where the ground is ambiguous, finishing at the summit. That snow-to-rock transition at about 8,100 ft is the test. If you are still on talus and scree on the south side of the saddle with no snowfield below you, you have not crossed over. If you are working up a broad crest with no snow anywhere, you are on the wrong saddle: the correct one lies due north of the point at which you left the Fisher Creek Trail, between Cosho and Kimtah.

runs: downscoping ribbon of white rock and the first
hits.text: There are three markers above the lake and they come in order. First, at about 6,800 ft the grade mellows and the trail turns north. Two parties record the same elevation for it. Second, at about 7,600 ft the trail ends — it does not fade, it disappears into a loose gully, and three accounts agree on the height. That is where the scrambling starts. Third, and this is the thing you can see: the gully is marked by a downscoping ribbon of white rock and the first of several yellow painted X marks. One climber calls it pretty hard to miss once you know to look for it. Negative marker, and it is important because the marking itself is the trap: the paint tempts you straight up that gully. It starts well and turns steep and loose with rolling pebbles higher up. A party who followed the paint up found on the way down that the better line traverses across the gully and around the corner, where cairns lead upward. Once you reach a yellow arrow, the ground improves markedly for the rest of the way. How you know you have finished the hard part, corroborated four ways and genuinely reassuring: the scrambling ends well below the summit and real trail resumes. A mellow path runs the last quarter mile to the top, past the remnants of an old tramway at the top of the cliff section. If you are still scrambling within sight of the summit, you are off the line. There is one false top, a bump on the south ridge, and the trail bypasses it to the west — the real summit sits directly behind it and is not visible from below. Two things to have straight before you go, because both are commonly stated wrongly. The historic lookout stood on the highest summit, not a lower one; the second, lower lookout site is on a peak about a mile east. And the lookout tender here was Gary Snyder in 1952 — Jack Kerouac was on Desolation Peak, a different mountain some fifteen miles away, four years later. The summit register itself carries a card that conflates the two.

runs: of pinnacles on loose class 4 5 ledges
hits.text: Cross the glacier from camp to the foot of the northwest couloir and climb it: 40-45 degrees of snow, usually simul-climbed on pickets or flukes, and three to four hours of it. Above the couloir a narrow snow-and-rock gully gains the north ridge, then an exposed traverse around a line of pinnacles on loose Class 4-5 ledges leads to the headwall — a short, near-vertical crack at 5.8+ (or 5.2/A1). Ledges on the upper west face above it lead onto the south summit ridge. Treat every hold on the ridge as suspect and budget hard for the descent, because parties routinely run out of daylight here and end up bivouacking.

runs: from the ridge crest down to a lower cliff band
hits.text: At the top of the headwall that bars the upper west face, immediately beyond the band of giant boulders. The headwall runs from the ridge crest down to a lower cliff band and forms a near-impasse; the crossing is the roughly 10-ft vertical crack, the third of four lines evaluated across it — the ridge crest, a high catwalk ledge, this crack, and the bottom nose. Reached on the way down after downclimbing the summit ridge and the loose ledges below it.

runs: a small horn draped with several rappel slings
hits.text: A small horn draped with several rappel slings, on the exposed traverse around the north ridge's pinnacles. It is passed on the way UP, between the notch at the top of the couloir and the easier ground beyond, on loose class 4-5 ledges — note it on the ascent, because it is the descent anchor.

runs: onto the second pitch of rise and fall skip the belay out right
hits.text: Look up and right for a lone black-hangered bolt. Undercling the roof as for the right variation of Davis-Holland, reach a jug under the bolt, then a short tricky section (horizontal takes a #2 Camalot) leads onto the second pitch of Rise and Fall. Skip the belay out right, clip the next black bolt up-left, and follow crystal edges up a dike; the crux is getting past two roofs at the end. Three-bolt belay.

runs: long pullout on the north side of the
hits.text: Drive the North Cascades Highway (SR-20) to the long pullout on the north side of the road about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, roughly half a mile west of the Blue Lake Trailhead. The climbers' track leaves the east end of the pullout. SR-20 over Washington Pass is closed in winter, typically from late fall until spring.

runs: buttress into the basin east of cutthroat peak
hits.text:
From the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, follow the cairned climbers' track from its east end down through timber, cross State Creek, and climb toward the basin below the south side of the peak. Then traverse over the rib that extends south from the South Buttress into the basin east of Cutthroat Peak, where the East Face routes begin.

Avoid the steep, loose scree chimneys directly below the wall on the way in.

runs: buttress into the basin east of cutthroat peak
hits.text: Traverse over the rib that extends south from the South Buttress into the basin east of Cutthroat Peak. That second basin is where the East Face routes begin. So the count is two basins, and the rib between them is the thing you cross: first the basin below the peak's south side, which is where the South Buttress and North Ridge parties go, then over a rib, then the east basin. If you have not crossed a rib, you are still in the south basin and you are under the wrong side of the mountain. The negative test against the North Ridge, which leaves the same boulder field: that route bears right and north into the basin beneath the North Ridge Notch, and gains it by a loose runout 5.7 pitch. If you are roping up for a single hard pitch to reach a notch, you are on the North Ridge, not on the East Face. A hazard that is also a route-finding instruction, and it is stated in both routes on this side: avoid the steep, loose scree chimneys directly below the wall on the way in. If your line into the base is up a confined chimney full of scree, you have picked the wrong way through and should back out and go round. There is no named crack or flake at the start; the basin, the rib and the chimneys to avoid are the ground features to go by. Descent: parties commonly descend the South Buttress with multiple rappels, or the West Ridge on fixed-anchor rappels plus downclimbing, rather than reversing the technical face.

runs: long pullout on the north side of the highway
hits.text: Drive SR-20 to the long pullout on the north side of the highway about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, at roughly 5,200 ft. The climbers' track leaves the east end of that pullout — it starts on the west side of a clump of trees near the eastern end and is usually cairned, but it takes some hunting the first time and is easy to walk past. It is genuinely hard to find in the dark, so spend a minute at the east end before committing to a pre-dawn start.

runs: the left side of the gully to the ridge crest
hits.text: Climb the left side of the gully to the ridge crest, then about 12 pitches up to 5.8 along the buttress, past a chockstone crawl, a stembox crux and an offwidth near the false summit. Drop off the false summit and climb the final pitch to the true summit.

runs: sews up the crux pitches a few doubles in the 0.5 2 range
hits.text: A single rack from 0.3 to 3 inches sews up the crux pitches; a few doubles in the 0.5-2 range stitch the whole route. An optional #4 protects the short summit-ridge offwidth. Bring lots of single and double-length runners. A single 60m rope suffices for the descent.

runs: west of washington pass the trail leaves from the east end of
hits.text:
Park in the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass. The trail leaves from the east end of that pullout and drops straight into the woods; the climbers' track actually starts on the west side of a clump of trees near the pullout's eastern end and is usually cairned, but it takes some hunting the first time and is easy to walk past.

The path drops through timber, crosses State Creek — fill up, it is the last reliable water — and then climbs steadily up into the big meadow and basin below Cutthroat Peak. Reports put roughly an hour and a half from the car to the foot of the entry gully.

Above the meadow the trail steepens into a boulder field beneath the south buttress.

hits.text: From the saddle at the foot of the west ridge, traverse ledges east along the south face about 100 ft to a shallow, blocky gully. Scramble the lower gully (Class 3-4, mostly solid), then belay the last section up to the ridge crest past two fixed pitons; a double-bolt station sits in the gully. Do not take the second, harder southwest gully by mistake.

hits.text: From Dayton, follow North Touchet Road out of town toward Ski Bluewood; it is paved for roughly the first 15 to 16 miles, then turns to gravel as Forest Service Road 64 at the national forest boundary. The Dikes sit along that road in the East Fork Touchet River valley below Ski Bluewood, in the Walla Walla Ranger District of the Umatilla National Forest. The road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter; snow on the crags and approach slopes is what limits climbing, to roughly May through October, sometimes from April. You do not park at this trailhead: for Megadike South, keep driving about 1.2 miles further south on FR 64 past it and pull off on either side of the road just before the bridge over the river.

hits.text: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike South: drive 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and park on either side of the road just before the bridge over the river. Scramble up the steep hillside on the NW side of the road above the bridge abutment, then continue uphill along the dike to a passable gully.

runs: forest service road 64 at the forest boundary
hits.text: Paved North Touchet Road out of Dayton becomes gravel-to-dirt Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary as it climbs toward the Bluewood ski area; the climbing dikes sit right along this road roughly 18 miles in (about 1-2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, which is 16-17 miles from Dayton). Approach paths to individual crags (Megadike, Minidike, Weeping Wall, Joe's Rock) are unofficial, brushy, and easy to lose.

runs: the right side of the glacier is reported as
hits.text: Dark Peak is regarded as an adventure/remoteness objective more than a technically hard one. After a boat-and-shuttle approach into the roadless Stehekin Valley, parties hike the Agnes Creek Trail (PCT) to a high camp, then leave the trail for a long, routefinding-heavy cross-country push -- either up the historically brushy, officially abandoned Swamp Creek climbers' path, or via a newer variant farther south on the PCT to Hemlock Camp -- gaining a basin below "Dark Fin Col." From the col, parties rope up, descend a loose slope onto the crevassed Dark Glacier, pick a line across it (the right side of the glacier is reported as a good line), and finish with a belayed crossing of the summit moat/bergschrund onto the rock ridge leading to the top. Reported early-to-mid-summer conditions give firm, well-bridged snow with minimal crevasse danger; by late summer more crevasses are exposed and the glacier becomes less stable.

runs: steep forest veering right at the end to a natural saddle
5 500 ft below the slabs of the receding glacier
hits.text: This is the line most descriptions still call standard, and it is the brushy one. From the road end at the bridge, follow the crest trail south to the first creekside camp and on to the camp at the Swamp Creek fork. Leave the maintained trail there for the long-abandoned climbers' path: cross Swamp Creek on a large log to its east side and force about a quarter mile of dense slide alder and vine maple. Above that a headwall bars the basin; the way up it is at the far left, and the route then climbs steep forest, veering right at the end to a natural saddle around 5,040 ft. Beyond lies a further, higher basin near 5,500 ft below the slabs of the receding glacier.

runs: right at the end to a natural saddle
slope under the north side of the summit
hits.text: The headwall has a tempting wrong line on it, and the glacier has a tempting wrong line above it. Coming up the basin the headwall looks formidable; the way up is at its far left, through a brushy gully where the headwall corners, and there is an appetising forested cut up the wall to the right of the waterfall that must not be taken — cutting right early forces you onto the low end of the rock wall in the trees. Above, steep forest veers right at the end to a natural saddle around 5,040 ft, where a piece of orange flagging has marked the way. Beyond that, a third and higher basin near 5,500 ft sits below the slabs of the receding glacier, and a natural cut on that basin's southwest side leads through the slabs onto the ice: easy snow early in the season, later a gully with a stream in it. Once on the glacier, the second trap: a snow and talus slope under the north side of the summit looks enticing and leads to the northeast ridge, which is far more exposed and saves nothing. Do not take it.

runs: up and left up and left up and left to
8 200 ft east of the actual saddle
hits.text: Open forest and slopes, not brush, is the sign you are on this variant. Leaving the crest trail farther south, the climb northwest gains roughly 3,500 ft through timber and open slope that stays walkable; if you are fighting slide alder and vine maple you have started up the Swamp Creek drainage instead and are on the older, much harder line. Veer left near the top of the drainage to reach the drop-in point onto the glacier — parties have needed a rappel to get off the ridge here, so carry the means to do it. Once on the ice, ignore the snow and talus slope running up under the north side of the summit: it looks enticing from the glacier and leads to the northeast ridge, which is much more exposed and saves no time. Leave the glacier by crossing the moat onto the rock instead, then take the three step-ups — up and left, up and left, up and left — to gain the west spur around 8,200 ft, east of the actual saddle.

runs: the northeast ridge of dark peak continues over to
hits.text: About nine miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail and roughly three beyond Fivemile, this is the working base for Needle Peak, Mount Lyall at 7,892 ft and the ridge between them. The unmaintained Swamp Creek trail leaves the corridor here and climbs toward Needle Peak's north ridge; the ground above is class 3 and 4 scrambling with real exposure and a helmet is wanted, and the northeast ridge of Dark Peak continues over to Lyall, so a party willing to spend the days can link several of these summits off one camp. Budget five days for the full set including the boat at both ends, and something close to forty miles of walking. The approach is all of the difficulty. These are not hard climbs by North Cascades standards; they are remote, brushy and slow, and the price of admission is the boat, the shuttle, the mileage and a good deal of unpleasant bushwhacking once you leave the corridor. Nothing about this is a weekend. Cedar Camp further up the valley is the alternative if this one is taken; Hemlock Camp above it is unsafe from falling insect-killed timber and should be skipped.

runs: when the rest of the route is dry

hits.text: Jam the hand crack at the far left of the upper walls, where the approach trail arrives. It is often damp even when the rest of the route is dry; stemming off the left wall helps on the slippery opening layback. From the ledge, wander right and then back left over small terraces to a bolted belay in a right-facing corner.

runs: around the roof then back left into a right facing corner
hits.text: Make a bouldery move up and right around the roof, then back left into a right-facing corner; a variation goes directly left past a bolt on balancy friction that may be harder. The crux is in the corner, on delicate footwork and small edges protected by small nuts, so carry extras. It ends at a bolted ledge where most parties rappel or continue up Lovin' Arms.

runs: bank of the creek this is a quiet residential
hits.text: Turn into Diablo at milepost 126. Older directions run you to the northernmost street and across a lawn to find the unmarked Stetattle Creek trail on the east bank of the creek; this is a quiet residential neighbourhood, so bypass the houses and drive the lakeshore past the powerhouse to the large public parking lot with restrooms built for the Seattle City Light dam tours, and walk the extra distance. Since the climb finishes at the Gorge Creek bridge at about milepost 123, leave a shuttle car there.

runs: to the bridge over gorge creek about 2.6 miles
hits.text: Drive SR 20 to the bridge over Gorge Creek, about 2.6 miles east of Newhalem and about the same distance west of the Gorge Lake causeway and the Diablo turnoff. Watch the sharp curve at the east end of the bridge. Park in the lot at the west end; the east lot is signed for motorhomes and oversize vehicles. There is no trail: the route leaves the highway directly.

runs: with light bivy gear and no cook food
hits.text: Late spring is the consensus best window. Snow still suppresses the salal and slide alder, snowmelt provides water on a slope that otherwise has none, and avalanche danger on the south side is minimal. Mid-summer turns an entirely south-facing 6,000-ft slope into an oven and the brush reaches full leaf; late summer and fall add a genuine water problem on top of that. Winter ascents have been made — one party climbed it over the first weekend in January, camping in sub-zero weather (down to -22F) and passing huge cornices, and reported that the brush at least was minimised. With light bivy gear and no-cook food in warm spring weather, one party found it very pleasant, which is the strongest endorsement this route gets.

runs: to the bridge over gorge creek about 2.6 miles
hits.text: There is no trailhead in the usual sense — you step off the highway into the forest. Drive SR 20 to the bridge over Gorge Creek, about 2.6 miles east of Newhalem near milepost 123, or about the same distance west of the Gorge Lake causeway and the Diablo turnoff. Watch the sharp turn at the east end of the bridge. There are parking lots at each end; the east lot is signed for motorhomes and oversize vehicles, so park at the west lot. Elevation here is 1,096 ft, and there are accessible restrooms and a short interpretive trail to the Gorge Creek Falls viewpoint. Walk across the bridge to its east end, go a few feet farther east, cross the highway, and pick the easiest place to start uphill into the woods. That is the whole approach: the route and the approach are the same thing from here, 6,000 vertical feet of it. Round trip is about 6.2 miles with roughly 6,000 ft of gain in three miles. Carry water. The slope is south-facing and dry once the snow is gone, and there is no reliable source between the highway and the snowfields high on the mountain. In late spring, snowmelt on the route solves this and simultaneously suppresses the brush, which is why that window is the usual recommendation.

runs: room for two tents on a snow ledge
hits.text: Feasible in one very long day or, more comfortably, as an overnight. Day trip: leave the Gorge Creek bridge before dawn; the South Davis saddle at 5,700 ft is about 4.4 hours from the car and the summit about 8.3 hours; allow 4.1 hours down, for roughly 13.5 hours car to car and 10 miles travelled with about 7,400 ft gained and lost if you take the Gorge Creek/South Buttress line with its detours. The round-trip figure for the direct line is 6.2 miles. Overnight: one party camped at the 5,720+ ft saddle, where there was room for two tents on a snow ledge; what is there when the snow has melted is not documented. That splits the trip into a long brushy climb on day one and a short summit push plus the full descent on day two, and it is the version to choose if you are unsure of the slab above the saddle. An overnight requires a wilderness permit.

runs: to the bridge over gorge creek about 2.6 miles

hits.text: Drive SR 20 to the bridge over Gorge Creek, about 2.6 miles east of the Seattle City Light company town of Newhalem near milepost 123, or the same distance west of the Gorge Lake causeway and the Diablo turnoff. Watch the sharp turn at the east end of the bridge — the deck is open steel grating and rings under the tyres. Parking lots sit at both ends; the east lot is for motorhomes and overlength vehicles, so use the west lot. Elevation 1,096 ft, with accessible restrooms and a short interpretive trail to the falls and the Gorge Lake overlook.

runs: on a fin like flake right off the ground mount
into face climbing to a small ledge below a roof
hits.text: Deep Blue begins on a fin-like flake right off the ground — mount the flake and pull a small bulge into easier climbing. Lower/mid pitches include an overhang leading into face climbing to a small ledge below a roof, a pitch through a roof with technical edges to a ledge, and a stretch of 5.11 climbing to a higher ledge below the crux. Higher up, steep 5.10+ lieback flakes lead to an alcove, then a roof with a bouldery V6 crux on perfect edges (~25m pitch), before steep, sequential climbing on good holds leads toward the 5.13c crux pitch itself (~35m, sustained overhanging climbing to a vertical-face crux) and a further 5.12 pitch (~35m) through another roof. The route was developed over several years and finished in 2020; it climbs in 12 pitches with link-up options for parties wanting to move faster, and multiple parties have completed it car-to-car in a day without simul-climbing.

runs: left of vanishing point on a fin like flake
hits.text: Begins about 100 ft left of Vanishing Point on a fin-like flake that reaches the ground. Water can be found just left of this pitch through June and early July.

runs: upper international run from the top of upper international
hits.text: From the Alpental base area, ascend barren lower slopes to snowline, then follow the Lower International run and the steep, double-black-diamond Upper International run. From the top of Upper International, a wide ramp leads to a clump of alpine fir below the summit block; a steel cable protects a down-sloping, exposed rock-ledge traverse, followed by a short Class 2-3 scramble to the summit, which carries a radio tower and marker pole. runs: cross bird creek at the northern lake and hike
hits.text: From Bird Creek Camp (~4,200 ft) on the Devore Creek Trail, traverse to open meadows and a waterfall cirque, then climb semi-open slopes and snow ramps into the ~7,000 ft basin between Wy'North Peak and Devore Peak (the Bird Lakes basin). Cross Bird Creek at the northern lake and hike southeast up talus/scree to a col at roughly 7,500 ft on Devore's southeast ridge. From the col, scramble west along Class 3 terrain, working past a false summit block, to an unavoidable ~20-ft rock step (Class 5.0-5.4) just below the true summit; a short final Class 3-4 pitch tops out at the 1940 first-ascent register.

runs: the glacier peak wilderness boundary at 2 300 ft
hits.text: Devore Peak is only reachable by a multi-day approach out of Stehekin, at the head of Lake Chelan — there is no road access. Drive to Fields Point Landing (or Chelan) and take the Lady of the Lake II or Lady Express passenger ferry up-lake to Stehekin (roughly a 2-4 hour boat ride depending on which boat); the National Park Service shuttle bus or a short water-taxi hop then covers the last few miles to Weaver Point Campground on the north shore, which is the trailhead (some parties instead bike or hike the road from Stehekin to High Bridge/Harlequin Bridge and pick up the Stehekin River Trail on foot). From Weaver Point (~1,160 ft), pick up the Devore Creek Trail (USFS Trail #1244). The trail switchbacks steeply — roughly 30 switchbacks over about 2 miles — up through open forest to the Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary at ~2,300 ft, then settles into a steady, unrelenting climb alongside Devore Creek for another 3+ miles; this middle section sees little maintenance and can be brushy underfoot. Devore Creek is crossed/paralleled repeatedly and is the reliable water source through this stretch. At roughly 4-5 miles from Weaver Point you reach Bird Creek Camp (~4,200 ft), the last established campsite and a common bivy for a two-day itinerary. From here leave the maintained tread and follow the open-forest use path/animal trails up along Bird Creek about another mile to a higher, unofficial camp at ~5,400 ft — many parties who want a single big summit day push to this basin instead. Continue upvalley along Bird Creek through heather benches and a talus staircase into a broader open basin holding the Bird Lakes (~7,000 ft); cross Bird Creek near the northern lake (last reliable water before the summit ridge). From the lake basin, climb loose Class 2-3 talus/scree southeast to a col (~7,500 ft) on Devore's southeast ridge, passing beneath a pair of distinctive rock towers locally called "the Bottles." Expect lingering snow in this basin and on the col approach well into July, sometimes requiring an ice axe/crampons on a short ~40-degree traverse; loose rock and occasional avalanche debris are the main hazards on this upper section. From the col, the route turns west along the summit ridge/west flank — ledges and shallow gullies of variable rock quality (some solid, some "kitty-litter"-covered slab) lead through Class 3-4 scrambling with a route-finding crux threading the ledge systems below the summit block.

Cross Bird Creek at the northern lake, climb SE to a col (~7,500 ft) on Devore's southeast ridge, then work west across scree/talus and short Class 3-4 rock steps to the summit; reverse the same line to camp.

runs: staying on the east bank of downey creek
hits.text: From the Downey Creek Campground trailhead (~1,450 ft) on Suiattle River Road (FR 26), take the Downey Creek Trail #768, staying on the east bank of Downey Creek through old-growth forest. The trail is rough and lightly maintained — expect brush, downed timber, and washed-out sections; a footlog or ford may be needed at Bachelor Creek (~6.5 mi in), which has been scoured by past avalanches that swept debris across the valley and buried sections of trail. Beyond Bachelor Creek the trail climbs steeply out of the valley toward Cub Lake, gaining roughly 4,000+ ft from the trailhead; this stretch crosses open avalanche paths below Spire Point that should be assessed for stability in early-season snow. Camp is typically made in meadows southeast of Cub Lake (~5,300 ft) or, better positioned for summit day, up on the ridge above at ~6,200 ft (add ~1 hr from the lake). Reported car-to-camp time is 9-11 hours given the distance, brush, and elevation gain — budget this as a genuine multi-day approach, not a day hike-in. From high camp, a boot path crosses the south ridge toward Spire Point, then the route drops ~200 ft and traverses cross-country (roughly 80° bearing) below cliff bands, over glacier-polished slabs (bare rock in late season, snow-covered early season) and a boulder/snow slope, to gain the base of the Dome Glacier. This traverse is unmarked route-finding on exposed, sometimes loose terrain — a map/compass or GPS track is strongly recommended.

runs: the col between pt 8386 and dorado needle
hits.text: From the Eldorado East Ridge high camp (~7,400 ft), rope up and cross the Inspiration and McAllister Glaciers to the col between Pt. 8386 and Dorado Needle. The route starts with a loose, thinly-protected 5.5 pitch off the col, eases into several ropelengths of class 3-4 ridge terrain (with a glacier traverse and moat crossing to regain the ridge partway up), then several ropelengths of 3rd-to-low-5th-class climbing to a sub-summit tower. Two short rappels drop into a notch below the true summit, followed by two sustained, high-quality 5.7 pitches to the top. Most parties take 8-12 hours round trip from high camp to summit and back, descending via the technical Northwest Ridge.

runs: the head of eureka creek to shellrock pass
hits.text: Shellrock is the camp for Ptarmigan Peak and Dot Mountain, both of which are otherwise out of reach. The standard line leaves Slate Pass, follows the Middle Fork Pasayten to Berk Creek, climbs to Freds Pass and crosses the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass, which puts a party in position to scramble Ptarmigan the following day; Dot is taken from the same country on the way through, usually in combination with the Lago and Carru group. This is genuinely remote — thirty-five miles and thirteen thousand feet of gain over four days is a fair description of a trip that collects three or four summits here — and there is no short version. The meadow ground is soft and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on the timber edge or on gravel rather than in the open grass. Snow lingers on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the single biggest constraint on when this is worth attempting.

Identical to the Serpentine approach as far as the moraine: Stuart Lake Trailhead, left at the junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail, about four miles and 2,280 ft to Colchuck Lake — roughly an hour and a half of uphill from the trail junction. Fill water and use the toilet near the lake's south end; there is nothing above.

Past the campsites you drop out of the forest into large talus blocks and follow cairns, then pick up the climbers' path along the moraine, passing a small creek on your left, until the face opens up in front of you.

A perennial snow patch sits below the start; its size varies year to year and it is usually short enough that crampons and axe are a convenience rather than a necessity by midsummer. Above it, a loose gully and gravel ledges lead to the scrambling.

Parties report roughly four and a half to five and a half hours from car to the first roped pitch.

Stay left: a few hundred feet up the path crosses to the left of the creek, and at about 6,400 ft keep left of the small cliff band with the waterfall and ignore side paths toward it.

Stuart Lake Trailhead at 3,400 ft. Stuart Lake Trail #1599 to the signed junction at 2.6 miles, then Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about 4.3 miles and 2,200 ft of gain.

From the lake's west side follow the cairned climbers' path up Aasgard Pass, gaining roughly 2,200 ft in about three quarters of a mile.

The pass itself is where people get hurt, and the rule is simple: stay left. A few hundred feet above the lake the path crosses to the climber's left of the creek and stays there. At the first grove of larches keep well clear to the left of the rock, in any season. At about 6,400 ft stay left of the small cliff band with the waterfall in it and ignore every side path leading toward the waterfall — deaths are on record on that side, and the right-hand ground cliffs out.

From the top of the pass head right and south along a short ridge above a tarn to reach Dragontail's east saddle, then cross the Snow Creek Glacier basin — a mellow slope with little crevassing, snow-covered through most of the summer — to the saddle on the east ridge.

runs: snow ramps just right of the low point of the face
hits.text: Also called the North Face route. First climbed in summer as mostly 4th/low-5th class rock with a couple of 5.7 cruxes; in recent years it has become a sought-after winter/spring alpine ice and mixed objective, following snow ramps just right of the low point of the face and then the runnels splitting the dark rock band two-thirds up. Winter conditions are highly variable with multiple line options; in good nick it's described as offering more sustained exposure than the neighboring Triple Couloirs.

runs: to the stuart lake mountaineer creek trailhead at 3 400
hits.text:
Icicle Creek Road is plowed only as far as Bridge Creek Campground, at the junction with FR 7601, which leaves about 3.7 miles of road to walk, snowshoe or ski to the Stuart Lake / Mountaineer Creek trailhead at 3,400 ft. Plan for that; it is a substantial part of the day and it is why so many parties do this route on skis.

The trail follows the creek about 1.5 miles, crosses to the west side, and continues another three-quarters of a mile to the fork. Take the left fork, cross back, and continue south — about four miles from the trailhead in total — to the north end of Colchuck Lake. Campsites are on the western banks.

When the lake is frozen, cross it directly. That is the fast option and it puts you under the north face in minutes rather than an hour of shore boulders. It is also a judgement call about ice, and it stops being available once break-up starts.

Once FR 7601 opens for the season the road walk disappears and the approach shortens dramatically — but by then the couloirs are usually past their best.

hits.text: From I-90 Exit 54 (Hyak), follow Hyak Drive onto Forest Service Road NF-9070, continuing past where the pavement ends to the junction at Ollallie Meadow where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses the road. Take the left fork of NF-9070 and follow it until the road terminates in a large turnaround just below Silver Basin. From that turnaround, it's roughly a 20-30 minute approach on foot up into Silver Basin to reach the base of The Citadel's walls, including Sofa King Buttress on the NW side of the basin's east wall. The road is not plowed and is generally only clear of snow from around July through November.

runs: to earl pass on the divide between bean and standup creeks at
hits.text: This is the overnight base for Earl Peak, and it is a contingency rather than the plan — Earl is a straightforward day from the car for most parties, and the reason to sleep here is a late start, a slow party, or a wish to link Earl with Bean Peak and the surrounding scrambles over two days. From the Beverly Creek trailhead at about 3,600 feet, take the right-hand branch at the first junction half a mile in and climb steeply up the Bean Creek valley, crossing the creek to reach the basin at roughly two miles. From the basin the route continues to Earl Pass on the divide between Bean and Standup Creeks at about 6,200 feet, then turns north up the southwest ridge, which carries bits of boot tread most of the way and stays easy scrambling to the summit. The basin is a flower meadow in early July and dry gold by September; mosquitoes are bad from snowmelt through mid-July. The last mile and a half of road to the trailhead is a rough, overgrown one-lane track that punishes a low car.

hits.text: This is the route's defining logistical fact: it uses a different trailhead from every other route on the peak. Start from the Cedar Creek trailhead near Mazama, at the end of Sandy Butte-Cedar Creek Road #200 about 4.25 miles west of Mazama off SR-20, not the Silver Star Creek or Wine Spires pullouts on SR-20 that serve the Glacier and Northeast Ridge routes. runs: the confluence of cedar and early winters creeks
hits.text: The trailhead is the test, and it is the most consequential one here because the two options are several highway miles apart. If you parked at a pullout on SR-20 opposite the Wine Spires, you are at the wrong trailhead for this route. The East Ridge is entered from Cedar creek, on the Mazama side. Arrival at the ridge: gain the crest near the confluence of Cedar and Early Winters creeks. Two named creeks meeting is a feature you can identify by sound in fog, and the ridge rises directly above it. From there the handrail is the crest itself, for roughly 3.5 miles north and west to the summit. That is a long ridge, and the navigation rule is the same as on any long ridge: keep it under your feet. Sidehilling off either side of a 3.5-mile crest at 5.9-plus is how a day here goes wrong. And the descent lands you at the other trailhead, which is the planning problem this route sets: from the summit, downclimb or rope down a short distance onto the Silver Star Glacier, descend it west and northwest toward Burgundy Col, then over the col onto the Burgundy Col climbers' trail, which drops to Highway 20 near milepost 166 about 4 miles from Washington Pass. That is several miles of highway from the Cedar creek trailhead you started at. Arrange a shuttle before you leave, not afterwards. Carry glacier travel gear, and an axe and crampons in early season: the descent crosses real crevassed glacier terrain, not just snow slopes.

From the Reflection Lakes trailhead, follow the maintained Pinnacle Saddle Trail 1.3 miles and about 1,000-1,050 ft to the Pinnacle-Plummer saddle. From there, continue on unmaintained boot path east and behind Pinnacle toward Castle Peak to reach the Castle-Pinnacle col. That segment typically takes roughly 2 to 3 hours and about 1,500 ft of gain.

The east ridge rises directly from the col. Pitch 1 scrambles mostly fourth-class ground to a belay ledge at a large dead tree. hits.text: The South Route climbs East Twin Needle from Crescent Creek Basin by the loose south-facing gullies to the Eye Col, the notch between East and West Twin Needle. Small chockstones low in the gully are scrambled past; the larger ones higher up are fifth class and are usually pitched, and a short scree walk finishes at the col. From the col the route climbs the steep summit block directly above, with a short hand-crack crux near the top that can hold ice early in the season; the summit is small, with a sheer drop to the east. Descend by downclimbing and rappelling back to the Eye Col, then down the south gullies with several short rappels off natural anchors. This is a different climb from the hard southeast ridge/face (east arête) put up during the 2003 Southern Pickets enchainment, which is reached along the crest from the east and is not gained from the Eye Col.

hits.text: Start at the Goodell Creek Cross-Country Zone Access Trailhead off SR-20 near milepost 119 (elev. ~600'). Follow the Goodell Creek Trail, an old forestry roadbed running through open forest along Goodell Creek, for roughly 4-4.5 miles. Near the trail's end, leave the maintained tread at a large cairn marking the start of the unmaintained Terror Basin/Barrier climbers' path and ford Terror Creek (can run high with snowmelt in early/mid summer - scout for a safe crossing). From the creek, the route shoots straight up the increasingly brushy crest of 'The Barrier,' a steep, dry ridge with essentially no water until small snowmelt puddles appear around 5,400'. Timberline is reached near 5,600', where travel opens onto slabs and heather in 'Stump Hollow' between the Barrier crest and the Chopping Block. Most parties camp on the Chopping Block ridge (~6,400'), making the car-to-camp day roughly 6-7.5 miles with about 5,800-6,000' of gain - a full, strenuous day, and the crux of the whole trip for many parties (loose talus, fading cairns/flagging, and route-finding through brush make The Barrier notorious for turning parties around). Parties wanting a camp nearer the Needles can instead drop about 200-250' off the ridge crest into Crescent Creek Basin and traverse roughly a mile cross-country (talus, slabs, occasional snow) staying near 5,800', to a camp below Mount Terror at about 6,050' near two streams fed by overhead slabs (reliable water, unlike the Barrier). From this basin camp, descend about 300' below the moraine to the head of Crescent Creek, then work up and around buttresses toward the braided, loose south-facing gullies beneath the Eye Col, the notch separating East and West Twin Needle. The final few hundred feet to the col and onto the route involve steep, loose gully climbing with real route-finding uncertainty (this south side has comparatively sparse route information and can feel disorienting in cloud or low light) before reaching the col, from which the route climbs East Twin Needle's summit block directly above.

hits.text: Reach the Monte Cristo townsite on foot or by bike from Barlow Pass, then take the Glacier Basin Trail less than a mile. The spire stands above the trail, roughly 2,000 ft above the basin. When it makes sense, leave the trail and start up toward the base of the ridge — a snowfield early in the season, extremely loose talus once it has gone. Snow or talus leads up a narrowing gully to the lower col, steepening as it goes, commonly 35 to 45 degrees, with the final couloir steeper and more exposed than anything below it. Best done early in the year while the gully still holds snow: melted out it is loose scree badly exposed to rockfall and a poor outing in late summer. Fixed stations exist in the gully and parties have used them to bypass melted-out gaps on the way down.

From it, scramble around the south face on very loose talus to the upper, east notch, and belay there: the first pitch climbs the east side of the spire a short way, then downclimbs a 5.5 crack about twenty feet to a ramp. hits.text: Start at the Eldorado Trailhead (Eldorado Creek Climbers' Path) at mile 20 of Cascade River Road, elevation ~2,100 ft (pit toilet at the parking area). From the parking area, backtrack downstream about 90 feet on the road and look for a log or a clump of three trees spanning the Cascade River — cross here (this crossing can be exposed and slick when wet or in high water; a rope/handline is prudent for less experienced parties), then walk roughly 100 feet perpendicular to the river to pick up the climbers' trail. The path climbs steeply through heavy timber, gaining about 1,500 ft before breaking out onto talus. Follow cairns and flagging up the boulder field, staying climber's right to avoid an unnecessary crossing of Eldorado Creek, until the talus eases into the open, beautiful alpine Eldorado Creek Basin (a common first camp at roughly 5,400–5,600 ft, ~3 miles and 3,300 ft from the trailhead). From the basin, climb up onto a rocky ridge at about 6,100 ft, then drop a few hundred feet on the far side into Roush Creek Basin (an alternate/second camp at 6,100–6,400 ft, with reliable running water). From Roush Basin, ascend broken talus and slabs onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier and continue up moderate glacier slopes to a high camp near 7,500–7,800 ft on the Eldorado–Inspiration Glacier saddle, with views of Moraine Lake, McAllister Glacier and Klawatti Glacier. Rope up for glacier travel here — the Eldorado and Inspiration Glaciers carry real crevasse hazard, worse as the day warms; parties have broken through hidden snow-bridged creek channels even in the lower basins in spring. From high camp, cross the mostly flat Inspiration Glacier aiming for the low gap on Eldorado's lower East Ridge, then follow the ridge/snow arete up to the base of the summit knife-edge. Total gain is roughly 6,700–6,800 ft trailhead-to-summit; guided parties budget 5–7 hours to high camp and another 3–5 hours (6–9 hours total on summit day) from camp to the top.

hits.text: Same trailhead and lower approach as the East Ridge: Eldorado Trailhead at Cascade River Road mile 20 (~2,100 ft), cross the Cascade River via the log/three-tree crossing about 90 ft downstream of the parking area, then climb the steep timbered climbers' trail into a dry boulderfield (roughly to 4,500 ft) and on into Eldorado Creek Basin. From there, continue as for the East Ridge over the Roush Divide and up the Eldorado Glacier, then trend toward the Eldorado–Dean's Spire col on the mountain's northwest side to reach the wild Marble Creek Cirque, with views of Dorado Needle and Early Morning Spire. The approach to this face is longer and more involved than the East Ridge approach — a long, somewhat complicated route across glaciated and crevassed terrain, so rope up for the glacier sections. High camp is typically established either in Eldorado Creek/Roush Creek Basin or higher at the Eldorado-Inspiration Glacier site (~7,500–7,600 ft). One recorded ascent (climbing from the trailhead in a single push) took roughly 5 hours to reach the couloir's base; that party also used a shortcut of a belayed downclimb (~35 m) and two 30-meter rappels down a snow/rock gully near the Eldorado–Dean's Spire col to drop directly to within about 100 yards of the couloir, which meaningfully shortens the standard glacier traverse but is a variation, not the only way in — most parties simply continue glacier travel around to the couloir's base at about 7,800 ft. Hazards on approach: crevasses on the Eldorado/Inspiration Glaciers, a long featureless glacier crossing that can be disorienting in whiteout, and the optional gully downclimb/rappel shortcut is itself exposed snow-and-rock terrain.

Same trailhead and lower approach as the East Ridge: Eldorado trailhead at Cascade River Road mile 20 near 2,100 ft, the log crossing of the Cascade River about 90 ft downstream of the parking area, the steep timbered climbers' trail into a dry boulderfield around 4,500 ft, and on into Eldorado Creek Basin.

The usual way in is from above: follow the East Ridge glacier track to about 8,100 ft, traverse to the notch between the North Ridge and the first rock spire — the same notch sometimes called the Eldorado-Dean's Spire or Dean's Tower col — and rappel from it into the cirque below. A full 60 m rope gets a party through in one; parties on shorter ropes have downclimbed the remainder. One party used a belayed downclimb of about 35 m plus two 30 m rappels to land within about 100 yards of the couloir. One single-push ascent took roughly five hours from the trailhead to the couloir's base.

The alternative is simply to continue glacier travel around to the couloir's base at about 7,800 ft.

hits.text:
Once you are in the cirque the route is obvious, and two separate parties say so in nearly the same words: on looking up from below the rappel, one recorded instantly seeing the line — steep, fat and unmistakable. The couloir splits the northwest face and there is nothing else in the cirque it could be confused with. So the navigation problem is not identifying the couloir; it is getting into the cirque at all.

The notch is the thing to find, and it is shared with the North Ridge. It is the obvious gap between the North Ridge and the First Rock Spire, at about 8,100 ft, reached by traversing north from the East Ridge glacier track. At that notch the two routes go opposite ways: rappel down the far side into the cirque and you are on this route; climb steep snow up onto the rock crest and you are on the North Ridge.

The base itself is the transition at about 7,800 ft where the couloir meets the glacier — which is the usual place to find the moat or bergschrund, and it widens as summer goes on. Rope up on the glacier before you reach it.

One branch point worth knowing: at least one party climbed a steep line just to climber's left of the main gut of the couloir rather than the gut itself. Both go; the gut is the route as described.

Confirm on the climbing: the line runs from about 7,800 ft to about 8,800 ft, roughly 1,000 ft, usually two or three long pitches or simul-climbed blocks, and the character is a succession of short ice steps broken by lower-angle snow rather than one continuous wall. Steps around 70-80 degrees with occasional near-vertical bulges for a body length is right; sustained vertical ice for a full pitch is not this route in any season.

Switchback up the woods above and cut right to the wall. Ellation starts in the shallow grooves above and left of the single-pitch crag, at a bolt near the ground. About an hour and 1,200 ft of gain.

hits.text:
Rappel the line of ascent on a single 70m rope used doubled. The descent is not one continuous rappel line and does not map onto the pitches: five rappels bring you down the main wall to a gear belay at its toe, then you downscramble a 3rd/4th-class gully to the big treed ledge, then three more rappels reach the ground. Seven of the eight are too long for a 60m rope, and the last is 115 ft — the whole reach of a doubled 70 — so knot the ends.

Two stations need naming in advance. The rappel down pitch 6 is where ropes jam: a crack at the top of the ramp catches the pull, and parties have had to re-climb the pitch to free it. Clip the pull strand through a leaver biner on the second bolt below that station and it stops being a problem. And the station off the big treed ledge is a tree on slings, roughly 30-40 ft to climber's left of the top of pitch 3 — the only anchor on the route without fixed metal, so inspect what you find.

From the base, retrace the brushy climbers' path down through timber and mossy slabs to the Hannegan Pass Trail and out to the trailhead.

From the white-boulder clearing, work up to a mossy slab and, standing literally at its base, cut left and up a slight hill on a reasonably well-defined trail running along the foot of the slab. About five minutes of that reaches a dry streambed under a gully. hits.text: A car-to-car loop from the Stuart Lake trailhead that links the nine tallest summits of the Enchantments area: Mount Stuart, Sherpa, Argonaut, Colchuck, Dragontail, Little Annapurna, McClellan, Enchantment Peak and Cannon Mountain.
