hits.text: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike North: park 1.1 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, where a dirt road intersects the paved road on the left (SE side), or continue to 1.2 miles and use the large pull-off. Cross the main road and pick up the approach trail between the two parking spots, marked by a short steep drainage topped with a downed tree.

runs: the 5 300 ft saddle between bedal peak and sloan peak
hits.text: From the Mountain Loop Highway, turn onto FR 4096 (Bedal Creek Trailhead spur) and park at the trailhead, 2,790–2,800 ft. Follow the Bedal Creek Trail #705 through old-growth forest along Bedal Creek's steep banks; the maintained tread peters out roughly 1.5–2.5 miles in, at a large brushy washout coming down off the basin below Sloan's West Face. Scramble up the boulder- and blowdown-choked washout — this is the crux of route-finding on the approach — until a cairn marks an exit onto a climber's path (often flagged with pink tape) that switchbacks steeply through forest from about 3,500 ft to 4,900 ft. Above treeline the path crosses talus and a meadow bench (4,900–5,300 ft) with summit views, passes a stagnant tarn near the 5,300 ft saddle between Bedal Peak and Sloan Peak (last reliable water is here or at the cascading streams just below), then continues on rocky, exposed scrambling terrain to about 5,800 ft at the toe of the glacier — crampons/axe may be needed here depending on season. For the Southwest Face (Fire on the Mountain's start), do not follow the standard Corkscrew line onto the glacier; instead cross the low ridge that separates the West Face basin from the Southwest Face basin/meadows to reach the base of the face. Total car-to-base time runs about 3 hours for a fit, familiar party; expect a long day given ~8 pitches of technical climbing still ahead. An alternate approach via the Cougar Creek/North Fork Sauk trailhead (FR 49) converges with the Bedal Creek route around 5,000–5,500 ft but requires fording the North Fork Sauk River, a crossing that is deep, swift, and best avoided solo or in high early-season flow.

hits.text: From Chelan, take the Lady of the Lake ferry (or a floatplane) to Stehekin Landing. Ride the NPS shuttle bus 4.4 miles up Stehekin Valley Road to Harlequin Bridge ($5 fare), cross the bridge, and follow the road past Harlequin Camp and the Stehekin Airport to pick up the Stehekin River Trail. Follow this mostly flat trail southeastward about 3 miles to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction. The Devore Creek Trail then climbs steeply through rock bluffs and open forest for about 1 mile, enters the Glacier Peak Wilderness, and traverses brushy, dry hillside for roughly 3 more miles to Bird Creek Camp (4,200 ft) — the only designated camp in the area, with room for about three tents. From Bird Creek Camp, most parties do Flora as a long day round trip: bushwhack through open forest (spiderwebs, chest-high brush, and blowdown reported) toward the saddle south of Enigma Peak, then follow the route description above to the summit.

runs: up an increasingly steep and unstable talus slope to an obvious saddle
hits.text: Two elevations tell you you are in the wrong place, and both are worth memorising. Leave the trail at about 5,000 ft, cross the creek and bear east-southeast; if you have climbed to 5,200 ft you have gone too far along the trail and risk dropping into the wrong basin when you turn off. Then, if you find yourself heading cross-country into a narrow basin as early as 6,200 ft, you are too far south — contour northward at once, round the corner below the steeper ground, and get into the next basin over. The correct basin leads to a divide at about 7,460 ft on the south ridge of the neighbouring peak, reached up an increasingly steep and unstable talus slope to an obvious saddle on climber's left, the rock starting as large solid boulders and degrading into loose softball- and football-sized stuff. From the divide, descend about 600 ft off its east side toward the creek, contouring around at roughly 6,800 ft to avoid steeper ground, then aim for the high southwest basin, from which a simple talus scramble reaches the top. The true summit is the south end of the massif; the north point is about a hundred feet lower.

runs: the two spires and scramble to a flat ledge
hits.text:
Stay right of the gully that divides the two spires, and scramble to a flat ledge. Those are the two things to find: the dividing gully, kept on your left, and a flat ledge where the route starts.

Why the gully is the right handrail to use here: North and South Early Winters Spires are separated by a single continuous cleft, a chockstone-filled chasm on the west side and a gully on the east. It runs the full height between the two peaks, so it is the one feature on this side you cannot lose. Keep it on your left and you are on North Early Winters Spire's ground; cross it and you are on South Early Winters Spire, where the Direct East Buttress and Southern Man start.

Arrival: a flat ledge, gained by scrambling. Flat ground on a steep east-facing wall is the confirmation.

The trailhead test, which is the one that costs an hour if you get it wrong: this route is on the east side and is reached from the hairpin pullout. The other two North Early Winters Spire routes here, The West Face and Labor Pains, are on the west side and are reached from the Blue Lake Trailhead, which is about 2.5 miles away by road on the far side of Washington Pass. Those are different cars.

And the descent crosses back over the mountain, which you should plan for before starting: from the summit, traverse to the west side of the peak and rappel either the Chockstone Route with a 60 m rope or the bolted West Face anchors with a 70 m rope. Both require crossing over from the east-side climbing line to the west-side descent infrastructure.

runs: in the area with large trees on it
hits.text: The only ridge in the area with large trees on it, then a cliffy nuisance ridge. Cross Glacier Creek above the falls and traverse nearly level to the base of a timbered ridge — unmistakable, because it is the only rib on this slope carrying big trees while everything either side of it is brush and talus. That ridge is the first landmark and it is climbed, not skirted. The second comes at the end of the upper traverse near 5,100 ft: a cliffy ridge that has to be got around rather than crossed. Once past it, turn right and go straight up the talus slopes toward the summit gully. At the gully entrance the season decides the day — in a good year the snowfield runs continuously into the gully, and where it has pulled back, the rock immediately to its left has gone at short class 4. The gully above is mostly class 3 and finishes at a notch on the skyline just west of the true summit; aim for that notch, not for the summit block. A gully topping out at the summit, or east of it, is the wrong one.

runs: grassy traverse east to the next rock rib
hits.text: The East Ridge is not reversed as a rappel line in its own right; two descents are used instead. The standard one is the East Ledges, dropping climber's-right/northeast directly off the summit: three rappels trend northeast from the summit area, then a short, exposed grassy traverse east to the next rock rib, followed by two more rappels onto the East Ledges proper, about 5 rappels in all. From there, several hundred metres of loose, sandy and grassy class 3–4 ledges and slabs, marked by intermittent and sometimes doubled cairn lines, lead east above the cliffs over the crevassed Boston Glacier to a gully about 100 ft below the Solitary Gendarme; go up and over the East Ridge through it, then down snow slopes on the south side to the small glacier below Forbidden's south face and the walk back across Boston Basin. The alternative is to reverse along the ridge crest past the gendarmes to the West Ridge notch and descend the West Ridge line: about three rappels on the ridge and about five down the Cat Scratch gullies, roughly eight on a single 60 m rope. It is longer, but it is more travelled and easier to follow, and many parties prefer it to the East Ledges, which are faster but loose, exposed, rockfall-prone and easy to lose. Either way, expect mostly natural slung-horn and block anchors with some tat and a handful of fixed or bolted stations, and carry a 60 m rope.

hits.text: From the Boston Basin trailhead near 3,200 ft on Cascade River Road, the old Diamond Mine roadbed runs about a mile to the mine site, then the climbers' path climbs hard through forest with four stream crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft. Camp low at about 5,300 ft or high at about 6,400 ft. From high camp, follow the moraine and the west edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier up to about 7,500 ft and climb to Sharkfin Col at 7,720 ft — roughly 10 ft of 5.7 rock and 200 ft of a class 3 gully to gain it, on loose scree underfoot. The col is the commitment. From it you rappel roughly 100-150 ft, in one or two stages depending on snow, down a loose gully onto the Boston Glacier; retreat after that means re-climbing to the col. Traverse north through crevassed ground toward the north end of the glacier, then re-ascend to the ridge. Three Forbidden routes cross Sharkfin Col and use this rappel. Where you leave the Boston Glacier is what separates them.

The section is rated old-style grade III and was first protected with a few pitons; expect no fixed gear, and treat this outline with caution because the face sees very few ascents.

runs: steep somewhat loose 4th to low 5th class
hits.text: Forbidden's tallest, steepest, and most remote established route, first climbed by Fred Beckey and Ed Cooper in July 1959. It is a notably pure line whose mixed character demands real climbing ability and adaptable alpine skills. From a high bivy, roughly 500 ft of steep, somewhat loose 4th-to-low-5th-class terrain gains a knife-edge section (5.6), leading into four 60m pitches up to the 5.8 crux before the face blends into the upper West Ridge near the summit.

runs: one of the fifty classic climbs of north america and
hits.text: One of the Fifty Classic Climbs of North America and Forbidden's standard route: a sweeping, exposed arête of clean North Cascades granite. The crux is a single sustained 5.6 move near a prominent gendarme tower (stay left to avoid straying onto the harder West Ridge Direct variation), followed by a narrow knife-edge crest and a final false-summit downclimb — losing roughly 10 ft of elevation — before the true summit.

runs: the old diamond mine roadbed for about 1 mile
hits.text: From the Boston Basin trailhead off Cascade River Road, follow the unsigned but well-beaten Boston Basin climbers' path. It starts by following the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about 1 mile, then splits off the roadbed to climb steeply and directly through forest. The trail crosses four seasonal creeks/streams (reliable water) as it switchbacks up through increasingly open timber, breaking out above treeline around 5,300 ft. Above treeline it continues into the broad boulder-and-heather Boston Basin cirque, past the usual high-camp sites around 6,300–6,600 ft (roughly 4–5 miles and 3–4 hours from the car, ringed by Sahale, Sharkfin Tower, and Mt. Torment). From camp, make an ascending traverse across talus and the Quien Sabe Glacier remnant toward Forbidden's south face; when the glacier is melted out, a class 3 rock spur on climber's right is often a faster, drier alternative to crossing snow/ice. Rope up if the glacier is crevassed or snow-covered. Aim for the obvious ~500-ft snow-and-ice couloir splitting the left edge of the south face — the standard gully leading to the West Ridge notch. This couloir steepens to 40–50°+ near its top, typically wants crampons/axe (and sometimes a picket) into mid-summer, and is guarded by a moat near its top, against the rock walls approaching the notch, that can require a short steep step or a band of loose rock to surmount. Exiting the couloir at the ridge-crest notch is roughly 4–5 hours and about 4,500 ft above the trailhead.

runs: the highest point in the lake chelan sawtooth wilderness
hits.text: Gardner Mountain (8,898–8,902 ft) is the second-highest summit in the Methow Mountains — a North Cascades subrange — after neighboring North Gardner Mountain (~8,956 ft, the Okanogan County highpoint), about a mile to the northwest; Gardner itself is the highest point in the Lake Chelan–Sawtooth Wilderness. The standard route is a long, non-technical Class 2 scree/talus ascent via the Wolf Creek Trail and Gardner Meadows, almost always done as a 2–3 day backpack rather than a day trip. This route (West Ridge / Saddle Traverse) links Gardner to North Gardner via the connecting ridge over Point 8,487, which steps up to loose Class 2–3 terrain with real exposure.

runs: the saddle southwest of the true summit between the mountain's two highpoints
hits.text: Stay west of the stream, and do not climb the gully it comes out of. Three gullies drain this face and they are not equivalent. The eastern one is where the stream originates, and it is the one that can cliff-band you out — which is exactly why every description of this route tells you to stay west of the stream from the meadows upward. The central open gully and slopes just west of the stream is the most direct line and tops out at the saddle southeast of the summit. A further large gully west of that reaches the saddle southwest of the true summit, between the mountain's two highpoints. The transition to watch for is at about 7,100 ft where meadow turns to rock and the scree begins; above it you climb directly up steep rocky slopes, picking over scree and rock buttresses. At the top the ground flattens onto a high plateau and the summit sits on the ridge crest, wide and gentle. If you are standing on a pointed bump with higher ground to the north, you are on one of the sub-peaks southeast of the true top.

runs: trail a few hundred feet west of the small stream
hits.text: The higher option for a party that wants to shorten summit day rather than take both peaks in one long push from the meadows. Heading north out of Gardner Meadows the ground rises to a small meadow basin at about 6,200 ft, and an old boot path leaves the main trail a few hundred feet west of the small stream to reach it. Stay between roughly 6,200 and 6,400 ft on the way across — drop lower and you land in groves of silver snags with jack-strawed deadfall that cost far more time than the elevation saves. From a camp here the scree slope to the ridge is about 1,400 ft of gain in half a mile, which is the steepest and loosest section of the whole climb and much better done early and on firm ground. It is an exposed spot with no shelter to speak of and it is cold; the compensation is the position and the head start. Use it when the forecast is settled and when you have confirmed water. In a dry August the meadows below are the safer plan.

runs: 12.3 miles to the middle fork taylor river
hits.text:
I-90 Exit 34 east of North Bend, east on Edgewick Road, then right at the stop sign after 0.4 miles onto SE Middle Fork Road, which becomes FR 56. Drive about 12.3 miles to the Middle Fork / Taylor River junction just after the Taylor River bridge, keep right on the Middle Fork Road and go about a mile to a small gravel pulloff — five cars at most — near 47.54604, -121.52151 at about 1,174 ft. Washouts on the Middle Fork road have periodically added a mile or more of walking.

The path leaves the road a hundred to two hundred yards further along, on the left, marked by a cairn. From there it climbs steeply through forest switchbacks for roughly 30 to 45 minutes. The tread is not signed but it is genuinely worn: if you have been walking more than a few minutes on ground that does not look like a trail, you are off it.

runs: a single rope rappel off the steep section of the wooded ramp
hits.text: Descend the line of ascent. A single 70 m rope handles it (60 m would probably work) via five or more rappels off trees and horns, linked by long stretches of downscrambling in the gully. Rappelling off the overhang near the summit into Gully #2 has been done, but getting out to that rappel is described as quite scary and it is not recommended. Below the Y Notch you are back on the Main Peak's South Route descent — a single-rope rappel off the steep section of the wooded ramp, then the slab (two double-rope rappels if you rope it) and the dirt gully. Loose rock is the constant theme; the descent is where parties get hurt.

runs: over the main west peak summit and down the west ridge
hits.text: No fixed rappel line on the route. Descend over the main West Peak summit and down the west ridge, or - if you have carried two 60 m ropes - rappel Infinite Bliss instead: counts for this rappel line differ - about 20 to 25 double-rope rappels. Do not head straight down the northwest backside slope.

runs: up and over the main west peak summit and
hits.text: From the sub-summit, walk down and left through the small gap in the trees onto the gentle northern slope, then go up and over the main West Peak summit and descend the west ridge. Do NOT head straight down the northwest backside slope — the first ascensionist flags this specifically. The alternative, if you have carried two 60 m ropes, is to rappel Infinite Bliss (about 20 rappels off the chain stations); a single 70 m or 80 m is not long enough for those stations. Either way this is a long descent on brushy, disorienting terrain and should be started with hours of daylight in hand.

runs: dirt gully slab canyon edge tiny notch razorback glade saddle key ledge traverse y notch 2 gully

hits.text: The old sketch landmarks are still the way people navigate it: dirt gully, slab, canyon edge, tiny notch, razorback, glade saddle, key ledge traverse, Y notch, #2 gully. Walk up the dry creek bed from the road; partway up the route leaves the streambed into the woods on faint trail and flagging. At about 2,200 ft you reach the dirt gully — fill water at the creek here, it is the last certain water on the route. Four hundred vertical feet of loose dirt and rock, then the trail exits left into brush-free timber for another 400 ft, then the slab, which is two pitches of comfortable soloing on intersecting dikes. Above the slab continue in dirt along its upper left edge, traverse under a rock outcrop, over the razorback and tiny notch to the Glade Saddle, where there is a tight, well-used two-person bivy site. The wooded ramp above has a sporty 20-foot step. The Key Ledge Traverse is the most overstated part of the description — after the dirt gully it feels like a walk. It ends at the Y Notch, the confluence of #1 and #2 Gullies at the head of the Great Canyon. A short exposed step around a rock band, then several hundred yards of very steep brush and brush-tunnel on faint trail, brings you to the base of #2 Gully. The gully is a nightmarish mix of impossibly loose rock on one side and polished mossy rock on the other — do not attempt it unless bone dry. Simulclimb the lower section with short belayed steps, then pitch out the harder ground; a fixed ring piton partway up may date to the 1940 first ascent. The 'Chimney Variation' (two leads of easy class 5 above the chimney, a good idea if the chimney is wet) rejoins the standard line at the top of #2 Gully around 5,200 ft, from where easy slabs and steep heather lead to the summit.

hits.text: From the summit scramble down to the top of the easy slab and rig a single-rope rappel to the col at the top of #2 Gully. From there scramble to a bolted rappel station and make the first of about four double-rope rappels with two 60 m ropes, traversing 100-yard stretches of slab between stations on the east side of the gully; the lower stations are on trees and chockstones with slings dating back to the 1990s. Pack the ropes near the base of the gully and downclimb — this is where the west-side rock is loosest and where a party member was struck by a 500-pound block that cut loose under hand pressure in 2001. Cross back over the Y Notch and the Key Ledge Traverse, make a single-rope rappel off the steep section of the wooded ramp, and continue down past the Glade Saddle. Two more double-rope rappels land you at the base of the slab at 2,900 ft; from there it is the wooded ridge, then the dirt gully to the creek at 2,100 ft, then the faint trail and the dry creek bed to the car. Expect to lose the trail in the dark at least once.

runs: a clean blocky chimney to the right of the route that looks good but
hits.text: Gato Negro is a full-day alpine rock climb with fairly sustained 5.10a/b climbing spread across 12 long pitches. Most pitches span 180-190 feet with none shorter than 150 feet. The route features a spectacular hand-crack first pitch, bolted 5.10a face climbing on fragile flakes, rising traverses under roofs, and splitter cracks on the final headwall. Route-finding is somewhat challenging; avoid a clean blocky chimney to the right of the route that looks good but is not as good as it appears. Cruxes are mostly well-protected, but a few slightly runout 5.8 sections on loose granite and a 5.9+ offwidth chimney section present additional challenges.

No exact count is published, so carry a rope and gear for several rappels and cord to build anchors.

hits.text: The descent does not reverse the route. Make a few rappels over the top of the spire into the steep gully between Whine Spire and the west summit of Silver Star, then work down the gully with long sections of loose 4th-class downclimbing and a few more rappels. The gully is extremely loose, with rock coming down through it constantly, so keep the party out of one another's fall line and clear of the ropes. Do not attempt it in rock shoes. Plan on 2.5 to 3 hours in good conditions; parties benighted here describe about three hours of complex route-finding in the dark, and advise against starting it after dark.

runs: the south and west sides of the mountain
hits.text: Ghost Peak is normally climbed as an add-on from a high camp shared with neighboring Crooked Thumb Peak and Phantom Peak, since all three summits are within a few tenths of a mile of one another in the Northern Pickets. The way from camp is obvious once you're established there. The first-ascent party climbed from the notch south of the peak, reaching it from the west, then kept to the south and west sides of the mountain along obvious weaknesses — easy-to-moderate 4th/low-5th-class climbing on comparatively solid Pickets rock.

runs: just before the third crossing of the nooksack river
hits.text: From Bellingham, drive SR-542 east about 46 miles, which is 13 miles past Glacier, and just before the third crossing of the Nooksack River turn left onto FR-32, then follow it 5.3 miles to its end at Hannegan Campground, where the trailhead is.

runs: stayed on the south and west sides of the mountain following obvious weaknesses
hits.text: Ghost is climbed from the high camp shared with Crooked Thumb and Phantom, all three being within a few tenths of a mile of each other. From that camp a roped glacier crossing reaches the foot of the peak. The original line gained the notch south of the peak, and gained it from the west rather than by attacking the notch directly from the glacier below, then stayed on the south and west sides of the mountain following obvious weaknesses at easy-to-moderate fourth and low fifth class. Access from camp is described as obvious once you are established there; the difficulty is knowing which of the three summits you are under.

runs: the east side of the conrad glacier to the
hits.text: Walk the road a quarter mile to the gate and take South Fork Tieton Trail #1120 about 4.5 miles to the loop junction; go right (north) about 2 miles, then near 5,100 ft turn right up an unmarked pack trail to a ridge crest and on west and north through benches to a Conrad Creek waterfall at 6,000 ft. Pass Barren Lake, climb the east side of the Conrad Glacier to the 7,200 ft saddle, traverse the Meade Glacier west-southwest to the south ridge and scramble it to the summit.

runs: the east side of the conrad glacier to
hits.text:
From the South Tieton Creek and Conrad Meadows trailhead, approach the north side of the peak and ascend the east side of the Conrad Glacier to a saddle at about 7,200 ft. From the saddle, traverse onto the Meade Glacier, then finish over boulders, scree and a summit snowfield.

The Conrad is the more active of the peak's two small glaciers, so this line wants a rope, a harness and a crevasse-rescue kit rather than just an axe and crampons.

Descent reverses the traverse: back over the saddle and down the Conrad to Conrad Meadows. It is normally done over two or more days given the long approach through the drainage and the talus.

runs: the east side of the conrad glacier to
hits.text:
Two glaciers with one saddle between them. That sequence is the route and it is the test.

You climb the east side of the Conrad Glacier to a saddle at about 7,200 ft, and from that saddle you traverse onto a second glacier — the Meade — before any of the summit ground. Glacier, saddle, glacier, then boulders, scree and a summit snowfield, in that order.

The negative at the saddle is the one worth carrying: if you reach a saddle and the ground beyond it is boulders and scree with no second glacier, you are on the wrong saddle. This route's saddle opens onto ice. A saddle that opens onto rock belongs to the ridge line, which is the peak's other route from the same trailhead.

The elevation is a cross-check rather than a marker: about 7,200 ft. Well above that and you have climbed the glacier past its col; well below and you are still on the apron.

Which side of the glacier matters and it is easy to get wrong in the dark: the east side of the Conrad. Drifting west takes you up the glacier's other flank and away from the saddle.

The approach-side finding: this route comes at the peak from the north. If you have climbed onto a long ridge with the peak in view along it, you are on the Klickton Divide line instead — a fine route, a different day, and it does not need a rope.

hits.text: Two approaches are used, both longer and more involved than the standard Sitkum route. (1) Via the White Chuck River, no longer usable since a 2003 flood destroyed the trail and road: the old line followed the White Chuck River Trail (FST 643) about 6 miles to the Kennedy Ridge Trail (FST 639) junction, then Kennedy Ridge Trail 1.7 miles up to the PCT. Head north on the PCT past the Glacier Creek crossing (water) to an unmarked climbers' path leaving the PCT on Glacier Ridge about 0.7 miles beyond the creek, which climbs snow and pumice to the standard high camp near 7,200 ft on the Kennedy Ridge shoulder. (2) Via North Fork Sauk Trailhead: North Fork Sauk Trail to White Pass (~9 miles, ~5,900 ft), then a long traverse north on/near the PCT to the same Kennedy Ridge camp area — a 20-mile-plus approach day used by some parties. From high camp, the route proper begins by traversing the upper southwest slopes of the Ptarmigan Glacier just below the ridgeline to about 8,000 ft, rounding Kennedy Peak to an 8,000 ft saddle between the Vista and Kennedy Glaciers. Ascend the Kennedy Glacier — a 'crumbling mess' of loose moraine and boulders low down — to an 8,800 ft saddle where Frostbite Ridge proper begins. The ridge itself mixes loose pumice/dust scrambling on narrow, exposed steps with sections of steep snow (45–50°) protected with pickets or ice screws, passing directly beneath/through the Rabbit Ears — twin eroded lava pinnacles — where loose rock is a real hazard, especially in warm, dry conditions (cold, snowy conditions lock the rock in place and make the scramble more manageable). Above the Rabbit Ears the route steepens further into a section of alpine ice, anywhere from a single ~40-foot ice step to roughly 200 feet of AI2, typically simul-climbed with ice screw protection, before crossing the crater rim and descending briefly into the crater to reach the 10,550 ft summit.

runs: above the steep ice north of the rabbit ears
hits.text: Frostbite Ridge is essentially a one-way, committing line — once on the ridge there is no turning back — and virtually all parties descend a different, easier route rather than reversing the ridge. The standard descent is down the Sitkum Glacier: from the summit, descend the gully east of the summit into the upper Sitkum Glacier, traverse and descend to a saddle at roughly 8,000 ft, then continue down the lower Sitkum Glacier to Boulder Basin, picking up the climbers' path back to the PCT, then south on the PCT to White Pass and down the North Fork Sauk Trail to the North Fork Sauk Trailhead (some parties instead reverse to the Cool Glacier/Gerdine Ridge side if that's where their car is staged). The single rappel belongs to the ridge itself rather than to this walk-off descent: there is a natural belay-horn anchor (a rock horn, typically backed by old slings — inspect before trusting) just above the steep ice north of the Rabbit Ears, used to lower one pitch of steep ice into a notch referred to as the 'doorway gap' in the summit rib. This is a single-pitch rappel — a 30m single-strand rope is sufficient for the drop described — encountered while working through the crux ice/rock step near the Rabbit Ears (i.e., on the way up for most parties, since the standard descent avoids the ridge entirely); some parties simul-climb this step with screw/picket protection instead of rappelling, depending on ice conditions. Carry 3–4 ice screws and/or pickets for this section and for the steep snow/ice above the Rabbit Ears regardless of whether you end up rappelling it.

runs: the upper south west slopes of the ptarmigan glacier just below the
hits.text:
The high camp at about 7,200 ft on snow and pumice is the staging point, not the route. From there the approach continues across the upper south-west slopes of the Ptarmigan Glacier just below the ridgeline to about 8,000 ft, rounding Kennedy Peak to a saddle at 8,000 ft between the Vista and Kennedy Glaciers, then up the Kennedy Glacier — loose moraine and boulders low down — to a saddle at about 8,800 ft. That saddle is where Frostbite Ridge proper begins, and it is the last bivy site before the crater.

The critical navigation warning is about the Rabbit Ears. They are the route's famous feature, a pair of eroded lava pinnacles, and they are not visible until you are immediately below them, slightly east of the ridge crest. Do not try to navigate toward them from a distance and do not conclude you are off route because you cannot see them — get to the 8,800 ft saddle and follow the crest, and they will appear.

Above the Ears the ridge steepens into alpine ice, reported anywhere from a single short step to a couple of hundred feet, before the crater rim.

The historic line starts at the White Chuck River Trailhead at the end of FR-23 and follows Trail #643 about four miles, then Kennedy Ridge Trail #639 for 1.7 miles to the Pacific Crest Trail near 5,000 ft. Turn north on the PCT and follow it about two miles to the Glacier Creek crossing, where there are established camps with reliable water near 5,300 ft. Four to five hours is the usual pack-in.

FR-23 has been closed from milepost 3.7 to its end, so the reliably open option in recent seasons has been the North Fork Sauk Trail and the PCT over Red Pass to the same Glacier Creek camps. That is a much longer walk to the same place, and it changes nothing above camp.

From the Glacier Creek camp a climbers' trail runs up a gully to the crest of Kennedy Ridge. Everything above is glacier, and the character of the day is set by how well you read the upper glacier rather than by any technical difficulty — the headwall at the top is about 40 degrees and short, while the crevasse field below it is the part parties spend hours on.

From the Bridge Creek Trailhead on Highway 20 near milepost 159, just over a mile east of Rainy Pass at about 4,400 ft, head south on the Pacific Crest Trail roughly nine to ten miles down Bridge Creek to the North Fork Bridge Creek junction near North Fork Camp, then up the increasingly brushy North Fork trail.

The total approach is on the order of twelve or more miles with several thousand feet of gain before any roped climbing. Most parties bivy low on the ridge; water is reliable along Bridge Creek and scarce once you are on the rock, so tank up before you leave the creek.

runs: stay in the scree climber's right of the
hits.text: Start at the Barlow Pass trailhead on the Mountain Loop Highway (19.3 miles east of the Verlot Public Service Center), on the Weeden Creek Trail / Gothic Basin trail (USFS #724). The first ~0.7 mile follows an old closed mining road before singletrack begins climbing steadily through forest; the trail fords Weeden Creek around the 1.1-mile mark (no bridge — the main reliable water source low on the route). From there the trail switchbacks up a steep, root-and-rock staircase, gaining close to 1,000 ft/mile through a roughly 2-mile crux band; this section holds lingering snow patches and old avalanche run-out debris across the tread well into early summer in heavy-snow years, and can require an ice axe. Around 3.5–4 miles the trail breaks out of timber into the open slabs and tarns of Gothic Basin (around 5,000 ft) — the last dependable water before the final push and a good bail-out point in poor weather. From the basin, continue up talus and slab benches roughly another 0.5–0.6 mile to the saddle above Foggy Lake (total to the lake is about 9.2 miles / 2,800–3,100 ft round trip per multiple trail sources), then drop slightly and traverse roughly 0.3–0.4 mile along/above the lake's shore to its outlet. At the outlet, leave the maintained tread for an intermittent, cairned climber's path onto Gothic Peak's SE ridge; stay in the scree climber's-right of the ridge crest rather than on the crest itself, following cairns past a small tarn at the base of a snowfield and up broken rock to the base of the summit block. Route-finding is the main approach-specific hazard: in early season, snow can bury the cairned line, and many parties inadvertently stray onto exposed Class 4 rock to climber's-left of the correct, easier line just below the summit block.

hits.text: The scramble begins at the lake's outlet, not from a random point on the shore, and getting on it early or late is the usual error. From the outlet, look up at the obvious low point on Gothic's southeast ridge. The line is not the ridge crest: stay in the scree on the climber's right of the crest and follow the cairns, which are numerous and continuous, past a small tarn at the foot of a snowfield. Cairns underfoot and scree, not rock, is the confirmation. At the very top, where the summit block stops the scree, cut left onto a narrow sidewalk of downsloping rock — slightly exposed easy friction — and switchback back up and right to the base of the block; the final scramble is about 30 ft of low-exposure class 3. Two negatives: if you are on the crest itself you have drifted left off the easy line, and if you find yourself on exposed class 4 to climber's left just below the summit block you have gone too far left, which is where most parties who get into trouble end up. In early season the cairns can be buried and the correct line is genuinely hard to hold.

runs: to stay in the basin below and right of the broken rock ridge until you can gain the saddle between the twin summits
hits.text:
The climb begins where the tread ends, and the arrival test is the saddle between Tyler Peak and Baldy. You know you are there because the trail stops going up in a line and the ground opens on both sides — navigation shifts from following tread to reading a ridge. There is also a signed Olympic National Park boundary marker in a saddle on this stretch and a spring path dropping off the crest. From here on you are on the crest and the crest is the route.

The test that actually matters on this route is at the far end, and it is a false summit with a name and a number: point 7076. From below, 7076 reads as the summit. It is not. The true summit of Gray Wolf is 7,218 ft and it lies further north along the crest and is higher. So the fog rule is simple: after Baldy you drop about 600 ft, climb back up over a prominent bump, and that bump is not the top. Keep going north over the last of the talus, detouring briefly round the occasional gendarme, and finish with a short Class 2-3 scramble on loose rock. If you turned round on the first big bump past Baldy, you turned round on 7076.

Second test, on the way to 7076 itself: the crest gets steeper and broken approaching it. The published avoidance is to traverse west at about 6,500 ft and then swing back to gain 7076 by its northwest aspect, and to stay in the basin below and right of the broken rock ridge until you can gain the saddle between the twin summits — 7076 has twin tops with snowfields between them. There is no trail at these decision points, which is why they are written down.

Third test, earlier: Point 6537 is a rocky gendarme and false summit below Baldy, normally skirted on its south side rather than climbed over. If you are scrambling straight over a tower before you have reached Baldy, you have taken the crest too literally.

Honest limit: long stretches of this crest are unmarked and off-trail and the whole thing is above treeline. Carry a map or GPS; the ridge is the handrail but the summit identification is not obvious by eye.

hits.text: Gunsight Peak is a multi-towered granite spire in the remote Dome Peak massif of the Glacier Peak Wilderness, guarded by the Chikamin Glacier to the west and Blue Glacier to the east. It neighbors Dome and Sinister Peaks on the classic Ptarmigan Traverse and requires a full 2-day approach (either from Downey Creek in the west or Stehekin/Agnes Creek in the east) before any climbing begins. The true summit is a tiny horn of rock roughly the size of a barstool, and parties typically take turns tagging it.

hits.text: A reddish-black basalt dike is the line, and it is softer than everything around it. From the 7,000 ft snow dome and rock outcrop, boot up the snow finger between the main and south spires; from a breach in that finger, a short wall leads to a broad ledge, then leftward to a steep dihedral of black rock whose top fifteen feet is the exposed 5.6 crux on solid granite. Above it, traverse left on Class 3 granite into a distinctive dike of reddish-black basalt — this is the feature that carved the gunsight notch in the first place, eroding faster than the granite either side, so if the rock you are on is the same colour as its neighbours you are not in the dike. It scrambles easily, if loosely, to the high notch between the main and north spires. There a vertical headwall blocks a direct exit: descend about twenty feet and traverse right across steep, solid, well-broken rock into a shallow parallel gully. Short chimneys and cracks to 5.5 end at the crest beside a large horn slung with old rappel tat — that horn is not the summit; the summit is a separate horn about the size of a barstool further along the ridge.

hits.text: A short winter day. From the PCT North trailhead, hike about 1.4 miles up the old Commonwealth Basin trail until the peak is directly west-northwest, then break uphill to the base of the gully. Climb 1,400 ft of snow that steepens from 45 to about 70 degrees, top out on the ridge between the true and false summits, and walk off east down Commonwealth or west over Cave Ridge. Start before dawn so the gully is still frozen: the sun-exposed half of the route softens quickly and the entire line becomes a wet-slide problem once it warms. runs: at the ridge between the true and false summits
hits.text:
Take a bearing, because this one can be done blind. Walk the old Commonwealth Basin trail about 1.4 miles until the summit of Guye bears roughly 290 degrees — west-northwest — from you, then turn and go straight uphill. The start of the route is at about 47.4411, -121.4026. In cloud that pair of numbers settles it and nothing on the ground has to be seen.

What the ground should do, in order, once you commit: the route starts by going 45 degrees straight up. Only then does the gully proper develop, turning northwest for about 40 m and steepening as it turns. After that it runs directly at the summit, which stays visible for much of the climb on a clear day. If the ground you are on stays uniformly angled and never turns northwest, you are on the open slope beside the gully rather than in it.

The angle is the other test: this is the steepest of Guye's gully lines. About 45 degrees for the first few hundred feet, then progressively steeper, reaching roughly 70 degrees near the top. A gully that stays moderate all the way is one of the peak's other lines.

Where it puts you: it finishes at the ridge between the true and false summits — not on a summit. If your line tops out on a summit block, it is not this one.

And a conditions test that is part of the finding here: roughly half the gully sits in shade and half in sun, which is what gives it solid snow under the surface. It also means the two halves can be in quite different condition on a warm day.

FS-37 normally runs 12.7 miles to the Skyline Divide trailhead. FS-37 has been closed by the 2021 flood washout at milepost 3.1, and during the repair work it is gated near its start (mile 0.03), so the trailhead is not reachable by vehicle. Confirm before planning around it.

When open, Skyline Divide Trail #678 climbs through old-growth switchbacks into meadows and reaches the ridge crest at about 2 miles and its high point near 6,563 ft at about 4.5 miles. From there the route is cross-country along the open ridge — roughly three miles of it — to Chowder Ridge and the base of Hadley's summit block.

The trail's high point on the crest near 6,563 ft is the landmark parties use to re-find the maintained trail on the way back.

hits.text: Drop off the saddle through open heather and easy slopes into the Diobsud basin, aiming for the uppermost pair of the four Diobsud Lakes. Heather and open ground with route-finding required, but no technical terrain. On-file timing puts this camp at roughly 6 to 6.5 hours and about 7.4 miles from the trailhead, with around 3,600 ft of gain and 500 ft of loss, and it is the standard base for the south-slopes climb.

runs: around the ice apron of the hagan glacier
hits.text: From the col at the southwest end of the crags, make a rising, crevasse- and moat-aware traverse around the ice apron of the Hagan Glacier to reach the second col, the one between Hagan's twin summits. This short glacier section is the technical crux of the route despite the Class 2-3 billing: carry rope, harness and a crevasse-rescue kit, and put crampons on - both are recommended even in midsummer. The moat is the same hazard in both directions on the way back. From the twin-summit col a short Class 2-3 scramble on slabs gains the summit ridge. Hagan carries several rocky bumps of similar height along that crest, so identify the true high point (7,067-7,080 ft) before committing to the last moves.

runs: around the ice apron of the hagan glacier
hits.text: Park at the Baker River Trailhead, the end of FR 11 (Baker Lake Highway), elevation roughly 800 ft. Start on Baker River Trail #606, which follows the true-right bank of the Baker River upstream through mossy old-growth forest — mostly flat, easy tread. At about 0.6 mile the trail crosses the river on a suspension bridge. Shortly after, a rerouted section drops steeply down a bank to ford a side creek and climbs back out through deadfall; this crossing gets wet and can be genuinely difficult or impassable during high runoff (spring snowmelt or after heavy rain) — plan around low-water conditions. The trail then enters North Cascades National Park and continues roughly another mile to Sulphide Creek Camp near the Sulphide Creek/Baker River confluence, about 2.6 miles and only ~170 ft of gain from the trailhead — this is the last maintained tread, the last reliable easy water, and a common bivy for a two-day trip. From near Sulphide Creek Camp, leave the trail and begin a steep, unmarked, use-path-at-best bushwhack climbing north/northeast up the valley wall through old growth and brush toward a small unnamed tarn at roughly 4550-4600 ft informally called 'Hidden Lake' (not the maintained, signed Hidden Lake Trail #745 near Marblemount, which is a different area entirely) — this gains close to 3,700 ft in a little over a mile with no tread. From the tarn, continue bushwhacking north up steep forest, working through two distinct rock cliffbands that form the route-finding crux of the approach; parties pick brushy ramps and weaknesses to keep the grade climbable. Above the cliffbands the forest breaks into open heather and grass benches on Hagan's south flank around 6000-6400 ft, with seasonal snowmelt water and rough camps. From the benches, ascend a broad talus-and-scree couloir to the southwest end of the Hagan Mountain crags, then make a rising, crevasse/moat-aware traverse around the ice apron of the Hagan Glacier (rope and crampons recommended even in summer) to reach the col between Hagan's twin summits, finishing with a short Class 2-3 scramble on slabs to the summit (listed 7067-7080 ft). Overall this is one of the more sustained, taxing approaches in the North Cascades — heavy old-growth/slide-alder bushwhacking, two cliffband route-finding sections, loose scree, and a glacier crossing — which is why it is very commonly combined with Mount Blum (and sometimes Bacon Peak) into a multi-day traverse rather than done as a single out-and-back day.

hits.text: The pass sits between the south and middle peaks, and it is the south peak you climb. Arriving at 6,831 ft, you should have a summit on either hand: this is a pass between two of Hagan's own peaks, not a col on the outside of the massif, and if only one side of you rises to rock you are in the wrong gap. The climbing then goes up the south peak's north side to a notch on its upper east side — that notch is high on the peak, not at the pass, and it is on the east flank, so a notch you can walk into from the west is the wrong one. From the notch, traverse onto the south face and gain the summit ridge, work up a spur on the east, then bear around to the south, where slabs lead to the summit at Class 3. The finish is south-facing slab, not a gully: if you are grovelling up a loose gully at the top you have missed the traverse around to the south side.

hits.text: Start in the deep notch north of the peak and climb the broad buttress above it toward the ridge crest. The first pitch has hollow, friable rock that improves steadily on the second. From there the line stays on the crest or just west of it, belaying at ledges, with steeper crack climbing in the middle of the route. High on the ridge a pitch traverses the west side of the narrowing crest with big exposure over the west face before working back to the crest. The last pitch is easy climbing on the crest, then a short scramble to the summit. Seven pitches is the usual count; belay at the obvious ledges rather than running pitches together, which causes rope drag.

hits.text: Park at the large hairpin-turn pullout on Highway 20 near milepost 163 (roughly 5,100 ft), just east of Washington Pass. From the east end of the pullout, drop into the woods and pick up the unsigned but well-used climbers' path toward Kangaroo Pass. It runs south, staying west of and well above Early Winters Creek — angling down toward the creek itself is the common route-finding mistake. Beyond the first mile the path climbs through boulder fields and slab benches with intermittent cairns, and the tread all but disappears on the slabs, so route-finding is tricky in fog or fresh snow. It also crosses the toe of the avalanche path that sheds off the col between South Early Winters Spire and Cornice Peak, a hazard in early season or after new snow. About two miles from the car, cross the last soggy meadow before the path climbs toward Kangaroo Pass and leave it: look up and left (east) for the prominent talus and scree gully that angles back to the deep notch just north of Half Moon. Climb it — a loose slog at the end — to the notch, where the route starts. Water is only reliably available near Early Winters Creek low on the approach; carry what you need above it.

hits.text: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike South: drive 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and park on either side of the road just before the bridge over the river. Scramble up the steep hillside on the NW side of the road above the bridge abutment, then continue uphill along the dike to a passable gully.

hits.text: Helmet Butte is normally climbed as part of a Buck Creek Pass backpacking trip rather than a car-to-car day climb, given the ~17.6-mile round-trip approach. From a point at 5,600 ft on the Buck Creek Pass Trail ('Waypoint 86'), the recommended line turns off-trail toward Pass No Pass on a well-defined but braiding boot path, gains a notch around 7,200 ft below the summit block, then finishes with a short, low-exposure Class 3 scramble on solid rock, aiming for the block's south (left) side for the easiest line. An alternate line continues past the trail junction to Buck Creek Pass itself, then climbs steep grass and heather slopes to the west side of the summit block before the same short scramble - this option is likely hazardous when wet.

runs: to the south side of the summit block
hits.text: Start at the Rachel Lake Trailhead (Trail #1313, elev. ~2,800 ft) at the end of Box Canyon Road/FR-4930. Follow the Rachel Lake Trail as it climbs gently through forest along the Box Canyon Creek drainage — the grade is easy and well-graded here, mostly Class 1 hiking. At roughly 2–2.2 miles and about 450–500 ft of gain (~3,300 ft elevation), the trail crosses a brushy avalanche-path clearing where Hibox's summit block comes into view on the ridge to the northeast; this clearing is the key landmark. Just past it (some parties note it's after the second such clearing), watch on the right/climber's-right side of the trail for an unmarked but well-established boot path (the 'Hibox climbers' path') leaving the maintained trail and heading northeast/uphill into the forest — it's easy to walk past if you're not looking for it. From here the character changes completely: the bootpath climbs steeply (mostly Class 2, with fallen timber to step over) before breaking out of the trees near a band of cliffs around 5,300 ft. Stay right of this first rock band, then work left around a rock outcrop, continuing through patchy timber to a second, higher cliff band; a gully on the right provides passage through it. Above this the trail opens into a large sloping subalpine meadow (wildflowers in season) that funnels into a loose talus/scree slope — this is the most tedious and slip-prone section of the route, so careful foot placement matters more than pace. A thready boot path threads up through the talus to the south side of the summit block. There is no reliable water past the lower forest/creek section, so carry what you need from the car or treat water low on the mountain. The route-finding through the two cliff bands and the avalanche-path junction low on the trail are the two spots parties most often go astray; a GPS track or recent trip report beta is worth having.

runs: to the south side of the summit block
hits.text: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than glissading the scree, which is loose and eroded. From the summit, downclimb the short exposed notch/cleft back to the south side of the summit block (good rock, low exposure, easy Class 3 moves), then pick your way back down through the loose talus/scree field to the sloping meadow. Some parties descend via a slightly different line on the east side of the summit block/east ridge before rejoining the ascent boot path lower down — functionally the same route, just avoid cutting new paths through the scree to limit erosion. Continue down through the two cliff bands (reversing right/left as on the way up) and back into the timber, staying alert for the boot path's exit point onto the maintained Rachel Lake Trail near the ~3,300 ft avalanche clearing — it's easy to miss in the trees when descending. Once back on Rachel Lake Trail #1313, it's an easy, well-graded 2+ miles back to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no rappelling required — the summit block's only technical move is a short, low-exposure Class 3 downclimb, not a rappel. Watch the weather: afternoon thunderstorms are common in this range and parties often report hurrying off the loose upper slopes ahead of incoming storms.

runs: to the south side of the summit block

runs: ed cooper glen denny joan firey joe firey and george whitmore
hits.text: Himmelhorn (originally Himmelgeisterhorn, "Horn of the Sky Spirit") is one of the most sought-after summits of the Southern Pickets, sitting on the crest between Ottohorn/Frenzel Spitz to the west and Twin Needles/Mount Terror to the east, with the small Mustard Glacier draped on its north side. It was first climbed September 8, 1961 by Ed Cooper, Glen Denny, Joan Firey, Joe Firey, and George Whitmore, who approached via the west notch (the Himmel-Otto col) and found a class 4 line up a ledge system onto the north/northwest face — no summit cairn was found, confirming the true first ascent. The peak remains a serious objective less for sustained technical difficulty than for its position deep in one of the most remote, brush-choked corners of North Cascades National Park; parties commonly link it with neighboring Ottohorn and/or Frenzel Spitz from a shared Crescent Creek Basin camp. Other established lines on the peak include the classic Wild Hair Crack (5.7, west face, Kroeker/Roper/Wild, 1981) and the harder South Face "Stonehenge" (5.10-, 8 pitches, Schilling/Halder, 2015).

runs: between the barrier ridge and the chopping block
hits.text: Top off water at Goodell Creek before leaving the roadbed: there is none reliable again until treeline. From the cairn, the boot path leaves the creek bottom and switchbacks steeply up into old-growth forest toward Stump Hollow. Expect steep root-and-duff footing with slide alder and devil's club low down; the path stays reasonably distinct with flagging and cairns higher up, but multiple trip reports on this approach describe losing it, and it is especially easy to lose in fog - track it deliberately rather than trusting the tread to hold. Around 5,000-5,600 ft the timber gives way to the heather benches and slab of Stump Hollow, a slabby basin wedged between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block.

runs: between the barrier ridge and the chopping block
to the himmel otto col in early season
hits.text: From the Goodell Creek Campground/Trailhead on SR 20 just west of Newhalem (~600 ft), follow the old decommissioned logging roadbed along the true left (south) side of Goodell Creek. This grassy/gravel roadbed is flat and easy hiking for roughly 4 to 4.5 miles, gaining only a few hundred feet to about 1,700-1,800 ft. Watch on the right for a cairn/stone marker (climbers call it the 'stone arrow') at the end of the roadbed - this marks the unsigned but well-boot-beaten climbers' path that leaves the creek bottom and switchbacks steeply up into old-growth forest toward Stump Hollow and Terror Creek Basin. This user trail is steep, root-and-duff footing, and brushy in spots (slide alder, devil's club low down) but stays reasonably distinct with flagging/cairns in the upper sections; there is no reliable water between the roadbed's end and treeline, so top off at Goodell Creek. Around 5,000-5,600 ft the forest opens into Stump Hollow, a slabby heather-and-snowfield basin wedged between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block - a scenic, easier-angle respite after the timber grind. From Stump Hollow, rising-traverse on meadow, slab, and (early/mid-season) snow to a broad saddle on the Barrier ridge at roughly 6,200 ft. Cross the Barrier itself by one of two options: a lower crossing on a loose, exposed ledge system at the toe of the Terror Glacier, or a higher crossing over moat terrain and steep choss just below Mt. Degenhardt; either takes under an hour but involves loose rock and some exposure, so care with rockfall onto any party below is essential. Descend the far side into Crescent Creek Basin (good bivy sites and reliable running water, roughly below Mt. Terror) - this is the standard camp for Himmelhorn objectives. From camp, ascend the narrow gully leading to the Himmel-Otto col: in early season this is a straightforward snow climb with a bit of scrambling near the top; by late season the gully turns to icy hardpack with choss-filled moats along the rock margins, and an overhanging boulder near the col often forces a loose, exposed class 3-4 bypass on the left (climber's) side. From the col, the standard route continues up easier ground (scrambling to low 5th class) onto Himmelhorn's northwest flank to the 7,880 ft summit. Total approach distance to the summit and back runs on the order of 15-16 miles round trip with substantial elevation gain and loss, so most parties treat this as a 2-4 day trip with a basecamp in Crescent Creek Basin rather than a car-to-car push.

hits.text: From the Goodell Creek Campground and trailhead on SR-20 just west of Newhalem at about 600 ft, follow the old decommissioned logging roadbed along the south side of Goodell Creek. It is flat and easy for roughly 4-4.5 miles, gaining only a few hundred feet to about 1,700-1,800 ft. Watch on the right for a cairn and stone marker, which climbers call the stone arrow, at the end of the roadbed. This marks the unsigned but well-boot-beaten climbers' path that leaves the creek bottom and switchbacks steeply into old-growth forest toward Stump Hollow and Terror Creek Basin. Steep, root-and-duff footing, brushy in spots, but reasonably distinct with flagging and cairns higher. No reliable water between the roadbed's end and treeline, so top off at Goodell Creek. Around 5,000-5,600 ft the forest opens into Stump Hollow, a slabby heather-and-snowfield basin wedged between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block. From there, rising-traverse on meadow, slab and early-season snow to a broad saddle on the Barrier ridge at roughly 6,200 ft, then cross the Barrier into Crescent Creek Basin, the standard camp for Himmelhorn objectives.

runs: to the himmel otto col in early season
hits.text:
The route starts at a col you reach by a narrow gully, and the gully's character changes completely through the season. From the Crescent Creek Basin camp, ascend the narrow gully leading to the Himmel-Otto Col. In early season that is a straightforward snow climb with a bit of scrambling near the top. By late season it turns to icy hardpack with choss-filled moats along the rock margins, and an overhanging boulder near the col often forces a loose, exposed class 3-4 bypass on the left, climber's left.

So the marker is the boulder, and it is a countable one: there is one overhanging boulder near the top of the gully, and getting past it on its left is the last obstacle before the col. If you have bypassed several such blocks, you are in the wrong gully.

Arrival: you are at the col when the gully tops out into a gap with ground falling away on the far side. From there the standard route continues on easier ground, scrambling to low 5th class, onto Himmelhorn's northwest flank to the 7,880 ft summit.

Two crossings of the barrier exist and both are correct: a lower crossing on a loose, exposed ledge system at the toe of the Terror Glacier, or a higher crossing over moat terrain and steep choss just below Mount Degenhardt. Either takes under an hour. Both are loose enough that a party above another is the real danger.

What going too far looks like: descending north from the Himmel-Otto col rather than climbing from it. The north side is a different and harder proposition and leads onto the Mustard Glacier.

runs: between the barrier ridge and the chopping block
hits.text: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.

hits.text: From Sahale Glacier Camp traverse the boulder-and-heather plateau east, downclimb the steep snowfield, and gain Sahale Peak's sharp southeast ridge; follow a cairned climbers' trail down it, past one short 4th-class step, descending easterly to about 7,100 ft. Pick up the southeast rib that forms the west edge of Horseshoe Basin and follow it southeast to the top of the so-called secret gully at about 6,700 ft — full of snow some years, completely melted out and loose in others. Below it, traverse a wide ledge at 6,600 ft rising gradually to the base of a cliff at 6,800 ft where old mining workings sit, then contour loose scree until you are due south of the peak. Fill up at Doubtful Creek or Pelton Basin: the water in Horseshoe Basin is contaminated by historic mine tailings and should not be drunk.

runs: the twin spired formation with a u shaped notch
hits.text: An alcove with old mining equipment stashed in it is the unmistakable marker. Dropping into Horseshoe Basin you use a narrow rock dike about eight feet wide that loses roughly a hundred feet: it starts Class 3, then a short downward Class 4 step lands you in that alcove with mining gear cached inside it, after which the dike stays Class 3 but loose and exposed. Nothing else on this ridge looks like it. Get the peak itself right before you commit: the crag climbers call Horseshoe is the highest point on Ripsaw Ridge, nearest Buckner, with the sharp Lick of Flame spire standing between the two. The twin-spired formation with a U-shaped notch in the middle of the ridge is the older, historical Horseshoe and is not the summit anyone bags — aiming at it puts you on the wrong tower. From the basin floor a snowfield at 30 to 45 degrees sits at the base of the peak and spills onto a large ledge about a hundred feet below the top; from there work leftward around a small buttress into the loose gully that leads to the notch just east of the summit, where the rope comes out for five feet of 5th class.

hits.text:
Lake Serene trailhead off Mount Index Road at about 600 ft. Lake Serene Trail #1068 runs about 4.1 miles and 2,000 ft to the north end of the lake, where the trail ends.

Traverse the west side of the lake over talus and huge boulders to the south end. In snow, stay lower, closer to the water — the slope is less steep near the shore. Expect massive avalanche debris on this stretch.

From the south end of the lake head east to the saddle, then take the ridge running southwest from it. That forested ridge is the crux of the approach and the reason this is a spring route: roughly the next 1,000 ft is dense brush and intermittent cliffs, plus one airy ten-foot rock step usually climbed by grabbing roots. Snow cover makes the ridge dramatically easier; bare, it is a fight. Plan on 12+ hours car to car and over 6,000 ft of gain despite the peak being under 6,000 ft.

runs: on the right side via a short chimney
hits.text: Follow the ridge until it runs into the cliffs of Index, then traverse under the cliffs and take the first wide gully on your right. That is the Hourglass. Its shape is the check: it is wide and easy where you enter, constricts high up, then opens again. A gully that is narrow at the point where you step into it is not the one — keep traversing. Once melted out, the constriction holds a large wet rock step; that step is the reason the route is climbed as a snow line rather than in summer, and passing it dry would be mid-to-high fifth on the right side via a short chimney and face, or harder on the left.

hits.text: A genuine Cascade backcountry big-wall problem rather than a route in the usual sense. The line takes the left-facing corner systems that lead directly to the summit, with rope-stretcher pitches through the 6-10 range and a leftward traverse of the wall's distinctive tiger-stripe ledges to avoid the overhanging upper section, reaching the summit ridge about 100 ft from the top. Twelve pitches, climbed all free at 5.9, with one shallow piton placed and removed and no bolts on the entire route - Cascade ground-up ethics applied to a wall that barely accepts hardware. The first ascensionists' own summary is the best warning available: the face is very large, much steeper than it appears from below, the rock is friable, and there are almost no protection cracks, even for thin pitons. One published account rates the line V 5.9+ R/X rather than the published IV 5.9, and the R/X reflects reality better than the number does. What the rock lacks in solidity and protection it partly returns in a plethora of in-cut features, which climb well where they are attached. Larson and Wehrly bivouacked atop pitch 10, about 100 m below the summit.

runs: there are almost no protection cracks even for thin pitons
hits.text: Sparse, poor and often absent. The defining feature of the Zorro Face is that there are almost no protection cracks, even for thin pitons, across a very large and steeper-than-expected wall of friable metamorphosed basalt. This is R/X terrain in one published account's rating. Leaders must be comfortable running out easy-to-moderate 5th class ground on rock that may detach, and the belays are as much of a problem as the pitches. Do not treat 5.9 as the difficulty - the difficulty is 5.9 with nothing between you and the belay.

runs: almost no protection cracks even for thin pitons
hits.text: There is no good bail from this wall. Retreat means building rappel anchors in rock that will not take gear, on a face the first ascensionists describe as having almost no protection cracks even for thin pitons. Make your commitment decision at the base, from the launch point, with the whole day and the weather in front of you. The low-cost bail is earlier: from the camp north of the peak, or partway through the 4.5-hour approach traverse, at which point you can retreat to camp and go climb the north-side scramble instead. Once you are several pitches up, the realistic exit is upward and over the summit.

runs: the route goes up the right side of the east ridge
hits.text:
Leave the PCT when the summit is due west of you — a bearing, not a landmark, which is exactly what you want in cloud. From that point head cross-country west up steep heather or talus.

The base of the climb is where the mellow terrain ends and the ground turns rocky, at about 6,100 ft, marked by a rocky buttress. That change underfoot is the arrival, and it is felt rather than seen.

And then comes the one decision that decides which route you climb, which is the most valuable thing on this page. At the base of the rocks you have two options: left takes you into a steep loose gully leading to a notch and the summit block — that is the older gully line, and it has turned parties around with rockfall. Right takes you up the ridge on class 3+ terrain — that is the East Ridge, the historic first-ascent route, and it is what most parties now climb. If you are in a loose gully, you have gone left.

How to follow it once committed, because it does not look obvious from below: the route goes up the right side of the east ridge, essentially linking clumps of trees, tree patch to tree patch. Looking up at it, the line is genuinely hard to piece together by eye; once you start, the next move is usually clear. Staying towards the right is correct at the beginning.

Checkpoints higher up: about halfway, maybe a little further, leave the ridge proper by heading left on a short traverse to a blocky ramp, which you climb to a high point just before the summit block. Then descend about 20 ft to the notch at the foot of the block — either straight down, or skiers' right and a class 3 traverse to a ramp leading down to the notch.

The summit block itself: go up the middle to an obvious slabby ramp. From there either a short class 5 crack — one piece, a #1 Camalot at its start, protects it — or follow the ramp climbers' left to exposed class 3/4. Bring a 60 m rope: a 30 m is insufficient for the rappel off the block.

Scale of the thing, so nobody underestimates it: there is no walk-up on this mountain, the scrambling is stiff class 3 with class 4 moves, and one of the 1915 first-ascent party wrote his will on his shirt cuff over doubts he would survive the descent.

hits.text: Park at the PCT North Trailhead at Snoqualmie Pass (I-90 Exit 52, large lot off SR 906/Alpental Rd; Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass required). Head north on the Pacific Crest Trail; most parties cut the corner via the Commonwealth Basin/Red Pass climbers' shortcut, which rejoins the PCT and trims about a mile off the standard trail. Climb the well-graded PCT switchbacks up to Kendall Katwalk (roughly 5 miles and 2,600 ft of gain from the trailhead) — a dramatic ledge blasted into a cliff face with real exposure in a fall-on-snow scenario early season. Continue north on the PCT past Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, skirting the base of Alaska Mountain, to where the trail runs above Joe Lake, about 10 miles from the pass. For the West Route, leave the trail at a flowery meadow northeast of Joe Lake and head up a talus slope into the basin below the west face, which is clearly visible from there. Alternatively, take the Gold Creek Trail to Joe Lake and hike upslope to the PCT. Water is reliable at Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, and at Joe Lake below the trail. Hazards on the approach include lingering snow on north-facing benches into July, loose rock in the approach gullies and talus once off-trail, and route-finding in poor visibility. Because of the length, many parties split this into 2-3 days with a camp at Ridge Lake or Gravel Lake.

runs: at the northern end of the ptarmigan traverse
hits.text: Hurry-up Peak (7,821 ft) lies on the Skagit-Chelan county line at the northern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse, just south of Cascade Pass and Cache Col, between Magic Mountain and Spider Mountain (its line parent). It is not part of the Sahale-Boston/Horseshoe Basin group on the opposite side of the pass; instead it's reached from a Kool-Aid Lake camp on the traverse's first day. A quiet, seldom-solo-targeted scramble, it is usually tagged as a short side trip by parties already committed to the Ptarmigan Traverse rather than climbed on its own.

hits.text: Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead (~3,600 ft) at the end of Cascade River Road (about 23 miles of pavement then gravel from Marblemount; the upper gravel section is gated and typically doesn't open until snow clears, often not until late June/July). From the trailhead, follow the well-graded, heavily-used Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft of gain, switchbacking up through forest and avalanche-path meadows to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft) — the last reliable trailside water is at the creek crossings low on the trail, so top off bottles before the switchbacks. At the pass, leave the maintained tread and pick up the climbers' path/boot track heading south-southeast, making a rising traverse across snow or heather on the flanks of Mixup Peak to the base of the Cache Glacier (~6,000 ft); this stretch is loose, choosy, and crosses several snow patches that can be firm in early morning. Ascend moderate glacier/snow slopes (crevasses can open by late summer — rope up if the party isn't comfortable soloing them) to the notch at Cache Col (6,900 ft). From the col, descend and traverse south-southeast about 1 mile over loose rock and heather benches, crossing occasional snowfields, down to Kool-Aid Lake (6,120 ft), the standard base camp for this side of the Ptarmigan Traverse and the only dependable water source in the basin (may be partly frozen early season). Car-to-camp is roughly 5-6 miles with about 3,300 ft of gain, generally a half-day carrying overnight gear. From camp, the peak itself is climbed as a side trip: head up toward Hurry-up Peak's south/southwest flank, crossing a band of steep snow around 7,100 ft (carry an axe/crampons even mid-summer) before gaining broken granite slabs and the south ridge crest; follow the crest/upper gully system with sustained Class 2-3 scrambling and a couple of exposed but short moves along the summit ridge to the 7,821 ft top — about 1 mile and 1,400-1,500 ft above camp, roughly 1-1.5 hours for a fit party.

Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. runs: at the dogtooth go right for the traditional approach gully
hits.text:
The target is visible from the lakeshore: the cleft between the North and South peaks, with a single pointed spire sitting in it. That spire is the Dogtooth. Aim just left of it and let it draw you up the slabs.

At the Dogtooth, go right for the traditional approach gully. The last gully is scree. If the gully you are in is green and lush it is the wrong one and it will carry you too high — traverse right out of it onto clean scree.

Arrival is physical: a short section of Class 4 up a crack of roughly forty feet at the top of the gully lands you on a ledge. That ledge is where the rope comes out. Pitch one is the low-angle slab above it, taking the large crack system up the middle.

Touch test at the start: the rock here is green serpentine, an odd slick band quite unlike the surrounding granite, sitting just up from the Dogtooth crag. Large hexes work in it where cams skate. Confirmation higher up — the pitch-three ledge carries two big bolts and there are three more at the top.

Negative marker, and this is the one that matters. This route climbs the south ridge of the north peak, and the North peak (7,662 ft) is the true summit. The South peak (7,640 ft) is a separate Class 3 scramble that starts from the same notch. If you reached the notch, dropped about fifty feet down its west side and scrambled easy gullies back to a top without ever roping up, you climbed the South peak. That is not this route and not the high point.

Second marker: finishing the technical pitches does not put you on the summit. There is a few hundred feet of walking left to tag the actual high point, so a summit that arrives the instant the climbing ends is the wrong one.

Identical to the Northwest Buttress: Upper Dungeness Trailhead at the end of FS 2870, Trail #833 to Camp Handy at about 3.4 miles and Boulder Camp at roughly 6.1-6.4 miles, then the trail climbs into Olympic National Park to Home Lake at about 9.3 miles, short of Constance Pass itself. Basecamp is the large boulders directly northwest of the summit, just south of Home Creek. The northwest face comes into view from below the lake.

This route and the Northwest Buttress share their approach, their camp, their scree field and their first pitch. They are one climb until the top of that pitch. The first-ascent party's round trip from camp — climb plus the descent into Avalanche Canyon and back round to the Home Lake cirque — ran about 12.5 hours.

runs: scree field to the obvious ramp and follow it
right of the prominent dihedral to a steep class 3/4 gully
hits.text:
The base is shared with the northwest buttress and so is the test for it: from the boulder camp, up the scree field to the obvious ramp, and follow it round climber's right of the prominent dihedral to a steep Class 3/4 gully. Right of the big corner, not left.

The test that separates this route from the buttress comes at the top of pitch one, and it is a decision rather than a landmark — which is why it is worth knowing before you leave the ground. At that point the Northwest Buttress steps climber's left onto an obvious ledge along a green-lichen-covered face. Sean's Route does not. It stays with the crack system and follows it straight on up rotten loose rock for roughly three pitches in total.

The confirming test is tactile, overhead and unmistakable in any visibility: about three pitches up, the crack system ends at a cave beneath an overhanging roof. You cannot mistake being under a roof. That cave is the route's crux and its identity — you build an anchor in it and make a committing move out by underclinging the roof and traversing right about 10 to 15 feet onto the ramp leading to the slab above. If you have climbed three pitches and there is no roof over you, you are on the Buttress or on neither.

Honest limit: this is a shared base with a pitch-one divergence rather than a route with a base of its own, and it is recorded that way rather than dressed up. Above the roof it is a few pitches of Class 4 to low fifth to the southwest false summit, then it rejoins the Northwest Buttress for the last pitch to the true top. Protection averages one usable placement every 20 to 100 feet.
