hits.text: Iron Cap Mountain (6,347 ft) rises above the Williams Lake and La Bohn Gap country near the heart of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Despite its modest elevation, it has striking local relief, climbing about 2,500 feet above the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Valley in less than a mile. The mountain straddles two drainages: its south side sheds into tributaries of the Snoqualmie River via the Williams Lake basin, while the north side drains toward the Foss River. It was first climbed in 1925 by a party led by Seattle mountaineer Joe Hazard. This route comes in from the north on the West Fork Foss River trail off US 2, past Trout, Copper and Big Heart lakes to a camp at Chetwoot Lake, and finishes on Iron Cap's west and north ridges.

runs: working upward to the southeast on a series of
hits.text: The scrambling begins on rock ledges above the outlet of Iron Cap Lake. Cross the outlet stream and start working upward to the southeast on a series of ledges — the change from vegetated, dirt-over-rock ground to continuous clean ledges is the tell that you are on the route, and the rock here is genuinely solid, unlike everything below it. The line curves around the nose of the north ridge rather than attacking the summit block head-on. Higher, a short third-class downclimb drops into a notch, which reads as a dead end and is not one: beyond it a wide ramp traverses below the summit block, taking you across without sidehilling, and meets the broad north ridge. From there easy red-tinged rock and dirt lead to the true summit. Losing that ramp is the way parties end up cliffed out on the steeper east-side rock bands, so note the line as you go and retrace it exactly on the way down.

hits.text:
The col between Old Snowy and Ives is the arrival, and you get to it by leaving a trail, not by following one.

Leave the PCT north of the Snowgrass Trail junction, at roughly 6,700 ft, and go off-trail northeast up talus. There is no tread. Occasional cairns are the only marks. If you are still on maintained trail you have not started the route.

You know you are at the col because you are between two peaks at about 7,250 ft — Old Snowy behind you, Ives ahead. A high point on one side only is not the col.

The bump is the trap and it is countable: from the col the ridge crosses a rounded intermediate high point before you reach the true summit block. That bump is not the summit. If you have not passed one rounded bump, you have not reached the summit block, whatever the ground in front of you looks like.

The base of the scramble is a notch between two rock outcrops, reached by a boot path up scree. And here is the test that settles it beyond doubt, because it is the opposite of what you expect at a summit block: above the notch is a short cliff band, and the route goes down first. You downclimb slightly and traverse a narrow, exposed ledge to gain the upper south face, then scramble about 40 ft to climber's right on loose blocky rock to easy ground and the summit.

So: if the line in front of you only goes up, you are at the wrong notch. Having to lose a little height at the notch is the confirmation.

Descent finding worth making before you start: dropping straight southwest off the col into the basin is faster and is the loosest ground on the mountain. Traversing back over Old Snowy and down its established south-ridge path avoids the worst of it.

runs: grade vi big wall in the pacific northwest
hits.text: This is the only repeatable Grade VI big wall in the Pacific Northwest with bolted stainless steel anchors and portaledge bivy opportunities achievable by experienced wall climbers in 3-4 days. Climbing follows a continuous crack system featuring varied aid pitches including thin pins, rivets, hooks, and roof passages. The Fang Roof (Pitch 8) stands out as a classic pitch with hand crack free climbing through an overhang. Plan for 7 days of capsule-style climbing with portaledge camps to complete the first ascent.

runs: on the left side of the buttress about
hits.text: The start is on the left side of the buttress, about a hundred yards left of the Doorish line, in a crack system that runs continuously from the ground. That continuity is the tell — the neighbouring weaknesses on this side peter out within a couple of hundred feet, so if the crack you are looking at closes above you, you are not on it. Use the Doorish line as your reference and count leftward from it rather than trying to identify the start in isolation; from the talus the whole left flank looks alike. Do not sort gear at the foot of the wall: the base is a rockfall alley fed by North Index above and by the deep cleft between this buttress and Middle Index, so stay low near the lake to rack up and keep time directly beneath the face as short as you can. Below the clean granite is a band of steepening mossy slab and brush that is part of the approach rather than part of the route, and roping up for it is normal rather than timid.

hits.text: This is an early-season snow climb, done when the north cirque is still filled in. From the East Bank Trailhead follow the East Bank Trail roughly 8 miles to the May Creek camp, then leave the trail and climb about 3 miles of steep, bushy, cliff-banded forest — cliff bands start around 3,200 ft and are passed on game trails — to reach snowline near 4,800-5,000 ft and a camp either on the flats around 5,200 ft below the glacier or higher on the glacier itself around 7,400 ft. The Nohokomeen Glacier runs from about 6,100 ft to 8,200 ft, is over 340 acres, and is heavily crevassed after the midpoint of its descent, so rope up. Above the glacier the headwall is the crux: it is variously described as 700 vertical feet of snow at slopes up to 60 degrees, and as a sustained 50-55 degrees for about 800 feet with steeper steps. Most parties simul-climb it, taking turns kicking steps, with a rope over the shoulder for the bergschrund; winter parties have pitched it out with pickets, cams, nuts and screws through a mixed cliff band. The bergschrund is the main obstacle and normally goes on a single bridge on the left side. Above, exit onto the ridge and finish along a narrow, corniced summit ridge with rocky drops — the last few hundred feet are the most exposed of the route.

runs: between the creeks on the west side of jack mountain
hits.text: From SR 20 milepost 138, park at the East Bank Trailhead (~1,800 ft) and descend briefly to the bridge over Ruby Creek. Follow the East Bank Trail — mostly flat and fast — roughly 8 miles north along Ross Lake to the May Creek camp. (Ross Lake Resort's water taxi will drop parties on the eastern shore and is a legitimate way to skip most of the trail; check current rates and schedule directly with the resort.) At May Creek leave the trail and climb steeply east, loosely ascending between the creeks on the west side of Jack Mountain. Cliff bands begin around 3,200 ft and are threaded on boot and game trails; snow generally appears around 4,800-5,000 ft. About 3 miles of this off-trail work reaches a flat camp just over 5,200 ft below the glacier toe. Strong parties push a second camp onto the upper glacier around 7,400 ft, which shortens summit day considerably. Before the highway opens, parties have biked about 4 miles from the MP 134 gate to the trailhead and continued on foot or ski.

hits.text: Jack Mountain (9,069 ft) is a massive, glaciated summit rising directly east of the south end of Ross Lake, on the boundary between the Ross Lake National Recreation Area (North Cascades National Park Complex, NPS) and the Pasayten Wilderness (Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest). It is one of only ten non-volcanic Washington peaks over 9,000 ft, and one of the least climbed — published and modern trip-report accounts both note it sees on the order of only a few ascents a year, owing to a 20+ mile, multi-day approach and constantly loose rock. The mountain carries five small glaciers on its upper flanks (largest is the Nohokomeen Glacier, which nearly fills a cirque on the north side); the standard South Face/Southeast Ridge line stays off the glacier and instead climbs a long, complex face of ramps, gullies, and cliff bands to reach the southeast ridge near 8,600 ft before finishing on class 3-4 terrain to the summit block.

It also has one of the shortest approaches of any major North Cascades alpine route, but the couloir itself is the most direct and objectively dangerous way up the peak: a sustained roughly 3,400 ft gully of continuous 30-50° snow squeezed by the Sill Glacier, which threatens the lower two-thirds with icefall and opens dangerous, increasingly unbridged crevasses as the season progresses. Above the Cascade-Johannesburg col (~6,760 ft), about 1,400 ft of exposed, loose, mossy/broken-gneiss ridge — with rock pitches, gullies, ribs, and a knife-edge traverse up to low 5th class — leads to the summit.

hits.text: From the basin camp south of Mesahchie Peak, gain roughly 800 ft to a bench near 7,400 ft, then traverse west holding somewhere between 7,400 and 7,600 ft. The traverse is an endless maze of ribs and gullies and you will cross easily over a dozen of them. The hardest section is a rib about halfway along: drop to around 7,200 ft and look for two ledges that give passage, at the cost of some elevation to regain and a short stretch of class 4. Where a line looks like the easiest way through, it usually goes. There is no reliable water past the basin camp late in the season.

runs: crosses at the base of a couple of the grotesque gendarmes
hits.text: The red ledge is the proof, and it is obvious when you are on it. Somewhere along the westward traverse the ground organises itself into one reddish ledge that cuts straight across every rib and gully — it runs almost like a trail, and it is the feature that makes this traverse reasonable instead of desperate. It crosses at the base of a couple of the Grotesque Gendarmes, the ragged towers standing on the crest above you, then carries on across roughly 7,800 ft through a cliffy cave section and delivers you to a couple of gullies that lead to the summit. If you are picking your way up and down individual ribs and gullies with no continuous ledge underfoot, you are above or below the line and should hunt for it rather than force the terrain. Take the broad, solid-granite gully to the ridge just west of the true summit; from its top a short class 3 scramble crosses a scree saddle east to the true top.

hits.text: The maintained trail ends at White Pass. Traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin and White River Meadows, the usual base camp, either by way of Red Pass or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck basin. From camp climb to Foam Pass and cross the White Chuck Glacier to the gap — this is glacier travel on largely featureless snow, so carry a track or the navigation skill to retrace it in cloud, and be roped for the crevasses low on the glacier, which can be fully open.

hits.text: The standard approach follows the North Fork Sauk River Trail (USFS Trail #649) from the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (~2,050 ft), reached via Forest Road 49 off the Mountain Loop Highway south of Darrington. The trail climbs gently through old-growth forest along the river valley for about 5.5 miles to Mackinaw Shelter — a possible camp, though tight for a larger party — crossing several tributaries en route, including Red Creek, which parties describe as interesting but not difficult to ford in normal flow (a trekking pole/sturdy stick helps with balance); it can run considerably higher during spring snowmelt or after rain. Past the shelter the trail turns uphill in earnest, climbing roughly 3.2 miles of sustained switchbacks through subalpine forest to a junction with the Pacific Crest Trail in a meadow (~6,000 ft) with the first real views of Glacier Peak and the White Chuck/Kololo massif. Turn right (north) on the PCT and follow it about a quarter mile to White Pass (5,900 ft) — roughly 9 miles and 4,800+ ft of gain from the trailhead, and the last reliable, easy water source before the high traverse. From White Pass the maintained trail ends and the route becomes a boot path: traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin / White River Meadows (~6,300-6,500 ft), the common base camp, either via Red Pass (1.2 miles from the PCT junction) or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck River basin (the 'Foam Pass' variant). From camp, climb to Foam Pass and cross the White Chuck Glacier and Glacier Gap onto the White River Glacier — this is glacier travel, and rope/crampons/axe are standard gear here; crevasses are typically open and visible to weave around by late summer but can be harder to read under early-season snow bridges. From the gap, drop a short way onto the White River Glacier and come at the peak from the south, climbing the snow headwall to the summit ridge and an easy talus-and-ledge scramble to the summit (Class 2+). This is a long approach in its own right — the round trip runs roughly 28-30 miles — so almost all parties camp at White River Meadows or Foam Basin rather than attempting the trailhead-to-summit push in a single push. There are two long approaches: this North Fork Sauk line, and the alternate White River Trail approach from the east, which reaches a similar high basin by a comparably long trail-plus-cross-country line.

hits.text: From the North Fork Sauk Trailhead near 2,050 ft at the end of FR-49, Trail #649 runs about 5.5 miles up the valley on an easy grade through old growth, fording several tributaries. Red Creek is the first crossing that can actually stop you: manageable at normal flow, considerably higher during snowmelt or after rain, and worth a pole. Mackinaw Shelter at 2,950 ft is a possible camp but tight for a big party, and it is where the trail leaves the river — fill water there. Above the shelter the trail climbs about 3.2 miles of sustained switchbacks to a meadow junction with the Pacific Crest Trail near 6,000 ft, then a quarter mile north on the PCT to White Pass at 5,900 ft. That is roughly nine miles and 4,800 ft from the car and the last easy water before the high traverse. Maintained trail ends at the pass. Traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin and White River Meadows around 6,300-6,500 ft — the usual base camp — either by way of Red Pass or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck basin. Almost nobody does this from the car in a day, and the round trip is long enough that the two published distances for it disagree.

hits.text: Kyes Peak (7,280+ ft) is the highest summit of the Monte Cristo group, sharing a remote high basin with Columbia Peak and Monte Cristo Peak that holds the shrinking Columbia Glacier on its north/northeast flank above Blanca Lake. Formerly known as 'Goblin Peak' and 'Mount Michigan,' it was renamed for Rear Admiral James E. Kyes, an Everett native who commanded a destroyer in WWII; two Everett Boy Scouts (Kyes and Reginald Bachelder) made the first recorded ascent on August 15, 1920, with a possible earlier USGS survey ascent by Thomas Gerdine around 1897. The peak sees two common lines to the same summit block: the classic, brushy South Ridge climber's trail above Blanca Lake, and a Columbia Glacier approach that some parties consider the more enjoyable 'real' standard route.

hits.text: La Bohn Peak (6,585 ft) is a granite summit at the head of Necklace Valley in the eastern Alpine Lakes Wilderness, rising directly west of La Bohn Gap — a broad, tarn-dotted saddle around 5,900 ft between the peak and Mount Hinman (7,492 ft, 1.7 mi east). The standard line follows a climbers' path west from the gap up the ridge and face above La Bohn Lakes, gaining a final ~1,000 ft of Class 2 (occasional Class 3) talus and rock to the summit. It's rarely climbed on its own — most parties tag it as a half-day add-on from a Necklace Valley or Dutch Miller Gap-Williams Lake-Chain Lakes backpack, often paired with Mount Hinman.

hits.text: The high camp for La Bohn Peak and the launching point for the west route on Mount Hinman, and the single most useful piece of ground in this zone for a climber. La Bohn Gap is a broad boulder-covered saddle at roughly 6,000 ft on the crest between the Foss and Snoqualmie drainages, with the tarns of the La Bohn Lakes scattered on the benches around it and the Chain Lakes sitting lower at about 5,515 ft in the gully on the south side of La Bohn Peak. From Necklace Valley the climb to the lakes goes either up to the gap itself or by a steeper line beside the waterfall; both are straightforward in summer and both hold snow into July. La Bohn Peak is a short class 2 walk west from the gap. For Hinman the ground continues east and then north, half a mile of easy going to gain the gap area and then a long open ascent to the summit — worth knowing that the Hinman Glacier shown on older maps has essentially gone, so what you will actually cross is a shrinking snowfield with the moat and loose-rock problems that come with that, and conditions vary enormously year to year. The gap is also the hinge of the whole area on foot: north drops into Necklace Valley, south drops toward Dutch Miller Gap and the upper Middle Fork Snoqualmie, and the view takes in Bald Eagle, Silver Eagle and Big Heart Lake off to the west. Camping here is committing. It is fully exposed, the weather arrives without warning, and a bad night in the gap is a real one — carry proper shelter or drop back to the Necklace lakes.

hits.text:
The Chockstone Route's start is the anchor point and it is the most unmistakable feature on this side of the mountain: it is obvious, at the base of the massive chasm separating North and South Early Winters Spires. A chasm splitting two spires is not something you can be uncertain about, in any weather where you can see the rock at all.

From there the instruction is two words and a feature: up and left, to a ledge below a clean slab. Clean rock is the marker. This route takes the clean face; the ground either side of it does not read as clean.

So the route is sandwiched, and you can bound it both ways: the Chockstone Route is to its right, in the chasm. The west face is to its left. If you are in the chasm you have not left the shared start; if you have traversed all the way left to the shared start with the Northwest Corner, you have gone past.

Confirm by what you are standing on: a ledge, below a slab. Not a chimney, not a corner.

Descent, and it is not a reversal: rappel down the Chockstone Route line, using the same bolted stations that route uses, rather than reversing the Labor Pains pitches. That means you finish where you started, back at the chasm.

hits.text: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike North: park 1.1 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, where a dirt road intersects the paved road on the left (SE side), or continue to 1.2 miles and use the large pull-off. Cross the main road and pick up the approach trail between the two parking spots, marked by a short steep drainage topped with a downed tree.

hits.text: Same trailhead as the Classic Route: park at the Reflection Lake pullout on Stevens Canyon Road when it's open, or at the Narada Falls pullout in winter/spring when the road is snow-gated (a short, steep ~200 ft climb from Narada Falls regains the road). Walk the road about half a mile to the 90-degree bend, then drop south through open forest toward Tatoosh Creek (~4,500 ft), as with the Classic Route. Rather than climbing right toward the south-face saddle, stay low and work into the basin directly below Lane Peak's north face — the Zipper is the obvious left-leaning couloir splitting the center of the face, visible from the road. From the basin, hike up and across a large triangular apron of avalanche/rockfall debris fanning down from the base of the couloir. From the top of this debris cone, angle climber's left and climb roughly 1,000 ft up the couloir itself to a dead tree at a notch in the peak's east ridge, which marks the top of the technical climbing and the rappel/tie-in point. Snow conditions range from styrofoam neve to alpine ice depending on season and aspect; the basin and lower couloir cross avalanche-prone terrain, so this is a start-early, check-the-forecast approach, especially in winter/spring when most ascents happen. Total approach is roughly 2-2.5 miles one-way from the road to the notch; no water past Tatoosh Creek. In the couloir itself, expect the angle to build from about 40° to 45° near the top, the walls narrowing from roughly 40 ft to 20 ft wide, and up to three short ice/mixed steps (about 15 ft, 8 ft, and a 25 ft crux) depending on fill.

hits.text:
Left to right on this face the three couloirs are: Lover's Lane, the Zipper, the Fly. Learn that order before you leave the car. All three drop onto the same debris apron and on a busy weekend all three have parties on them at once, which means overhead hazard from other people as well as from the mountain.

The Zipper is the middle one, and it is the one that leans left and splits the centre of the face. From the top of the debris cone, angle climber's left. If you are working right, you are heading for the Fly.

The strongest test is width, and it is a thing you feel rather than see: the Zipper narrows. About 40 ft wide at the base, closing to about 20 ft near the top. The Fly is broad — 40 to 50 ft — and it stays broad. If the walls are not closing in on you as you gain height, you are in the Fly, one couloir to your right, on easier ground than you came for.

The second test is countable and it is the one that settles it: the Zipper has up to three short steps — about 15 ft, then about 8 ft, then a 25 ft crux near the top. The Fly has none worth the name. If you have climbed a thousand feet of continuous 45-degree snow and met no step at all, you are not in the Zipper.

The top-out is an object, which is the best kind of confirmation: a dead tree at a notch in the east ridge. That tree carries the fixed rappel slings. If you have topped out onto open ridge with no tree, you are on something else — Lover's Lane finishes on the ridge above this notch, and the Fly finishes at the west-ridge notch.

What the angle should do: build from about 40 degrees to about 45 near the top. It does not exceed that. Ground steeper than 45 sustained means Lover's Lane, which reaches about 60.

hits.text: The stair starts where the ridge rises sharply and falls away on its north side. Climb the trail and talus up the forested ridge and watch the crest: at the point where it rears up and drops off on the right, or north, side, a precipitous path of compacted dirt and rock leads up through a small gully to a grassy ledge fifteen to twenty feet wide. Walk west along that ledge and make a full 180-degree turn at its far end to pick up the path to the top of the ridge — that reversal is what earns it the name, and if the ledge you are on runs out with no way to double back, it is not the stair. Follow the ridge to a rock outcropping immediately beneath Le Conte's north face; this is where parties drop their packs and it is the base of the climb proper. Peak 7004 is a hump on the ridge that is very hard to get around directly: bypass it on its east slope. Above, a loose rock gully gains a ridge on the north side and short steep snow near 7,200 ft leads to the east notch, then a quick, exposed traverse of a narrow ledge to the top.

runs: gain the ridge where it looks easiest it is
hits.text:
The arrival is a rock step, called a chute in published descriptions, and it sits below the main summit after you have crossed the glacier basin and traversed north under Lemah Two.

The touchable sequence at the step, from a party who did it: pass a small waterfall, climb a wet gully for about ten feet, then work right onto dry rock. Those ten feet are the fourth-class move and the landing beneath them is relatively safe. That waterfall-then-wet-gully-then-step-right is the thing to look for; it is the crux of the whole climb and it is where the approach ends.

There is a tempting alternative that does not work: a ramp far to the left looks as though it would let you bypass the rock step entirely, but reaching it means an unpleasant moat crossing, and the party that looked at it came back down and took the step.

Above the step, the recorded mistake is worth more than the recorded route. Between Lemah Two and Lemah Three there is a small snowfield. A published sketch puts the line just left of the summit rocks, and following that into a mostly snow-filled gully leads to a difficult top, a snow bridge onto loose rock, and about a hundred feet of loose third and fourth class. The party who did that found on the way down that the honest instruction is simply: gain the ridge where it looks easiest. It is.

One route people have taken and should not repeat: descending a gully from Lemah One to reach the glacier. It melts out into very unstable talus blocks.

The Spectacle Lake approach is documented but has been explicitly superseded — the slide area between the lake outlet and the shoulder has grown into ten- to twelve-foot slide alder on a thirty-degree slope, dense enough that you cannot see over it to aim at anything.

runs: from the trailhead at the north end of cooper lake
hits.text: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.

hits.text: Day 1 follows the well-graded Lena Lake Trail 3 miles to Lena Lake, then a steep, primitive trail up West Fork Lena Creek to Upper Lena Lake (6.5 mi, 4,000 ft gain from the trailhead). Day 2 leaves the trail entirely: climb southwest across meadows/heather toward the ridge south of Mt Lena, follow intermittent way trails west past Scout Lake, over Scout Pass (5,200 ft) and Upper Scout Lake/Scout Basin, over Ullin's Pass (5,000 ft, with views of the 'Ullin's Bathtubs' tarns), then up the steep snow/dirt 'St. Peter's Ramp' to St. Peter's Gate (5,950 ft) — the high point of the traverse and an obvious notch in Mt Stone's SE ridge. Lake of the Angels lies half a mile southwest of the gate in a grassy bowl. The optional Mt Stone summit side-trip climbs a class 3-4 gully on the mountain's south face to a rock bowl, joins the standard west-ridge route, and finishes with a class 2-3 scramble on solid pillow basalt to the summit (about 1,100 ft gain round trip, ~3 hrs). Day 3 descends the Putvin Trail — historic and primitive, with cliff sections (one with a fixed handline, one requiring tree roots) past Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet — to the Putvin Trailhead, about 4 miles by road from the Lena Lake Trailhead where the trip began.

hits.text: Start at the Lena Lake Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25, ~600-750 ft). Follow the well-maintained Lena Lake Trail (#810) about 3 miles through second-growth and old-growth forest along Lena Creek to Lena Lake (~1,800 ft), a popular backpacking destination with reliable camping and water. Beyond Lena Lake the trail narrows to a steep, primitive tread that climbs the West Fork Lena Creek drainage; continue roughly 3.5 more miles and about 2,700 additional feet to Upper Lena Lake (~4,000 ft total gain, ~6.5 mi from the trailhead), the last reliable water and the last maintained-trail camp before the traverse goes cross-country. From Upper Lena Lake, leave the trail and head southwest/west: pick up the Scout Lake way-trail across meadows and huckleberry-heather slopes past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass (~5,200 ft), descend slightly to Upper Scout Lake, contour high around it into Scout Basin, and climb to Ullin's Pass (~5,000 ft) overlooking the tarns known as "Ullin's Bathtubs." From Ullin's Pass, a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp that angles across a steep hillside below Mt. Stone and ends at a loose, grungy moraine; the final approach to St. Peter's Gate (~5,950 ft, the traverse's high point) is exposed dirt-and-mud slopes with real route-finding demands, about 2.2 miles and 2,200 ft above Upper Lena Lake. This entire off-trail section crosses loose moraine and talus, can hold snow patches well into summer (many parties carry an ice axe), and has no dependable water between Upper Lena Lake and the small tarns near Ullin's Pass; fog is common and has caused parties to lose the route. From St. Peter's Gate, most parties descend about 300 ft to the base of a basalt cliff and cache overnight packs there, then follow a vague climber's path up a Class 3-4 gully on Mt. Stone's south face into a rock bowl below the summit block, joining the standard west-ridge route for a final ~100 ft of Class 2-3 scrambling on solid pillow basalt to the true (south) summit.

runs: the top of pitch 7 on thin red line
hits.text:
The start is about 10 metres right of Thin Red Line, and ten metres is the entire margin for error on this wall. That is a measured offset from a known line, which is the best that exists here, and it means you must locate Thin Red Line first.

How to bound it without seeing the whole face, using the order along the base: Freedom Rider about 100 ft left of Liberty Crack, then Liberty Crack, then Freedom or Death on a small leftward-trending ramp with bolts above, then Thin Red Line, then this route 10 m right of it, then Live Free or Die, then the Independence Route at the far right or north edge under a red roof.

The strongest confirmation is the hardware, and it is countable: every station on this line is a two-bolt anchor with fixed biners. If you top out a pitch and find no bolts and no biners, you are not on it. From the top of pitch 3 you can skip the pitch-2 anchor and rappel directly to the pitch-1 anchor, so two rappels get you back to the ground from P3.

What going too far looks like: keep walking right and the next thing you meet is the ground Live Free or Die and the Independence Route use, at the far right end of the face. The Independence Route's own marker is unmistakable when visible: a red-coloured roof and alcove, the Baer Ceiling, about 85 m above its start.

And where it goes: at five pitches the route joins the top of pitch 7 on Thin Red Line, from which you either continue climbing or rappel this route's own anchors with two ropes back to the base.

hits.text:
Park at the Blue Lake Trailhead on the south side of SR-20, roughly 1 mile west of Washington Pass, at about 5,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required and the lot is small enough that it fills on summer weekends.

Walk the maintained Blue Lake Trail for about 1.7 miles. The turnoff is a signed junction — the sign points straight on for Blue Lake and left for Liberty Bell Trail #727, Climbing Access — and it sits just past a small stream in a meadow, with a large cairn beside it. That stream is the last water you can count on.

Trail #727 climbs hard through granite slabs, talus and heather benches toward the gully that drains the notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower. In the gully itself the loose ground is least bad if you keep to climber's left for the lower two thirds, then cross and hug climber's right for the rest. Where the boot path forks a couple of hundred feet below the notch, take the left branch; the right branch leads on toward Lexington and Concord's south side.

hits.text:
Standard East Face approach: park at the pond pullout near the hairpin turn east of Washington Pass, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile to the East Face talus.

Fourteen pitches. Although it is technically the easiest all-free route up the East Face, the route takes about one and a half times as much effort as Liberty Crack, on often poor rock and gear, and apart from where it intersects Liberty Crack there are no bolted belay stances.

runs: loose corner system about 100 ft left of liberty crack
hits.text:
This is the only route on the east face that starts to the left of Liberty Crack, and that makes it the easiest start on the wall to confirm by elimination. It begins at a loose corner system about 100 ft left of Liberty Crack.

So the test is directional and countable: from Liberty Crack, walk left roughly 100 ft to a corner system. Every other line here is to the right of Liberty Crack. If you are walking right along the base, you are walking away from this route, and everything you meet in that direction belongs to something else: Freedom or Death, Thin Red Line, Liberty and Injustice for All, Live Free or Die and the Independence Route in that order.

And Liberty Crack itself is found by traversing 40 ft left on third and fourth class ledges from the base of the talus, so this route is roughly 140 ft of leftward travel from where the path meets the rock.

A hardware test that cuts the other way from the rest of this face: there are no bolted belay stances on this route except where it crosses Liberty Crack. Several of its neighbours are fully bolted. If you reach a bolted anchor early, you are probably not on Freedom Rider.

What to expect so you do not second-guess the find: the corner system is described as loose, and the rock and gear on the route generally as often poor. Poor rock at the start is consistent with this line, not evidence you are off it.

Descent: the shared East Face rappel line into Beckey Gully, or downclimbing the sheltered Beckey Route slab in good conditions. Both put you on the west side of the mountain, away from the East Face pullout.

Stop short of the notch. A couple of hundred vertical feet below the top of the Liberty-Concord notch, locate a side gully on climber's left with a large cave in it. Walk partway up that side gully, then move right onto a treed ledge to start.

So there are three things to find and all three are tactile rather than visual: a side gully on the left, a large cave inside it, and a ledge with trees on its right-hand side. Trees on a ledge are unmistakable underfoot.

The negative test is the most useful line here, because the error is always the same one: if you have reached the notch, you have gone roughly two hundred feet too far. This route leaves the main gully below its top. Everything at the notch itself belongs to the Beckey Route, Overexposure and the standard descent.

A second route shares the cave, so the ledge is what separates them: Sidewinder also scrambles to a major shelf or ramp below the cave feature. This route goes partway up the side gully and then steps right onto the treed ledge. Below the cave is Sidewinder's ground; up and right of it is this one.

Where it goes: three pitches rejoining the Beckey Route near its top, then the standard two single-rope rappels off chains to the notch and the gully back to the trail.

hits.text:
The route starts right at the top of the notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower, and specifically it begins above the notch rather than at it. That distinction is the whole find: Beckey Route parties stop at the notch and start climbing from it. This route asks for a little extra scrambling up from the notch into the initial belay.

Which notch, because there are two on this ridge and they are only a few hundred feet apart: the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, at about 7,300 ft, is the one this route uses. The Concord-Lexington notch is further along and serves Concord's south face and Lexington's north face. The discriminating test at the top of the gully is what the wall in front of you offers: the Liberty Bell-Concord notch faces a crack system. The Concord-Lexington notch gives onto low-angle, gravelly ledges.

So: crack system in front of you at the top of the gully means you are at the right notch for this route.

Confirm by the length of the climb, which is short and countable: four pitches at Grade II 5.8, and the second pitch tops out at the same bolted anchor system that starts the standard Liberty Bell descent. Most parties either stop there or continue a few hundred feet of fourth and low-fifth scrambling to the true summit. If you have climbed four pitches and are nowhere near a bolted descent anchor, you are not on this route.

Budget extra time and care for the scramble into the first belay compared with Beckey Route parties, because it is exposed and it is where this route differs.

hits.text:
The route is climber's right of Liberty Crack, and the published method for finding it is to work downward from the features above rather than along the base. Look climber's right of Liberty Crack and connect the line down from the features higher on the wall. Some mellow snow travel is usually necessary to reach the base.

So this is the one east face route whose start is honestly described as a sighting problem, and that is worth knowing before the cloud comes down. Fix the line from the talus while you can see the wall. If you cannot see the wall, you cannot locate this start by walking the base, and no description will change that.

What you can do without a view is bound it, because the order along the base is known. Left to right: Freedom Rider about 100 ft left of Liberty Crack, Liberty Crack, Freedom or Death just right of it on a leftward-trending ramp with bolts above, Thin Red Line, Liberty and Injustice for All about 10 m right of Thin Red Line, Live Free or Die, and the Independence Route at the far right or north edge of the face beneath a red roof and alcove called the Baer Ceiling about 85 m up.

So: if you are standing at a leftward-trending ramp with bolts above it, you are one route left, on Freedom or Death. If you can see a red roof about 85 M above you, you have walked all the way right to the Independence Route.

The descent decides which car you end at, and this route has both options: from the top of the route near M&M Ledge, work climber's left to good bolts and make four double-rope rappels essentially to the ground at the base of the East Face, returning to your pack and the East Face approach. If you instead continue to the true summit and take the standard Liberty Bell notch descent, you finish on the west side of the mountain and need a shuttle or a road walk back.

runs: rainier between willis wall and liberty wall two of the most dangerous alpine walls in the lower 48
hits.text: Liberty Ridge splits the North Face of Mount Rainier between Willis Wall and Liberty Wall, two of the most dangerous alpine walls in the lower 48 states. The route is considered the premier unguided climb on Mount Rainier and is included in Roper and Steck's Fifty Classic Climbs in North America. Approximately 100 climbers attempt Liberty Ridge annually; however, the route accounts for roughly 25% of Mount Rainier climbing fatalities due to persistent objective hazards and the committing nature of the climb. Fast, experienced parties can complete the climb in two days, while average parties typically require three to four days. Early-season timing (May to mid-June) is critical to minimize rockfall and avalanche hazard as temperatures warm and snow/ice conditions deteriorate.

From camp, either take the short steep ice step in the middle of the rock band directly or traverse up and left around the cliff, then climb the ice gully between the rock walls, which can also be bypassed on its right. Above that the ridge steepens into sustained ice runnels. The whole stretch funnels rock and ice, so it wants to be climbed frozen and in the dark.

runs: out onto the east face of the ridge
hits.text: Move out onto the east face of the ridge to get past the Black Pyramid, on exposed snow and ice up to about 60 degrees, with the angle easing back to 30 to 40 once you are around it. Several pitches of 40 to 60 degree ice and steep glacier ground then gain the Liberty Cap Glacier at around 13,500 ft. The bergschrund below the cap is usually the crux and varies year to year from a walk up a ramp to a short vertical ice step; the bridges and icy ledges across it are seasonal, so plan to climb it rather than count on finding a way over. Easier snow leads to the top.

hits.text: From Thumb Rock, ascend either a short vertical ice pitch (70-80 degrees) in the center of the rock band, or traverse left around the cliff. The ice pitch is a 10-20 foot technical section requiring confident ice climbing and secure placement of ice screws for protection. It is one of the steepest steps on the route and is where parties often spend significant time; the summit bergschrund higher up is usually the technical crux.

runs: the liberty cap glacier around 13 500 ft

Several short icy sections and potential bergschrund crossings require rope belays or simul-climbing. Final approach to Liberty Cap summit involves a bergschrund crossing that varies by year from an easy snow bridge to a short vertical ice step and final snow/ice approach to the summit area.

runs: the broad low angle snow ramp of the liberty cap glacier
hits.text: Above the rock band you reach the broad, low-angle snow ramp of the Liberty Cap Glacier. Follow it up to Liberty Cap. Rime crust is common, and many parties unrope partway up. The technical difficulty is over, but it is a long, tiring climb at altitude after a big day.

runs: a bridge just left of a rock outcropping
hits.text: The walking and the climbing are cleanly separated here and the boundary is a flat spot, but the climb does not start above camp — it starts several hundred feet below it and on the far side of the ridge, and that is what parties get wrong. Follow the crest south from the saddle beside Observation Rock until the ridge stops rising and levels out at about 10,200 to 10,300 ft. You will know the place without being told, because four things sit together there and nowhere else: room for a couple of small tents on flat ground, a steep 2,000 ft drop to the Carbon Glacier immediately east of you, huge banded ice cliffs standing directly south above you where the Liberty Cap Glacier ends, and a clean view straight across at Liberty Ridge. From that camp the route drops west off the crest a few hundred feet onto the upper Mowich Glacier and crosses the bergschrund at about 9,800 ft, aiming for a bridge just left of a rock outcropping near the middle of the face. Look that crossing over from camp the evening before, because it is in plain sight from up there and its condition changes year to year. The traverse down to it passes under the run-out of the ice cliffs and is usually walked across old avalanche debris and stray boulders sitting on the ice, so it is done in the dark and fast. Two ways to know you are wrong. If you have descended onto the Mowich Glacier and kept going west or south, you are wandering out onto Mowich Face ground rather than to the schrund. And if you cross a bergschrund with no ice cliffs above and to your left, stop: from the schrund the route rises back east, climber's left, toward those cliffs, not away from them. The route finishes on Liberty Cap; Columbia Crest is a separate trip across the summit plateau and is not part of this climb.

hits.text: The way in that is actually available during the ice season, because the White River road opens in late spring while Mowich Lake has had no road access since the 2025 bridge closure, and it puts you back at your own car after the Emmons descent instead of on the far side of the mountain. It is the Liberty Ridge approach as far as the Carbon: Glacier Basin, then a boot track up snow and scree to St. Elmo Pass, given variously as 7,400 or 7,600 ft, then onto the Winthrop Glacier and a roped traverse at roughly 7,200 to 7,400 ft around to Curtis Ridge, where there are good bivy sites near 7,500 ft. Next morning drop and cross the Carbon around 7,000 ft, staying clear of its seracs and north of the ice cliffs where the Russell calves onto it, then take snowfields up onto the Ptarmigan crest at about its 9,000 ft point and follow the ridge to high camp. It is longer than the Mowich walk, it crosses three glaciers, and it spends hours under actively shedding walls, so it wants to be done cold and early. One thing to fix in your head before the descent: parties coming off Liberty Cap routes routinely wander onto the busy Disappointment Cleaver at Columbia Crest instead of the faint Emmons track, which is the wrong side of the mountain if your car is at White River.

hits.text: Lincoln Peak's SW Face route, known as the 'X Couloir' (sometimes referenced as 'X Couloir – Emancipation Proclamation'), is the historic line up this seldom-climbed, seriously loose Black Buttes summit. First climbed by Fred Beckey, Wesley Grande, John Rupley, and Herb Staley on July 22, 1956, it was the only documented route to the summit until a 2015 first ascent opened a second line on the NW Face. Only about a dozen ascents are known; the peak is guarded by near-vertical walls on every side.

hits.text:
The highest trees in the basin are the camp, and the camp is the last thing you can navigate to. Above treeline the southwest side of Lincoln is open snow and there is nothing to hold on to in cloud. So the arrival marker is vegetative rather than topographic: climb until the trees stop, and camp at the last of them, below Seward Peak, around 6,100 ft.

The bergschrund is the base of the climb. From camp an alpine start takes you into the southwest basin and to the schrund while the snow is still cold and firm. Above it is roughly 1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step in it.

Do not expect one clean couloir — this is the trap the name sets. Parties who have climbed and skied it describe it as less a couloir and more a series of steep chutes and faces, and the line drops from the high point to the highest notch, then down a narrow chute, and trends right out of view. So 'find the obvious couloir' is the wrong instruction and will have you standing in the basin looking for something that is not there. Work from the notch downward: the correct line is the one that connects to the highest notch on the skyline, and it is narrow where it leaves the basin.

The serac step is the confirmation. Somewhere in that 1,500 ft you meet a steep serac step. A line with no ice step in it is not the X Couloir.

And the aspect settles the coarse error: this route faces southwest and this approach reaches it from Rankin Creek. If you are standing on the Coleman Glacier looking at a shaded north-facing cirque, you are under the other route on this mountain.

hits.text: From the Elbow Lake Trailhead on Forest Road 38 (Middle Fork Nooksack Road), the Elbow Lake Trail reaches the Middle Fork Nooksack River within a few minutes. The bridge is gone and has been for decades — the Forest Service states plainly that there is no bridge over the river to reach the north trailhead and that fording may not be possible during high flows. Parties cross on whatever log is currently in place. One group used a log crossing roughly 200 yards east of the trail junction; another used an unofficial log about a quarter mile downstream of the usual crossing. Assume you will have to hunt for it, and treat the crossing as the crux of the day in terms of consequence. Once across, follow the Elbow Lake Trail — reported in remarkably good shape — through old-growth for about 1.5 miles. Just before a sharp switchback (near Hildebrand Creek), find the blazed Green Creek climbers' path branching off and heading up the Green Creek drainage. It is marked with small blue diamond trail markers. Follow it past the Wiseman Lake outlet at about 2,850 ft, then up through the brush-filled Green Creek valley, past a rock buttress around 3,800 ft, and onto loose scree, boulder fields and rolling slabs with class 3 scrambling to gain the Green Creek Glacier. For the South Couloir specifically, continue up the basin and climb snow to the 6,240+ ft col southeast of Little Sister, then traverse onto the south side and up into the gully. runs: the crest between the fryingpan and whitman glaciers
hits.text: The highest of the three camps, in the prominent gap on the crest between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, just under the base of the peak itself. It reduces summit day to a short glacier walk and the East Shoulder scramble, which is its whole justification. Everything else about it is a cost: it is cold, wind-hammered, waterless, and small enough that a third party arriving has nowhere to go. Little Tahoma's summit block is notoriously loose volcanic rock and the peak is the site of one of the largest rockfalls recorded in the range, so where you site a tent relative to the slopes above matters more here than anywhere lower on the route. Sound judgement is to camp high only if the freezing level is low enough to keep the mountain frozen overnight.

From the Paradise parking lot, climb the standard Camp Muir route to about 8,600 ft. Leave it there and traverse east onto the Paradise Glacier and across the Cowlitz, holding elevation to stay above the cliff and serac band below, then through a notch in the Cathedral Rocks cleaver and across the Ingraham Glacier to a snow or rock ramp at the base of Little Tahoma's south and east face near 8,900 ft.

Camps are made on the Cowlitz or Ingraham glaciers, or on the more exposed Cathedral Rocks cleaver.

Above the ramp the route climbs the Whitman Glacier and exits its upper left-hand corner into a gully, climbs about two-thirds of it to a short step, continues up a gully-chimney to the summit notch, and finishes with a short loose scramble along the crest.

The Paradise road stays open far later into winter than the roads on the north and east sides, which is the whole reason this variant exists.

One single-rope rappel with a 60 m rope reaches a sandy ledge; work right and down to a bolted station, then make two single-rope rappels of about 25 m from bolted anchors into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft. Parties who stop at M&M Ledge can instead take Thin Red Line’s rappel line: from M&M Ledge, rappel with two ropes off a fixed pin and wire, then work climber’s left to bolted anchors and make four more double-rope rappels to the talus at the base of the East Face.

hits.text:
The route is sandwiched, and the sandwich is the test: it lies to the left of the Independence Route and to the right of Thin Red Line. Those two neighbours are the most identifiable lines at that end of the face, so bound the ground between them and the route is inside it.

The right-hand bound is the one you can see from furthest away: the Independence Route starts at the far right, or north, edge of the East Face, and a red-coloured roof and alcove, the Baer Ceiling, sits about 85 m above its start. If a red roof is above you, you have walked one route too far right.

The left-hand bound: Thin Red Line is climber's right of Liberty Crack, and Liberty and Injustice for All sits about 10 m right of Thin Red Line on two-bolt anchors with fixed biners. If you are at a two-bolt anchor with fixed biners a rope length up, you started too far left.

An honest warning from the first ascent, and it changes how you read the wall: the party recorded that the route's initial crack pitches were 700 ft up the wall and seemed to have been reached by rappel from other routes, with no obvious way to reach them from below. So the visible feature that names this route is not at its base. Do not try to identify the line by the cracks; identify the ground between Thin Red Line and Independence and start there.

Descent from M&M ledge, for parties who do not top out, is Thin Red Line's: from the ledge, rappel with two ropes off a fixed pin and wire, then work climber's-left to a set of bolted anchors and make four double-rope rappels back to the talus at the base of the East Face. Every station after the first is bolted; no natural or v-thread anchors are involved. Parties who finish on the summit take the standard Liberty Bell descent on the west side instead.

hits.text: Lizard Mountain has no trailhead of its own. It is climbed from a camp at White Rock Lakes, which parties reach from the north over the first half of the Ptarmigan Traverse and leave the same way. Start at the Cascade Pass Trailhead (~3,600 ft) at the end of the Cascade River Road, 23 miles from Marblemount. The maintained trail switchbacks about 3.7 miles and 1,800 ft up to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft), the last built tread of the trip. From the pass a climbers' path traverses south-southeast across the flank of Mixup Peak to the Cache Glacier; rope up for the glacier to Cache Col (~6,900 ft), then drop to Kool-Aid Lake (~6,100 ft), the usual first camp. Beyond the lake the Red Ledge crosses the cliff band, and a roped crossing of the Middle Cascade Glacier leads to the gap beside Spider Mountain and down to Yang Yang Lakes (~5,800 ft). From there climb onto the Le Conte Glacier, work around Sentinel Peak, cross the broad South Cascade Glacier and top out at Lizard Col (~6,800 ft) on Lizard's south ridge, then descend to White Rock Lakes (~6,200 ft). From camp, regain the col and follow the south ridge roughly 600 vertical feet to the summit, a short but loose Class 2-3 scramble; stay near the crest to avoid the worst rubble on the flanks. Most parties take three days to reach White Rock Lakes, and the whole outing is about 35 miles round trip with some 11,000 ft of cumulative gain. The southern approach from the Downey Creek Trailhead is not usable at present: the Suiattle River Road has been closed at the milepost 4 washout since the 2025 floods, and washouts cut off the trailhead; check status before planning on it.

hits.text: Lost Peak sits deep in the Pasayten Wilderness and is climbed as the summit day of a multi-day loop, not from a roadside trailhead. Start at the Robinson Creek trailhead (about 2,500 ft, on Lost River Road beyond Mazama) and follow the Robinson Creek trail about 9 miles to Robinson Pass (6,220 ft), then drop about three miles into the Middle Fork Pasayten valley and camp on the river flats. Next day follow the valley down past Fred's Lake, climb over Rolo Pass (7,100 ft) to the head of Eureka Creek, cross Shellrock Basin and go over Shellrock Pass (7,500 ft); the tread through this high country is faint and easy to lose in fog. Camp at the small pond in the North Monument Creek basin below Butte Pass, the base for the climb. On summit day walk up to Butte Pass, go over Point 7275 and along the ridge toward Pass Butte (8,140 ft), which many parties climb on the way, then from the col between Pass Butte and Point 8107 follow the connecting ridge southeast over several false summits to Lost Peak's summit. The ridge keeps you off the loose scree of the peak's west and southwest slopes. To close the loop, move camp to Lake of the Woods, cross Pistol Pass to the Eureka Falls camp where Eureka Creek meets the Lost River, then ford Eureka Creek and walk out the lower Monument Creek trail to the Monument Creek trailhead (about 2,400 ft), on the same road as the start. The upper Monument Creek trail beyond Eureka Creek looks like a shorter way in to the North Monument Creek basin, but it has not been maintained for decades and is overgrown and choked with deadfall. Hazards: faint or missing tread above the passes; a long ridge of false summits that is disorienting in whiteout or after dark; cold fords of Eureka Creek during snowmelt; afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter above treeline; and multi-day self-rescue distance from any road.

hits.text: This is the staging camp that makes Mount Carru and Mount Lago short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. What you pay for the position is water and weather. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.

hits.text: From the White River Trailhead (~2,300 ft, at the end of White River Road/FR 6400, reached via WA-207 and White River Road from Coles Corner off US-2), follow the White River Trail (#1507) upstream along a mostly level grade through old-growth forest for about 4 miles to its junction with the Boulder Pass Trail (#1562, also called the Boulder Creek Trail). Water is abundant the whole way — the White River parallels the trail, and Boulder Creek is a dependable source at the junction (the crossing here can be a ford depending on the year/season, so check recent trip reports before committing). Turn onto the Boulder Pass Trail and climb switchbacks through forest, gaining roughly 2,500-2,700 ft over about 3 miles to break out into the open basin below Boulder Pass (~5,000 ft). Because the round trip from the trailhead runs in the 20+ mile range with well over 6,000 ft of gain, most parties do this as an overnight, camping in the Boulder Pass basin or pushing on to a high camp in Upper Boulder Basin (~5,800 ft). From the basin, leave the maintained trail for the unmaintained 'sheepherder's path,' a boot track that sidehills west across a series of cirques (Clark Basin, then Luahna Basin), losing roughly 1,000 ft as it traverses below Clark Mountain's south spur before regaining elevation near a 7,200 ft spur. This traverse is the route-finding crux of the approach — brushy, exposed to sidehill slips, and easy to lose in poor visibility or snow cover. The arrival at the climbing is a glacier, and the thing that gets you to it is a col that belongs to the next peak. From the 7,200 ft spur, make a rising traverse across broad benches — often snow-covered well into summer — and easy Class 2 ledges to the roughly 7,600 ft col west of Clark Mountain. You are navigating to a gap beside a different summit, which is what makes it findable: Clark is the big thing on your left.

From that col, the route is one rising traverse across the Upper Richardson Glacier to Luahna's east ridge. Rope up at the col. The glacier crossing is the route; the ridge above it is a scramble west to the summit.

The critical negative marker is about which glacier you are on: the Pilz and Butterfly Glaciers are on Luahna's north slope and belong to a separate route approached from the Napeequa side. This route uses the Richardson, which lies to the south-east of the summit. If the glacier you have stepped onto is north of the peak, you are on the other mountain's business entirely.

The second negative marker is simpler: if you never touched a glacier at all, you are on the south-west slopes and south-east ridge line, which is the other route on this peak and is deliberately glacier-free. Both finish on the same summit and neither is a variation of the other.

Coming down, the one piece of technical ground is below the east ridge: a short, steep step reported as low Class 4 and sometimes verglassed in an adjacent gully. Strong parties downclimb it; a single 20-30 m rappel off a horn or block is common practice when it is wet or icy. There is no fixed anchor — carry webbing.

Do not take the thunder creek exit on the strength of the map. Dropping south into Thunder Creek looks shorter and is reported slower and rougher, with heavy blowdown, avalanche debris and a boot path that disappears near the creek crossing. Reversing the ascent line over Boulder Pass is the reliable way out.

You find the base of this route by counting basins, and the answer is four. From the Boulder Basin camp the sheepherder's path crosses cirques in order: boulder, then Clark, then Luahna, and the peak's base sits above the fourth — Chalangin Basin. Nothing about the ground tells you which cirque you are in, but the character does: the first is where the path keeps disappearing, the second is open and park-like, the third has good tread. Count them.

The intermediate marker is a number on the ridge: make a rising traverse across Luahna Basin toward the roughly 7,500 ft ridge point, then follow a faint trail across scree and talus above the fourth cirque to the peak's base. Above Chalangin Basin, not in it.

The positive test at the base is the grade, and it is easier than you expect: the scramble begins on easy class 2 ledges on the south face, leading up to the right-hand skyline ridge. Class 2 ledges, south-facing, and a ridge on your right at the top of them. If your first ground is steep, or if you are on a glacier, or if the ledges lead left, you are not on it.

The confirmation comes high and it is on the wrong side of the mountain: just beneath the summit the route crosses an exposed class 3+ traverse on the north side before the final Class 3 scramble straight up. So the sequence is south-face ledges, gain the ridge, cross to the north beneath the summit, then straight up. A route that never leaves the sunny side has not reached the summit block.

The negative marker against the peak's other route: the east slopes line crosses the upper Richardson Glacier from a col west of Clark Mountain and needs glacier gear. This route touches no glacier at all. If you are roping up for crevasses, you are on the other one, and it is a different day.

A note on what is published versus what parties find: this is described as a second-class line, and most parties meet a short Class 3 or better traverse or step to bypass a gap in the ridge below the true summit. Expect it rather than treat it as evidence you are off route.

The route is the glacier immediately south of the peak, and the test is that it narrows. From the floor of Luna Cirque, get onto the hanging glacier that lies directly south of Phantom and follow it up to where it narrows and steepens as it flows down from higher on the mountain. That constriction is the route; there is nothing subtle about walking into a narrowing throat of ice with rock on both sides.

Arrival at the rock, which is the actual base of the climbing: where the narrows end, turn north and climb over a rock step to reach the highest snowfield on the peak. That turn is the transition from snow to rock and the point at which the party commits to the upper route. The whole climb above the cirque is only about 400 ft in four pitches, so if you have been climbing rock for more than a few rope lengths without reaching a summit block you are not on this line.

Countable confirmation: one rock step, two to three pitches of easy slab to the ridge, then a summit block of about 25 ft. Four pitches, 4th class with a move of easy 5th. Parties carry runners and a few pieces rather than a full rack, because placements on the slab are where the features allow rather than where you want them.

The turnaround test, which is the most useful thing about this route: the hanging glacier has to be recrossed to get home. A party that finds it in poor condition on the way up should treat that as the turnaround decision rather than pressing on. Timing is the main decision this route asks of a party, and the answer is taken at the base, not at the top.

This route contours where the south ridge climbs, and the difference starts above camp rather than at the col. From the Access Creek basin, ascend broad talus gullies, snow-filled early season, southwest toward an obvious gap in the ridge above. Once on the ridge, traverse south of point 6,730 on grass and heather benches into a large basin on Luna Peak's southeast side, then cross that basin at about the 6,600 ft level to Luna Col at 7,200 ft.

So the fog test is an altimeter test: the basin crossing is held at roughly 6,600 ft. Losing height into the basin or gaining it toward the crest both cost you, and both are what happens when you navigate by feel. Hold the contour and it delivers you to the col.

Arrival: Luna Col at 7,200 ft is the notch between Luna Peak and a smaller tower to its left. You are there when the ground drops away on the far side.

Confirm on the climb, and the count is short: above the col the route is roughly 1,100 ft of class 2-3 talus and scree to the false, southern summit, then one short connecting ridge to the true summit. Snow lingers on and just below the false summit well into the season and is often the first unavoidable snow of the ascent, so an axe is worth carrying even when the lower slopes are dry. Poles are commonly left at the false summit.

The one technical spot, and its tell: drop roughly 5 ft off the false summit onto a narrow, very exposed 4th-class crest with a snow-covered cliff falling several hundred feet down the northwest face on one side and a snow-free cliff dropping the southeast face on the other. A commonly used variation avoids the worst of it by dropping onto a ledge on the southeast side and scrambling back to the ridge behind the summit. If you are on a crest with snow on your left and bare rock on your right, you are in the right place and there is one short section of it.

No water above the access creek basin. The summit push is done on what you carry.

This climber's trail is intermittent and route-finding becomes more important in early season when it's snow-covered. hits.text:
The bergschrund is the route's identity and it is the one-look test against both its neighbours on this side of the mountain. This is the only Magic Mountain route from the Kool-Aid Lake side that crosses a schrund. The Northwest Ridge walks up easy slopes to rock and a chimney; the Southwest Cirque goes up heather gullies. If you have not crossed a gap between glacier and rock, you are not on the west ridge.

The positive landmark above the schrund is a named shape: shelves lead up to a blocky open book — a dihedral corner. That open book is the 5.6 crux and the best-protected pitch on the route. If you cross the schrund and find no open-book corner above you, you have crossed it in the wrong place.

Count the four features in order, because they are all different shapes: schrund, shelves, open book, slab. The slab is taken on its easier left side, not up the middle.

The finish tells you which summit you are under: from below the ridge between the false and main summits, an easy chimney on the left gains the crest. So the route deliberately arrives on the ridge between the two tops — if the chimney you climbed put you straight onto a summit, you are on the false one and the ridge continues.

And if you have to retreat below the summit, the schrund has to work in both directions: a retreat reverses the chimney and slab, downclimbs the open book and re-crosses the schrund. Look at it on the way up with that in mind, because there is no walk-off from this side of the mountain; the walk-off starts at the summit and goes down the South Ridge.

hits.text: McClellan Peak forms the high, sprawling rampart on the southeast side of the Enchantments, a granite massif with substantial prominence that rises above the Snow Lakes and Nada Lake basins. It sits about 1.3 miles east of Little Annapurna and 1.6 miles southwest of The Temple, and was first climbed July 5, 1946 by Ken Prestrud, Keith Rankin, and William Herston. The mountain is composed of Late Cretaceous tonalitic plutons; its broad summit ridge carries subsidiary towers (the Prong, and 'the Pawn' — first of the Chessmen) that offer 5th-class rock climbing for parties who want more than the standard Class 3 scramble to the true summit.

runs: around to the south side of mcclellan peak
hits.text: This route's crux move is on the ridge itself, not a technical descent: from the ridge crest (reached via the ascent line west of the Prong), drop roughly 70 vertical feet off the crest and wrap around to the south side of McClellan Peak, then scramble up class 3 rock to the true summit. Descend by reversing this exact sequence: downclimb the class 3 south-side rock back to the ~70-ft notch below the ridge crest, regain the crest, and drop back down the steep talus/scree/snow slope west of the Prong to the flat area between Leprechaun and Sprite Lakes at ~7,000 ft. From there, rejoin the Snow Lakes Trail (No. 1553) and retrace it past Lake Viviane, the Snow Lakes, and Nada Lake back to the trailhead — summit-to-trailhead typically takes roughly 5–5.5 hours. This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling required. Watch for loose rock and exposure on the class 3 downclimb (parties have noted going down 20 ft and wrapping to an easier gully when the direct line felt too exposed), ice on the ridge slope in late season, and the same logjam crossing between the Snow Lakes on the way out. Carry an axe/microspikes if snow lingers on the upper slope, since a slip there has real runout consequences.

runs: a talus slope leads to the base of the summit
hits.text: From High Bridge the trail passes Howard Lake, climbs a long, hot, dusty switchback up an open southwestern shoulder, then drops into subalpine fir/pine forest and crosses a clear creek before reaching the lower of two glacial cirques on a rocky, sandy moraine. Heaton Camp (~6,700 ft), the only established camp, sits just above the terminal moraine. Another set of switchbacks above camp ends in about a third of a mile at a rocky outcropping, where the maintained trail stops. From there a talus slope leads to the base of the summit; the scramble is 'not particularly technical' but steep, with loose footing and real exposure in places, marked by faint red paint arrows, and crosses a snowfield above the Sandalee Glacier before reaching the old fire-lookout site and the radio tower at the true summit.

A steep snow/ice gully (steepening to roughly 40 degrees near the top) leads to the ~7,200 ft col between Inspiration Peak and West McMillan Spire. hits.text: Start at the Easy Pass/Fisher Creek Trailhead on SR-20 (marked pullout near milepost 151, about 5 miles west of Rainy Pass, elevation ~3,700 ft; room for roughly 10 cars, pit toilet, no water at the lot). Follow the Easy Pass Trail, which climbs steadily through forest and then open meadows/talus, gaining roughly 2,800 ft over about 3.6 miles to Easy Pass (~6,500 ft); budget 1.5-2 hours at a good pace. There are reliable streams along the lower trail but none right at the pass, so top off water before cresting. Do not descend into Fisher Creek: leave the trail just west of the pass, before it starts switchbacking down, and begin an uncomfortable cross-country sidehill traverse west-northwest across gullies, scree, talus, grass and blocky ground, well above the valley. Around 6,500 ft the route crosses a waterfall almost directly below Mesahchie on an easy bench - the ground above and below that bench is much harder. Beyond it, climb to the basin below Mesahchie Col, a common high camp with water. From the basin, work up the crest of the shoulder between Mesahchie and Katsuk (some class 4 moves getting established) to gentler but loose, cairned terrain, then traverse slabs down to the col at the foot of Mesahchie, which has a good bivy site. From the col, cross talus to the base of the first obvious gully leading up the southwest/west ridge - steep class 3/4 at its bottom, then broadening and easing after a string of cairns - and follow it to the ridge crest, then the exposed but moderate ridgecrest to the summit. The whole approach beyond Easy Pass is loose and unmarked, so GPS or a photo of the route is worth having. Total one-way distance/gain to the summit run around 12 km and 4,900 ft of the route's overall 24.1 km / 7,480 ft round trip.

hits.text: Mandatory NPS wilderness permit for any overnight stay: $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee, youth 15 and under free. Reserve in advance on Recreation.gov (watch the mandatory safety/rules video, then email noca_wilderness@nps.gov up to 3 days before the trip) or get a walk-up permit in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount (about 40% of permits are held for walk-ups). No camping is allowed at Easy Pass or in the surrounding meadows; nearest designated camps are Fisher Camp (~2 mi past the pass) and Cosho Camp (~6 mi along Fisher Creek). Day climbs with no overnight stay do not require a permit.

hits.text: The climbing starts at Mesahchie Col, the col at the foot of Mesahchie's west ridge. From the basin, the shoulder crest leads up to cairned ground; follow the cairns to the base of the small peak between Mesahchie and Katsuk, turn right, and traverse slightly exposed slabs down to the col, which holds a well-built bivy site. From the col, cross talus to the first obvious gully leading up the west ridge. The right gully is steep Class 3/4 at its base, then enters a broader, gentler gully past a string of cairns and tops out on the ridge crest; the crest is then followed east, exposed but moderate, to the summit. Negative marker: if you reached the peak along the crest from the east and are starting from a flat spot at the foot of the summit pyramid, you are on the East Ridge, not this route.

hits.text: Start at the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (2,350 ft, end of FR-4065). Follow the Sunrise Mine Trail (Trail #707) north; the first mile crosses two significant creeks with no bridges (a log crossing, a root crossing, and one more insistent ford), so expect wet feet and use caution in early season high water. The trail then climbs steadily through forest and, after roughly 2.5 miles and about 1,950 ft of gain, reaches the last major switchback (~4,300 ft) just before the tread begins zig-zagging steeply up toward Headlee Pass. Leave the maintained trail here and traverse northeast on a surprisingly easy, cairned line across a talus field toward the Mile High buttress (the striking pillar also called Eros Tower / Vega North Tower, a 5,280 ft sub-summit north of Morning Star's main summit). Route-finding landmarks: pass just above a large flat-topped boulder near the first stand of trees, thread a natural gap through the trees into a second open talus field, cross open heather and more talus, cross a strip of trees near a rocky bluff, then ascend to the obvious red gully to the right of the buttress. A convenient seep just below the Mile High gully is the only reliable water on the approach, and only runs through mid-season. From the gully, scramble up and left on rubble-strewn, loose ledges (careful footing/rockfall management for parties below) to a lone fir tree, then follow a narrow ledge about 20 ft to a single bolted belay marking the start of Pitch 1. Plan roughly 1–1.5 hours from the trailhead to the base once you know the line; it is unmarked past the switchback and has caught out parties who don't have beta or GPS coordinates for the turnoff.

runs: anchor at the base of pitch 7 rap 2
hits.text: Descend by rappelling the route itself, back down the same line you climbed — do not try to walk off. Eight single-strand rappels, all off bolted, fixed anchors (this is a sport-bolted line, so no natural gear or v-threads needed): rap 1 from the P7/summit anchor down to the anchor at the base of pitch 7; rap 2 face-rappels to an anchor set left and above the dihedral; rap 3 is a short drop to a ledge-side anchor beside the dihedral; rap 4 goes to one of two anchors at the pitch 4 stance (favor the left one); rap 5 is a short, free-hanging rap off an upper-P3 anchor aimed at a ~10 ft tree left of the line, with an intermediate anchor in a nook below it; rap 6 is a vertical face rappel down lower P3 to a large ledge at the pitch 2 anchors; rap 7 drops to the pitch 1 anchor (10–15 ft left of the original belay); rap 8 finishes at the base. A single 70m rope is sufficient for all 8 raps; two 60m ropes also work if you'd rather split gear or prefer doubled-rope security, and some parties carry a single 60m instead but report tighter/more numerous transitions. Because you rappel the entire route back to the start, many parties leave approach shoes and packs stashed at the base. Descent hazards: loose rock sitting on several of the belay ledges (manage ropes and stack carefully to avoid kicking debris onto the party below), some rope-stretch/rope-snag potential given the zigzagging (not straight-down) line of anchors, and lingering steep snow in the approach gully in spring that can complicate the walk back to the Sunrise Mine Trail after the last rappel.
