hits.text: Start at the Sunrise Mine trailhead at the end of the forest road. The first mile crosses two unbridged creeks — a log, a root crossing and one more insistent ford — so expect wet feet and treat them seriously in early-season high water. The trail then climbs steadily through forest to the last major switchback before it starts zigzagging steeply up toward the pass. That switchback is where you leave the trail; the pass is not. From there a cairned line traverses northeast across talus. Route-finding markers on the traverse, in order: pass just above a large flat-topped boulder near the first stand of trees, thread a natural gap through those trees into a second open talus field, cross heather and more talus, cross a strip of trees near a rocky bluff. A seep just below the gully is the only reliable water and only runs mid-season.

runs: scramble up and left on rubble strewn ledges to a lone fir tree
hits.text: The traverse ends at the obvious red gully on the right-hand side of the buttress. From the gully, scramble up and left on rubble-strewn ledges to a lone fir tree, then follow a narrow ledge about twenty feet to a single bolted belay — one bolt, on a ledge, past one tree. That belay is the start of the first pitch and there is nothing else like it on this tower. Negative markers: if you are standing on open talus under a dark grey face with two large boulders at its foot and a long line of bolts running away up a fifty-five-metre pitch, you are one line left of here, on the west-face route that shares this tower's summit; if you left the traverse into a gully on the right-hand (east) side of the tower and climbed cedar and heather to a notch on the skyline, you are on the neighbouring tower entirely and the route above you is a different climb.

runs: one mile south of cascade pass on the
hits.text: Mix-up Peak (7,440 ft) sits one mile south of Cascade Pass on the Skagit–Chelan county line and marks the northern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse. First climbed in 1947 by Wesley Grande and Jack Kendrick, its East Face is a compact, mostly solid-rock 'staircase' of class 3–4 scrambling with a short mid-5th-class step near the top, reached by a glacier/snowfield crossing from Cascade Pass. It's a popular objective (7-9 hours from the trailhead to the summit alone) for parties already in the Cascade Pass basin, but the approach's moat and rockfall-prone notches keep it a genuine alpine outing despite the modest elevation.

runs: belay station at the top of the second climbing pitch from
hits.text: Descend by reversing the final scramble pitches/downclimbing back to the top of the technical face (the uppermost section is a downclimb/scramble to the top of the East Face), then begin a rappel sequence rather than trying to downclimb the buttress itself — the rock is loose enough that down-climbing the route is not recommended. From a small ledge/anchor on the east side just below the summit, a 50 m rappel gets you down the steepest upper wall (rockfall-prone — the next rappeller should move off to the side immediately, not straight down, to avoid anyone above). Below that, from the bottom of the shoulder, one rappel on a single 60 m rope reaches the belay station at the top of the second climbing pitch. From there the line drops over an overhanging section to just below the north side of Gunsight Notch: one double-rope rappel with two ropes, or two rappels on a single 60 m rope. That is four rappels on one 60 m rope, which is what parties report, or three with two ropes. Anchors are fixed natural slings and cord rather than bolts, and parties regularly add cord or rebuild one, so carry some. Move off the fall line as soon as you are down each rappel; rockfall knocked loose by the party above is a recognized hazard here. Below the notch, re-descend the glacier and snowfield and Mixup Arm to Cascade Pass.

hits.text:
There are two notches at the head of the Cache Glacier on Mixup's east side, and picking the wrong one is the standard mistake.

A U-shaped notch sits on the left and a V-shaped notch on the right. The East Face is accessed from the V-notch. It is common — and accepted — to go up through the U-notch on the left and wrap around the back side to reach the V, so being at the U is not a failure, but starting to climb from it is.

Gunsight Notch, the prominent notch west of Cache Col, is the portal that serves Mix-Up, the Triplets and Cascade Peak, and the snow tongue leading to it is short, about a hundred feet, but steep at roughly 50-65 degrees. Bergschrunds flank the tongue on either side, dropping ten to fifteen feet to a rock floor, and the ground between the snow and the rock is wet, tight and swept by rockfall.

From the south side of the notch the sequence is specific and is your confirmation: go west about 100 ft down a side gully, then ascend northwest up a wide, loose gully to a saddle. At that saddle the White Staircase begins — an easy, exposed class 3 staircase of pale grey rock on the right-hand side of the large summit pyramid. If you are looking at a grey staircase-like ramp on the right side of the pyramid, you are exactly where you should be.

The hardest and dirtiest climbing on the whole approach is the first fifty feet out of the moat where the glacier meets rock — perhaps mid-fifth on loose ground. That difficulty is itself a tell: if the entry felt trivial, check that you have actually crossed the moat at the right place.

Season matters for this specifically. As the Cache Glacier recedes, getting to the notch has been getting harder year on year, and by August the moat can be the deciding problem rather than the climbing.

hits.text: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike South: drive 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and park on either side of the road just before the bridge over the river. Scramble up the steep hillside on the NW side of the road above the bridge abutment, then continue uphill along the dike to a passable gully.

hits.text: From the Barlow Pass Trailhead (end of the paved Mountain Loop Highway drive), the approach is in two clearly different stages before you ever leave a maintained tread. Stage one is 4 flat, easy miles up the gated, washed-out Monte Cristo Road along the South Fork Sauk River to the Monte Cristo ghost town (~2,800 ft) — a couple of cable/suspension bridges cross the river en route, and this stretch is runnable/bikeable in dry conditions. At the townsite, walk past the old cabins, cross the bridge over 76 Creek, and follow "Dumas Street" through the settlement to pick up signed Glacier Basin Trail #719. Stage two is the real climb: the first half-mile follows an old mining road grade along Glacier Creek, then the trail turns into slick rock scrambling more than hiking — steep, eroded, hands-on-rock terrain climbing past Glacier Falls, with numerous cascades and slick, root-braided rock steps that are notably harder (and slicker) descending than ascending. The trail crosses into Henry M. Jackson Wilderness and skirts the northeast edge of Mystery Hill before leveling out into Glacier Basin (~4,500 ft) after about 2.5 miles and ~1,700 ft of gain from Monte Cristo — roughly 6.5 miles and ~2,100 ft from the car. Glacier Creek parallels the whole climb and is a reliable water source, but it drains historic mine workings — treat/filter and be aware of elevated arsenic/heavy-metal readings noted by the Forest Service, especially in the lower reaches near the old townsite. From Glacier Basin the maintained trail ends; leave it and climb open talus and (typically) persistent steep snow — up to ~45° for a few hundred vertical feet — directly toward the obvious North Col (~6,760+ ft) on Monte Cristo's north ridge, with the Wilmans Peaks and Wilmans Glacier looming close overhead to climber's right. An ice axe and comfort on steep firm snow are essentially mandatory into midsummer; a moat can open at the col and the step across it can be intimidating or, late season, impassable. From the North Col, contour south (skier's/climber's left) across snow or talus below the summit cliffs, scouting for the obvious break/gully in the rock that gives the easiest way up to the base of the short summit chimney.

hits.text: Monument Peak is the most rugged and inaccessible peak in the Lago group, deep in the eastern Pasayten Wilderness near the Eureka Creek country. Double-nubbed and built of granite, it sits almost as an island: Eureka Creek wraps its north, west, and south sides while Monument Creek drains the east side. The mountain has a precipitous north/northeast side, a cliffy east face, a rugged west face, and a comparatively gentler (though still remote) south slope that forms the standard scramble line. A disheveled connecting ridge links it to 8,397-ft Blackcap Mountain a half-mile north; 8,745-ft Mount Lago, its line parent, lies about 2.4 miles further north. First ascended in 1978 by Fred Beckey and John Roper.

hits.text: From the Killen Creek Trailhead (FS Rd 2329, ~3 miles from Takhlakh Lake), follow Killen Creek Trail #113 through open, dusty lodgepole forest. Around 2.5 miles in you cross East Fork Adams Creek and its meadows (last reliable easy water before the high basin), then the trees thin as the trail climbs rockier terrain to meet the PCT (Trail #2000) at roughly 6,100 ft, about 3.1 miles from the trailhead. Continue straight across the PCT onto the High Camp Trail #10 for about 1.0 mile to High Camp / Adams Glacier Meadows at the edge of the Adams Glacier moraine (~6,900 ft) — a common base camp. From High Camp the route leaves maintained trail: traverse east/southeast, off-trail across lava fields and around or over the toe of Lava Ridge, crossing the toe of the Lava Glacier, to reach the base of the Lyman Glacier at about 8,000 ft. This traverse is glacier/talus travel with real route-finding, especially in low-snow years — a rope and crevasse-rescue gear are standard once on glacier ice. The Lyman Glacier itself splits around a rock outcrop; the north lobe (original route) and south lobe (40° lower half on unbroken neve/ice, upper half broken by crevasses and serac walls) both lead to a crux chute near 10,000 ft that varies 45–65° for about 50 ft depending on the year, then easier snow to the summit plateau.

hits.text:
From the Killen Creek trailhead, follow Trail #113 through open dusty lodgepole forest. Around 2.5 miles you cross East Fork Adams Creek and its meadows — the last easy water before the high basin. The trees thin as the trail climbs rockier ground to the PCT at about 6,100 ft, roughly 3.1 miles in. Continue straight across onto High Camp Trail #10 for about a mile to High Camp at Adams Creek Meadows, near 6,900 ft.

From High Camp the maintained trail is done. Traverse east and southeast off-trail across lava fields, across the toe of the Lava Glacier and around or over the toe of Lava Ridge, to the base of the Lyman Glacier at about 8,000 ft. This is glacier and talus travel with real route-finding, worst in a low-snow year; rope and crevasse-rescue gear are standard once on ice.

Most of the route can be simul-climbed with a running belay on pickets. The standard descent is the North Ridge, not a reversal — long, loose volcanic scree, occasionally narrow, with a real chance of knocking rock onto parties below.

runs: around or over the toe of lava ridge
hits.text:
Count the ridges, and for this route you must get past two.

East of High Camp the order is: Adams Glacier, North Ridge, Lava Glacier, Lava Ridge, Lyman Glacier. You cross the Lava Glacier and then go around or over the toe of Lava Ridge. Lava Ridge is the second ridge and it is the gate. If you have crossed only one ridge and stopped at a glacier, you are at the Lava Glacier Headwall — a different climb with a triangular face — not at the Lyman.

The positive test is a fork, and it is unmistakable once you are on it: the Lyman splits around a narrow rock outcrop into two lobes. The north lobe is the original line; the south lobe runs 40-degree unbroken neve on its lower half and is broken by crevasses and serac walls on its upper half. A glacier that forks around an island of rock is the confirmation you are where you meant to be.

The crux confirms it a second time, higher: both lobes lead to a chute near 10,000 ft that runs anywhere from 45 to 65 degrees over about 50 ft depending on the year. One short steep chute, then easier snow to the summit plateau. If you meet no constriction at all, you are on a neighbouring glacier.

The base elevation is the third check: about 8,000 ft. Arriving on ice much higher than that means you gained the glacier well above its toe and may have come onto it over the ridge rather than around it, which is fine but changes where the lobes sit relative to you.

What the descent means for the approach, and it is worth deciding at the car: you do not come back this way. The walk-off is the North Ridge, back toward High Camp. So the ridge you counted past on the way in is not the ridge you come down.

From the Austin Pass / Artist Point trailhead at the end of SR-542, follow the signed Lake Ann Trail #600. It drops about 800 ft into the Swift Creek headwaters basin before climbing back up to a saddle at 4,900 ft northwest of Lake Ann, about 3.9 miles one way; the lake itself is a short way farther down the trail.

hits.text: Mount Arriva (8,215 ft) is a long, broken summit ridge at the east end of the Ragged Ridge group in North Cascades National Park, about 1.6 mi southwest of Easy Pass — though it stays hidden from both the pass and SR-20 despite that proximity. The ridge has two high points: East Peak (~8,160+ ft), first climbed by Fred Beckey, Jim Crooks, and Ed Kennedy in August 1940, and the higher true (west) summit, first reached July 6, 1966 by Joe and Joan Firey with John and Irene Meulemans. There is no trail to the peak — parties approach off-trail through Fisher Creek Basin and the Silent Lakes basin, then climb class 3 (occasionally class 4, depending on the exact line) rock on Arriva's south/southwest ridge and ledge systems to the summit. It's commonly combined with nearby Fisher Peak, Kitling Peak, or Graybeard Peak as a multi-day trip.

From a high camp near 6,600-7,000 ft, the route crosses the broken lower Coleman Glacier to the base of the headwall around 8,500 ft, then climbs roughly 10-14 pitches of sustained 45-50 degree snow/ice with several short steeper steps (occasionally 60-80 degrees) and a crux bergschrund passage near 10,000 ft before easing onto the summit plateau. Most parties start well before dawn and take 8-12 hours camp-to-summit.

hits.text: The face begins near 8,500 ft on the northwest side, bounded by the Roman Nose on the climber's right and serac walls on the left. Getting established means crossing a bergschrund, and there are two on the route; depending on the year the crossing can involve a very short vertical step and is often the most committing and least reversible move of the day. hits.text: The North Ridge of Mount Baker is the peak's premier moderate alpine ice route and a Cascades classic, first climbed by Fred Beckey, Ralph Widrig, and Dick Widrig in August 1948. From the Heliotrope Ridge approach, cross the Coleman Glacier laterally to the base of the ridge, then ascend snow slopes on the ridge's west flank (with crevasse crossings) to the ice cliff that forms the route's crux — 2-6 belayed pitches of 50-85 degree ice depending on the year and line chosen. Above the cliff, moderate snow/ice leads toward the summit cap, which steepens in its last few hundred feet with real exposure over the west face and a possible crevasse crossing near the summit plateau.

hits.text: Shares the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead (~3,500-3,700 ft) and the same Trail 677 approach as the Coleman-Deming route: switchback through old growth to the Kulshan Cabin site/treeline fork (~2.25 mi), then up the Hogsback moraine to the standard high camp at ~6,000 ft (about 3 mi and 2,300 ft of gain, 4-5 hours for a laden party). From high camp, the North Ridge approach diverges from Coleman-Deming: rope up and cross the Coleman Glacier heading climbers' left (east), navigating crevasses and icefall, to gain the base of the North Ridge proper on the glacier's true right side. The standard start crosses a double bergschrund via a bridge or narrow snow ramp (can be a difficult, exposed step depending on the season) and climbs a broad 40-degree snow gully to the crest of the ridge. Hazards: crevasse and bergschrund crossing is the technical crux of the approach and is season-dependent (can close out entirely by late summer), icefall exposure on the glacier traverse, and the route sees far less traffic than Coleman-Deming so tracks/bridges may be unbroken.

hits.text:
From the Trinity / Buck Creek Trailhead, hike roughly six miles of Buck Creek Trail through an old burn recovering in fireweed, then drop through a meadow and ford Buck Creek — an easy crossing in normal summer flow.

Across the creek, climb to the crest of Mount Cleator's east ridge through logged and burned forest with a great deal of downed timber. The forest opens considerably above about 4,800 ft, and around 5,500 ft a faint trail appears and contours left.

That faint path leads to an Alder tunnel at the base of some cliffs. Breaking out of it, traverse slippery heather and blueberry slopes across a basin beneath a waterfall, then climb steep goat trails to a grassy knoll beside a talus field.

The route is nearly 2,000 vertical feet of generally low-angle, low- to mid-fifth granite, broken by a distinct notch and a burly 5.8 chimney crux, then towers and gendarmes to the summit. Rock is consistently solid enough for fast simul-climbing except at the crux — which is what makes this the peak's one technical line.

hits.text: This is the base camp for both peaks and effectively the only one. Getting here is the whole difficulty of the trip: leave trail 606 a short distance past the Baker River suspension bridge, before Blum Creek, and find the faint path that works away from the creek through old timber. The first section is genuine devil's club, fern and deadfall bushwhacking, and the path comes and goes; above that it settles into a steep, tiring forest ridge, then an ascending traverse along the south side of that ridge into the lake basin. Five hours from the car is a good day, and parties routinely take longer. For Mount Blum, the south ridge and southeast slopes go from here up through gullies and snow to the east ridge. For Hagan, climb southeast from the lower lake to about 5,600 ft on the east-west ridge, then traverse south toward the pass below the Hagan peaks. Best from mid-July into September; earlier and the traverse to the lakes is a snow slope with a long runout, later and the water thins. There is no shelter of any kind and no cell coverage.

runs: a red talus gully east of the carru lago saddle
hits.text: This is the staging camp that makes Mount Carru and Mount Lago short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. What you pay for the position is water and weather. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.

runs: keith and ruth rankin made the first ascent
hits.text: Mount Chaval (7,127 ft) is a craggy, three-summited peak straddling an east-west ridge (East Peak and Middle Peak, each 7,040 ft, plus the true 7,127-ft summit) in the Glacier Peak Wilderness of the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, roughly 15 miles northeast of Darrington in Skagit County. It sits immediately southwest of its taller, more massive neighbor Snowking Mountain (7,433 ft, 2.5 mi NE) and is built from the Late Cretaceous 'Chaval pluton,' a pyroxene-bearing diorite/tonalite. Richard Merritt and Keith and Ruth Rankin made the first ascent on September 20, 1946. Despite over 1,800 ft of prominence and striking relief above the Illabot Creek and Suiattle River drainages, Chaval is one of the least-visited named summits in the North Cascades — not because the final scrambling is hard, but because every approach (the shorter Illabot Creek Road/west-ramp line, or the longer historical Jug Creek/Bluff Lake/Jug Lake route from the Suiattle side) involves miles of pathless old growth, brush, and steep sidehilling before the climbing even starts.

From camp, climb talus/scree/snow over the moraine rim and across Surprise Basin to 6,920 ft Surprise Col, the Clark-Johnson col. From there the corkscrew route works around south and east ledges before an exposed Class 3-4 finish on the north side of the summit block. runs: the south chute as soon as the cat ears
hits.text:
From the lake, follow the boot path around the shore, out onto a large scree cone, and north into Avalanche Canyon between Inner Constance and Mount Constance. A large rock called the Thumb sits on the canyon's left side; the South Chute lies on the south side of the Thumb, and due south of the Cat Ears.

The most useful rule on this mountain: start up the South Chute as soon as the Cat Ears come into view, not when the chute starts to look obvious. Entering low keeps you on firmer ground, where there is a path in places; parties who keep walking up the canyon and attack the chute higher get the worst of the loose scree. If the Cat Ears have been visible for a while and you are still walking north, you have overshot the entrance.

From the lake the chute line climbs roughly 1,900 ft of scree to a saddle near 6,560-6,600 ft below the Cat Ears. Descend about 150 ft, then a second gully leads to a notch near 7,300 ft.

Above that is the exposed upper maze, and identifying which traverse you are on is the thing to get right. The Finger Traverse is a downsloping ledge above a cliff with old rusted pitons on it — the pitons are the identifier, and some parties clip them as a solo-belay anchor. The Terrible Traverse is a hard-snow traverse of roughly 45 degrees above a big cliff and a nasty drainage. Both feed into class 3, occasionally class 4, ground leading to the base of the summit block. If you are on a traverse and the summit block is not visible above and ahead of you, you are on the wrong ledge.

The actual climbing is only the summit block, about 60 ft, with the North Chimney taking its north side at 3rd class — reported by plenty of people as feeling like easy 4th.

hits.text: A more sustained, technical alternative to the standard scramble: roughly 1,100 feet of mostly broken class 3-4 rock with a few low-fifth-class steps over 5+ pitches, the hardest about 5.4-5.5, climbing the arete that rises directly above Crystal Pass at the head of Avalanche Canyon to the summit ridge. From Crystal Pass, traverse around a small tower to the start; climb a vertical crack protected by fixed webbing, then right-trending class 3 ledges to the arete crest. The route crosses occasionally snowy sections along the crest to a large ledge, then the crux: a right-trending ledge that cuts back left past a couple of fixed pitons into a chimney, followed by short face climbing and a hand traverse (sometimes snow-covered) before easing into scree near the summit ridge. Several belays use fixed pitons or slung anchors left in place.

hits.text: From Crystal Pass (base of the West Arête), begin a rising traverse on the right side of the ridge crest at ~10:30 AM (typical timing). Terrain involves fairly broken Class 2 and 3 with occasional 4th or low 5th steps. Bypass towers via a ledge on the right side. Reach the crux step on the arête proper—traverse up and right on a groove (5.4), clip existing pitons, move straight up (5.4) then back left to a small alcove below a chimney. Anchor and ascend the chimney leftward to a sloping ledge, then traverse left to easier ground. Continue to ridge crest with talus climbing above, then cross to east side following the standard route descent to summit horn.

runs: washed out dosewallips river road to the lake constance
hits.text: Same trailhead and grueling approach as the standard route: a road-walk/bike of roughly 5 miles up the closed, washed-out Dosewallips River Road to the Lake Constance climbers' trail (~1,450 ft), then a steep, unmaintained boot path gaining roughly 3,300-3,400 ft in under 2.2 miles — no switchbacks, hand-over-hand in places — to Lake Constance (4,800 ft); figure 2.5-3.5 hours. Camp at the established sites on the lake's north end. From there, instead of cutting into the South Chute, continue up into Avalanche Canyon past the 'Thumb' rock feature and stay toward the climber's-right side of the canyon passing below the 'Cat Ears' landmark, following a rough path through scree and talus that fades out below the South Chute turnoff. The canyon is roughly 1.5 miles of steady uphill slog to Crystal Pass at its head; this terrain is loose, poorly consolidated talus/scree when snow-free and considerably faster and safer when covered in firm early-season snow (carry an ice axe June into July). The final few hundred feet to Crystal Pass steepen and often hold softening snow by mid-morning, so an early start pays off. Plan roughly 3-4 hours from the lake to the pass.

runs: a remnant of ice below the scree fan leading
hits.text:
Same start as the standard route: the closed Dosewallips roadbed for roughly 5 miles, then the Lake Constance climbers' trail, which gains about 3,300-3,400 ft in under 2.2 miles with no switchbacks and hand-over-hand pulling in places. Figure 2.5-3.5 hours on that section. Camp at the established sites at the north end of the lake; a wilderness permit is required and the site is reservable for the May 15-October 15 summer season.

From the lake, take the boot path around its eastern shore, come out onto a large scree cone, traverse north across the cone and into Avalanche Canyon. Do NOT turn off into the South Chute — that is the standard route. Instead keep going north up the canyon, past the Thumb, roughly 1.5 miles of steady uphill to Crystal Pass at the canyon's head.

The canyon is loose, poorly consolidated talus and scree when snow-free and much faster on firm early-season snow; carry an axe June into July. The final few hundred feet to the pass steepen, there is often a remnant of ice below the scree fan leading up to it, and softening snow by mid-morning is a good argument for an early start.

crystal pass at the head of avalanche canyon and
hits.text:
There is no ambiguity at the top: the West Arete is the prominent ridge rising directly out of Crystal Pass at the head of Avalanche Canyon, and it runs straight up to Constance's summit ridge crest. If you are standing in a windy col with the canyon behind you and a ridge going up on your right toward the summit, you are at the start.

The negative marker is a turn made much lower down. If you found yourself climbing a scree chute out of the east side of the canyon with the Cat Ears above you, you are on the standard South Chute route and will end up in the upper maze and the traverses, not on the arete. The arete approach never leaves the canyon floor until the canyon itself ends.

On the arete, the climbing stays close to the crest on broken class 2 and 3 with the odd class 4 or low fifth step, so easy ground at the start is correct here and is not a sign you are off route.

runs: no sites are held as same day walk ups
hits.text: A wilderness permit is required and Flapjack Lakes is a named quota area, limited year round, so this is the one booking in the zone that will actually stop your trip. Permits are issued only through the federal recreation booking site; the online reservation window for this camp runs mid-June to mid-October, and the whole summer season releases in one drop on April 15 at 7 a.m. Pacific. No sites are held as same-day walk-ups — the old half-reserved, half-first-come arrangement is gone, and availability now updates live, so cancellations are the only late route in. For dates outside the online window you have to arrange it directly with the park's wilderness information office. Fees are a non-refundable per-permit reservation charge plus a per-person nightly charge for anyone sixteen and over, with an annual wilderness pass available that covers the nightly half. Parties of seven or more must take the group site. Bear canisters are required. Campfires are prohibited — the lakes are above the 3,500 ft parkwide fire line. Camping is in designated sites only. Stock is not allowed on the Flapjack trail, and dogs are not allowed on park wilderness trails. A park entrance pass is needed for the drive in, and the access road up Lake Cushman is unpaved for its last stretch and closes for snow and weather. Weekday permits here are usually gettable; summer weekends are not.

hits.text: From the Staircase Ranger Station (~770-850 ft, at the end of Lake Cushman Rd/North Fork Skokomish Rd), the approach starts on the North Fork Skokomish River Trail, a gently graded old decommissioned roadbed that runs up-valley through old-growth forest for about 3.7-3.8 miles to the former road-end/Spike Camp junction with the Flapjack Lakes Trail. Bear onto the Flapjack Lakes Trail, which climbs steadily and then steeply (with one rough slide/washout bypass to pick through) for about 4 more miles, gaining about 2,000 ft, to reach Flapjack Lakes (~3,850 ft, about 7.5-8 miles from the trailhead) - the standard base camp. Flapjack Lakes is a designated, permit-limited backcountry camp, so reserve ahead for summer weekends. Reliable water is available at the lakes and at several creek crossings on the lower trail; treat before drinking. From camp, continue about 1.5 miles on maintained trail up-basin toward Gladys Divide; just before the divide, leave the trail and climb southeast up a steep snow/scree couloir (several hundred feet of gain, often 35-40+ degrees) to Needle Pass. This couloir holds firm, icy snow well into summer, and crampons plus an ice axe are advisable for most of the season - it's the single biggest hazard of the approach, since a slip on hard snow here has real consequences. From Needle Pass, turn left (east) and scramble exposed Class 3 terrain to the summit of Beta Peak, descend through its right-most summit notch (one Class 4 move and a short gully), traverse high toward Cruiser, then drop down a longer connecting gully to reach Cruiser's base, where the roped climbing begins (a Class 4 gully leads to a large chockstone; go left around it and squeeze through a short tunnel to reach the platform below the 5.0 pitch). All told this is roughly 8-9 miles from the trailhead to the base of the technical climbing, crossing Needle Pass at about 5,700 ft on the way, typically 5-7 hours to camp and another push to the base the next day. Fog and low cloud are common on the ridge and ridge-basin route-finding above Flapjack Lakes is easy to lose in flat light, so know the boot-tread line before committing.

The base of the roped climbing is the mouth of a Class 4 gully and you identify it by the large chockstone wedged in it above you — pass that block on its left and squeeze through the short tunnel behind it. That tunnel is the Cannon Hole, and coming out of it puts you on the broad, airy platform where the rope comes out; from the far end of the platform the low-fifth face pitch runs to a belay on the summit crest. Two decoys: the couloir up from Gladys Divide has more than one apparent exit and the correct one is Needle Pass itself, not the first gap in the rock, and Beta Peak's other notches cliff out below. Above the platform, look hard at the anchor before you weight it — the good two-bolt station sits near older rusted hardware that should not be trusted.

hits.text: A wilderness permit is required and Flapjack Lakes is a named quota area, limited year round, so this is the one booking in the zone that will actually stop your trip. Permits are issued only through the federal recreation booking site; the online reservation window for this camp runs mid-June to mid-October, and the whole summer season releases in one drop on April 15 at 7 a.m. Pacific. No sites are held as same-day walk-ups — the old half-reserved, half-first-come arrangement is gone, and availability now updates live, so cancellations are the only late route in. For dates outside the online window you have to arrange it directly with the park's wilderness information office. Fees are a non-refundable per-permit reservation charge plus a per-person nightly charge for anyone sixteen and over, with an annual wilderness pass available that covers the nightly half. Parties of seven or more must take the group site. Bear canisters are required. Campfires are prohibited — the lakes are above the 3,500 ft parkwide fire line. Camping is in designated sites only. Stock is not allowed on the Flapjack trail, and dogs are not allowed on park wilderness trails. A park entrance pass is needed for the drive in, and the access road up Lake Cushman is unpaved for its last stretch and closes for snow and weather. Weekday permits here are usually gettable; summer weekends are not.

Start from Ouzel Lake (~5,700 ft) and head eastward up the west slopes, which are semi-open initially and transition to alpine terrain around 6,200 ft. hits.text: Mount Daniel is the highest point in both King and Kittitas counties — a broad, multi-summited massif above the Cle Elum headwaters. It has five named summits (East Peak 7,899 ft, Middle Summit 7,959 ft, the true high point at West Summit, West Pyramid, and Northwest Peak); USGS topo maps historically mislabel the "Daniels" benchmark on the East Peak, so parties that stop at the Middle Summit have not reached the actual top. The mountain carries a shrinking glacier complex (Daniel, Lynch, and Foss Glaciers) that, together with neighboring Mount Hinman, included nine distinct glaciers as recently as 1984. First climbed in 1925 by a Mountaineers party via the north-side glacier route.

The approach has a hard edge and it is the ledge traverse into Peggy's Pond. That half-mile of narrow ledges with exposure is the last thing between trail and mountain, and it is the point at which a party knows it has left the walking behind. Peggy's Pond is the base camp and the last water.

From the pond, the finding is an altitude and a shape: braided boot paths head northwest then west across heather benches and talus, gaining roughly 1,500 ft over about a mile, to the broad southeast ridge at 6,800 to 7,000 ft. You are on the right ridge when it narrows westward with the Hyas Creek Glacier on your right and Circle Lake far below on your left. That pairing — glacier right, lake left — is the confirmation, and it does not need the summit to be visible.

The next checkpoint is a saddle at about 7,600 ft between the East and Middle summits, reached by traversing climbers' trail and open scree below the East Summit at 7,899 ft. The path is faint where it first leaves the ridge and well defined afterwards, so a faint start is not evidence you are off route.

Where the glacier comes in: to use the Daniel Glacier proper, enter it just north of a prominent spire on the Northeast Ridge and traverse west across it to the Middle Summit.

And the one thing not to do near the top: the true West Summit at 7,960 ft is reached over loose talus, lingering snowfields and the rocky margin of the Daniel Glacier remnant. Stay on the rock and scree spine. Wandering onto the glacier ice on the north side is where the crevasses are.

hits.text:
The arrival test is a lake you walk across. Traversing below the Daniel Glacier you come to Lynch draw and, in season, to frozen Pea Soup Lake. Walk straight across it and get onto the ice above the low rocks on its far side. That is the base of the Lynch Glacier, and standing on the lake surface is an unambiguous confirmation you are in the right basin.

What to do when the lake has melted out, which is the common case from mid-July: do not try to force the draw, which can be flooded. Instead climb the ridge separating the Daniel and Lynch glaciers for a couple of hundred yards to the first minor notch at about 6,600 ft. Drop roughly 100 ft off it to a snowfield hugging the ridge, then work climbers' left via a second snowfield and rock benches onto the Lynch Glacier. First minor notch at 6,600 ft, then down 100 ft and left: that is a counted sequence rather than a described one, which is what you want in cloud.

Getting onto the ice, in either season: early, take the snow finger on climbers' right. Late, bypass on climbers' left by class 3 scrambling, and expect a moat at the transition. The loose rotten rock used to reach the ice is repeatedly reported as more dangerous than the glacier itself.

And the top tells you which summit is which: the glacier leads to the gap between the two highest summits. From the notch, the west summit — on your right — is the true high point. Late in the season expect a detour around crevasses about two thirds of the way up.

A scope note that matters to peak-list parties: reaching the upper Daniel Glacier from Peggy's Pond by the Southeast Ridge or the Hyas Creek Glacier is a scramble and is not this route.

From Dip Top Gap the traverse is west until you are on the shoulder looking down into the Foss River drainage; the descent from that shoulder lands at the lake outlet. hits.text: Start at the Goodell Creek Trailhead (Goodell Creek Group Camp, ~500-600 ft) off SR-20 just west of Newhalem. The first stretch follows an old logging-road grade/climbers' path along Goodell Creek for a little over a mile before it narrows to a boot-beaten track. Roughly 4 miles in, near Terror Creek, watch for the unmarked junction where the Terror Creek climbers' path splits off — historically flagged only by a rock arrow, a post, and a large cairn, so route-finding here is a genuine crux; the path is well-defined at first but dies out into creek-bottom brush and devils club lower down. Ford/cross Terror Creek at about 2000 ft: the customary crossing is a large log roughly 500 ft upstream of where the path hits the creek, but in high water this log is sometimes submerged and parties have had to scout alternate logs — treat this as a conditions-dependent obstacle, not a given. From the creek, the path grinds directly and relentlessly up the opposing hillside, gaining close to 4000 ft in under two miles through forest, then open heather slopes above treeline — steep and loose in spots. The climbers' path eventually merges into 'Stump Hollow' and follows the narrow crest north to the standard basecamp area near 'Chopping Block Camp' (~6000-6400 ft), the usual base for Southern Pickets objectives. The south ridge starts at the notch at the top of the Barrier — the long rocky rib dividing Terror Basin from Crescent Creek Basin — immediately south of Degenhardt's summit, and it can be reached from either basin. From Terror Basin, climb the Terror Glacier to its upper end (open crevasses can usually be walked around; crampons and an axe are standard here even in summer), then broken rock, heather benches and steep, loose dirt to the notch. From Crescent Creek Basin — reached by traversing Stump Hollow to the roughly 6400 ft saddle near the Chopping Block and descending about 200 ft — a snow ramp rises to the same notch. Parties moving between the two basins cross the Barrier either low, over loose ledges at the base of the Terror Glacier, or high, over moats and steep choss near the top of the glacier just below Degenhardt; both are loose, exposed, and consistently described as 'Pickets Class 3' — sustained, serious, low-fifth-class-feeling terrain despite the modest rating. Total trip is roughly 18.7 miles round-trip with about 600-8100+ ft of elevation range; water is available at Goodell Creek and the Terror Creek crossing, with seasonal snowmelt/tarns higher up that can dry out late season.

hits.text: Mount Fairchild (6,899 ft) is the second-highest peak in the Bailey Range, a glaciated subrange deep in the interior of Olympic National Park's Daniel J. Evans Wilderness. It carries the small, retreating Fairchild Glacier on its northeast flank and sits about 0.84 mi northeast of higher neighbor Mount Carrie (6,995 ft). No trail comes anywhere close to the summit — nearly all ascents are made as a side-trip during the multi-day Bailey Range Traverse rather than as a standalone climb, and the peak sees only a handful of ascents most years. First climbed in 1963 by Denny Pruitt, Dan Baker, Jack Christiansen, and Roy Etten.

Named by the 1889-90 Seattle Press Expedition for Governor Elisha P. Ferry. It is almost never climbed as a standalone objective -- nearly every ascent is a side-summit tagged mid-trip during the multi-day Bailey Range Traverse, the off-trail alpine high route linking Sol Duc's High Divide to the Elwha valley. The summit block itself is a straightforward walk-up over loose 'Olympics dagger' scree from Ferry Basin; the real difficulty of this route is the days of off-trail travel, routefinding, and exposed ridge traverses required just to reach its base.

This is the last maintained tread; everything beyond is boot-path/climbers'-trail, the start of the Ptarmigan Traverse. From the pass, leave the trail and climb/contour east and north below Cache Ridge toward Cache Col (~6,903 ft), crossing the toe of the Cache Glacier — generally a mellow, low-crevasse-hazard crossing in early/mid season but rope up if it's opened out or snow-covered, since crevasse hazard has caught parties off guard here in low-snow years. From Cache Col, descend a talus traverse on a good climbers' trail down to Kool-Aid Lake (6,100 ft), a small meltwater tarn that is the standard base camp for the route (no permit required, no fires) — roughly 3 hours and 5-6 miles from Cascade Pass, so plan on 5-7 hours trailhead-to-camp overall. From Kool-Aid Lake continue south past Art's Knoll to the broad, well-known 'Red Ledge' — an exposed traverse over loose rock and (often) lingering snow patches that many parties choose to rope for; it is the most consistently reported crux of the approach and is noticeably worse when snow-covered. Beyond Red Ledge, follow a rough climbers' path roughly a mile over meadows, snow, talus, and small rock ribs toward the Middle Cascade Glacier icefall (~6,500 ft), then rope up and ascend the glacier's left/SSE side, weaving through crevasses, to the Spider-Formidable col (7,320 ft). From the col, descend/traverse (plunge-stepping snow, crampons for icy sections) to a flat camp/staging area below the south face snow slope near a notch around 7,050 ft — this is the jump-off point for the climb proper. From there the final approach to the route gains the south-face snowfield alcove via one of two options: a hidden gully on the left (reportedly with 5th-class moves) or, more commonly, a winding ledge on the right rated 3rd class with one 3rd-class-plus section. Water is available at Kool-Aid Lake and from glacier meltwater streams along the Middle Cascade Glacier margins; carry enough for the long, exposed traverse sections beyond. Overall this is a long, remote glacier-and-ledge approach with real route-finding demands — most parties treat it as a 2-3 day trip with camp at Kool-Aid Lake or the south-face notch rather than a single push.

runs: at the end of the cascade river road
hits.text:
Cascade Pass trailhead at 3,600 ft at the end of the Cascade River Road. The maintained trail runs 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft to Cascade Pass at 5,392 ft — well graded, an hour and a half to two hours at a steady pace. Everything beyond is bootpath and it is the start of the Ptarmigan Traverse.

From the pass take the bootpath uphill to the south and traverse along Mix-Up Arm on heather, talus and snow, then up the mellow Cache Glacier to Cache Col at about 6,900 ft — corniced early in the season. From the col, a descending traverse south-south-east on more heather, talus and snow reaches Kool-Aid Lake at 6,100 ft, the standard base camp, roughly three hours and five to six miles from Cascade Pass.

South past Art's Knoll comes the Red Ledge: an exposed traverse over loose rock and lingering snow patches that many parties rope for, and by common consent the crux of the approach. It is noticeably worse when snow-covered.

Beyond it a rough path runs about a mile over meadow, snow, talus and small rock ribs toward the Middle Cascade Glacier icefall at around 6,500 ft. Rope up, ascend the glacier's left side weaving through crevasses, and reach the Spider-Formidable col at 7,320 ft.

runs: a spur ridge to reach a third gully and
hits.text:
This is the part that is easy to get wrong, and it is a counting exercise rather than a description.

From the col, go through the narrow eastern notch and descend roughly 150 vertical feet of steep snow — or in the moat beside it — before it becomes feasible to start contouring right, to the west. Do not try to contour immediately from the notch; you have to lose that height first.

Continue west over slabs and snow, then heather and small rock outcrops. Leave the snow onto class 3 rock, climb up and then left to a distinct ledge. From that ledge make a rising traverse to the north-west, scrambling across two gullies. Then cross a spur ridge to reach a third gully — and it is the third gully that you climb.

So the test is: from the ledge, the first two gullies are crossed, not entered. If you start up the first gully you meet after the ledge you will be on steeper, looser ground short of the line. If you have crossed a spur ridge and are looking up a gully, that is the one.

Some trip reports also describe reaching the south-face snow alcove from a staging camp near a notch at about 7,050 ft below the col, by either a hidden gully on the left with fifth-class moves or, more commonly, a winding ledge on the right at class 3 with one harder step. The right-hand ledge is the usual choice; if you are pulling fifth-class moves you have taken the left option.

runs: by don bechlem ne peak and jack newman sw peak
hits.text: Mount Fricaba (7,139 ft) is a rain-shadowed, double-summit peak in the north-central Olympic Mountains, straddling the boundary between Olympic National Park and the Buckhorn Wilderness of Olympic National Forest — it is the highest point in both. It sits near Mount Deception and Mount Mystery and is composed largely of shattered Eocene sandstone, turbidite, and basaltic oceanic crust, producing loose shale and scree that make the climbing non-technical but tedious underfoot. First ascent 1957 by Don Bechlem (NE peak) and Jack Newman (SW peak). This route takes the standard approach via Home Lake and Constance Pass into Deception Basin, gaining the peak's Southwest Ridge; an alternate approach climbs the Northeast Ridge directly from the Upper Dungeness River/Royal Basin side (crossing the river near ~4,400 ft, over Point 6138, along the ridge crest to the summit), often used as a loop with the SW-ridge line and covered by the 'Deception, Mystery, Fricaba & Hal Foss' scramble.

Without the boat, add a six-mile shoreline walk. From Big Beaver Landing follow the well-maintained Big Beaver Creek Trail about 10-11.5 miles through old-growth cedar past 39 Mile Camp to Luna Camp, then continue roughly 1 to 1.5 miles further north. Watch on the left for a small cairn or a scratched arrow on a split log marking the cut-off, and cross Big Beaver Creek on a log just north of where Access Creek enters it; some years you have to wade. Then bushwhack up Access Creek: wade the valley-bottom devil's club, cross to the north side and climb directly upslope through huckleberry, then several hours of heavy forest, deadfall and alternating slide alder. Near 3,800 ft cross back to the south bank where the brush pinches out between a tongue of forest and a tongue of talus, and follow cairns and a faint climbers' path up talus into Access Creek Basin at about 4,300 ft - a good first camp. From the basin grind up a long, steep, grungy scree chute to Access Col at 6,100 ft, then make the notorious traverse on very steep heather, talus and slabs (ice axe out; some parties wear crampons for traction on the heather) to Luna Col / Luna Pass at about 7,100-7,200 ft, the standard high camp on glacially polished slabs. From Luna Col drop a few hundred feet east, then traverse right at about the 6,600 ft level across ribs, gullies and small basins to the crest of a subsidiary ridge running southeast, then cross the large basin in front of you dropping no lower than 6,300 ft. From 6,300 ft in the middle of that basin start the ascending traverse northwest to the 7,050 ft notch where the route proper begins.

runs: class 3 gully to the flat upper fury glacier
hits.text: About 50 ft short of Point 7,850's high point, cross to its west side on a ledge and scramble down a Class 3 gully to the flat upper Fury Glacier at roughly 7,750 ft. Do not continue to the summit of the sub-peak.

runs: in front of you dropping no lower than 6 300
hits.text:
The route begins at a numbered notch and the whole approach is a contour to reach it. From Luna Col drop a few hundred feet east, then traverse right at about the 6,600 ft level across ribs, gullies and small basins to the crest of a subsidiary ridge running southeast. Cross the large basin in front of you dropping no lower than 6,300 ft, and from 6,300 ft in the middle of that basin start an ascending traverse northwest to the 7,050 ft notch. That notch is where the route proper begins.

So the test is an altimeter test, and it works in cloud because it needs no view: the traverse is held between 6,300 and 6,600 ft, and then and only then does it climb. If you are below 6,300 ft you have dropped too far into the basin and will pay for it; if you never got below 6,600 ft you are still on the ribs and have not crossed the basin at all.

Arrival: a notch is a gap you can stand in with ground falling away on both sides. From it the ridge runs west toward Fury and there is an exposed, level stretch the route's own account calls the sidewalk in the sky. Reaching an airy horizontal crest immediately above the notch confirms it.

What going too far looks like: continuing the ascending traverse past the notch, or contouring on around, puts you under the Southeast Glacier, which is the standard route's ground and a different climb.

Countable feature on the route itself: there is one 20 ft step on the east ridge that parties rappel on the way down off a medium cam or chock. One step, not several.

runs: one of the longest ridgelines in the lower
hits.text: This is Wayne Wallace's solo masterpiece, first ascended August 24-27, 2006, in four days (exiting/reporting on the 28th). The route ascends the south buttress as a continuous skyline ridge featuring four major pinnacles separated by deep notches: Rooster Comb (knife-edge horizontal traverse) and the Pole of Remoteness (notable pinnacle near summit) are the most famous features. Technical climbing is moderate but committing (5.9–5.10), mixed with extensive scrambling and mandatory rappelling. Rock quality is variable (granodiorite and choss); many ascents done unroped to save time, increasing risk. First ascent involved free-soloing sections up to 5.8. The route is one of the longest ridgelines in the lower 48 and one of the most remote alpine objectives in North America.

hits.text: The West Peak route starts from the East Peak via the Southeast Glacier approach. The traverse between summits is a wild and fun scramble with decent exposure and more technical difficulty than the East Peak ascent. Three distinct towers require climbing up and over; rock quality on this connecting ridge is notoriously poor — climbers describe it as 'shockingly mobile' loose talus and standard chossy 4th class, not sound rock. The route involves low Class 5 rock climbing up to 5.4, though many climbers solo the final sections. A 50-60 meter rope is recommended for rappelling 4th and 5th class terrain.

hits.text: From the PCT-Northbound (Rainy Pass) trailhead on SR 20 (elev. ~4,855-4,900 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail north. The trail climbs steadily through subalpine forest and larch parkland past Porcupine Creek, reaching Cutthroat Pass (6,820 ft) at about 4.9 miles / ~1,900 ft gain (roughly 2-2.5 hours at a hiking pace). There is no water at the pass itself; Porcupine Creek below is the last reliable source before the high country dries out in late summer, so top off there. From Cutthroat Pass continue north on the PCT, which drops to Granite Pass (~6,300 ft) and then contours across open, sparsely-treed slopes to Snowy Creek Meadow (~6,400-6,900 ft) - a common camp/water stop, with a short side-trail up to Snowy Lakes if you want a higher, more scenic bivy. From the meadow, stay on the PCT northbound roughly another 1-1.5 miles / ~350 ft gain (about an hour) to Methow Pass (~6,600 ft). Leave the trail here: travel west/southwest, off-trail, through open heather and talus benches toward Mount Hardy's east ridge. Gain the ridge and follow moderate slopes of sand, scree and talus - loose in spots, with real route-finding required - up to the saddle between the true summit and a lower false summit (roughly 7,200-7,600 ft). From the saddle, several hundred feet of enjoyable Class 2-3 scrambling over blocky rock leads to the summit at 8,097 ft; some parties note a notch below the true summit block that's crossed before a short, shallow summit gully. Total one-way distance from the trailhead to the summit is roughly 11-12 miles with about 5,100 ft of cumulative gain, matching the recorded figures - this is a long day for strong parties or, more commonly, a 2-day trip with camp near Snowy Creek Meadow/Snowy Lakes. Snow can linger on the upper ridge and in north-facing gullies near Cutthroat and Granite Passes well into early summer; the highway itself (and both this trailhead and the alternate Swamp Creek pullout used for the shorter South Ridge route) sit inside WSDOT's SR 20 winter closure zone, so the route is typically only accessible from around late April or May through November depending on snowpack. Carry an ice axe and know how to use it if attempting before the passes fully melt out.

hits.text: The North Fork Skokomish Trail from Staircase to First Divide and the Home Sweet Home Trail from First Divide down to the Duckabush have been closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, with no reopening date; check the park's trail conditions before planning. When open, the standard way in starts at the Staircase trailhead (~785 ft) and follows the North Fork Skokomish River Trail up the valley through old-growth forest, past Camp Pleasant to Nine Stream Camp, where the trail fords the river (deep and swift in high snowmelt or heavy rain). Above Nine Stream it climbs steeply past Two Bear Camp, brushy between Two Bear and the divide, to First Divide (4,688 ft), about 12.5 miles from the trailhead. The much longer alternative comes up the Duckabush River Trail and climbs over First Divide from the north past Home Sweet Home. Just below First Divide on the Skokomish side, the long-abandoned Mount Hopper Way leaves the main trail; its tread has gone under brush, so expect to bushwhack south and east through forest, then climb open talus and subalpine meadow toward Mount Hopper's basin below the summit rockwall (high point ~6,120 ft). This upper stretch has real route-finding difficulty: numerous gullies and ribs look equally plausible from below, snow can choke the gully well into summer (ice axe advisable), and the final scramble features loose rock underfoot — expect to backtrack if you pick the wrong line. Most parties make it a multi-day trip, camping at Two Bear Camp, First Divide or Home Sweet Home rather than pushing car-to-car.

hits.text: Mount La Crosse is a Class 2 scramble summit on the Duckabush/Dosewallips divide in the seldom-visited southern interior of Olympic National Park, part of what is locally called the 'Dosewallips Group.' It rises above La Crosse Pass and Lake La Crosse (the peak's namesake), with White Mountain 0.95 mi SW and the Mount Anderson massif roughly 2.7 mi N. First climbed in 1928 by Richard Paulson, William Ryer, Paul Wiseman, and Frank Woodworth, it remains a multi-day objective with no day-hike trailhead access — reaching it requires backpacking in via the Duckabush River Trail or West Fork Dosewallips River Trail, then leaving maintained trail to scramble open Class 2 slopes above the pass.

runs: a red talus gully east of the carru lago saddle
hits.text: This is the staging camp that makes Mount Carru and Mount Lago short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. What you pay for the position is water and weather. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.

hits.text: Descend by reversing the ascent line exactly: down the North Ridge to the top of the chute, then down-climb the loose chute back to the valley floor — this is the most hazard-prone part of the descent, since the same scree and rockbands that were merely tedious going up become genuinely slippery and rockfall-prone with tired legs and no rope; move one at a time through any narrows and stay alert for parties below. At the bottom, re-ford the North Fork Quinault River (same knee-to-thigh-deep crossing as the approach — check levels, as afternoon snowmelt can raise it) to regain the maintained trail, then simply walk the North Fork Quinault River Trail back out to the trailhead, re-fording Elip and Wild Rose Creeks en route. There is no rappelling on this route: it is a scramble/walk-off (Grade I, Class 3 via the North Ridge, 'Basic Snow/Rock Scramble', or Class 2 hiking), and nothing on it involves fixed anchors, bolts, or rope work — a hand line could be a reasonable precaution for a mixed-experience party on the loose upper chute or on lingering early-season snow, but it is not a technical necessity.

runs: no sites are held as same day walk ups
hits.text: A wilderness permit is required and Flapjack Lakes is a named quota area, limited year round, so this is the one booking in the zone that will actually stop your trip. Permits are issued only through the federal recreation booking site; the online reservation window for this camp runs mid-June to mid-October, and the whole summer season releases in one drop on April 15 at 7 a.m. Pacific. No sites are held as same-day walk-ups — the old half-reserved, half-first-come arrangement is gone, and availability now updates live, so cancellations are the only late route in. For dates outside the online window you have to arrange it directly with the park's wilderness information office. Fees are a non-refundable per-permit reservation charge plus a per-person nightly charge for anyone sixteen and over, with an annual wilderness pass available that covers the nightly half. Parties of seven or more must take the group site. Bear canisters are required. Campfires are prohibited — the lakes are above the 3,500 ft parkwide fire line. Camping is in designated sites only. Stock is not allowed on the Flapjack trail, and dogs are not allowed on park wilderness trails. A park entrance pass is needed for the drive in, and the access road up Lake Cushman is unpaved for its last stretch and closes for snow and weather. Weekday permits here are usually gettable; summer weekends are not.

runs: past a good log bridge with a handrail
hits.text:
The usual way in while SR 20 is open. From the Easy Pass Trailhead near milepost 151, climb about 3.5 miles to the 6,500-ft pass, drop into Fisher Basin, and follow the Fisher Creek Trail down the valley — past a good log bridge with a handrail — to the stream that drains the lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier. About ten miles one way. The trailhead sits inside the highway's winter closure, and the pass is often snowbound until July.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge, sometimes called Christmas Tree Col, which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the Banded Glacier on the far side and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.

runs: a vast field of slide alder and other brush
hits.text: Start at Easy Pass Trailhead at Highway 20 mile 151 (elevation 3,700 ft). Hike 3.5 miles gaining 2,800 feet to Easy Pass (6,500 ft). Descend into Fisher Basin via steep scenic trail through alpine meadows and forest (1.5 miles). Continue to Fisher Creek valley floor and established campsites. From camp area, cross Fisher Creek via large fallen log and travel east side of Douglas Creek valley on faint climber's path. This transition from forest to open terrain is where the route becomes extremely challenging—travelers encounter a vast field of slide alder and other brush, 10+ feet high, virtually impenetrable in many directions, with small rocky stream channels crisscrossing the ground. Progress is measured in inches per minute. Off-trail navigational skill critical.

runs: south along the edge of a steep scree slope
hits.text: The 7,300 ft notch is the first proof and the white rock strip is the second. From the broad basin below the peak, turn south along the edge of a steep scree slope dotted with larch and make a beeline through talus and snow for the notch on the southwest ridge at about 7,300 ft. That notch is the gateway; a gap without the scree-and-larch slope leading to it is the wrong one. From the notch, walking up the southwest ridge leads directly into cliffs — this is expected and is not a sign you are off route. The fix is to drop about a hundred feet on grass to get round a buttress, then traverse upward beneath a striking vertical strip of white rock, hugging the edge below an overhang and taking care on the small loose rock lying over sloping slabs. That white band is unmistakable and is the confirmation you are on the correct traverse. Above it, keep scrambling just below the ridgeline rather than following the jagged crest itself, and finish over stacked boulders to the summit block.

hits.text: Nothing marks the turn — the tell is what happens if you carry straight on. Past Merritt Lake the maintained trail climbs to the ridge trail; a short way along it an unsigned junction sends the climbers' path uphill toward this peak's south slopes. There is no cairn, no post and no blaze, and parties carrying a track have still needed to hunt for it. The overshoot tell is the useful part: going straight on at that junction descends toward Lost Lake, so losing height toward water means you are past the turn and should come back. Higher, the route gives you the one genuinely visual landmark on the mountain — climb the ridge until the snow gives way to a rocky, jagged, narrow crest, which looks impassable at first glance. The line follows the moat between rock and snow just off to the left, stepping up onto the rock to cross ledges, then wraps a big rock tower on its right side, staying close in at its base, and scrambles dirt and ledges to a knoll and one last snowfield. The summit above is bare and flat rather than a point, and the register does not sit on the high point but off to the south of the flat area.

hits.text: The North Face is not descended — after topping out on the summit ridge (9,082 ft), descend via the standard South Slopes / south ridge walk-off: down the south ridge and upper talus to about 7,700 ft, then southwest down broad open slopes to the 6,840 ft saddle. The trail up the valley is the same tread hikers use for Spider Meadow. Walk the Phelps Creek trail, #1511, about three and a half flat miles to where it meets Leroy Creek near 4,120 to 4,140 ft. Cross on a large tree or by rock-hopping — awkward in early season with the creek up — and pick up the well-worn but unsigned climbers' trail, #1512, on the north side of the creek. It is sometimes called the Carne Mountain High Route, but the two are also treated as different paths, so do not assume the names are interchangeable. It climbs steeply, then eases into the Leroy Creek Basin meadow at about 6,100 ft, roughly five miles from the car and a little over two hours for a party moving well with light packs. Above the basin, one party continued on the high-route path less than a quarter mile and then went directly into the upper basin below Maude by way of a gully with a small waterfall. runs: a rib on the right side of the face
hits.text:
The col is not the route, and that is the thing to internalise before you get there. From the col you have to go down about four hundred feet, and not in one clean line — it comes in a series of forced descents alternating with traverses.

The recorded sequence: from the col, take the option toward the Entiat River valley side, downclimb roughly a hundred feet of face to a moderate bench, traverse a couple of hundred yards, be forced down again, traverse again, and eventually arrive at a steep snow slope beneath an overhang. That slope is the steepest ground of the day, around sixty degrees for the first moves, easing above.

The test is visual and it is unambiguous: you have descended far enough when the face comes into full view. Until it does, you are still traversing. One party took an hour and a half from the col to standing on continuous snow at the foot of the face.

Once on it, the lower face runs around thirty-five to forty degrees. A rib on the right side of the face is the line parties choose, not because it is named but because it keeps you out from under the cornice.

What not to expect: a bergschrund. The 1957 first ascent, coming from below on the Ice Lakes side, stood at a schrund between the glacier and the ice sheet above. Parties arriving by the col traverse enter partway up the face and bypass that ground entirely, and modern reports of this approach do not mention a schrund at all. The hazard people actually record here is the cornice at the top — one party had a piece of it come down and sweep across their tracks.

Honest gap worth knowing: nothing published tells you how to distinguish Maude's north face from Seven Fingered Jack's. The two, with Fernow, form one continuous headwall at the head of the Entiat, so the col is your positional anchor rather than the look of the wall.

On the way down, stay south and descend toward Ice Lakes. Parties regularly drop into one of the gullies cut into Maude's west side, either by mistake or thinking it a shortcut, and it is not.

It can be reached from Leroy Basin by the climbers' path heading south, or from the long Entiat River approach.

hits.text: Approach as for the North Face: Phelps Creek trailhead, the Phelps Creek trail to the Leroy Creek crossing, then the unmarked climbers' trail up the north side of Leroy Creek into the basin, and on up toward Ice Lakes. Parties bivy on ledges above the south side of the lake, below the South Ridge. That is the sensible camp because the South Ridge is the descent — but be clear that it puts you on the wrong side of the mountain for this route, so the morning starts with a long traverse over a cliff band to reach the access notch. One party set themselves a turnaround rule of two hours from camp to the notch, on the grounds that any slower and there would not be time to finish. Cross the talus above the lake to the notch that lets you onto the Entiat Glacier. Rope up and descend to find a short crossing through the ablation zone of the receding glacier — this is harder than the old published photograph suggests. Skirt below the rock spur and head up toward the icefall.

hits.text:
The notch is the thing you can get wrong, and there is a documented decoy. The access notch is at about 7,200 ft. A climbers' path leads to a different notch at about 6,900 ft, and a party who took it for the right one paid for the error with a long detour in the wrong direction up an ugly scree bash. If the notch you have reached is around six-nine rather than seven-two, keep going.

Once through the correct notch and onto the glacier, the sequence is: descend, cross the ablation zone, pass under the rock spur, then work rightward beneath the headwall. Arrival at the climbing is a change in the ice — you move from walking to big crevasses with short vertical steps, and above those the angle relaxes to about thirty-five degrees of ice running up to the base of the rock.

That base of rock is the second, unmistakable transition: roughly nine hundred feet of fourth and low fifth class above it, with several ramps to choose between. Take the line of least resistance trending slightly toward the ridge crest. The rock is crumbly and protection is scarce, so running belays are the usual method rather than pitching it. There is a distinctive step-across at the top of a couloir partway up.

A note on how much ice you will actually find: in a heavy snow year one party bypassed roughly two pitches of the icefall on steep snow slopes off to the side, and the whole icefall took them an hour of running belays where they had budgeted six. Do not plan the day around a pitch count from an older description.

Descent is the South Ridge, which took that party half an hour — which is exactly why the camp is where it is.

There is no maintained trail to the top; the standard scramble route climbs the east side via the Noyes-Meany col, reached only after a multi-day wilderness approach. hits.text:
From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead on FR-2870 — large parking area, vault toilet; an overnight stay needs an Olympic National Park wilderness permit booked in advance — take Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 about a mile. The trail forks just before the Royal Creek footlog bridge; bear right onto the Royal Basin Trail #832. A short way up, stay left where the Maynard Burn Way branches off; it is easy to mistake in early light.

Royal Creek Camp, about 4 miles in, is a common first night. Royal Lake at about 7.2 miles and 5,100 ft is the main basecamp, with designated sites and a seasonal ranger post — the last dependable water before the dry climb. Many parties push on to camps around 5,800-6,200 ft in upper Royal Basin.

From upper Royal Basin, climb a moraine and a snowfield of roughly 35-40 degrees to the notch on the Royal-Deception divide at about 6,500-6,560 ft, then descend shower-tile scree to grass and heather benches above Deception Basin.

runs: a jade green moraine bounded lake sits at the
hits.text:
The base of the climb is the lower left corner of the Mystery Glacier, and the thing that marks it is a lake you cannot mistake for anything else: a jade-green moraine-bounded lake sits at the glacier's base. Drop off the benches into Deception Basin, cross a dark moraine, and the lake is at the foot of the ice. Get on the glacier at its lower left corner. Colour is a fog-usable marker at short range and there is one such lake here.

The test for the glacier crossing is a diagonal: you enter at the lower left and exit at the upper right, at a col at about 6,700 ft on the peak's east side. The ice is stagnant and low-angle with a few small crevasses to step over — this is a walk with a rope on, not a serious glacier. If you are climbing straight up the fall line rather than trending right, you are not heading for the col.

Second test, above the col, and it is a specific distance and a specific side: from the col traverse mixed rock and snow to reach open snow about 200 ft south of the col, then climb those slopes staying south of the blocky rock band immediately above. South of the rock band, not through it. Snow angles reach around 40 degrees and take pickets well. The gullies feeding this section are where the rockfall comes from, so move one at a time and keep the party to three or fewer.

Third test, and it is the commitment point: a short class 4 step on poor rock, with steep runout dirt below it, gains a notch near 7,500 ft. Trend climber's left on the approach to it. This step has to be downclimbed on the way out, usually unroped, and one party rated a single move on the reverse at 5.8 — so it is worth being certain about before you commit. A moat over 30 ft deep has been reported below the gully late in the season, which changes how the section is entered and exited.

What confirms you are through: beyond the notch a clean Class 3 gully leads to the summit block, and the rock gets markedly better than anything below it. Good rock on this peak means you are nearly there.

runs: the base of the 80 ft summit rock
hits.text: Descend the same North Ridge/Blue Glacier line in reverse. From the base of the ~80 ft summit rock, the roughly Class 4 with one Class 5 (5.4-ish) step is reversed by rappel rather than downclimbed by most parties: build/clip the fixed summit anchor (recent parties note slung horns/blocks and a semi-permanent thin rappel line has appeared in some seasons, though this should not be trusted blindly) and rappel the north side of the summit block. A single-strand rappel with a 40-50m rope reaches the notch/belay ledge for most of the season; a 60m rope (doubled, ~30m per strand) is the safer bet as summer progresses and snow recedes below the block, and some parties join two ropes to make one long rappel to the base of the block instead of two shorter ones. An alternative is a single-rope rappel off the northwest edge to a belay ledge, then downclimbing the original route. Anchor material is a mix of fixed slings on horns/chockstones and natural gear (small cams in the 0.3-0.4 range have been used to back up or build anchors) rather than bolts — inspect any in-place tat before trusting it. Below the summit block, reverse the snow slope (mind the runout) back to the Snow Dome plateau, re-rope for the Blue Glacier crossing, regain the lateral moraine catwalk, and retrace the Hoh River Trail 17+ miles back to the trailhead, watching for the ladder/washout section and any lingering steep snow between Glacier Meadows and Elk Lake.

up the north face on mostly solid rock
hits.text:
The only technical climbing on this route is the summit block of the West Peak, and finding it is the crux of the day, because the true summit is not visible from the north side. A party that keeps navigating toward the highest thing it can see from Snow Dome ends up at the five-fingered false summit, which is east of where it wants to be.

The rule that works: go south-southeast through one of the two gaps to the left, or far left, of the five fingers, and come at the summit from the east or southeast — approaching an objective you cannot yet see.

Once through, a rising traverse leads to a loose rocky gully; you go up that, over, and down into a second rocky gully, then up a final steep snow slope that delivers you to the foot of the block.

You are there when you are standing under a discrete rock tower roughly 80 ft high. The standard finish is class 4 on loose rocky ramps; there is also a line of about 80 ft straight up the north face on mostly solid rock, around 5.4. If you are under a snow slope with no rock tower above it, you have not arrived — keep going.

Expect a bergschrund or moat immediately below the block. Its state changes through the season and it can force a short detour or a stretch of short-roping; on the pinnacle just east of the West Peak parties have found a schrund below it and deteriorating scree above, and have grouped tightly or moved one at a time because of the rockfall.

hits.text: The path begins on the north side of the creek where the road fords it, and follows the north bank through old growth, boulders and windfall. The brush thickens, then the path makes a rising traverse into a rocky gully; climb that gully — talus, sometimes snow-filled — to a small basin at about 4,300 ft. Fix that basin in mind, because on the way down it is the aiming point before you drop back to the creek and losing it puts you in the wrong drainage. From it, continue straight up and then cut left up a second gully into the basin east of the summit near 5,400 ft. That upper basin is the base of the climb proper, and two lines leave it for the south ridge: a centre gully, and a left-hand one giving 45 to 50 degree snow followed by a short loose, brushy Class 4 rock step. hits.text: Mount Queets (6,476 ft) is a remote summit in the interior Olympic Mountains, sitting on the divide near the headwaters of both the Elwha and Queets rivers, just southwest of the Bailey Range and Dodwell-Rixon Pass. It is built of Eocene basalt, and heavy winter snowfall sustains the small Queets Glacier in a cirque on its north slope despite the peak's modest elevation. Harry Fisher (recorded as James B. Hanmore) and Nelson Linsley made the first recorded ascent in 1890 during the Army's O'Neil Expedition. There is no maintained trail to the peak; it lies deep in Olympic National Park wilderness and is normally climbed either as a side objective from the multi-day Bailey Range Traverse or via a dedicated cross-country backpack up the Elwha River to Elwha Basin.
