hits.text: There is no direct trailhead-to-summit trail. Vehicle access to the Elwha Valley has been closed since a May 2021 washout on Olympic Hot Springs Road; you now walk or bike an extra ~6-7 miles from the Madison Falls parking area (past the washout, then up Whiskey Bend Road) just to reach the Whiskey Bend trailhead. From Whiskey Bend, follow the Elwha River Trail to Chicago Camp, where it fords the Elwha short of Low Divide, then leave the trail and continue about 3 miles cross-country up into Elwha Basin and over Dodwell-Rixon Pass (4,763 ft) to reach the north ridge of Mount Queets. Most parties treat this as a multi-day (4+ day round trip) wilderness objective, commonly combined with the Bailey Range Traverse via Queets Basin to the west. The lower third of the north ridge is mostly 2nd-class scrambling on crumbly rock and heather; where it becomes impassable, drop a few hundred feet to traverse steep, firm scree around 5,300 ft on the east side to bypass a cliff band, then regain the ridge for an easy 2nd-class scramble around its west side before a moderately steep snow slope on the east side leads to the summit. Microspikes and an axe have been used here even in late August.

runs: halfway along the east side of the ridge then
hits.text: Dodwell-Rixon Pass is the divide between the Elwha and Queets drainages, with a small tarn just below it and Mount Olympus in view to the west. The north ridge is gained directly from the pass, so the base is the pass itself and the lower third of the ridge is straightforward Class 2 on crumbly rock and steep heather with brushy patches. The identification that matters is where to leave the crest. About a third of the way along, the ridge ahead becomes impassable; the move is to drop a couple of hundred feet off the east side onto steep, firm scree and traverse. Hold that traverse until you have passed below a steep cliff roughly halfway along the east side of the ridge, then climb back up talus, steep heather and crumbly slabs to regain the crest for the final third. From there it is easy Class 2 around the west side of the ridge, then a moderately steep snow slope on the east side to the top — snow that has needed an axe here even in late August. If you are still on the crest and the rock ahead of you is vertical, you have missed the drop-off point and should go back for it.

hits.text:
The Glacier Basin trailhead is in Loop D of White River Campground (about 4,300–4,400 ft), reached by the White River road off SR 410. That road and the campground are seasonal and open on the snowpack, not on a date.

The trail follows the Inter Fork of the White River on an old mining road grade, 3.5 miles to Glacier Basin Campground (~5,935 ft): six designated sites, a toilet and a bear-proof food cache. This is the last reliable water and the last forested camp.

Above Glacier Basin a climbers' path continues about a mile up the lateral moraine — conspicuously yellowish once it melts out — to the toe of the Inter Glacier at roughly 7,000 ft. The Inter Glacier is about 1,500 ft of moderate snow; it is the mildest glacier on the route but it opens real crevasses as the season goes on, and roped travel is standard. It leads to Camp Curtis on the rim at about 8,700 ft.

From Camp Curtis the route drops slightly and traverses onto the lower Emmons Glacier, rounding the southern side of Steamboat Prow to Camp Schurman (about 9,460 ft), where the Emmons and Winthrop glaciers split around the Prow. There is an NPS ranger hut, an emergency radio on the front of it, toilets and a blue-bag barrel; tent platforms are dug into snow on the Emmons side.

Camp Schurman's nightly capacity is small — far smaller than Camp Muir's — so a permit here is worth reserving. The same Rainier permit structure applies: a per-person climbing permit for glacier travel or ground above roughly 10,000 ft, plus a wilderness permit for each overnight.

hits.text:
From Paradise (5,420 ft) follow the paved trail about a mile to Glacier Vista, then the Nisqually Moraine climbers' path to roughly 6,300 ft where boot paths drop onto the Nisqually Glacier. Rope up here — the crossing is through crevassed ground exposed to icefall from above and is dangerous in poor visibility.

From the east side of the glacier there are two ways onto the Wapowety Cleaver ground. One is a flat traverse to the base of a gully known as The Fan, climbed directly to a bench at about 7,300 ft; The Fan carries avalanche, rockfall and steep-snow hazard. The other climbs the Nisqually/Wilson margin at about 6,800 ft through an often-crevassed gully to the same 7,300–7,400 ft bench.

Above the bench, snow slopes lead to a string of established camps: Wilson Moraine (8,200–8,600 ft), Lower Castle (9,250 ft) and Upper Castle (9,400–9,500 ft), the most common base, with running water from about mid-June. Higher again, rock islands along the west edge of the Turtle snowfield between roughly 9,500 and 10,500 ft hold good bivouacs, and there is usually flowing water at the snowfield edges in warm weather.

Camp Hazard (about 10,800 ft) is the traditional high camp and is named for what sits above it: the Kautz Ice Cliff. Many parties deliberately camp lower and climb through Camp Hazard early rather than sleep under the cliff. On the Turtle, keep to the western, climber's-left side — the centre and east are raked by ice and rock off the cliff.

Rainier permits apply: a per-person climbing permit for glacier travel or ground above roughly 10,000 ft, and a wilderness permit for each overnight camp in the high-use season.

runs: and around the toe of the icefall to
hits.text:
The single most useful fact about this route is that the technical climbing starts below Camp Hazard, not above it. Parties who expect to walk out of camp and start climbing walk straight under the ice cliff.

From camp, pick up the climbers' path on the rock and follow it to a short rappel, which often has a fixed line on it. That rappel is the confirmation you are on the right line — it drops you about 150 ft into the drainage gully at the bottom of the ice cliff. You should be losing height before you gain any.

From the bottom of that gully, traverse west, underneath the ice cliff, until you can see an obvious snow-and-ice ramp running up on your left. That ramp is the Kautz ice chute, and it is the start of the route. The older description of the same ground is: down over the ridge, down the gully about 150 ft, then either cross the icefall into the broad chute or continue down and around the toe of the icefall to reach the bottom of the chute.

What you should find in the chute: two steps of alpine ice separated by lower-angle snow. The first is the easier, anything from a short pitch of steep snow to about 250 ft of ice; the second is the crux, from a short pitch to more than 300 ft, steeper, and where a second tool earns its place. Both change a great deal from year to year. In lean years the ice can be thin, rotten or frozen dirt rather than good ice; the angle, not the quality, is what identifies it.

Negative marker: if you are climbing directly up from Camp Hazard toward the ice cliff, stop. That is the serac fall line, and it is the reason the camp has its name.

Cross the prow and descend the Inter Glacier into Glacier Basin, then follow the trail out to the White River trailhead. This returns to the trailhead you started from, but it does not retrace the approach: the St. Elmo Pass, Curtis Ridge and Carbon Glacier leg is not reversed. Do not plan on downclimbing Liberty Ridge itself. Parties who instead carry over the summit and descend the Disappointment Cleaver to Camp Muir finish at Paradise, a different trailhead that needs a car shuttle.

hits.text:
High camp is not the start of the climbing — and the mistake this route invites is treating the ridge you camped on as the ridge you climb.

From camp at around 10,000–10,300 ft you descend, on loose rock or steep snow, onto the Mowich Glacier. If you are gaining height straight out of the tents along a rocky crest, you are still on the approach ridge.

The first real feature is the bergschrund, usually crossed by a bridge just left of a rock outcropping near the centre. Above it the climbing is 40–45 degree snow for about 1,000 ft, and it ends in an obvious way: you run up under large rock cliffs. That is the signal to traverse left into an hourglass-shaped snow face rather than to keep going up.

The next decision point is a rock buttress at about 11,500 ft, where the route splits — left and around toward Liberty Cap between the buttress and the icefall, or right through mixed ground, a minor rock rib and the left margin of the Mowich Face to a second rock gully. Either way there is a short section of real rock or mixed climbing above 12,000 ft; if you have got that high on pure snow, you have probably drifted onto the Liberty Cap glacier ground.

Descent is normally the Emmons, not this route.

hits.text: Sunset Ridge climbs the long spine separating the upper Mowich Face from the Sunset Amphitheater on Rainier's remote west/northwest side. After the long Westside Road/Wonderland Trail approach to St. Andrews Park, the route climbs a series of steep 50-55° gullies and open faces; at about 12,800 ft the ridge forces climbers out onto the upper Mowich Face, which is followed on steep snow or ice to 13,200 ft before the route regains the ridge crest to Liberty Cap and the true summit. The road is gravel and open to vehicles only for the first few miles; beyond that it is foot or bike travel, and has been that way for years because of flood damage in the Tahoma Creek drainage. Treat the walk as part of the route rather than as an inconvenience that might be lifted.

Walk the road about 3.8 miles to Round Pass, then take the South Puyallup River Trail to the Wonderland Trail and on to St Andrews Park. Leave the trail there and climb north through alpine meadows onto the Puyallup Cleaver, passing Tokaloo Spire.

Leave the cleaver at about 8,500 ft and traverse the Puyallup and South Mowich glaciers into the Sunset Amphitheater. Camps are used on Colonnade Ridge, on the Puyallup Cleaver near 9,000 ft, in the open near 9,600 ft, and at the bergschrund in the amphitheater itself.

hits.text: A notorious roughly 4,000-ft north face — the headwall of the Carbon Glacier's cirque — capped by a 200-300 ft band of hanging ice (seracs) that has historically deterred most attempts and is the wall's defining objective hazard. Named for geological engineer Bailey Willis, who helped build the first trail to the Carbon Glacier in 1881. The wall's West Rib was first climbed in June 1961 by Charles ('Charlie') Bell, though credit for the first ascent was disputed for years; Jim Wickwire (who climbed the East Rib in 1963 and made the first winter ascent in 1970) later corroborated Bell's claim by comparing notes and photographs directly with Bell.

runs: first climbed in 1930 by jimmy cherry and bob ross
hits.text: Mount Redoubt is one of the highest and most striking peaks in the remote Chilliwack (Custer-Chilliwack) group of the North Cascades, in the Stephen Mather Wilderness just 3 miles south of the Canadian border. Composed of resistant Skagit gneiss, it carries the Redoubt Glacier on its south/east slopes and is ranked among the North Cascades' 'Classic Eight' summits for its remoteness, glaciated approach, and exposed, rotten-rock summit block. First climbed in 1930 by Jimmy Cherry and Bob Ross, it remains one of the more committing standard climbs in Washington largely because the approach paradoxically requires driving and hiking through British Columbia, Canada, before crossing back into the US at the Monument 65 border marker to reach the mountain itself.

runs: mount saul is the fourth highest point on wenatchee ridge a
hits.text: Mount Saul is the fourth-highest point on Wenatchee Ridge, a spur of the Cascade crest in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. It has a bare granitic summit with jagged rocks, a sheer northwest face, and a south side that drops nearly 4,000 ft to Indian Creek Valley in about a mile — the mountain punches well above its modest elevation for alpine character. There is no maintained trail to the top; climbers approach via the Indian Creek Trail from the White River drainage, then leave the trail near Airplane Creek for an off-trail scramble past Airplane Lake to the upper east slopes and summit rocks.

hits.text: The staging point for the whole trip, and worth its own entry because the drive is where this approach most often fails. The White River road leaves the Lake Wenatchee end and turns to gravel several miles before the trailhead, ending at about 2,300 feet where the White River trail, the Indian Creek trail, the Mount David trail and the Boulder Creek trail all begin. Getting the right one matters: only Indian Creek leads to Mount Saul. There are small developed forest campgrounds spaced along the road below the trailhead which are a better place to spend a night than the parking area itself if they are open, but they are primitive, first come and first served, and carry no potable supply. The road is the fragile part, and it is closed right now. Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-07-2026-40 (Little Giant Fire), effective 3 September 2026 through 31 October 2026 unless rescinded sooner, closes FSR 6400 to the end of the road and lists the White River Trailhead. It is not named in the Wenatchee River District storm-damage road order (06-17-07-2026-11, 20 May 2026 through 31 December 2027), which closes seventeen other roads. When the road is shut low, the trailhead is a substantial road walk or bike ride further on and the trip changes character completely.

hits.text: The standard/easiest and most commonly climbed route on Sefrit. From Ruth Creek, climbers cross the creek and bushwhack up through slide alder to the base of the 'Wall Street' couloir, a roughly 1,500-vertical-foot snow gully about 50 feet wide at 30-35 degrees. The couloir tops out on the Northwest Glacier at about 5,000 ft, crossed (roped, with pickets/flukes for crevasse hazard) to a broad saddle at 6,500 ft just west of the summit. From the saddle, parties either climb a steep, narrow chute due south to a notch just west of the summit pinnacle, or traverse southeast across a shallow snow bowl beneath the summit — the traverse exposes climbers to cornices and is usually roped with snow protection. The route finishes on the southeast ridge: a straightforward Class 2 scramble broken by about 100 ft of exposed Class 3 traversing near the middle. routeFt here (3,691 ft) is a computed total combining the couloir, glacier crossing, and final ridge scramble, since no aggregate route length is known.

Drive SR-542 to Hannegan Pass Road (FS-32); at 1.3 miles bear left onto Ruth Creek Road and continue to the pullout near milepost 3, just past where a creek flows over a concrete weir, at about 2,950 ft. This is NOT the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at the end of the road.

The couloir runs roughly 1,500 vertical feet and opens onto the Northwest Glacier around 5,000 ft; from there the route crosses the glacier to a saddle near 6,500 ft and scrambles the southeast ridge to the summit.

Timing is the whole trade: earlier means more snow and more avalanche risk, later means thicker brush and discontinuous snow.

runs: about 50 feet with very steep rock walls on both sides
hits.text:
Wall Street is a corridor with walls on both sides, and that is the test. Once you are in it, the gully holds a remarkably uniform gradient of 30-35 degrees and a uniform width of about 50 feet, with very steep rock walls on both sides, for roughly 1,500 vertical feet. Nothing else on this side of the valley does that. In cloud you do not need to see the top: if you can touch rock on your left and rock on your right and the angle is not changing, you are in Wall Street. If your gully fans out, or has a wall on only one side, it is not.

Getting to it: the marker at the bottom is avalanche debris. After the creek crossing and roughly 45 minutes of alder and devil's club, the brush ends at the debris pile at the foot of the snow gully. Debris is what tells you the gully above you actually runs — and it is also the reason to be there early and cold.

The arrival at the top of the couloir is the glacier. The corridor opens onto the Northwest Glacier around 5,000 ft. Walls end, glacier starts.

The discriminator against the peak's other two routes, and it is decided in the car park rather than on the mountain. Three routes on Sefrit start from three different places: this one from the Ruth Creek pullout near milepost 3 on Ruth Creek Road; the Bloody Head Couloir from the Ruth Creek trail higher up the valley near 3,450 ft; and the Southwest Ridge from the Nooksack Cirque trailhead at the end of FR-34, a different road entirely. If you drove to the end of FR-34 you cannot reach this route today.

hits.text: A steep, seldom-climbed 7,191-foot summit rising abruptly above the North Fork Nooksack River, about three miles north of Mount Shuksan in the Mount Baker Wilderness (Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Whatcom County). Sefrit is notorious among North Cascades climbers less for technical difficulty than for its approach: a brushy, pathless bushwhack up steep timber and slide alder to reach a short but genuine Class 4 ridge/gully system leading to the summit. First climbed in 1930 by Jim Irving and Brick Spouse.

Baker Highway (SR 542) east about 12.5 miles, turn left on Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32), continue just over a mile to the junction with Nooksack Cirque Road (FR 34), and follow FR 34 one mile to its end at the Nooksack Cirque Trailhead (do not confuse with the separate Hannegan Pass Trailhead further up FR 32). Above the cliff band, the summit gully splits into several forks; the leftmost fork (or the one just west of a snow couloir to its right) is easiest, and rock is generally solid low but looser near the summit ridge. A separate, lower-angle line on the north side — Wall Street Couloir and the Northwest Glacier, finishing on the southeast ridge — is Class 2 with one exposed Class 3 traverse and is reportedly the more commonly climbed route on the peak. runs: to the summit of mount shuksan the fisher chimneys
hits.text: One of the most popular routes to the summit of Mount Shuksan, the Fisher Chimneys climbs the west side of the peak through a rocky chimney system before crossing the Upper Curtis and Sulphide Glaciers to the summit pyramid. It is a quintessential North Cascades outing, mixing scrambling, glacier travel, and a rock finish on a spectacular mountain.

Most parties take 2-3 days.

runs: the northwest edge of the upper curtis glacier
hits.text: After summiting via the central gully or the southeast ridge, several descents are used: reverse the Fisher Chimneys (complex route-finding and exposed), or descend the northwest edge of the Upper Curtis Glacier and cross onto the White Salmon Glacier around 7,050 ft, taking Winnie's Slide back down to the Chimneys. The White Salmon sits on Shuksan's northwest flank — the usual high camp sits near its upper edge, at the top of the Chimneys — not the east side, which is the Nooksack Cirque. Either of those returns you to the Lake Ann trailhead you started from. A third option loops around and descends the Sulphide Glacier, but that exits south to the Shannon Ridge trailhead and needs a car shuttle.

Go straight up its right side, then traverse left to a narrow rock rib. Crampons are effectively mandatory; late in summer it melts to glacial ice needing screws and a second tool.

runs: the white salmon cirque from the price glacier cirque
hits.text:
Price Lake must stay below you and to your north-east, and that is the test. From the bivy the day is a traverse climber's left, above and across the hanging glacier that sits over Price Lake and beneath the upper hanging glacier tucked under the first rock barrier. In cloud you will not see the summit and you do not need to: the lake is the reference and it belongs on your left-hand side, downhill.

Arrival: you are at the base of the technical climbing when you reach the shoulder — the snow-and-ice rib that divides the White Salmon cirque from the Price Glacier cirque. It is the only place on this traverse where the ground stops being a sidehill and becomes a defined rib with a cirque falling away on each side. Stand on it and you should be able to look down into two separate basins.

The error that kills people here is drifting left, and it is worth stating as a hard rule: stay right during the traverse. Going further left puts you onto the true North Face, which sheds avalanches frequently, especially early season. Left feels like progress toward the mountain and is the wrong direction.

After 500 ft of traverse the line goes up, on a firn-and-ice finger west of the upper hanging glacier. If you are still traversing horizontally after a long way, you have gone past the finger and are running out under the face.

runs: to the ridgecrest directly opposite the ski area follow
hits.text: Follow the dirt road up the White Salmon Creek drainage for under a mile, then drop off-trail across White Salmon Creek and climb to the ridgecrest directly opposite the ski area. Follow that crest to the base of the mountain's north side and gain the northwest arete, a long line of loose, runout rock, moderate ice and glacier travel, to the summit.

runs: by parking at the lower white salmon lodge

to the ridgecrest directly opposite the ski area
hits.text: Two realistic approach options both start by parking at the lower White Salmon lodge on SR 542 (White Salmon Road, FR-3075) and following a dirt road up the White Salmon Creek drainage for under a mile. The more direct option drops off-trail across White Salmon Creek and climbs to the ridgecrest directly opposite the ski area, then follows the ridgecrest to the base of the mountain's north side. The alternative continues up the road as far as it goes, then travels off-trail up the valley until open slopes allow access to the lower White Salmon Glacier. From there, gain the crest of the northwest arête itself -- a long, remote line combining bushwhacking, complex route-finding, runout and loose rock, moderate alpine ice, and extensive glacier travel.

Camping at Lake of the Angels, which lies inside Olympic National Park, requires an Olympic National Park wilderness camping permit. If approaching via Flapjack Lakes inside Olympic National Park, an overnight wilderness camping permit is required, reservable on Recreation.gov for the Flapjack Lakes zone (bookable mid-April, camping dates mid-June through mid-October); contact the Wilderness Information Center at (360) 565-3100.

runs: ridge then take a broad gully southwest and
up and around left to the true summit which is large and broad
hits.text:
Stand at Lake of the Angels and the cirque itself tells you which way to go: Mount Stone is on your right, another peak is on your left, and Mount Skokomish is straight ahead. That three-way check is the arrival test, and it fixes your orientation before you leave the lake.

The turn is around the right-hand side of the lake, on a way trail heading west to the ridge. Then take a broad gully southwest and up toward the saddle just north of point 5945. That is the base of the climb and it is a named, mapped point — the saddle you want is the one immediately north of 5945, not the next gap along. A map point is the strongest thing you can navigate to in cloud.

Second test, past the saddle: the route does not go straight up from it. From the saddle a boot path contours south and southwest across scree, grass and rock benches around the east and south flanks of the peak, passing a large tarn. The tarn is the confirmation. Turn right and start climbing when you are above the large tarn — that is the trigger, and it works because a tarn is a thing you stand beside rather than a thing you see from a distance. Turning up before the tarn puts you on the steeper cliffy ground on the north side of the upper mountain.

Third test, near the top: the final ground passes through rock bands and scrubby trees across a section known as the hanging or fingertip traverse, then goes up and around left to the true summit, which is large and broad. This peak has three summit horns and parties have mistaken a lower false summit for the true south high point. A broad top is the right one; a narrow horn is not.

A directional warning: contouring too far right (north) near the ridge crest gets sketchy, exposed and dangerous. Cut west over the ridge instead.

runs: to the 7 380 ft custer spickard saddle
hits.text: Two camp options are used. Via Silver Creek: arrange a Ross Lake Resort water taxi (reservation required) roughly 25 miles up Ross Lake to a drop-off at the Silver Creek mouth (1,600 ft); a trail climbs the north side of Silver Creek about 2.5 miles to an old cabin at 2,900 ft, after which the route continues cross-country (occasional blazes) across slide-alder and forest slopes to the Silver Lake basin camp (6,763 ft). Via Ouzel Lake: use the Depot Creek approach (see the Southwest Ridge route) to Ouzel Lake (5,700 ft), then climb toward and over the Custer-Spickard saddle. From Ouzel Lake, climb north-east from the lake's north side up the obvious wide gully to the 7,380-ft Custer-Spickard saddle and step onto the Silver Glacier beyond it. From Silver Lake there is no saddle to cross: walk round the north side of the lake to its south-west end, then south across moraine and snow, skirting a small buttress, to the glacier toe at about 7,400 ft.

runs: you should be able to see at least the lower
hits.text:
From the Silver Lake camp the route does not go near a col. Walk round the north side of the lake to its far, south-west end, then head south across moraine and snow, skirting a small rock buttress, to the toe of the glacier at about 7,400 ft. Allow an hour to an hour and a half from camp.

You should be able to see at least the lower glacier from camp, so pick your line onto it before you leave. The ice comes down toward the lake from the north side of the peak; you rope up at its toe and climb it, with no saddle or gully on the way.

The wide gully and the col at about 7,380 ft between this peak and its neighbour to the north-west belong to the other approach, from the lake on the Depot Creek side. If you are climbing a gully toward a gap, you have left this line.

And the negative marker that matters most: the south-west route on this peak starts at the toe of a different glacier on the other flank, reached by traversing round a rock buttress into heather and moraine basins rather than by gaining any col. If you are roping up at the foot of an icefall with no saddle in sight, you have started the other route.

runs: north side up the obvious wide gully that leads to the
hits.text:
From the Depot Creek camp, climb north-east from the lake's north side up the obvious wide gully that leads to the col.

The fixed point is the same: the col at about 7,380 ft between this peak and its neighbour to the north-west. It is a gap with a summit on either hand and the glacier beyond. The wide gully you came up is the way back to camp; the glacier lies on the far side.

The test that you are at the right gap is that both summits are identifiable from it, and that the ice you are about to climb runs away from the col rather than up to it. A notch with only one summit beside it, or with no glacier beyond, is a different gap on the same ridge.

Do not confuse this start with the south-west route, which leaves the same camp. That route turns right around the toe of a rock buttress well before any saddle and ropes up at the toe of a glacier on the other flank. If you have not gained a col, you are not on this route.

runs: 5th highest summit in north cascades national park
hits.text: Mount Spickard is a massive, heavily glaciated peak straddling the Skagit/Fraser drainage divide just 2 miles south of the Canadian border, part of the Chilliwack Group of the Skagit Range. It is the 5th-highest summit in North Cascades National Park and the 16th-highest in Washington, and its roughly 4,779 ft of prominence ranks 9th-greatest in the state. The mountain is built of Tertiary-age gneiss; the Silver Glacier drains north over a mile to Silver Lake, while a separate glacier system on the southwest side extends over 3 miles toward Mount Redoubt. First ascent is credited to Walter B. Reaburn in 1904; the peak's current name was applied in 1963 for climber Warren J. Spickard Jr., who died climbing a nearby peak in 1961. The standard Southwest Route/Silver Lake line climbs broad talus and a southwest glacier to a final short but loose Class 3 rock scramble, and is notable as much for its remote, cross-border approach as for its technical difficulty.

runs: an extremely overgrown and sporadically muddy road for
hits.text:
From the road washout at about 2,600 ft, reached by a rough spur off the lake road on the Canadian side, walk the old roadbed about nine minutes to an inconspicuous spur on the left, follow that spur four minutes to a T-junction, and bear right onto an extremely overgrown and sporadically muddy road for about thirty-five minutes. That brings you to the boundary obelisk, where there is a register - carry a passport, because this approach crosses the international border on foot.

Above the boundary the way becomes a crude but discernible climbers' path along the creek through old growth, easy where deadfall has been cut and full of uncut logs where it has not. About three miles in it reaches the falls, which are the real crux of the approach: wet slick boulders and slabs at their base, with steep steps rigged with an old fixed hand-line. Treat the line as an aid rather than as protection, and back it up with a heavy pack on.

Above the falls the path continues through meadow and upper valley to the lake at roughly 5,700 ft - flat sandy mostly treeless benches at the toe of the talus, the standard base camp for this peak and its neighbour, with reliable water.

hits.text: Descent is the same Monitor Ridge line back to timberline and then the Ptarmigan Trail back to Climbers Bivouac — there is no rappelling on this route (0 rappels; it is entirely a walk-off/scramble descent). The critical descent hazard is at the top: the crater rim is corniced with wind-built overhanging snow/ice that has repeatedly broken away, including a fatal collapse and multiple large rim failures in recent years, so the Forest Service and USGS explicitly warn to stay back at least 30 ft (9 m) from the visible rim edge and never approach or stand on a cornice for the crater view. From the true summit, descend back to the false summit and pick up the wood-post line down through the loose pumice/ash upper slopes; below about 7,000 ft the marked posts guide you back toward timberline, but climbers should double-check they're following the correct post line on the way down, since it's easy to wander onto a neighboring, unmarked drainage in poor visibility. Depending on season and snow coverage, glissading is possible on sections of the upper mountain and can significantly speed the descent, but chutes are frequently thin, rocky, and mixed with bare ash/pumice patches later in the season, so glissading should be assessed conservatively (an ice axe for self-arrest is standard kit). Below timberline, follow Ptarmigan Trail #216A back down through the forest to the Climbers Bivouac parking lot.

hits.text: Camping itself is free, but the parking requires a Northwest Forest Pass, an Interagency pass, or a small day fee. Separately and unavoidably, a climbing permit is required year round for anyone going above 4,800 feet on the mountain, and camping above 4,800 feet is prohibited outright. From April 1 to October 31 that permit carries a daily quota and a per-climber fee of about twenty dollars: 350 climbers a day from April 1 to May 14, then only 110 a day from May 15 through October 31. Permits are sold first come, first served with no lottery, released a month at a time on the first day of the preceding month at seven in the morning Pacific time, and the summer dates sell out within minutes of release. From November 1 to March 31 the permit is free and self-issued at the trailhead with no quota. Blue bags are mandatory for all human waste above the tree line and are stocked at the trailhead kiosk.

hits.text: From the Marble Mountain Sno-Park (about 2,700 ft) trailhead, the route follows the Swift Creek Trail #244 (blue diamond blazes on trees in winter) north into forest. The trail climbs steadily through timber for roughly 2 miles, gaining to about 3,700-3,750 ft, where it breaks out of the trees near Chocolate Falls, a 40-ft seasonal waterfall on Swift Creek. Just above the falls, cross to the west side of Swift Creek — this ford can be tricky and swollen with meltwater in spring or after warm spells, and the crossing point/sign is often buried in winter snowpack, so treat it as a navigation checkpoint rather than a marked trail junction. Above treeline the route enters the open, barren Worm Flows lava/mudflow terrain; wooden route-marking posts guide climbers from about 3,700 ft up to roughly 4,800 ft, after which large posts thin out and occasional cairns (and, in winter, wands placed by parties) mark the line up broad ridges and open slopes. The route follows Worm Flow Ridge past an old seismic monitoring station near 6,200 ft, then continues up snow/scree slopes to merge with the summer Monitor Ridge climbing route at about 7,400 ft. From that junction it's another ~850 ft of climbing on open slopes to the crater rim, then about a quarter mile west along the rim to the true summit (8,363 ft). There is no reliable water past Swift Creek/Chocolate Falls, so carry everything you'll need for the round trip. Above treeline this is committing, exposed terrain: whiteout conditions, wind, and snow-covered cairns/posts make route-finding the main crux, so carry a map/GPS track as backup even though the line is well-established. Open slopes on the upper mountain can be avalanche terrain when wind-loaded — avoid loaded slopes and gully bottoms after new snow or wind events.

hits.text:
From the Marble Mountain Sno-Park at about 2,700-2,800 ft, follow the Swift Creek Trail #244 north into forest, marked in winter by blue diamond blazes on the trees. It climbs steadily through timber for roughly 2 miles to about 3,700-3,750 ft, breaking out of the trees near Chocolate Falls on Swift Creek.

Just above the falls, cross to the west side of Swift Creek. This ford can be swollen with meltwater in spring or after a warm spell, and the crossing point and its sign are often buried in winter snowpack.

Above treeline the route enters the open barren Worm Flows lava and mudflow terrain. Wooden posts mark the line from about 3,700 to roughly 4,800 ft; above that the posts thin out and occasional cairns, plus wands placed by parties, mark broad ridges and open slopes. The route follows Worm Flow Ridge past an old seismic monitoring station near 6,200 ft, then up snow and scree to merge with the summer Monitor Ridge line at about 7,400 ft, and roughly 850 ft more to the crater rim.

A Sno-Park permit is required to park in the winter months. This is the standard winter and spring access because the summer trailhead on the far side is snow-gated.

runs: cross to the west side of swift creek just above
hits.text:
Three hard markers, in order, and they work because they are objects rather than descriptions of slope — which matters here, since snow buries everything else.

One: Chocolate Falls, at about 3,700-3,750 ft, where the trail breaks out of the trees. You cross to the west side of Swift Creek just above the falls. In winter the crossing point and its sign are usually under snow, so treat the falls themselves as the marker and never a sign.

Two: wooden posts, from about 3,700 to about 4,800 ft. Above 4,800 they thin to cairns and wands.

Three: the old seismic monitoring station near 6,200 ft on Worm Flow Ridge. This is the last hard object on the whole route and the best single confirmation you are on the ridge and not on one of the broad open slopes beside it.

The negative that catches parties low: if you have crossed Swift Creek and are still in trees, you crossed too low — below the falls. Regain the east bank and keep climbing to the treeline break.

The merge at about 7,400 ft is the last check: from there you are on the summer Monitor Ridge line and it is roughly 850 ft to the rim.

The most important finding on this route is about coming down, not going up. Whiteout wrong-drainage descents are the documented failure here. From the rim the correct line is back down Worm Flow Ridge — a ridge, not a gully. Do not descend into a gully because it is going downhill; and record your bearings on the way up while you can still see the ridge you are on.

hits.text: From Marmot Lake Camp (~4,400 ft) leave the maintained trail and follow a small creek up into an amphitheater on the west side of the peak; easy Class 1 slopes lead from the amphitheater to the summit. The multi-day approach up the Duckabush valley (roughly 21-23 trail miles one-way to Marmot Lake) is the real crux of the trip, not the summit scramble itself. An alternate approach from the Staircase/North Fork Skokomish side reaches First Divide, drops into a basin with an unnamed lake, and climbs the saddle between Mount Duckabush and Mount Steel before turning north along the ridge to the summit block; the park lists that trail closed between the Staircase Rapids Loop and Home Sweet Home since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, with no reopening date on the park's fire-conditions page updated September 18, 2026, which leaves the Duckabush/Marmot Lake line as the open approach.

runs: on the west side of the summit where easy slopes lead to the
hits.text: The eastern base for this group of peaks, about 20 miles up the Duckabush River trail from Brinnon and roughly 1.1 miles and 1,700 ft above the Upper Duckabush camp, in a saddle a little over a mile from O'Neil Pass. Mount Steel and Mount Duckabush both stand directly above it, and Steel's less-travelled route from this side leaves the trail a few miles above the Duckabush camp and follows a small creek into an amphitheatre on the west side of the summit, where easy slopes lead to the top. Mount Duckabush is a scramble from the same basin. The approach is the obstacle, not the climbing. Twenty miles with the Big Hump early on, a river ford in the upper valley that is genuinely hazardous outside high summer, and a trail that goes long stretches between clearings — recent accounts describe dozens of downed trees between the trailhead and the upper ford and heavy brush. Most parties take two full days each way. The compensation is that this side stayed open when the Staircase side was closed by the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire: the park still lists the North Fork Skokomish and Home Sweet Home trails closed, with no reopening date, on the park's trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026, and while they stay closed this is the direct way in to Steel and Duckabush. Hart and LaCrosse Lakes a mile or two above make excellent extensions if you have the days. Season is mid-July through September.

hits.text: The drive ends at the gate where Olney Creek Road leaves the Sultan Basin Road, and the day starts on foot up the closed roadbed. Walk the road uphill for about 4.8 miles, past a first switchback and on to a second one where the grade noticeably eases around 3,700 ft — that second switchback is the key junction and there is nothing signed about it. Mapped road alignments in this area are known to be wrong, so trust the switchback you can see on the ground over the line drawn on a map. Leave the road there and pick up an unsigned but well-established boot path on the right, north side, which climbs onto a forest ridge crest and follows it. The path fades out somewhere around 4,050 to 4,200 ft; from there leave any tread and traverse southeast cross-country, aiming for a small pond just northeast of point 4875, then continue southeast to a second minor ridge and cross open slopes into the rocky basin holding One Acre Lake. It is the highest point in Mason County. The lower approach lies in the Mount Skokomish Wilderness (Olympic National Forest); the upper basin, lake, and summit sit just inside the Olympic National Park boundary. On a clear day the summit gives views of The Brothers, Mount Washington, Mount Anderson, Mount Constance, Mount Deception, and Mount Olympus.

runs: the south facing ridge just below the false summit
hits.text:
The north ridge rock rib is the discriminator, not the look of the ice. Standing in the 5,400 ft basin facing the mountain, in order from your left: Sherpa Glacier, then Ice Cliff Glacier, then the enormous rock rib of the North Ridge, then the Stuart Glacier beyond it.

So: if that rib is on your right, you are on the Ice Cliff. If you have walked around the rib and it is now on your left, you are on the Stuart Glacier and have gone too far west. If there is no hanging ice anywhere above you and the slope is a uniform moderate angle, you are on the Sherpa and have gone too far east.

The name is the second test. Ice Cliff is the only one of the three carrying a hanging ice cliff and serac band partway up. Sherpa has none.

The move itself: walk the moraine up to the foot of the North Ridge, then cut hard left and traverse east under the ice cliff at about 6,600 ft. You are aiming under the cliff, not up the rib.

Touch test at the base, and it is unmistakable in cloud: the ground is not clean snow. It is frozen avalanche debris mixed with fallen chunks of glacier ice, set solid — a talus field made of snow and ice. Standing on that is direct evidence you are underneath the ice cliff.

Both the far left and the far right side of the icefall are used, and which one goes is a conditions question rather than a route question. The same is true of the bergschrund: one published description passes it on the climber's right, another on the left. Do not treat either as fixed, and look before committing.

Exit: surmounting the cornice puts you on the south-facing ridge just below the false summit near 8,600 ft. Standard descent is the Sherpa Glacier, immediately east of the couloir exit, starting around 8,200 ft and dropping back into the same basin — so a party reversing the Ice Cliff is doing something unusual.

hits.text: Primary approach is from the north via the Stuart Lake Trailhead (reached via Icicle Creek Road and FR 7601 out of Leavenworth). From the trailhead, follow the Stuart/Colchuck Lake Trail as it rolls along Mountaineer Creek through forest; at the signed junction roughly 2 miles in, stay right on the Stuart Lake Trail (the Colchuck Lake Trail is the left fork). Continue up the Mountaineer Creek valley on the Stuart Lake Trail, then leave the maintained trail before reaching Stuart Lake itself, cross Mountaineer Creek, and follow its south fork upstream cross-country. After roughly 2 more miles of streamside travel, climb a steep, loose talus/boulder slope to gain the hanging valley beneath Sherpa Peak and the Sherpa Glacier — this valley has good bivy sites and is a common overnight stop. From the valley, angle directly up to the toe of the North Ridge, keeping the Ice Cliff Glacier on your left; the notch/base of the upper ridge sits around 8,200 ft, where a snow-filled gully (often climbed on 4th-class rock at its edge) gains the crest. All-in this is roughly 6-6.5 miles and 3,300+ ft of gain, about 4-5 hours to the base of the climbing. A well-known alternative is the southern approach via the Esmeralda/Teanaway trailhead over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek to Goat Pass, gaining the ridge from that side (~9 miles, ~4,800 ft gain, ~8 hours) — longer and higher-gain on the way in, but it sets up a much shorter car-to-car loop for parties planning to descend the Cascadian Couloir, since that descent drops back toward Ingalls Creek. Water is available at Mountaineer Creek and its south fork on the north approach, and at Ingalls Creek/seasonal snow patches near the 8,200 ft notch bivy on the south approach; above the notch there is no reliable water. Route-finding through the boulder/talus slope below Sherpa Glacier and the creek crossing (higher and faster in early season) are the main approach-specific hazards.

runs: off the right side of the ridge below the
hits.text: Nearly all parties descend via the Cascadian Couloir on the mountain's south side — this is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling required (0 rappels) under normal summer conditions. From the true summit, downclimb steep snow or scree, keeping right through sparse trees to drop into the head of the Cascadian Couloir, then follow the couloir down its full length (loose sand, scree, and rockfall-prone rock the entire way; an ice axe, and often crampons, are recommended into mid-summer for a lingering snow tongue) to the valley floor near Ingalls Creek, roughly 4,000 ft below the summit. The upper couloir splits into a confusing maze of climbers' paths and cairns — keep to the established talus path on the climber's left side around the 8,800 ft permanent snowfield; parties who drift onto the right side have run into old rappel-station remnants and much harder downclimbing. Because the North Ridge is climbed from the north (Stuart Lake/Mountaineer Creek side) while the Cascadian Couloir exits to the south (Ingalls Creek/Teanaway side), most parties face a long, tiring hike back around the mountain to a north-side vehicle — either via Longs Pass and a car shuttle, or a full trail loop back to the Stuart Lake Trailhead; parties using the southern (Esmeralda/Longs Pass) approach avoid this by parking on that side to begin with. Note: some parties opt for a short, optional ~75 ft rappel off the right side of the ridge below the Great Gendarme (using an established, well-traveled sling/fixed anchor, not bolted) to bypass the crux 5.9 pitches during the ascent — this is a mid-route bypass rappel, not part of the standard descent, and is not counted in the rappel total below. A single 60m rope doubled (or a single-strand lower) is sufficient for it.

From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737), take the trail over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek to Goat Pass, then traverse east beneath the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe of the ridge.

About 2,000 ft of the day is descent, so the round trip is more work than the raw gain suggests, and parties consistently report it taking longer than planned — budget eight hours and expect route-finding on the traverse rather than tread.

The reason to accept the longer, higher approach is that it removes the shuttle entirely. The Cascadian Couloir descent drops to Ingalls Creek on this side, so a party that walked in from Esmeralda walks out to its own car. Parties who came in from the north do not.

How much snow remains on the Goat Pass traverse is the recurring gear question here: sections have been reported at around 40 degrees, and whether you need an axe and traction changes week to week through the summer. Recent photos and current reports are worth more than any fixed answer.

hits.text: A classic steep snow-and-ice couloir splitting the north side of Mount Stuart above the Stuart Glacier, first climbed by Helmy Beckey and Larry Strathdee in June 1944. Most of the route climbs at 40-50°, with a narrow, sustained crux about halfway up that frequently holds around 100 ft of water ice up to 60°. The route tops out at or near the small notch on the West Ridge route; the exit rock is low 5th class on the standard finish, about 5.7 on the left-side variation.

hits.text: Start at the Esmeralda Trailhead (end of North Fork Teanaway Road, ~4,243 ft) and follow the Ingalls Way Trail. At about 0.3 mile, stay right onto Ingalls Way where it leaves the Esmeralda Basin Trail; at about 1.7 miles (5,440 ft), turn right at the Longs Pass junction rather than continuing to Ingalls Basin, and switchback up open slopes to Longs Pass (roughly 3 mi, ~2,100 ft gain from the trailhead, cresting around 6,400 ft) — the pass gives the first clear look at Stuart's west aspect. From the pass, descend steep, sometimes dusty/scree-y trail on the north side, losing about 1,300 ft in a mile, to reach Ingalls Creek in the timber below. Cross the creek (a straightforward rock-hop or wade in normal summer flow, the last reliable water source before the ridge) and pick up the climber's path heading west, up-valley, toward Stuart Pass. Well short of the pass itself (roughly 6,200–6,400 ft), leave the trail and traverse climber's-left (north) across open talus and heather benches toward the base of the West Ridge — this cross-country traverse is where parties most commonly go astray, since there is no maintained tread and several minor gullies look similar; aim for the obvious deep gully (the middle of three parallel gullies) marked by a large, house-sized boulder at its base. An alternate, longer northern approach via the Stuart Lake Trailhead and Stuart Pass exists but adds significant mileage and is not the standard line. Plan on 3.5–5 hours car-to-base depending on route-finding and snow conditions; some parties camp near Ingalls Lake or in the upper Ingalls Creek basin to break the day up. Hazards: the Longs Pass descent and creek-crossing slopes hold snow into early summer and can be icy at dawn; the final talus traverse to the ridge is loose and exposed to rockfall from parties above; there is no water beyond the Ingalls Creek crossing, so tank up there for the long day ahead. Getting past Long John Tower and the exposed West Ridge Notch traverse are the route's main route-finding dilemmas; high on the route, below the summit, a short dihedral with a fixed piton (5.4) or a layback further along the ledge (5.6) leads to easier fifth-class climbing to the top.

hits.text:
The start is just left of the snowfield at the bottom of the face, after the wall is accessed from its west side. From the Crescent Creek Basin camp the technical start is reached by crossing the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col and descending the Mustard Glacier into McMillan Cirque, then rounding into position under Terror's wall. Cross the glacier remnant beneath the face, then start just left of the snowpatch at the bottom.

The moat where snow meets rock at the base is the usual obstacle, and it is also the marker: you are at the base when you are standing at the gap between the snowpatch and the wall, on its left.

The decision that defines this route, and it is made before the hard climbing rather than during it: the face is split by two ribs, and this route takes the right, or western, one. The main risk on the lower face is not difficulty but committing to the wrong rib. Long, mostly third-class pitches climb above the snowfield while traversing steadily rightward; the face is over 2,000 ft tall with limited options to reverse. If your traverse is taking you left, you are on the wrong half of the wall.

Two confirmations higher, both visual and both usable in thin cloud: aim for the right or western crest of the buttress about two thirds of the way up the lower face, identifiable by the rock darkening. And A sharp prow marks roughly the lower third of the buttress. Darkening rock and a sharp prow are features of this rib and not of its neighbour.

What the upper face gives you: a long snow finger forming a ramp that carries the route a good distance, then scrambling on a wildly exposed crest, a traverse around a small tower to the notch between the false and true summits, an exposed easy-fifth hand traverse over the false summit, a downclimb, and the short climb to the true 8,151 ft top.

On the approach, when crossing from Stump Hollow into Crescent Creek Basin: do not drop into the low notch north of the chopping block. The correct line into Crescent Creek Basin is about 100 yards north of that notch, at a flat, bivy-site shelf on the ridge.

hits.text: The long snow finger on the upper face forms a ramp that carries the route for a good distance; carry what you need to climb it. Above its top, the climbing turns to scrambling on a wildly exposed ridge crest, then a traverse around a small tower to the notch between the false and true summits. The false summit is taken directly on an exposed easy fifth class hand traverse, then downclimbed before the short climb to the true 8,151 ft top. Rock quality deteriorates near the top, with steep, extremely loose ground reported; a fatal-consequence rockfall accident on this buttress involved a sizeable block that had appeared solid tearing loose. Descent is normally the West Ridge gully. This is one of the longest and most committing lines in the range and retreat from high on it is genuinely difficult.

hits.text:
Aim for the lowest point in the ridge, and know in advance that it is further left than it looks. From Bumblebee Basin, scrambling up scree, the beginning of the ridge that you can see from below is not where you want to be. The notch you want is left of it, at the ridge's lowest point, around 5,960 ft. That single correction is the most useful thing on this approach, because the eye pulls you right every time.

The notch is small, and its size is the confirmation: it holds about three people at most. If you have topped out on a broad, comfortable saddle, you are not at the start of the West Ridge.

Expect short fourth-class scrambling around gendarmes to reach it. Once you top out on the ridge you scramble over a small gendarme, traversing rightward toward the crest, to gain the notch itself.

The first move settles it absolutely: pitch one begins with a step left into a well-featured chimney. That step-left-into-a-chimney is the signature of this route and is probably the crux of the whole climb. If your first pitch is a face or a slab, you are not in the right notch. The first two leads run up a series of chimneys in solid rock.

And the other route on this peak is on the opposite side: the East Ridge is class 3-4 and is gained from a notch at about 5,600 ft on the ESE side, from the same basin. If you are on easy scrambling ground the whole way, you are on the East Ridge and you have circled to the wrong end of the mountain.

hits.text: Three options exist, and the choice depends on party speed and whether you're continuing to Forbidden Peak. (1) Reverse the South Ridge: downclimb interspersed with numerous short, traversing rappels off fixed slings/anchors that are 'in abundance' along the ridge — a single rope is generally sufficient for these short raps, but carry extra webbing/cord to back up or replace tat, since stations are alpine-style (slung horns, chockstones, occasional old fixed gear) rather than bolted. This option is slower but avoids the moat problems of the SE Face line. (2) Descend the Southeast Face: downclimb from the summit area to the top rappel station, then make 5-6 double-rope (60m) rappels down the SE Face gully/slab system back toward the Taboo Glacier — the second station is on climber's left, the rest are straight down or climber's right. The crux of this option is the final rappel, where you must cross a moat/bergschrund to reach the snowfield below; this can be genuinely difficult and its condition can't be scoped from above, so the first person down should carry a picket, ice axe, and crampons to help climb out of the moat if needed. Bring two ropes (or a single rope doubled) for these double-rope rappels. (3) Continue over the summit and descend via the Torment-Forbidden Traverse toward Forbidden Peak (sustained exposure, a 5.6 step and ~45-degree snow/ice) if that's the day's objective — this is a full traverse, not a simple descent, and commits you to exiting via Forbidden's West Ridge/Boston Basin instead of returning the way you came.

runs: the junction with the silver lakes trail 842
hits.text: Start at the Mt. Townsend Upper Trailhead (elev. ~3,300 ft), reached via Forest Road 27 off Penny Creek Road out of Quilcene — the trailhead has a small gravel lot and a Buckhorn Wilderness boundary sign where Trail #839 begins. From the lot, the trail climbs immediately into dense, heavily wooded old-growth forest via the first of three switchback sets; this opening stretch is the steepest sustained grade on the route and stays shaded most of the way. After the initial switchbacks the trail eases through forest before a second switchback section, then a third set of steep, fully sun-exposed switchbacks that break out onto the crest of a ridge — this exposed stretch is the hottest, most water-demanding part of the hike in summer, so carry all the water you need (there is no reliable creek crossing directly on-trail; the small streams crossed in the first mile or so are often dry by late summer, so shallow Windy Lake by Camp Windy is the last water). At about 5,300 ft, roughly 2.6 miles in, an unmarked spur trail branches off to Windy Lake/Camp Windy, a common rest stop and the last reliable flat ground before the alpine section. Continuing on the main trail, at about 5,500 ft you reach the junction with the Silver Lakes Trail #842 — stay right (straight/uphill) to continue to the summit; the left fork toward Silver Lakes involves loose, unmaintained scrambling and is not the standard route. From this junction the forest opens into subalpine meadow and the trail's grade eases considerably for the final ~1 mile to the broad, flat summit ridge (6,282 ft), passing through increasingly open wildflower meadows with the last quarter-mile crossing mostly open, low-angle grassy/rocky tundra. No technical terrain or exposure is encountered on the standard route; the main hazards are heat/sun exposure on the third switchback set, lingering snow patches on the upper meadows into early summer (which can obscure the tread and create a slip hazard on a steep sidehill), and occasional route-finding uncertainty at the Silver Lakes junction if signage is missing.

hits.text: One of eleven summits in The Needles, a range of jagged Eocene sandstone-and-pillow-basalt spires that radiate north from Mount Deception and form the west wall of Royal Basin in the dry, rain-shadowed eastern Olympics. Walkinshaw (7,378') is the range's northernmost and most accessible peak — first climbed in 1961 by Joe Munson and Jim Parolini — sitting just north of higher, harder Mount Clark (7,528') and range-highpoint Mount Johnson (7,680'). The group lies within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park, draining to Royal Creek on the east and the Gray Wolf River on the west.

hits.text: The easiest line is a Class 3 scramble that gains the col at the south end of Gray Wolf Ridge, northeast of the peak, and follows the northeast ridge to the top. There is no maintained trail to the summit; parties leave the trail system in the 3,500-5,500 ft band and travel cross-country over open ridge and steep, brushy forest. The forest band climbing out of Royal Basin toward the col is slow, brushy going; above it, Class 3 ground on the ridge, with perhaps one short Class 4 step, leads to the small, exposed summit block.

hits.text: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead (~2,550 ft, end of FR 2870), start on the Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2, which runs a gentle, mostly level mile through old-growth forest along the Dungeness River to a well-signed junction. Bear right onto the Royal Basin Trail and settle into a steady, moderate climb up the Royal Creek valley for about 5 miles, crossing several tributary creeks — the last reliable water before the high basin — through forest that opens into wildflower meadows around the 6-mile mark, with Mount Clark and Mount Walkinshaw's 7,000-ft summits visible ahead. The trail steepens for the final push through switchbacks into Royal Basin, reaching Royal Lake (5,100 ft, ~7.2 mi, ~2,500 ft gain) — the established backcountry camp area (bear canisters required, no fires, permits needed May-Sept). From the lake, a climbers' path continues roughly another 0.8-1 mile and 500 ft of gain across willow flats and boulder benches to Upper Royal Basin (~5,600 ft, ~8 mi from the trailhead), the day-use staging area for all Needles-area objectives (camping is not permitted in the upper basin). Beyond Upper Royal Basin there is no maintained tread: traverse cross-country north, contouring below Mount Clark's east flank on talus and boulder benches toward Mount Walkinshaw, the northernmost peak in the Needles chain — this stretch is rough, adds roughly 1.5 miles and several hundred feet of ascending/descending sidehill travel, and involves genuine route-finding (krummholz and short cliff bands can obscure the best line, as noted by parties working this same traverse from the Gray Wolf Ridge side). Aim for the prominent talus tongue below Walkinshaw's broken east face, then climb northwest over boulders and a bare scree rib to the col at the south end of Gray Wolf Ridge, northeast of the peak. From the col, skirt several steepening pinnacles on their east side with Class 3 moves on rotten shale (far looser than typical Cascades granite), then follow the northeast ridge through ledges and small gullies to an exposed blade of rock and the small (~10-ft-diameter) rocky summit at 7,378 ft — Class 3 overall, with perhaps one short Class 4 step. Keep parties tight and helmets on through the entire gully/ridge section — loose rock and rockfall onto climbers below are the defining hazard of this route. Total round-trip distance from the trailhead is on the order of 19 miles (matching the route's recorded 30.58 km), reflecting the extra cross-country mileage beyond Upper Royal Basin that standard figures for the closer Royal Basin peaks (Deception/Mystery, ~14 mi RT) don't include.

runs: 2419 and follow it up the big creek drainage
hits.text: From the T-intersection at the end of North Lake Cushman Road, continue right onto FS Road 24 for about 1.5 miles, then turn left onto FS Road 2419 and follow it up the Big Creek drainage for roughly 6.6 miles to its end at a small trailhead/parking area at about 3,026 ft. From here the 'trail' quickly becomes a boot path and then largely off-trail scrambling — there is no numbered maintained trail for most of the route. The path climbs directly and steeply through forest for the first stretch, hand-over-hand on roots and rock in places, gaining several hundred feet before breaking out of the trees into a couple of open meadow benches (the most reliable early-season water, via lingering snowmelt seeps, is generally found in this meadow band — by mid-to-late summer expect it to be dry, so carry all the water you'll need from the car). Above the meadows the route enters scree and talus slopes and stays primarily on the climber's-left side of a large, loose rocky gully; this section is tight in spots with a lot of unconsolidated rock, so groups should stay spread out (not stacked directly above/below each other) to avoid raining rocks on people below. In spring and early summer this gully can hold avalanche-prone snow and may require an ice axe. The path winds above the gully until it gains Mount Washington's southern ridgeline, then follows a faint, exposed climbers'/goat trail along the ridge crest — in multiple spots the tread narrows to barely one boot-width with real exposure on both sides (this is the section referred to as the 'Dog Walk Ledge'); solid class 3 with a couple of class 3+/4 moves, and not a place for hesitant scramblers. The ridge trail leads to a scree field below the false summit (greasy and slick if wet) and a 'goat trail' up its climbers'-right edge to a stone wind shelter on the ridge, from which a final short class 3–4 scramble gains the true 6,255 ft summit.

hits.text: Park at the Watson Lakes Trailhead at the end of FS Road 1107 (elev. ~4,300 ft), reached via Baker Lake Road (FS-11) south around Baker Lake on FS-1106 and out FS-1107 to road's end. From the trailhead, follow the Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail #611 into the woods; at about 1 mile you'll pass the junction with the Anderson Butte Trail #611.1 (stay straight/right for Watson Lakes). Around 1.5-2 miles, at roughly 4,700 ft, a second junction splits: right drops 0.5 mile to lower Anderson Lake, while the left fork climbs 0.5 mile to a small saddle entering the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness before dropping to the Watson Lakes (4,400 ft) near 2.5-3 miles in. The lakes are notoriously buggy in summer and are the last reliable water — treat before filling up, since there's no dependable source higher on the mountain. From Watson Lakes the maintained trail ends and the route becomes an open, cairned/boot-path climbers' route: leave the basin and climb talus (and snow well into summer) on Watson's north/west slopes toward the ridge crest. The standard and easiest line follows the widest gully east of the peak up to a saddle at about 5,900 ft on the ridge; a western gully alternative has a dangerous moat and rotten snow bridge late-season and should be avoided. From the 5,900-ft saddle, traverse along the ridge and across a steep slope to wrap around the base of the summit block. A short, loose class 2-3 dirt-and-rock gully (10-15 ft) gains the true summit ridge, which is a narrow (~30 ft), exposed class 2-3 catwalk with real drop-off on both sides — a hand line is commonly carried and recommended for this final airy section. Total round trip runs roughly 7-9.5 miles with 2,500-3,000 ft gain depending on exact trailhead/camp and route-finding; parties camping partway (e.g., ~5,400 ft on the north slopes) shorten the summit day considerably. Route-finding above the lakes is the main approach hazard in poor visibility since the line is unmarked talus/snow rather than trail.

hits.text: Turn off the highway a little over four miles east of Washington Pass, following signs for the Cutthroat Creek trail, and drive about a mile to the trailhead lot, which has restrooms. Do not confuse this with the Cutthroat Peak approach, which starts from an unmarked highway pullout well west of here and serves a different objective entirely. Start on the maintained Cutthroat Creek Trail, then leave it a short way along and walk up through the woods toward the wall — the ground gains elevation quickly at first, then the line traverses leftward through open forest and across slabby benches. There is no maintained tread on this section; parties report cairns and an intermittent climbers' path, but treat it as open-forest navigation rather than a trail. The traverse ends on a shoulder at the base of the wall's right-hand side, which is where the climbing starts. Allow the better part of a couple of hours from the car to the base.

runs: the base of the wall's right hand side
hits.text: The shoulder at the right-hand end of the wall is the arrival point, and the route starts on low-angle ground, not steep ground. The traverse through the forest and across the slabby benches deposits you on a shoulder at the base of the wall's right-hand side; that shoulder, rather than any point along the middle of the cliff, is where you should be standing. From it, the start of this route is clean, low-angle crack systems running up a big ramp that trends left as it rises. Low angle and left-trending together are the test. This wall holds only two known lines and the other one is several grades harder and sustained, so if what is above you is steep, continuous crack climbing with no ramp under it, you have walked past the start and are beneath the hard line. Likewise, if you are still in trees and have not come out onto a distinct shoulder with the right edge of the wall above you, you have not finished the traverse. Expect the cracks on the lower pitches to be bushy and dirty rather than clean — that is normal here and is another sign you are on the right, less-travelled line. The upper pitches merge into the harder route's corner and finish on its final blocky pitch, and the descent rappels that line.

hits.text: The summit path is now more worn than the trail it leaves, and the wrong turn has a name. Navaho Pass is unmistakable ground — small, rocky, sparsely vegetated and wind-exposed, with the Stuart Range filling the view — and it is where the trail meets the old crest trail along the county line. Head east out of the pass, paralleling the range. The old boot-path junction that descriptions still mention has effectively vanished: the beaten track now is the summit path, more worn than the crest trail beside it, so the thing to look for is the most-used tread rather than a faint branch. If instead you follow the connecting ridge left from the pass, you are heading for Wrong Turn Peak, which is what it is called and why. Two more confusions worth knowing: the prominent peak straight ahead on the walk in is Little Navaho, not this one, and the final ridge throws up several false tops before the true summit, which is small — barely higher than a rocky outcrop just east of it. On the way down, do not follow the southeast ridge all the way toward Little Navaho; there are cliffs below it.

runs: each pitch has a move or two of old school 5.3
hits.text:
You are aiming for the long broken ridge that runs between Cathedral Peak and The Pope, a separate small peak further north along the same crest, sitting right on the Canada–United States border.

That relationship is the base-finding and it is also the warning. The ridge has a peak at each end. If you keep working north along the crest past the point where the ground starts descending away from Cathedral, you are heading for The Pope and, shortly after that, for an international border it is illegal to cross here.

The route itself confirms as you go rather than at a single spot: each pitch has a move or two of old-school 5.3 with scrambling between, so seven pitches of mostly-easy ground with occasional short difficulties is correct here and is not a sign you have wandered onto the walk-up. The real crux announces itself — about 400 feet below the summit you cross a dike, and the two short pitches immediately above that dike are the hardest climbing on the route. A final airy fourth-class scramble finishes it.

Negative marker for the start: if you find yourself entering a deep gully with a detached tower on your right, you have walked to the SE Buttress start. The NE Ridge is gained from open grassy slope off the main trail, with no gully involved.

Descent is the ordinary walk-up route to the west, and a short rappel may be wanted to get off the summit ridge.

runs: 200 vertical feet and traverse to the first obvious gully
hits.text:
From the notch, downclimb about 200 vertical feet and traverse to the first obvious gully. That is the published test and it is the one that works in cloud, because it is counted rather than seen: you are not identifying a gully by its shape from a distance, you are walking beneath the face from a fixed point and taking the first one you meet.

Why that matters here more than anywhere else on this page: this face carries five closely spaced ice and mixed lines — Pineapple Express, Blue Moon, New York Gully Direct, New York Gully and LA Express — and they are near enough together that racking up under the wrong one is the normal failure. Count from the notch, do not pick by appearance.

The pitch-one confirmation, and it is a good one: ascend roughly 200 ft up the gully and then take an obvious ramp out to the left, belaying from a quasi-cave. Gully, then a left-trending ramp, then a cave belay. If your first rope length does not offer a left ramp at about 200 ft, you are in a neighbouring line.

The second confirmation is higher and unambiguous: the route runs up obvious weaknesses to a small headwall split by a 5.8 crack, historically aided and now freed. That crack is the route's signature. A line with no headwall crack is not New York Gully.

And a honest warning about the approach itself: most of it is through thick timber and the published advice is to go with somebody who knows it or follow an existing skin track. Without a track, expect it to be slow and to be the part of the day where you lose time.

runs: into the notch between north and south early
hits.text:
Two established ways off the summit; both are widely used and either works, but they return you to different spots relative to a gear stash at the base.

Bolted West Face rappel line (most direct back to packs at the base of NW Corner/West Face): from the summit, downclimb/walk skier's-left to the top of a clean, purpose-bolted rappel line down the right side of the West Face. Six bolted (2-bolt) rappel stations in a nearly direct line bring you back down to essentially the same spot where you left your pack at the base of the route. Pulls are reported as clean and the line is efficient — regulars find it a breeze. A single 60m rope is just barely sufficient (one station, reportedly the 3rd rappel, is tight enough that you may need to reach down to clip your PAS/daisy to the anchor and feed rope through your device to reach it); a 70m rope removes that squeeze and is the more comfortable choice. No natural anchors needed on this line — it's fully bolted.

Classic notch/chockstone descent (South/Southwest Gully): downclimb and rappel the south side into the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire, then continue down the Southwest Gully (the South Early Winter Spire "Chockstone Route" descent). This runs three single-rope rappels from near the summit down to the notch/gully (which often holds snow even in summer), followed by one spectacular, largely free-hanging double-rope rappel down and past a huge chockstone (~50 ft of air), then a final short rappel (~30 ft, off a tree anchor) or downclimb/scramble to reach the base. Total is about 4-5 rappels on this line. Anchors are natural/fixed slings around the chockstone and trees rather than bolts — inspect webbing before trusting it. Summit-to-base time on this descent is typically around 1.5-2 hours. This option is the standard descent if you climbed a route on the south/southwest side, or as a backup if the West Face bolt line is congested or iced.

runs: the bergschrund at the foot of the final
hits.text:
The bergschrund at roughly 6,500 ft is the base, and the couloir above it is the only one. Beckey and Schmidtke's own account of the first ascent puts them at the bergschrund at the foot of the final north face at 6,500 ft, with 800 ft of 50-degree ice couloir above. That is the arrival: a schrund, then a single steep couloir that guards the Tower.

The ridge between the two glaciers is the handrail. From the Price Lake moraine you climb a rib with the Price Glacier on one side and the East Nooksack on the other. In cloud you do not need the Tower: keep a glacier on each side of you and go up. If you only have ice on one side, you have come off the rib.

The saddle is the hinge, and it is counterintuitive. From the bivy the traverse is climber's right to an exposed snow saddle below the Tower, and then you drop down onto the main lobe of the Price Glacier. Losing height here feels wrong and is correct. A party that refuses to descend off the saddle stays high on the wrong side and never reaches the couloir.

Confirm at the schrund: the couloir starts around 50 degrees and steepens to about 60 at the top, with a single 70-degree step where it hits rock. If your line eases off rather than steepens, it is not the couloir. Parties have found the schrund hollow and swung wide left to avoid it entirely — that is a known variation, not a sign you are lost.

What going too far looks like: continuing up the Price Glacier past the Tower's couloir puts you on the Price Glacier route on Shuksan, which is a different mountain's climb reached from the same basin. Nooksack Tower is the freestanding tower below and north of Shuksan's summit; if the ground above your couloir keeps going for thousands of feet rather than ending on a tower in about 1,200 ft of fourth class, you are on Shuksan.

hits.text:
The whole route-finding problem is which glacier you end up on, and the answer is the east one. The rib above Price Lake has the Price Glacier on one side and the East Nooksack on the other. The Beckey route commits to the Price. This route commits to the East Nooksack. That single decision, made at the top of the rib, is the difference between a north-face ice couloir and a south-face rock climb, and once you are on the wrong glacier nothing further down the day will correct it.

The aspect settles it in fog, with no visibility at all. This route faces south. If the wall in front of you is in shade all morning and holds ice, you are under the north face and on the Beckey route's ground. If the wall catches the sun and is dry rock, you are where you meant to be.

Arrival: the south face rises directly above the glacier — there is no intervening basin, moraine or approach slope. You walk on ice until the ice ends at the wall. That directness is the marker; a wall you reach after scrambling up talus is not this one.

And the start is on the right. Having reached the foot of the face, the climb begins on its right side. A party that starts up the middle or the left of a twelve-pitch face on a rarely climbed tower has committed to unknown ground with a technical descent waiting for them.

Descent note that double-checks the start: the first-ascent party did not reverse this face. They descended the standard north-face route on the front of the tower, i.e. over the top and down the other side. If you are planning to rappel your line of ascent, you are planning something nobody has recorded.

runs: in the blocky line of face holds just left of
hits.text:
The face is about fourteen hundred feet of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs above a glacier and it carries several routes with nothing marked. Do not identify by name; identify by feature.

First, place the central buttress. Stand back on the glacier and find the summit, then look at the buttress directly beneath it — that is the neighbouring route, and this line is not on it. This route takes the left margin of that buttress system, so you want to be off to the left of the plumb line from the summit.

Second, find the gully or chimney at the buttress's left edge. The start is in the blocky line of face holds just left of it. Blocky face holds, immediately left of a gully or chimney, at the left edge of the buttress: that is the whole identification at the ground. The first pitch is long, mostly low fifth class, with a wide crack near its end.

Third, and this is the confirmation higher up that nothing else on the face gives you: this route follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke up the wall to avoid the dirtier rock either side of it. A yellow band running up the granite is not a subtle feature. If you never meet one, you are on a different climb.

Watch for an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock.

Negative markers, and they matter because two of the neighbours are hard: if the summit is directly overhead from your belay and your second pitch is desperate face climbing wanting an aid move, you are on the central buttress line. And the face's original route and at least two others also exist here, so the honest rule is that anything without the yellow dyke above it is not this.

Descent is not the route reversed and not a rappel: take the east ridge from the top to an obvious col, then a snow finger back down toward the approach glacier and basin.
