Whichever way you arrive, the glacier is the same and so is the identification, and this side has one advantage worth using: you come down toward the wall, which gives you the whole face in one view before you are under it. Take that view rather than sorting the routes out from the bergschrund.

From back on the glacier, find the summit and note the buttress directly under it — that is the neighbouring line and it is not this one. This route is on the left margin of the same buttress system.

The ground marker is a gully or chimney at the buttress's left edge, with the route starting in the blocky line of face holds just left of it. The confirmation above is a yellow quartz dyke, which the line follows deliberately to stay on clean rock and away from the dirtier granite either side. Yellow band, left margin, blocky start beside a chimney: those three together are the route.

Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat at the transition from ice to rock.

Negative markers. Directly under the summit with a very hard second pitch means the central buttress line. No yellow dyke anywhere above you means one of the other lines on this face, of which there are several and none is marked.

Second negative marker and it is not about climbing: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line across this ground. It is not a route and it is not a shortcut.

Descent is the east ridge to an obvious col and then a snow finger back to the glacier and basin.

hits.text: The base is the top of the notch between Concord Tower and Liberty Bell, reached by the gully — if you scrambled left out of the gully a couple of hundred feet below the notch onto a broad sloping bench, you are on Liberty Bell's west side and on a different mountain's route entirely. From the notch, the first pitch follows a crack system to a large ledge with some small trees growing on it; that ledge with trees is the confirmation you are on the North Face and not somewhere else on the tower. The second pitch is where this line parts from the standard route. From the tree ledge, head right toward a striking vertical crack and climb it until it gets harder, then traverse up and left across the face to a huge boulder or chockstone slung with tat. If you climbed straight up hollow, flaky rock to a short blank wall covered in huge huecos, you are on the standard North Face instead; going right after that hueco wall leads onto the Cave Route, not this variation. Expect severe rope drag on that long right-then-left pitch; extend everything.

hits.text: North Gardner Mountain (8,956 ft) is the highest point in Okanogan County and the 20th-highest peak on the Washington Bulger List (the state's 100 highest summits with 400+ ft of prominence). It sits within the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness on the east side of the Cascade Crest above the Methow Valley, joined by a high connecting ridge to 8,898 ft Gardner Mountain, 59 ft lower. The standard Southwest Slopes/South Ridge line is a long, remote scramble: roughly 10 miles of trail approach up Wolf Creek to Gardner Meadows, then off-trail travel through Wolf Creek Basin and a loose scree/snow bowl to the south ridge at Point 8,487, followed by a short final ridge walk to the true summit. Terrain is mostly Class 1-2 with a few short Class 3 steps; the crux for most parties is route-finding and about 1,400 ft of loose scree below Point 8,487, not technical climbing.

runs: groves of silver snags with jack strawed deadfall
hits.text: The higher option for a party that wants to shorten summit day rather than take both peaks in one long push from the meadows. Heading north out of Gardner Meadows the ground rises to a small meadow basin at about 6,200 ft, and an old boot path leaves the main trail a few hundred feet west of the small stream to reach it. Stay between roughly 6,200 and 6,400 ft on the way across — drop lower and you land in groves of silver snags with jack-strawed deadfall that cost far more time than the elevation saves. From a camp here the scree slope to the ridge is about 1,400 ft of gain in half a mile, which is the steepest and loosest section of the whole climb and much better done early and on firm ground. It is an exposed spot with no shelter to speak of and it is cold; the compensation is the position and the head start. Use it when the forecast is settled and when you have confirmed water. In a dry August the meadows below are the safer plan.

runs: short pitches of low fifth class to gain the north ridge notch
hits.text:
At the boulder field, bear right and north into the basin beneath the north ridge notch, rather than left toward the south buttress gully. That is the fork, and left versus right is the whole difference between two of this peak's routes.

The route's real base is the notch, and getting to it is itself a pitch: from the basin, A loose, runout 5.7 PG13 pitch gains the north ridge notch. Protection is marginal, one or two small cams and narrow-head-width pieces help, and this pitch should be treated as the technical and psychological crux of the approach, not of the ridge above it.

So the test is blunt: if the hardest, scariest thing you have done is the pitch that got you to the notch, you are on the right route. If you got to a notch by walking, you are somewhere else.

Arrival: a notch, a gap on the crest with the ridge running above it. Everything above is the North Ridge.

The northern alternative, which arrives at the same notch from the other side: from Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail into the Porcupine Creek drainage, then climb two or three short pitches of low fifth class to gain the North Ridge Notch from that side. That is a legitimate option for parties camping near Rainy Pass, and it adds significant approach time. Two or three easy pitches versus one hard runout one is how you tell which side you came up.

Descent does not reverse the approach pitch all the way: from the summit, reverse the North Ridge with several short rappels through the steeper fifth-class steps, then one longer rappel back into the North Ridge Notch. From the notch, descend via the standard South Buttress and West Ridge line, downclimbing to the first set of bolted chain rappel anchors and continuing down the same four-rappel West Ridge sequence, a single 60 m rope sufficient for each, before the final scramble through the scree bowl and boulder field back to the meadow and creek crossing.

runs: 6 000 ft at the toe of the borealis glacier
hits.text:
This is a genuinely obscure line and every recorded approach to it is a variation on getting round to the mountain's north side, which no other Primus route visits.

The first recorded ascent reached it from the Klawatti side: descend a couloir where the North Klawatti Glacier meets Primus's west ridge, then traverse an unnamed glacier north of Primus to the foot of the crest. The first-ascent account says in as many words that it was unlikely this approach had been used before.

Other parties have come from the Thunder Creek side instead — the same trailhead, creek crossing at McAllister Camp and climbers' trail up the ridge as the East Slope, to a bivy near 6,000 ft at the toe of the Borealis Glacier — and then reached the ridge by circling the glacial lake at the glacier's terminus and crossing a short section of glacier to the base, rather than climbing the glacier toward Lucky Pass. One party took that line specifically because conditions at the standard Primus-Tricouni saddle were hazardous that day.

The ridge itself is about 1,000 ft and took the first-ascent party roughly an hour.

The Aiguille is a small formation, not a peak of its own: it is the cockscomb dividing the high Forbidden basin from Torment basin, with the Taboo Glacier on its west side and an unnamed glacier on its east, sitting just south of the Torment-Forbidden traverse line. It is named for its resemblance to the Chamonix aiguille of the same shape — a deliberate echo, and a coincidence worth being clear about rather than a mistake.

Approach exactly as for Forbidden Peak: Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles to the small pullout near 3,200 ft opposite Johannesburg, the old Diamond Mine roadbed, then the steep unmaintained climbers' path with several stream crossings to treeline near 5,300 ft and the Boston Basin camps at about 5,300 and 6,400 ft.

From camp, head up toward the Forbidden Gully / Cat Scratch gullies area and traverse to the notch. It is a half-day objective from camp, which is most of its appeal.

runs: the notch to the right of the north ridge
hits.text:
The formation is the easy part: the aiguille is conspicuous on entering Boston Basin and reads as the letter it is named for. Use it to orient the whole basin. The route is the harder part.

The base is the notch to the right of the north ridge — you traverse to it from the Cat Scratch / Forbidden Gully side; you do not start at the toe of the ridge. A start at the very bottom of the crest is not this route.

Count the pitches, because the count is the route: three to four pitches of fourth-class scrambling to the base of a tower, and then one 40-ft pitch to its top. That is the whole climb. If you have run out four pitches and there is no tower standing in front of you, you are on the wrong side of the formation.

The most important thing to know about the top is that it is not the top. The route finishes on a subsidiary tower; the true high point of the Aiguille looks as though it is about to topple over and most parties deliberately stop short of it. So a summit that feels wrong is not evidence you are off route — on this formation it is the expected outcome, and it is the reason the descent is a single 40-ft rappel from where you stand.

Tell it from the south ridge by which side you walked round. The two routes differ only in which flank of the same small formation is climbed from the same camp; the South Ridge is the longer, harder and much less documented of the two, and its start is not published — so if you are unsure which side you are on, the four-pitch scramble to a tower is the one that can be confirmed.

runs: the small cirque at the base of the
hits.text:
Tiffany Springs Campground sits at about 6,760 ft and is reached by long gravel drives from Conconully by the North Fork Salmon Creek road, from the Methow Valley, or over Baldy Pass on the South Fork. The Conconully line is the roughest of the three. Expect an hour or more on gravel whichever you choose.

Trail #373 leaves the campground east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass at about 7,150 ft, about forty-five minutes of easy walking. From the pass, traverse south on the grassy east slope below the crest into the small cirque at the base of the north face, at roughly 7,360 ft, then climb the boulder field to the foot of the climbing at about 7,600 ft.

Compared with anything else in this corner of the state the approach is short and easy, which is most of this face's appeal. Roads are snowbound for much of the year and generally open around late June.

runs: bench and continue to the foot of the formidable glacier
hits.text: A deep objective reached along the same corridor as its neighbours, and the walk-in is a full day or more of committing glaciated terrain rather than a hike. From the Cascade Pass Trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road, take the maintained trail to the pass, then leave it and work south and east across the Mixup flank on boot path, talus and snow bands, up the Cache Glacier to Cache Col, and down the steep snow on the far side to the tarn at Kool-Aid Lake. From the lake, climb out of the basin toward the cliff band running west off the knoll above; the Red Ledge cuts through it, usually entered by scrambling through the moat at the snow-rock margin and a few feet of easy rock, and it is broad and walkable unless it is holding snow or verglas. Roughly a quarter mile past the ledge, descend several hundred feet to the bench on the Middle Cascade Glacier between the two large icefall sections, cross that bench, and continue to the foot of the Formidable Glacier. Note that this is a different objective from the peak's ordinary walk-up on the south side, which is the descent line rather than the approach.

hits.text:
This is one of the shortest approaches in the range and one of the least forgiving. From the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of Cascade River Road near 3,600 ft, walk a short way back down the road, descend a dirt embankment, ford or cross the infant Cascade River, and cross the terminal moraine and snowfield. Serious ground starts around 3,500 ft — you are on the route within an hour of the car.

Climb partway up the Cascade-Johannesburg couloir to the hanging glacier on the right, then take the leftmost rib to the summit. Twelve pitches, about 4,000 ft.

The descent is a separate expedition: the East Ridge's loose 3rd and 4th class gendarme ledges to the Cascade-Johannesburg col, then either the couloir or 'Doug's Direct' — beneath the Triplets buttress, sidehilling steep heather, across Mixup Peak's north ridge and down to the Cache Glacier. Parties have taken four and a half to nine hours from the col.

hits.text:
From the Stuart Lake Trailhead, hike the Stuart Lake Trail and go straight past the Colchuck Lake turnoff. Continue to about 4,700 ft, where a faint path leaves the trail for Mountaineer Creek. Follow it over and down to the creek, then up the creek to roughly 4,780 ft, and bushwhack up to a boulder field below Argonaut at about 4,925 ft.

Traverse the boulders following cairns south-southwest and cut through slide alder — this brush is the notorious part of the day, and staying on talus to climber's right where you can avoids the worst of it. Then head up in or beside the trees, through boulders, talus, scree and dry creek beds, past waterfall slabs, into the north basin below Argonaut at about 6,700 ft. Roughly four hours car-to-basin for an efficient party.

Expect to lose the boot path in the boulder field. Most of this approach is navigated by feel; there is no marked trail. Wet, mossy logs over Mountaineer Creek are a nuisance in both directions.

runs: the 5 300 ft saddle between bedal peak and sloan peak
hits.text: Same Bedal Creek approach as Sloan's other West Face routes. From the Mountain Loop Highway take FR 4096 to the Bedal Creek Trailhead (~2,790 ft) and follow Bedal Creek Trail #705 along the creek through old growth until the maintained tread ends at a washout below the West Face basin (roughly 1.5–2.5 miles in). Scramble the washout to a cairned exit onto a climber's path that climbs steeply through forest from about 3,500 ft to 4,900 ft, then crosses talus and a meadow bench to the 5,300 ft saddle between Bedal Peak and Sloan Peak (last water here or at nearby cascading streams). From the meadows below the broad West Face, the Northwest Buttress route begins on a corner of darker rock at the lowest, leftmost part of the face — no glacier travel is needed to reach the start, unlike the standard Corkscrew line, which continues past this point onto the ice. Expect brush and route-finding in the forest band; best conditions are mid-to-late season (July–September) once snowmelt clears the lower approach.

The ridge itself is deep, virgin choss rated 5.5 X, including a two-pitch section climbed à cheval (straddling the ridge crest) across rock with the consistency of feta cheese, followed by roughly 1,000 additional feet of similarly poor climbing. It is accessed along the basin rim from the direction of Sharkfin Tower. The road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter; snow on the crags and approach slopes is what limits climbing, to roughly May through October, sometimes from April. The Dikes lie farther on, upstream and south toward Bluewood.

hits.text: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike North: park 1.1 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, where a dirt road intersects the paved road on the left (SE side), or continue to 1.2 miles and use the large pull-off. Cross the main road and pick up the approach trail between the two parking spots, marked by a short steep drainage topped with a downed tree.

runs: forest service road 64 at the forest boundary
hits.text: Paved North Touchet Road out of Dayton becomes gravel-to-dirt Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary as it climbs toward the Bluewood ski area; the climbing dikes sit right along this road roughly 18 miles in (about 1-2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, which is 16-17 miles from Dayton). Approach paths to individual crags (Megadike, Minidike, Weeping Wall, Joe's Rock) are unofficial, brushy, and easy to lose.

From the summit, downclimb the upper pitch a short way and go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60 m rope reaches a sandy ledge; work right and down to a bolted station, then make two single-rope rappels of about 25 m from bolted anchors into the Liberty Bell-Concord notch at about 7,300 ft. Parties who downclimb the ridge and the 5.6 boulder problem to the first bolts instead of making the tree rappel do two rappels in all. hits.text: Same Hoh River Trail (17.4 mi) and Blue Glacier approach to Glacier Meadows as the standard route (5-Mile Island, Olympus Guard Station/High Hoh Bridge, Lewis Meadow ~11 mi as the common overnight, Elk Lake, Glacier Meadows at 4,300 ft), then the ~1-mi lateral-moraine crossing onto the glacier. From Snow Dome (~6,600–6,800 ft), the traverse follows the standard Crystal Pass line — over Crystal Pass, south of (below) Five Fingers Ridge, over the false summit — to the West Peak (7,980 ft), then continues east across intervening terrain to the Middle Peak (7,929 ft) and finally the East Peak (7,762 ft). This is a multi-day, largely off-trail glacier and ridge outing; expect sustained glacier travel with crevasse and icefall exposure the entire way, and carry a full rescue kit for the whole traverse, not just the West Peak summit pitch.

hits.text:
Do not stop at the obvious base. The first thing you reach under this wall is a granite patio where two other routes start about fifty feet apart. This route is not there. It is about a hundred and fifty feet climbers' left of and above that patio, so from the patio you keep walking left and gaining height rather than racking up.

The marker is vegetation, and it is specific: a small outcropping of trees uphill of the left-hand patio route's start. Find that patch of trees. The route begins in the rock-scarred open book just left of it. Scarred rock and an open book, immediately left of a small stand of trees, uphill and left of the patio — that is the whole identification, and it is the only start on this wall with a plant landmark.

Confirm by the feature above: this line takes the obvious left-facing broken corner system in the centre of the buttress, left of the blockier ground that carries the two patio routes. If the corner above you faces right rather than left, you are on the wrong side of the wall.

Negative markers. If you are standing on a flat slab platform with a second route start visible fifty feet away, you are still at the patio and have not walked far enough. If your line is wandering through featured ground past big gnarled trees and later a distinctly spiral tree, you are on the 5.9 that starts right of the patio.

This route is also the one on the wall whose descent is different, and knowing that is worth a lot at the top: parties find it faster to rappel the route — three full sixty-metre rappels reach the ground, starting from a tree slightly up and left of the belay at the top of pitch five — rather than take the shared notch descent. Watch for stacked blocks near the top of the second pitch's corner.

hits.text: Identical trailhead-to-basin approach as the Classic Route and The Roof: from the Snow Lake Trailhead on Stevens Canyon Road, hike the maintained Snow Lake Trail ~1 mile (about 350 ft of up-and-down) to Snow Lake, the last water source. Continue past the lake on the fading tread over a wooded rise, then pick a line up and right into the talus/dirt gully on the peak's NW side; a climbers' path reappears on a heather bench near the gully's top and leads into the basin beneath the summit block. Ascend moraine along the edge of the small basin snowfield to the saddle (Unicorn Col) just west/southwest of the summit, then follow the use trail traversing below the cliffs on the south side of the peak to the base of the summit horn. The Open Book line starts at two wide, left-leaning cracks about 50 ft right of the Classic Route on the same south face, so from the base of the horn move climber's-right before starting the technical climbing; it's regarded as the easiest of the summit-block lines (Easy 5th class / 5.0), a step down from the Classic Route (5.4-5.6) and The Roof (5.6). Total approach is roughly 2.5-3 miles one-way with about 2,400 ft gain, mostly on climbers' path and talus once past Snow Lake.

runs: at the stream crossing just before the lake
hits.text:
Leave the trail at the stream crossing just before the lake, not at the lake. Two independent accounts do exactly that: cross the stream, head north-east up into open forest, and break out of the trees onto talus.

The arrival test is the ground itself. The talus is continuous and endless — no benches, no trees, no interruption — running roughly fourteen hundred feet straight to the top. There is no elegant line on it; you put your head down and climb. If you are still weaving between trees and heather benches you have not reached the slope proper.

Negative marker for leaving too early: one climber went up toward what he took to be the south-west ridge, found it was not, and had to work up and down to reach the real one, where bits of use trail run through the least-bad talus. Use-trail fragments are a sign you are on the right slope.

Summit test: the top is ringed by cliffs on every side except the scree slope you came up. If you are on a summit with more than one walkable side, it is not this one.

How to know it is Osceola and not Carru: Mount Carru is about a mile east and it is higher — 8,595 ft against Osceola's 8,587. From the top of Osceola you look east across a deep notch at a higher peak. The ground between the two is described by one climber as somewhere between awful and impassable, so that notch is a wall, not a link. Osceola, Carru and Lago all keep their steep and cliffy ground on the north, which gives a broader check: a peak in this group whose easy ground is on the north side is none of the three.

Nothing published reports a false summit on Osceola.

hits.text: The Ottohorn is a slender granite spire in the Southern Pickets, rising directly across the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col from its larger neighbor Himmelgeisterhorn, deep in North Cascades National Park's Crescent Creek Basin. It was first climbed on September 10, 1961 by Ed Cooper, Glen Denny, Joan Firey, Joe Firey, and George Whitmore via the east ridge from the col (Class III) — the same trip that put up Himmelgeisterhorn and Frenzel Spitz, all three reportedly named after labels the Fireys peeled off a mustard bottle carried on the approach. One of the range's more obscure summits, Ottohorn is rarely climbed alone; most parties tag it as part of a Crescent Creek Basin enchainment with Himmelgeisterhorn and/or Frenzel Spitz.

runs: between the barrier ridge and the chopping block
hits.text: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.

runs: 500 vertical feet to the base of the wall
hits.text:
From the Icicle Road junction at the west end of Leavenworth, drive Icicle Road about 4.25 miles to the Snow Creek trailhead lot. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park.

Walk the Snow Creek / Snow Lakes trail uphill for roughly two to two and a half miles — about an hour — until the wall stands directly opposite you across the drainage. The trail never touches the rock, so what you are watching for is the wall coming abeam, not a junction or a sign.

At one of the first easy openings, branch right off the trail and scramble down into the flat ground beside Snow Creek to find the log crossing. On the far bank, climb up through boulders and talus until a bootpath forms; it gains about 500 vertical feet to the base of the wall.

Weekends are busy and this is the most popular route in Leavenworth — a queue at the base is normal.

runs: the long well cleaned crack splitting the upper headwall
hits.text:
Find the route by its top, not its bottom. Outer Space is the long, well-cleaned crack splitting the upper headwall — the Shield — and it is the most obvious single feature on the wall. Trace that crack downward to where it ends at a ledge with several bushes on it.

The route's own original start is the ledge-and-dihedral system about 80 ft right of that point and 100 ft down from it.

In practice most parties never use that start: they climb the first pitches of Remorse instead, which begins essentially where the climbers' trail arrives at the wall. That arrival point is the highest part of the wall's base, with a few small scrub trees on it. Standing there, the clean bolted slab straight in front of you is RPM's first pitch at 5.10d; Remorse's much easier line is the often-vegetated gully about 30 ft to the right of it.

So the single most useful test at the base: if your first move off the ground is a hard, blank, bolted friction slab, you are on RPM, not on the Remorse start to Outer Space. Step right into the scruffy gully.

runs: see the large cliff rising above the south side of the river at the
hits.text: From I-90 exit 34 go north, then right onto SE Middle Fork Road, FR 56, and follow it about twelve miles to the Taylor River junction. Bear right onto FR 5620 and continue to the Dingford Creek trailhead at roughly 1,500 ft. FR 56 is notorious for potholes and ruts and high clearance is genuinely useful; the stretch beyond the gate is reported to be in better shape than the public road. FR 5620 is decommissioned beyond Dingford Creek. The closed stretch to the old Dutch Miller Gap trailhead and Hardscrabble Horse Camp is given as seven, eight or ten miles, so do not plan on a precise number. A bike is universally recommended and cuts hours off both ends. Beyond the road, parties use three genuinely different lines, none of them confirmed by another, so read all three before choosing. The most specific of them fords the Middle Fork on a visual cue rather than a mileage: walk roughly four miles of trail until you can see the large cliff rising above the south side of the river at the foot of Overcoat. Push through about ten minutes of alder, ford there, and you land on the talus field at the base of those cliffs. Further north-east the alder gets much thicker. A second line crosses about a mile before the Dutch Miller Gap trail proper and climbs steep forest to camp at Overcoat Lake. A third crosses the river on rocks, climbs steep brushy ground into a two-mile rocky corridor sometimes called the Valley of the Chiefs, meets continuous snow around 4,600 ft, and goes over a pass at about 6,140 ft. On the traverse toward camp, one party's correction: they climbed to the ridge and then realised the line stays lower, and had to drop back to find the sloping rock crux and downclimb to the snow. A durable warning about the road rather than the mountain: the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road has a long-standing reputation for unsavoury activity, including gunfire, and at least one regular visitor reports it on every trip.

runs: to get back to the top of the
hits.text:
The snow finger is not visible until you are underneath it, so do not try to identify it from camp or from the glacier below.

The sequence that works: reach the Overcoat Glacier, make a long rising traverse of five hundred feet or so to the top of the mild glacier, and only then does the steep snow finger show itself, with dark towers standing above it.

The dark towers are the transition. You leave snow for rock at their foot, then round the corner east and the glacier reappears below you. From there it is steep gully climbing on solid holds with a few exposed steps over tall blocks to the summit.

The consistent fact across every published account, and the one to steer by: the summit pyramid is gained on its east or north-east side. Nobody describes climbing it from the south-east. If you are working around to the south side of the block looking for a way up, you have gone the wrong way round.

Grade opinions on that finish run from Class 3 to low fifth, and parties have pitched it out in two short pitches with a few small cams and nuts, with one rappel and some downclimbing to get back to the top of the snow finger. Expect thin protection and poor rock rather than a scramble.

Moats around the glacier margin and crevasses part way up the snow finger are the two things that most often force a detour here, and both were reported as more awkward than expected by parties who had read otherwise.

runs: a few exposed moves over tall steps to
hits.text: The final block stands roughly 400 vertical ft above the surrounding terrain and is steep on every side, so at least class 4 and arguably low 5th is unavoidable to reach the top. Climb the steep gully on the east side of the pyramid on generally good holds with a few exposed moves over tall steps to gain a roomy summit. Summit rocks have been described as wobbly — test everything, and be aware that anyone below is directly in the fall line. Descent is normally a downclimb through a dihedral and heather ledges followed by two full-length rappels back to the glacier, so bring enough rope and slings to build anchors.

runs: red mountain trail signed painted mountain lookout trail
hits.text: From the North Fork Sauk trailhead, hike the maintained Red Mountain Trail (signed 'Painted Mountain Lookout Trail') about 1 mile to its end near the old 1936-67 lookout site (~2,800 ft). Ascend roughly 70 vertical feet of steep, moss-and-dirt-covered rock ledges (Class 3, exposed in spots) to gain the southwest ridge. From there a faint boot path, sometimes marked with pink flagging, climbs open meadows and rock along the ridge/shoulder to an overlook of Ruby Lake near 5,800 ft, then continues on steeper ground to about 6,700 ft before scree slopes lead to the 6,975 ft summit. The whole outing (car-to-car) is roughly 8 miles round trip with about 4,875 ft of total elevation gain.

hits.text: Pernod and neighboring Chablis are the easiest of the Wine Spires, and this line is a reasonable day from a Burgundy Col camp. The climbing is moderate (about 5.5-5.7) and not sustained. It climbs from the east side up to the notch between Pernod and Chianti and then up the northeast corner to a tiny summit block; the South Face and the Direct West Face are separate, harder routes on the same spire.

runs: leads to the base of the west face
hits.text:
This line is climbed from the east, not from the west face gully. Stay on the main climbers' trail past the bench all the way to Burgundy Col; the gully that contours right off the bench leads to the base of the west face, which is the start of a different and much harder route.

From the col, cross to the east side and go south. Traverse below the east walls of Chianti and then Pernod, on snow and talus at the edge of the glacier basin. Pernod is the highest of the four spires and sits just south of Chianti.

The key feature is the notch between Chianti and Pernod. From below the east walls, climb obliquely up and around to that notch; the ground is mostly 4th and 5th class, roughly three pitches. Going south from the col you pass below Chianti first, and the notch you want is the one immediately south of it. The next notch beyond Pernod separates Pernod from Chablis and is the wrong one.

From the notch the route goes up the northeast corner to the small summit block, which carries old first-ascent bolts that are worth backing up.

For parties who camp high: Burgundy Col holds three or four bivy sites, one large enough for a two-person tent, with old rock wind-shelters built by past parties still standing. Those shelters are a positive identification of the col.

Descent is by rappel: back to the notch, then long rappels down the east side to the snow at the edge of the glacier basin. From there climb back up a few hundred feet to regain Burgundy Col, then descend the climbers' trail.

runs: of solid granitic rock with thrilling exposure on both sides
hits.text: The standard approach to Phantom Peak uses the Southwest Glacier and South Couloir with a snow ramp at approximately 40-45 degrees. Climbers cross a bergschrund, navigate a steep snow finger, then move onto broken rock with Class 2-3 scrambling before traversing the sharp, exposed summit ridge. The summit consists of solid granitic rock with thrilling exposure on both sides. A hand line or belay may be useful for the narrowest sections.

hits.text: From a roping-up ledge just above the 6,100' saddle in the ridge's lower reaches, pitch 1 starts with a short, steep crack system before rambling along the crest. Pitches 2-5 continue in the same vein — large corners, towers either bypassed or climbed directly, and exposed ridge running, mostly 5.7+. Pitch 6 holds the crux: a tough move over an airy four-foot-wide cleft, requiring a long 5.10-ish stemming move across a 100-ft-deep gap (the FA party rigged a nut-and-sling handhold to tension across, then top-roped it free). At the top of pitch 7 the ridge tops out on a tower, from which the party rappelled ~100 ft into a notch; pitches 8-10 offer aesthetic face and crack climbing on solid rock. As the difficulty eases, the rope is coiled and about 400 ft of 4th-class terrain is soloed to the sharp summit ridge, finishing with an exposed traverse to the final summit pinnacle.

hits.text:
An involved two-day approach. Roughly 10 miles on trail up and over Hannegan Pass, wading the Chilliwack River, then the scenic 5-mile traverse of Easy Ridge, soloing exposed 4th-class terrain across the Imperfect Impasse, climbing through Perfect Pass and over the Challenger Glacier, then descending and traversing steep snow, talus and more glacier to a bivy site.

The route was first climbed in July 2021 and is documented in a single first-ascent account, so treat everything about it as sparsely reported.

runs: a sprint across a snowfield exposed to rockfall
hits.text:
The bivy is the viewpoint and that is the point of it: the camp sits under Ghost Peak, Phantom's neighbour immediately to the north, and the first-ascent party chose it because the full west ridge comes into view from there. So the test is not a feature at the base of the climb but a named peak overhead: if the summit above your camp is not Ghost Peak, and Phantom is not the next summit south of you, you are camped in the wrong place.

Why that matters more than usual here: this ridge has one published ascent. Nobody has recorded a marker at its toe, and inventing one would be inventing the only fact that matters. What is recorded is the vantage point, so use it: from camp, with the ridge in view, pick the line and note it before the cloud comes in. This is a route to reconnoitre the evening before rather than to find in the morning.

What going too far looks like, on the approach: past Perfect Pass, the Challenger Glacier is crossed and then left again on the far side. If you are still gaining height on ice you have not started the descent toward the Ghost Peak bivy.

On the descent, and worth knowing before you start: the way off is the southeast face, including a sprint across a snowfield exposed to rockfall. The first-ascent party noted that crossing would be more straightforward earlier in the season with more snow cover.

runs: to the western slope of the range from
hits.text: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.

runs: the southwest and west slopes of pyramid peak between
hits.text: From the Longmire Wilderness Information Center (2,762 ft), pick up the Wonderland Trail toward Indian Henry's Hunting Ground. About 3 miles in, after climbing out of Longmire, the trail drops steeply (~400+ ft) to a log-bridge crossing of Kautz Creek — a braided glacial outwash channel whose crossing is periodically damaged or washed out by debris flows off the Kautz Glacier, so check current status at the Longmire WIC before you leave, since a failed crossing can force a long reroute. Beyond the creek the trail climbs by switchbacks through old-growth forest, fords Fisher's Hornpipe Creek, and traverses a ridge past Devil's Dream backcountry camp (~5 mi, reliable water) before breaking out of the trees into the subalpine meadows of Indian Henry's Hunting Ground at roughly 6.3–7 mi and 5,300 ft, marked by the 1915 patrol cabin and open views of the Tahoma/South Tahoma icefall. From Indian Henry's, leave the maintained Wonderland Trail and follow the Mirror Lakes spur/climbers' path (several plank crossings over marshy meadow, then end of maintained tread), continuing cross-country onto the southwest and west slopes of Pyramid Peak between about 6,000 and 6,300 ft to reach Point 6631 just north of the peak. Running water is often available here from snowmelt puddles into early summer, and the rock-slab camp below Pyramid Peak at ~6,300 ft (with running water nearby) is another common first-night camp for a 2-day ascent. From Point 6631, drop briefly NNE to a saddle at about 6,400 ft — the start of Success Cleaver proper. Many parties place a second high camp on the cleaver crest around 10,700 ft (snow platforms can be dug in), from which the route continues up the crest — including a knife-edge section that requires real scrambling once snow melts off it — before angling climber's-right up snow gullies that merge onto the Kautz Cleaver around 12,200–12,600 ft, then up steepening snow/ice (to roughly 45°, with an isolated ~15 ft step near 55° used to bypass a cliff band in some seasons) to Point Success at 14,158 ft. All-in this is roughly 12–13 miles and 11,500 ft of gain from Longmire to Point Success, so most parties split it over 2 days with an intermediate camp rather than going car-to-car in a single push.

runs: the basin between copper peak and pyramid peak
the southwest and west slopes of pyramid peak between roughly 6 000
hits.text:
Longmire (2,762 ft) is the start, on the Wonderland Trail toward Indian Henry's Hunting Ground. About 3 miles out the trail drops steeply to cross Kautz Creek — a braided glacial outwash channel whose crossing is periodically wrecked by debris flows off the Kautz Glacier. Ask at the Longmire wilderness desk before you leave, because a failed crossing means a long reroute rather than a wet foot.

Beyond Kautz Creek the trail switchbacks through old growth, fords Fisher's Hornpipe Creek and passes Devil's Dream camp (about 5 miles, reliable water) before opening into the meadows of Indian Henry's Hunting Ground at roughly 6.3–7 miles and 5,300 ft, marked by the 1915 patrol cabin.

At Indian Henry's leave the Wonderland for the Mirror Lakes spur — plank walkways over marshy meadow, then the end of maintained tread. The path fades into a boot track at about 5,600 ft in the basin between Copper Peak and Pyramid Peak. From there it is cross-country on the southwest and west slopes of Pyramid Peak, between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft, to Point 6631 just north of the peak. Snowmelt water is often available here into early summer, and the rock-slab camp below Pyramid Peak at about 6,300 ft is a common first night.

This is one of only two routes on Rainier that avoids significant glacier travel, which is its whole appeal; the cost is that it is long, loose and unfrequented, with about 12–13 miles and roughly 11,500 ft of gain to Point Success. Most parties take two days, often with a second camp dug into the cleaver crest around 10,700 ft.

runs: feet to the very edge of the face
hits.text: A huge shield streaked with dikes like bolts of lightning is the proof, and you can see it from out on the glacier. This is the southernmost of the prominent subsummits on the ridge between Mount Challenger and Crooked Thumb, and it is identified by one feature rather than by its shape: the base of the tower carries an enormous shield of dark granite crisscrossed by hundreds of pale dikes running across it like bolts of lightning. That streaking is unmistakable and visible from well out on the glacier, so pick the tower off before you commit to a line across the ice. The climbing starts in a clean dihedral just left of the dike-streaked shield, roughly twenty feet above the snow, and the bergschrund or moat at the foot of it is the first thing to assess, because it decides whether that start is reachable at all on the day. If the wall in front of you is uniform dark granite with no lightning-streak dikes, you are beneath the wrong subsummit and should continue south along the base. Once on it, the first pitch tiptoes rightward across parallel dikes for about forty feet to the very edge of the face; that stretch takes essentially no protection and a fall on it is long, with cracks only appearing higher up.

hits.text:
From the grassy saddle bivy, cross class 4 ramps to a shallow dihedral with a small tree in it, then continue to a dirt ledge at the base of a short wall. That dirt ledge is the start.

The small tree in the shallow dihedral is the discriminator. Miracle Ramps uses the same class 4 ramps but leads to a dihedral and then a starting wall ledge that it shares with this route's upper start, and the two only diverge higher; Nature's Way goes the other way, crossing the apron past Concerto's start to two-bolt ring anchors on the opposite wall.

This is an old-school ridge ramble: lichened overlaps and dirt-filled cracks low down are correct here, not evidence of being off route. The crux does not arrive until pitch 9.

runs: to prusik pass at the base of the west ridge
hits.text: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (Trail #1599) at the end of Eightmile Road/FS-7601, elev. ~3,400-3,600 ft. Hike the Stuart Lake Trail about 2.5 miles to the signed junction with the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599 continues to Stuart Lake; branch left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail). This spur crosses Mountaineer Creek on a footbridge/logs (last reliable, easy water before the basin) and then climbs a rocky, switchbacking 1.6 miles through forest and boulder fields to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft (roughly 4.1 miles and ~2,200 ft from the trailhead) - a good rest, filter-water, and gear-sort stop. Skirt the east/south shore of Colchuck Lake on climbers' trail to the large boulder field at its south end, then begin the Aasgard Pass climb: follow the outlet stream/drainage, staying climber's-left of the first band of cliffs, up steep heather, rock steps, and (in early season) snow. This is the approach crux - roughly 2,000-2,200 ft of gain in under a mile on what regulars describe as a 'jenga pile' of loose scree and talus with real fall-and-rockfall consequence; an ice axe (and crampons in early season/on residual snow) is worth carrying into July. Top out around 7,800 ft at the rim of the upper Enchantment Basin, then traverse/descend roughly 600-700 ft east through the basin's tarns and slabs, then climb north to Prusik Pass at the base of the West Ridge, the actual start of the climb. Total one-way approach is on the order of 9-10 miles with about 4,600 ft of net gain, typically taking strong parties 3.5-5 hours; a NW Forest/Enchantments overnight or day-use permit is required and quotas are tight, so many parties do this route car-to-car in a single very long day rather than camp.

runs: to prusik pass at the base of the west ridge
hits.text: From the summit, the standard descent drops down the north side of Prusik Peak via a sequence of rappels, then traverses back to Prusik Pass to rejoin the approach line. Most parties make four rappels, then downclimb loose 3rd-class ground; one or two optional extra rappels can replace that downclimb - the first anchor is typically right at your feet on a flat spot at/near the true summit, with subsequent stations found by rappelling roughly 20-30m and looking climber's-left; anchors are fixed gear (slings/webbing 'tat' and rap rings/chains left by parties over the years, not bolted), so back them up or inspect carefully. Rappel lengths run mostly in the 25-30m range with one shorter first pitch; a single 60m rope is adequate for every station for a party of two, though a doubled 60m (30m per strand) can feel tight on the last traverse-y rappel, and parties of three often prefer a 70m rope for margin. After the last rappel, traverse west (skiers'-left) across talus back to Prusik Pass at the base of the West Ridge - this is not a walk-off from the summit itself, but the technical descent is short (well under an hour for an efficient party) and feeds directly back into the approach trail. From Prusik Pass, reverse the approach: down into the upper Enchantment Basin, back up and over the rim, then down the loose, steep Aasgard Pass gully to Colchuck Lake (use extra caution here - the scree that makes for a grueling ascent is equally unpleasant and slip-prone descending with tired legs), and out the Colchuck Lake/Stuart Lake Trail to the trailhead.

runs: the head of eureka creek to shellrock pass
hits.text: Ptarmigan is one of the most isolated summits in this wilderness, sitting less than a mile from the most remote point in it, and the whole difficulty is getting underneath it. From the Slate Pass road end the standard line drops through larch and avalanche-lily meadows to the Middle Fork Pasayten trail, runs down-valley through a stretch with a long-standing reputation for blowdown, then climbs by Fred's Lake and over the pass at the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass. A broad bench just southwest of the pass is the standard high camp for this peak and its neighbours. From the south the mountain is a rounded, tundra-covered massif and the walking is genuinely easy; its north side is another matter entirely.

runs: heads due south across the hillside and over
hits.text: There are two ways onto this peak and each has its own recognisable base. From the south, the base is the Ptarmigan-Dot saddle at about 7,800 ft, a genuine meadow holding a small tarn, unmistakable ground after miles of talus and the last water on the day. From that saddle the south slopes rise as open alpine tundra, scree and easy talus and there is nothing to find; you simply walk up. Getting to the saddle from the Shellrock Pass camp means gaining the crest north of camp and travelling over or around the shoulder of Mount Lago, with a short exposed step or two on the connecting ridge near the two rock points south of Dot. From the north and west the base is a saddle at about 7,250 ft overlooking Ptarmigan Lake, and the marker there is better still: a well-trodden boot path leaves the maintained trail at the Tatoosh Buttes junction around 6,950 ft and heads due south across the hillside and over a low rise on Tamarack Ridge, and following it to the saddle puts you at the foot of the north ridge, which is broad and easy. Whichever side you come from, the same rule identifies the route: the ground under you should stay rounded, open and tundra-covered. Ptarmigan's north face is sheer and seldom seen, so any point where the slope stops falling away gently and starts breaking off is the signal that you have wandered onto the wrong aspect and should move back south.

runs: to ptarmigan creek northeast of the peak then
hits.text: The shortest line on the map, but it starts below 3,500 ft instead of high on the Slate Pass road. From the trailhead at the end of Eightmile Creek Road, cross Eightmile Pass and follow the trail past the Hidden Lakes to Ptarmigan Creek, northeast of the peak, then go a further two or three miles to the base. Expect a long day of trail before any climbing.

runs: the head of eureka creek to shellrock pass
hits.text: Shellrock is the camp for Ptarmigan Peak and Dot Mountain, both of which are otherwise out of reach. The standard line leaves Slate Pass, follows the Middle Fork Pasayten to Berk Creek, climbs to Freds Pass and crosses the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass, which puts a party in position to scramble Ptarmigan the following day; Dot is taken from the same country on the way through, usually in combination with the Lago and Carru group. This is genuinely remote — thirty-five miles and thirteen thousand feet of gain over four days is a fair description of a trip that collects three or four summits here — and there is no short version. The meadow ground is soft and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on the timber edge or on gravel rather than in the open grass. Snow lingers on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the single biggest constraint on when this is worth attempting.

runs: day 1 cascade pass to kool aid lake
hits.text: Day 1 (Cascade Pass to Kool-Aid Lake): 4-6 hours, ~3,300 ft gain. Hike Cascade Pass Trail to the pass (3.7 miles), then off-trail south to Cache Col crossing on Cache Glacier, descend to Kool-Aid Lake bivouac (elevation ~6,100 ft). Day 2 (Kool-Aid to Yang-Yang Lakes): 8-11 hours, 2,500 ft gain/loss. Cross the exposed Red Ledge below Art's Knoll (Class 3 scrambling), climb the Middle Cascade Glacier to Spider-Formidable Col, descend to Yang-Yang Lakes bivouac. Day 3 (Yang-Yang to White Rock Lakes): 7-11 hours, 2,000 ft gain/loss. Traverse Le Conte Ridge, cross Le Conte Glacier with crevasse hazards, descend to White Rock Lakes bivouac (visual highlight of entire route). Day 4 (White Rock rest day or peak day): Optional rest day. Dome Peak (8,924 ft) is climbed from the Itswoot Ridge camp instead, via the Dome Glacier route (35-degree snow and ice), as an extra day after Day 5. Day 5 (White Rock to Itswoot Ridge): 8-10 hours, 3,000 ft gain. Ascend Dana Glacier crossing bergschrund, summit Spire Point (8,264 ft) or traverse below on east face, descend to Itswoot Ridge bivouac. Day 6 (Itswoot to Downey Creek TH): 8-12 hours, 2,500 ft loss. Descend Bachelor Creek through forest, reach Downey Creek Trailhead. Alternative faster options: out-and-back from Cascade Pass (4-5 days), or extend to Dome Peak summit and add Sentinel Peak/Old Guard (7-8 days).

runs: at a small notch overlooking the vesper glacier
hits.text: From the saddle between Vesper and Wolf Peak, an obvious ledge system cuts across the north face at roughly 5,800 ft, starting at a small notch overlooking the Vesper Glacier. The climbing is sustained low-5th-class rock with the crux exposed traverse pitch reported on pitch 5 (some parties also flag a 5.7 slab on pitch 2); belays are a mix of fixed (bolted/pin) anchors and gear anchors atop pitches 1 and 3. No rappels are needed — parties walk off. Popular enough that other Vesper lines (e.g. True Grit) are sometimes used as a less-crowded backup.

runs: and follow an obvious talus ridgeline up to
hits.text: Same trailhead and trail as True Grit: Sunrise Mine Trail #707 from the Sunrise Mine Trailhead on the Mountain Loop Highway, through second-growth forest and an early creek crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish (log crossing, harder in high runoff), up through Wirtz Basin and out onto open, cairned talus, then through Headlee Pass (~4,720 ft, 2.7 mi, loose rock/rockfall exposure in the narrow couloir) and down to Vesper Creek and Vesper Lake (Lake Elan, ~5,000 ft, ~3.5 mi/~2,700 ft gain) — the last dependable water. From the lake the maintained trail fades; cross the outlet and follow an obvious talus ridgeline up to the saddle between Vesper and Wolf Peak, the small summit just northeast of Vesper. From there a slightly improbable but well-trodden heather ledge system (goat trail through it) cuts across the north face at roughly 5,800 ft to a small notch overlooking the remnant Vesper Glacier, where the route starts. This traverse crosses steep, exposed heather that's treacherous when wet and typically holds snow into mid-to-late summer, so an ice axe (and sometimes crampons) is worth carrying into early summer. Plan on 3+ hours from the trailhead to the base of the climb.

runs: a very loose slope to gain the left end of an obvious ledge system
corner system on the right side of the
hits.text:
This route is reached from high, not from low, and that single sentence separates it from the other line on this pinnacle.

There are two ways onto its ledge, described from opposite directions and they meet in the same place. Either cut right off the col trail before topping out, crossing a very loose slope to gain the left end of an obvious ledge system; or go all the way to the col and descend about three hundred feet along the pinnacle's flank to the same ledge. Both are quick.

Then walk the ledge rightward to its far end. This is the step people skip. The ledge is third class and it goes further than you expect; the route does not start where you step onto it. Keep going until the ledge runs out.

At the far right end of the ledge, a steep clean corner rises straight off it. That corner is the route. It is a big obvious corner system on the right side of the pinnacle's main face, and the climbing in it is continuous, clean and steep — the physical test is that the rock quality is conspicuously better than the loose slope you crossed to get there.

Confirm on the climb. Pitch one is moderate with a chimney-behind-a-block move. Pitch two is the standout: a steep continuous corner to a triangular roof, passed on finger locks. Pitch three is the hardest, off a detached flake into steep flaring finger and hand jams on the left wall. Pitch four is corner climbing into an offwidth section. A triangular roof on the second pitch and a detached flake on the third are the two features that settle it.

Negative marker: if you left the trail down at the bench around 6,600 ft, contoured right past a spring in a dry sandy gully, and found a chockstone at the toe of a ridge, you are at the other route on this pinnacle — several number grades easier and a different day. A chockstone at a ridge toe is not this climb; a corner at the far right end of a ledge is.

Second negative marker: the neighbouring spire's routes start from the col itself and are the usual link-up partner. Standing at the col with rock above you is not evidence you are here; you still have to lose height.

At the top, either scramble third-class ground north-east toward the neighbouring spire's north face to continue a link-up, downclimbing over precariously stacked blocks and flakes, or make two thirty-metre rappels down the gully back to the col.

runs: ascends a very loose gully to gain the ridge
hits.text:
The gully above the lake is the route and it is the worst ground of the day - that is how you know you are on it. From the lake basin, the line ascends a very loose gully to gain the ridge crest. Parties routinely exit the gully about half-way up onto the rib that parallels it, because the rib holds more solid rock; the rib is an escape from the gully rather than an alternative to it, so if you cannot see the gully from the rib you have wandered.

If the ground you are climbing is pleasant, you are not in the right gully. Several chutes rise out of this basin; the one that is the route is the one that leads to the saddle on the crest.

The critical negative marker is on the ridge, not on the approach: a small peak stands just west of the saddle, and it is not the summit. Once on the crest the true high point is reached by an easy scramble eastward along the ridge. If you topped out of the gully and went left to a summit within a few minutes, you are on the lower point west of the saddle.

The positive test at the top is the walk. The true summit is a ridge scramble away over talus and large boulders, with intervening bumps, rather than an immediate high point above the gully. Ground you can traverse in minutes is the wrong answer here.

Also note the name trap in the roads and lakes on this side of the range: the drainage this variant uses and the one the south-east ridge uses have similarly named creeks and lakes on the same forest road system, so navigate by the road numbers and the trailhead you actually parked at rather than by the name of a lake.

hits.text: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike North: park 1.1 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, where a dirt road intersects the paved road on the left (SE side), or continue to 1.2 miles and use the large pull-off. Cross the main road and pick up the approach trail between the two parking spots, marked by a short steep drainage topped with a downed tree.

hits.text: Drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to the Ross Dam Trailhead and walk down to Ross Lake, where most parties take the paid water taxi from Ross Lake Resort to the Big Beaver landing rather than walking the lakeshore trail. From the landing it is about 9.4 miles of nearly flat old-growth trail up the Big Beaver valley to Luna Camp, the usual first night. About a mile and a half beyond camp, leave the trail on a small boot path and cross Big Beaver Creek just north of where Access Creek comes in, around 2,460 ft. Depending on the year this is a log or a wade. Then climb the north side of Access Creek on a faint, brushy climbers' path through Access Creek basin, up the south gully and around the south side of Luna Peak to Luna Col, the usual high camp. From Luna Col, follow the ridge toward Fury over class 3 ground with many short ups and downs. Drop to traverse heather slopes on its south side to the Southeast Glacier near 6,700 ft, then climb the right side of the glacier to steeper snow and a possible bergschrund below East Fury's summit, where the traverse to the West Peak begins. Allow three to five days for the round trip. The Luna Fire closure has shut the Big Beaver Trail from Big Beaver Stock Camp to Stillwell Camp, including Luna Camp, and bars cross-country travel from the closed trail; check the park's current fire closures before planning.

runs: gravel fr 5400 to the robinson creek trailhead on the right
hits.text:
Drive Highway 20 west from Winthrop about fifteen miles, right onto Lost River Road, a half mile then left to stay on it, seven and a half paved miles and another mile and a quarter of gravel FR 5400 to the Robinson Creek trailhead on the right. The trailhead sits at 2,500 to 2,600 ft. Ballard Campground is a minute or two away and is the standard car-camp.

Walk the Robinson Creek trail #478 — an easy valley walk through big timber — about two and eight tenths miles to the Beauty Creek junction near 3,560 to 3,600 ft. Mileages for it range from two to two and eight tenths, so use the elevation and the landmark rather than a mile count.

The landmark is the second bridge, the one over Beauty Creek, with Beauty Creek Falls cascading beside it. The junction is thirty to a hundred feet past that bridge, on the uphill side, and it is unmarked. Two parties independently warn that it is far less obvious than you would expect, one describing it as covered in bushes and nearly walked past. If you get thirty feet beyond the bridge and have not seen it, stop, go back, and look up on climber's right.

Beauty Creek #579 — not #479, which is a different trail entirely — is unmaintained and does not appear on maps. It stays on the west and north-west side of the creek the whole way. One party notes their topo showed it on the east side and the topo was wrong; that is a usable check. Blowdown is the recurring nuisance, typically five to nine logs.

Total for the peak is fourteen to fifteen miles with somewhere between 6,200 and 6,900 ft of gain, and four separate parties report ten to fourteen hours car to car as a single day.

The last several hundred feet to the summit ridge are steep, with cornices along the crest overhanging the north face - stay well back from the edge, keeping to the trees while they last. A breakable wind crust over powder can make this slow going. Small glaciers lie on the north side of the summit ridge.

At the pass, an unsigned, unmaintained path (the old 'Ruby Mountain Way Trail') marked by a jagged 8-ft stump and orange flagging on the north side of the main trail climbs through deadfall and heather benches onto the open south ridge, finishing on wide-open scree and talus to the summit. Non-technical but long, with real route-finding difficulty in the mid-mountain deadfall zone.

runs: a long leftward traverse across grassy benches and moderate heather
hits.text: Above 4,950 ft the path switchbacks north through sparse forest on the south ridge, then makes a long leftward traverse across grassy benches and moderate heather, then up a steep southwest-facing heather slope on tight switchbacks. Above about 6,600 ft it becomes scree and talus and the ridge opens out — wide enough that it can be walked without a trail to the gentle summit ridge near 7,400 ft. Steep heather is slick when wet or frosted and holds snow late; snow on these slopes turns a walk-up into a self-arrest problem, so carry an axe outside of high summer.

runs: ascend talus and slabs below a rock ridge
hits.text: Shares its trailhead and lower approach with the South Slopes/Ruth Glacier route: Hannegan Pass Trail #674 from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (end of FR-32) up the Ruth Creek valley to Hannegan Pass (5,066 ft, ~4 miles, ~2,000 ft gain), then the climbers' path east and south past the pond below the pass (faint, easy to lose), around a cliff-band shoulder, and onto the Ruth Glacier's north slope to a camp near the notch northwest of Ruth's summit (~6,600 ft) — see the South Slopes route for full trailhead-to-glacier detail, including the documented crevasse-fall hazard on the lower glacier despite its mellow appearance. From camp, the traverse is conventionally done Ruth-to-Icy: tag Ruth's summit first, then descend roughly 800 ft south and west toward a gully on the peak's west side, pick up a faint boot path, and continue down another ~800 ft (about 1,600 ft total off Ruth's summit) to the low saddle/col between Ruth and Icy at roughly 5,700-5,800 ft. Parties choose between a steeper, more direct 'death gully' line or supposedly-cairned heather slopes and game trails to climber's left holding 2nd-3rd class ground — the heather-slope option is the safer, recommended line. From the saddle, cross a patch of trees and talus/boot-path along the connecting ridge to the Icy Glacier, then ascend talus and slabs below a rock ridge to gain the glacier proper, aiming for a notch/saddle just west of Icy's Northwest Spire (~6,500 ft). From that notch it's another ~500 ft of 2nd-3rd class scrambling up an obvious left-hand, light-colored gully system to the base of Icy's summit block, where a 100-ft, 4th-class gully (solid jugs and ledges but real exposure) leads to the top. Helmets are standard here given loose rock and traffic funneled through a single gully. Note the true (highest) summit is the SE point, about 11 ft higher than the peak most maps label as the top.

Shares its trailhead and lower approach with the Ruth Glacier route: Trail #674 from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead up Ruth Creek to Hannegan Pass at 5,066 ft, then the faint climbers' path east and south past the pond, around the cliff-band shoulder, and onto the Ruth Glacier's north slope to a camp near the notch northwest of Ruth's summit around 6,600 ft.

The traverse is conventionally done Ruth-to-Icy: tag Ruth's summit first, then descend roughly 800 ft south and west toward a gully on the peak's west side, pick up a faint boot path, and continue down another 800 ft or so — about 1,600 ft in total off Ruth's summit — to the low saddle between Ruth and Icy at roughly 5,700-5,800 ft.

From the saddle, cross a patch of trees and follow talus and boot path along the connecting ridge to the Icy Glacier, then talus and slabs below a rock ridge to gain the glacier proper.

The re-ascent of Ruth on the way home is the sting in the tail and cannot be avoided on the standard car-to-car version.

runs: ridge to the base of the ruth glacier
hits.text: This is the important one. Everything from Hannegan Pass south along the ridge to the base of the Ruth Glacier is Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, so no national park backcountry permit is required here — only the parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary lies above and beyond, so a party that camps on this ridge and climbs Ruth as a day trip avoids the park permit system entirely. Standard wilderness rules apply: small groups, no fires at this elevation in practice, pack out everything.

runs: 1961 by bert brown roy etten and victor nelson
hits.text: Ruth Peak (~6,841–6,850 ft) is the third-highest summit in the Bailey Range, a remote sub-range of the northern Olympic Mountains, between higher neighbors Mount Carrie (6,995 ft, 0.9 mi NW) and Mount Fairchild (6,900 ft, 0.9 mi N). The Fairchild Glacier drapes its northeast slope. There is no trail to the summit — Ruth Peak sits deep in cross-country terrain south of the Sol Duc/High Divide country and is almost always climbed as a waypoint along the multi-day Bailey Range Traverse rather than as a standalone objective. First ascent 1961 by Bert Brown, Roy Etten, and Victor Nelson.

hits.text: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike South: drive 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and park on either side of the road just before the bridge over the river. Scramble up the steep hillside on the NW side of the road above the bridge abutment, then continue uphill along the dike to a passable gully.

Approach paths to individual crags (Megadike, Minidike, Weeping Wall, Joe's Rock) are unofficial, brushy, and easy to lose.

hits.text: The Boston Basin approach starts at an unmarked climbers' pullout on Cascade River Road roughly 21.5-23 miles from Marblemount (about 3,200-3,300 ft) - there's no formal trailhead sign, so watch your odometer. From the pullout, follow an old mining road/track for about a mile with minimal elevation gain, crossing Boston Creek. Watch closely for the unmaintained climbers' trail breaking off sharply to the right (cairns/flagging mark it, but it's easy to walk past); it climbs steeply through forest and a brushy old avalanche-slide path with sections of deadfall and loose footing. The path gains roughly 2,500 ft over about 2.5-3 miles to reach treeline and the lower Boston Basin camp (~5,300-5,400 ft), continuing to established upper camps around 6,200 ft. Plan on 3-4 hours trailhead to camp. Because this is a genuine climbers' path rather than a maintained trail, route-finding through the lower forest and slide-alder sections is the main approach hazard, and it can be greasy and slick when wet. Water is available from Boston Creek and seasonal snowmelt through mid-summer near camp. From high camp, rope up around 6,700 ft and make a rising traverse near the cliffs below Sharkfin Tower, picking a line up the Quien Sabe Glacier while avoiding crevasses - two common ascent lines (a left-side line and a more direct one) merge partway up. Expect to navigate a bergschrund via snow bridges around 7,600 ft and again near 8,100 ft, where large open crevasses flank the route on both sides in late season, before climbing to the Boston-Sahale col. From the col, a short but exposed snow traverse (crampons and axe recommended even late season) leads to the base of the summit block, finished with class 3-4 scrambling to the true summit.

hits.text:
Drive Cascade River Road about 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the Boston Basin fork at roughly 3,200-3,300 ft. There is no trailhead sign — it is an unmarked pullout, so watch the odometer rather than looking for signage.

Walk the old Diamond Mine roadbed for about three quarters of a mile to a mile, past the derelict mine site, with almost no elevation gain. The point people miss is where the climbers' trail leaves the roadbed sharply to the right and goes straight up; it is cairned and flagged but easy to walk past.

Above that the path is steep and unmaintained, switchbacking through forest and a brushy old slide path with deadfall, and crossing four small streams over roughly the next half mile — that is the last reliable water before camp, so fill there. Treeline comes at about 5,300 ft. Low camp sits on heather benches around 5,300-5,700 ft; the higher camp on a meadow knoll at about 6,200-6,400 ft cuts real time off summit day.

From camp, stay on climber's left toward the left side of Sharkfin Tower, rope up around 6,700 ft, and make a rising traverse under the cliffs below Sharkfin onto a flatter part of the Quien Sabe, then pick a line up the steeper section. Two common lines (one further left, one more direct) merge partway up.

Boston Basin is a cross-country zone; overnight permits are picked up in person at Marblemount. Biting flies are notorious here in midsummer.

runs: saska peak is the third highest peak in the
hits.text: Saska Peak is the third-highest peak in the Chelan Mountains and rises just northwest of its taller neighbor Emerald Peak (8,422 ft), 0.66 mi away across a connecting col. It's almost always climbed in combination with Emerald via that col, and strong parties often add Cardinal Peak (1.5 mi southeast) for a three-summit outing sometimes called the Entiat Bulgers. The peak sits deep in the North Fork Entiat River drainage inside Glacier Peak Wilderness — a long, quiet approach through fire-damaged forest rewards climbers with a genuinely remote basin and, in October, larch color on the descent.

runs: path up the north side of the creek
hits.text: This is the climbers' basin for Mount Maude and Seven Fingered Jack from the west, and it is also the base most parties use for Mount Fernow. Reach it by hiking about three miles up the Phelps Creek trail, fording Leroy Creek at around 4,140 ft, then taking the steep unmaintained climbers' path up the north side of the creek to the flat at 6,100 ft. The ford is the crux of the approach rather than an afterthought: Leroy Creek runs high and fast through early summer and often does not settle until August, so an early-season party should plan the crossing for morning and be prepared to turn round. From camp, Seven Fingered Jack's southwest slopes and Maude's south side are both reasonable days, and the two are frequently combined. Maude's north-side lines, including the ice fall and the couloir, are a different proposition entirely and are approached from the far side of the peak. Larch colour makes this a heavily visited basin in the first half of October.

hits.text: Start at the Park Butte Trailhead (elev. ~3,360 ft) at the end of Forest Service Road 13, reached via the Baker Lake Highway/Sulfur Creek Road turnoff (do not repeat the drive-in here — this covers the hike only). From the trailhead register, follow Park Butte Trail #603 south into Schriebers Meadow. The trail crosses Sulfur Creek on a footbridge just past the trailhead; at about 0.7 mile it crosses Rocky Creek — braided, silty glacial melt in a boulder field that can run high and fast on warm afternoons, usually bridged by a seasonal footbridge from about July. Beyond the creek the trail climbs through timber and brushy avalanche-path terrain, crosses a couple of additional meltwater streams, then switchbacks up a forested slope into Morovitz Meadows (~2 miles in). Near the meadow, stay left at the signed junction with the Scott Paul Trail #603.1 (which splits right) to stay on Park Butte Trail, then take the next right fork onto the Railroad Grade Trail #603.2 toward Baker Pass/the glacier (straight ahead leads to the Park Butte lookout instead). Railroad Grade Trail #603.2 climbs onto the crest of a narrow lateral moraine left by the receding Easton Glacier — a distinctive, uniformly graded ridge (hence the name) with exposed, steep drop-offs on both sides in places; use care in wind or on icy/frosty mornings. Designated Railroad Grade camps sit at 2.25–2.75 miles from the trailhead; High Camp sites are at about 3.75 miles and 5,600 ft; Sandy Camp, at roughly 5,900 ft, marks the end of maintained tread. From Sandy Camp the route continues cross-country over snowfields and rocky moraine to the toe of the Easton Glacier, typically 3–4 hours car-to-camp for most parties. Rope up for glacier travel around 6,800–7,200 ft (conditions-dependent) and ascend the Easton Glacier heading north toward the Sherman Crater rim; the standard line stays east (climber's right) of the glacier's major crevasse bands, though route-finding through the crevasse field is the technical crux of the approach and shifts season to season — wanding the route is standard practice given frequent whiteout/cloud cap conditions on Baker's south side. Above roughly 9,600–9,800 ft the route skirts the rim of Sherman Crater, where active fumaroles vent sulfurous steam (occasionally noticeable by smell and visible venting) — stay on the established boot path here and keep gear away from the acidic, degraded rock near the vents. No potable water exists at the trailhead itself; plan on treating water from Sulfur/Rocky Creek near the start or from snowmelt at High/Sandy Camp.
