runs: the ridge crest east of the balanced rock
hits.text: Start at the Longs Pass Trailhead (Esmeralda TH) at the end of Teanaway River Road (USFS Rd 9737) out of the North Fork Teanaway. Take Longs Pass Trail #1229 climbing steadily through open pine forest and sagebrush switchbacks for about 2.5 miles and 1,950 ft of gain (roughly 1.5-2 hours) to Longs Pass at approximately 6,200-6,400 ft, which opens up the first views of Mount Stuart, Ingalls Peak, and the Stuart Range crest. From the pass, drop off the north side on a steep, loose, eroded boot path (sometimes called the 'tapeworm') losing about 1,400-1,600 ft over roughly a mile to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft; this descent tread is dirt/scree and can be slick and hard on the knees. Ford Ingalls Creek (a rock-hop in low water, but a genuine wet crossing during early-season snowmelt) and pick up the Ingalls Creek Trail, following it east/downstream about half a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction at roughly 4,700 ft - the last dependable water source before the alpine basin above. From the junction, a climbers' boot path (referenced in trip reports as 'Variation #1' toward Mount Stuart) switchbacks up through forest and talus; around 6,000 ft it narrows into a gully system. Traverse east several hundred feet to a divide separating two gullies, then drop into the eastern gully, which leads more directly toward Sherpa Peak. Class 2 slopes above the gully lead to 'Table Rock,' a large flat boulder at about 7,400 ft in the boulder-choked Sherpa-Argonaut basin, a common high bivy for parties splitting the approach over two days. From Table Rock, a short Class 3 scramble gains a notch on the Stuart Range divide, putting climbers on the ridge crest east of the balanced rock; follow the crest west over blocks and sandy, exposed benches (Class 3-4) to reach the base of the balanced rock formation itself, where the Standard Route begins with a shoulder-stand or rope-lasso move to gain the east-side pedestal, then bolt-protected friction climbing (5.7) to the summit block. Car-to-base is roughly 6-7 miles one-way with roughly 6,000 ft of climbing on the way in, and Longs Pass to regain on the way out; expect loose rock and real route-finding through the gully/basin section, and carry all the water you'll need above the Beverly-Turnpike junction since the upper basin is dry.

Before the lakes, leave the maintained trail, cross Mountaineer Creek, and pick up a boot path and cairns climbing talus benches on the slope west of the creek — staying a couple of hundred feet above the trees before dropping back toward the water — aiming for the Sherpa-Argonaut basin.

Do not follow cairns out into the boulder field: parties specifically warn that the cairned line invites you off the better path. Stay with the creek.

Around 5,800 ft the ground steepens into sustained loose talus. The usual bivy is at the top of a talus field in the basin, and from there it is another hour and a half to two hours of talus-hopping to the toe of the ridge.

A southern approach over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek exists but is a longer, less direct way to this particular route.

Aim for the double V and camp just inside the lower one. Approaching the Sherpa-Argonaut col from the basin, the skyline reads as two V-shaped notches. The bivy sits at the top of a talus field just inside the lower V, and that pairing — two Vs, camp inside the lower — is the most reliable landmark on this approach because it is a skyline shape rather than a feature you have to be close to.

From the basin, the move is west-northwest and up a deep gully. Ascend talus west-northwest to a deep gully that runs to a notch on the ridge at about 7,000 ft. That gully is the way onto the route; contour up and climber's right out of the basin to reach the base of that lower notch.

Arrival: at the notch there are easy slabs that can be scrambled before you rope up. Easy slabs at a notch at roughly 7,000 ft, reached by a gully, with about 1,500 ft of ridge above you — that is the start.

What getting it wrong looks like, and it is expensive here: the ridge is largely Class 2-4 and you want to stay just on the east side of the crest. Straying onto the crest itself at the wrong point adds unavoidable 5.6-5.8 pitches on a route that is already long. So a party that gains the ridge somewhere other than the notch will find the climbing immediately harder than advertised — that is the signal to downclimb and traverse rather than to press on.

Confirmation low on the route: the first section ends with a roughly 25 m rappel from slings into a notch. If you have climbed a long way with no rappel, you are not on the ridge proper.

The landmark that settles this route is Sherpa's balanced rock — a distinctive perched block on the summit ridge, and it is visible from the basin below. Use it.

From the basin, climb class 2 snow and talus past the table rock to the Stuart-Sherpa col at about 8,100 ft, aiming for the notch closest to Sherpa. That is the start: the ridge rises east from the col to the summit, and the balanced rock stands beyond the summit on the crest to the east.

So the check in cloud is: at the col, Mount Stuart's east ridge rises behind you to the west and Sherpa's summit is ahead to the east, with the balanced rock beyond it. If you reach the crest with the balanced rock to your west, you have come up the East Ridge side of the peak.

The flat table-rock at about 7,400 ft is the intermediate confirmation on the way up — it is a distinct flat platform in otherwise broken ground and it sits on the correct line. Do not confuse the table rock (7,400 ft, a bivy shelf) with the balanced rock (on the summit ridge, a perched block); they are different features doing different jobs.

The descent uses a rappel line back to a notch west of the technical climbing, so know where the notch is before you go up.

hits.text: Park at the broad pullout/overlook on SR-20 near milepost 165–166 (about 4 miles east of Washington Pass), where a sign points toward Silver Star Mountain. From the pullout, drop down the embankment roughly 150–200 ft to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log (logjams shift year to year — scout up- and downstream for the best crossing, and be ready to ford in high water/early season, when the creek runs cold and fast with snowmelt). On the far bank, pick up the unofficial but well-defined climber's trail that climbs the timbered rib on the west (left) side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. From here the trail climbs relentlessly and steeply through forest and brush for roughly 2,500–3,000 ft with almost no switchbacks and only fleeting creek-side water access early on — treat the crossing at Early Winters Creek as your last reliable water until camp. At around 6,000–6,400 ft the grade eases at 'the Bench,' an open larch-and-heather shelf with several established campsites and usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby; this is the standard overnight camp for a two-day trip and a natural break point/turnaround check for day-trippers. Above the bench, continue up open subalpine terrain toward Burgundy Col. Do not take the obvious direct gully to the col — it is loose and exposed; instead stay left, follow the trail up the gully directly above camp, and near its head make an ascending traverse right under the cliffs on heather-covered slabs into the col itself (roughly 7,800 ft). Total gain from the highway to the col is on the order of 3,500–4,400 ft depending on exact trailhead/camp used. Hazards on the approach: the Early Winters Creek crossing (cold, log can be wet/mossy or washed out), steep eroding/brushy tread that's easy to lose in the timber, and loose rock ('kitty litter') on the final gully/traverse into the col.

The col is not the start of the climbing — the glacier is on the far side of it. From Burgundy Col, descend roughly 200 feet of steep snow down the east side onto the Silver Star Glacier; that descent is the moment the route begins, and parties rope up at the edge of the glacier below it. Head east, climb to the flat top of a spur ridge, then traverse east onto the main body of the glacier and ascend south to the saddle just west of the summit.

The finish is where people get it wrong. From that saddle the summit is a short scramble east, but only on one line: look for an easy ramp about 40 feet below the summit. Take it and the summit is class 3 to 4. Miss it and you end up on a short pitch of low fifth class instead. In poor visibility, work generally left off the saddle and hunt for the ramp rather than committing to the first steep line you meet.

The unmistakable break on this approach is the bench, at roughly 6,400-6,700 ft: the grade suddenly eases onto an open larch-and-heather shelf with several established campsites and usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby. That is the standard overnight camp and the natural turnaround check for a day trip.

Above the bench there is a gully running obviously and directly to Burgundy Col. That gully is the wrong one — it is loose and exposed. Instead stay left and follow the trail up the gully directly above camp. Within it, stay climber's left of the gully proper: the bed holds loose microwave-sized blocks, while the left side is unpleasant kitty-litter-covered slab but far less dangerous. Near the head of the gully make an ascending traverse to the right, under the cliffs, over heather-covered slabs into the col at roughly 7,800 ft. This gully and traverse is where parties describe the real crux of route-finding, both up and down. The col — not the glacier — is where the route proper begins; from there trend toward the northeast side of the west summit.

hits.text: From the Downey Creek Trailhead (elev. ~1,450') on the Suiattle River Road (FR 26), follow Downey Creek Trail #768 for 6.5 miles (easy, well-graded, mostly flat, forested trail with a suspension-bridge crossing of Downey Creek) to Sixmile Camp (2,440'), a good first-night camp with reliable water from Downey Creek. From Sixmile Camp the maintained trail ends; continue on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path, staying on the north side of the creek initially and fording to the south side around the 9.5-mile mark (~3,700') — treat this as a real creek crossing, harder and more dangerous in high water/early season. Around 4,500' the tread largely disappears through a large avalanche-debris zone (a major slide wiped out this stretch in 2002); expect slow, brushy route-finding through slide alder and downed timber here even in good conditions, and continuous snow well below this elevation in early season. Above the debris zone the path climbs to a pass (~5,900') just northwest of Cub Lake (about 14 miles in), then drops to Cub Lake (5,338', another good camp with water). Most parties push on from Cub Lake up onto Itswoot Ridge (6,400–6,900', ~15 miles and ~5,500' of gain from the trailhead) for high camp, with sweeping views of Dome and Sinister. From high camp, traverse climbers' paths and snow benches through the upper basins (staying near 7,000') to gain the Dome Glacier, cross over the Dome–Chikamin col, and descend the Chikamin Glacier (crevassed — rope up and carry crevasse-rescue gear) to about 7,200'. Traverse right (east) across the glacier to reach the 7,640' Dome–Sinister col; a bergschrund here can be difficult to cross in late season and has occasionally required a short rappel to get down onto or across it (see descent notes — same feature is encountered both ways). From the col, contour on an easy snowfield and climb up into a loose, unpleasant gully on Sinister's south side to gain the upper west ridge, then follow a Class 2–3 scramble along the ridge to the 8,444' summit; some parties instead take the exposed Class 3+ ridge directly from the col. Loose rock in the gully is the main climbing-specific hazard on the approach to the summit block.

Most parties downclimb the same loose south-side gully back to the Dome–Sinister col — it is one of the loosest, most unpleasant sections on the mountain, so expect care-intensive downclimbing with real rockfall risk to anyone below. A commonly preferred alternative, used by several recent parties instead of re-descending the gully, is to descend via the lower west ridge: a newer, more direct line involving sustained Class 3–4 scrambling on semi-solid rock with considerable exposure. One crux move on this ridge variant has a fixed sling left in place for protection/handline use, but this is not a rappel station — parties downclimb through it. Either way, the descent rejoins the gentle snow slopes leading back to the 7,640' Dome–Sinister col. At the col, the bergschrund that guards access to the Chikamin Glacier can be broken/unbridged in mid-to-late season; when it is, parties have used a single rappel (one 60m rope) off natural anchors (rock horn/sling or v-thread in snow, depending on conditions) to get down onto the glacier safely rather than risk a fall into the schrund — in good snow conditions or earlier in the season this same spot is often just a step-across or short downclimb with no rope work needed. From the glacier, re-ascend roughly 1,000' back to the Dome–Chikamin col, then descend to high camp on Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake and reverse the long Bachelor Creek/Downey Creek trail back to the trailhead. From the Mountain Loop Highway take FR 4096, a rough narrow spur where high clearance genuinely helps, to the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,790 ft. Distance and gain above are the full round trip by this line.

Walk the old Bedal Creek trail roughly 1.5 miles and 700 ft. It is overgrown in stretches but stays followable. The critical junction is around 3,500 ft, where a climbers' path turns off to the left near 48.0560, -121.3631; it has carried pink flagging tape in recent years. Missing that turn is the standard error here — the old tread continues and dies in a brushy washout below the basin.

The climbers' path gains about 1,400 ft steeply through forest. At roughly 4,900 ft it breaks out into talus, then bends southeast through meadow and scattered timber to the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft, where a shallow, somewhat stagnant pond marks the usual camp. This is the last easy water; cascading streams just below the saddle are the alternative.

Southeast from the saddle the ground opens into scramble terrain. At about 5,800 ft you cross a minor rock ridge and get your first view of the glacier. Snow from here is often firm in the morning and may want axe and crampons.

At 2.1 miles and about 1,500 ft of gain you reach Pyramid Lake (~2,600 ft) - top off water here, since the next several hours offer little. From the lake's south/right side, pick up the unmaintained but well-trodden climbers' path; it is steep and brushy from the outset and gains roughly 2,000 ft more, switchbacking up to the East Ridge of Pyramid Peak (~4,000 ft), then follows the narrow, knolly ridge crest past Point 4,555 ft toward Pyramid Peak, with loose rock and short routefinding steps. Just short of Pyramid Peak, descend slightly and traverse - often on lingering snow - across scree and boulders to the terminal moraine and small lake at the base of the Colonial Glacier (~5,900-6,100 ft), the standard first camp, with a tarn for water. From camp, rope up for glacier travel (crevasses present) and climb the Colonial Glacier south to the broad Colonial-Neve col (~6,800-6,900 ft; a stream/waterfall here is a second good camp and water source), then descend about 200 ft onto the Neve Glacier and cross it - a moderate, usually well-tracked but crevassed glacier crossing requiring a rope - to the rocks just below Snowfield's summit pyramid on its northwest side. From there a long class 3 gully leads to a notch below the true summit; the final short traverse/scramble across the notch to the south side and up to the summit (8,351 ft) is exposed class 3, with one move occasionally rated low class 4. Given roughly 7,300 ft of total gain and sustained glacier travel, most parties treat this as a 2-day (overnight) objective rather than a single push.

From Marblemount, drive the river road about fourteen miles and turn right onto forest road 1570, which crosses the river on a concrete bridge. Within roughly half a mile the right fork is blocked by boulders and washout; park at that Y-junction around 1,200 ft. The spur beyond is permanently closed to vehicles by windfall, brush and washouts, so the trip opens with a two to three mile road walk rather than at a trailhead.

The climbers' path above is unsigned and has no trail number, and it climbs hard through brush and then old growth on boot-beaten tread over roots and rock, with no water until well upslope. The grade eases at a boggy bench near 4,800 ft with room for a tent and seasonal water. Higher, a cairn-marked fork sends a fainter fisherman's trail down toward a lake; stay on the climbers' path. The ridge then rolls constantly over several small points rather than climbing steadily, before dropping to the meadows by the lake, which are the best camp on the route.

From the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass, follow the maintained trail as it climbs through fir and larch and out onto open slabs. After roughly a mile and a quarter to a mile and a half the ground opens up and the Liberty Bell-Concord-Early Winters skyline comes into view; the climbers' track leaves the maintained trail here, at a minor stream draining the basin, sometimes marked with a cairn. This is well short of Blue Lake itself, which is another mile-plus along the maintained trail — if you reach the lake you have gone too far.

The climbers' path works up through granite slabs and heather benches and then up open talus roughly parallel to the stream. The stream is good water low down and vanishes into the talus higher up, so fill there.

Higher, the path loses definition on the talus and slab benches and braids. Rather than chasing one cairn line, navigate to the feature: the southwest corner at the end of the ridge on the right.

runs: in the rightmost and larger of the two
hits.text:
Two tests, one at the gully fork and one at the wall, and you need both.

First, the fork at about 7,100 ft. The gully you have been climbing splits. The standard line is the left branch. The right branch also reaches the mountain but is far less travelled, so a party that drifts right will find progressively less sign of passage — that absence is the signal to come back down and cross over.

Second, the wall itself, and this is the one that matters in fog because the gully fork can be ambiguous under snow. At the base of the south face there are two short left-facing corners side by side. The route starts in the rightmost and larger of the two. Not a corner — two corners, and you take the bigger, right-hand one. If there is only one corner in front of you, you are not at the start.

What the climbing should feel like, as a check on all of the above: blocky, generally solid rock, three pitches, graded 5.6 — but an old-school 5.6 that parties consistently report climbing like modern 5.9 or harder. So sustained-feeling climbing is not evidence you are off route here. Watch for a few loose blocks low down.

A separate feature worth not confusing with the start: high on the mountain there is a 50-foot gully with a chockstone near its top, Class 4, taken by stepping right at the overhang, which tops out on the east ridge a short way from the summit. That is the finish of the ordinary scramble line, and the approach description on this route describes it as though it were the route. It is not the base of the 5.6 face climb, and a party navigating to it will end up on the scramble.

Climbers wanting more technical terrain can continue directly up the steep summit block at class 4/low 5th class, which requires a rope for the exposure. This is the most solid rock found on the peak (large slabs), in contrast to the notoriously loose rock elsewhere on Red Mountain.

runs: hiking finish on the west side of the south ridge
hits.text:
The rock is the marker and it is bright red. You are looking for a low-angle gully or ramp of solid, bright red rock at the base of the mountain — solid is the operative word, because it is the most solid rock on a peak otherwise famous for being fractured. The colour and the low angle together identify it; nothing else on this flank looks like it.

And the overshoot test is the one to remember, because it works without seeing anything: if you reach Red Mountain Pond, you have gone too far. Popping out of the trees on the flank of Red commonly puts a party too far west; the pond tells you so unambiguously. Turn back east and traverse on heather until the red gully appears.

What the first ground should feel like: class 3, no gear required, two pitches of it. If you are pulling on anything hard from the ground you are not in the ramp.

Where it leads, so you can check yourself later: you pop over a small ridge into the main gully below the summit. Keep going up that until the summit block above you turns steep and roofy. That roofy steepening is the signal to move left onto the class 2 hiking finish on the west side of the south ridge — or, if you want it, to continue directly up the block at class 4 or low 5 with a rope.

runs: looking from the notch start up the obvious crack in the middle of the wall
hits.text:
You are at the right saddle when Concord is on one side of you and Lexington is on the other, and the Concord wall in front of you gives onto low-angle, gravelly ledges rather than a steep crack system. If you are facing a crack system, you are at the Liberty Bell-Concord Notch and looking at the north face.

That is the notch test, and it is the one that matters, because the two saddles are a few hundred feet apart on the same ridge and both are reached from the same trailhead by the same path.

Arrival at this particular route, which is a different question from arrival at the notch: looking from the notch, start up the obvious crack in the middle of the wall. This route takes the centre of Concord's south face, climbs through a bulge, and continues trending left. Two right-facing corners put you at a tree right below the summit block.

So the count is: one crack in the middle, one bulge, two right-facing corners, one tree. If your line runs up the edge of the wall rather than its centre, you are on the tower's other south-face route.

Why the notch test and the route test both mention cracks without contradicting each other: at the Liberty Bell-Concord notch a steep crack system rises directly in front of you, which is the North Face. At the Concord-Lexington notch the wall reads as low-angle and gravelly overall, and this route's crack is the obvious feature up the middle of that easier-angled wall. Judge the wall first, then the line.

Descent: downclimb or make one full double-rope rappel from the summit back to the notch; with a single rope, use two shorter rappels off intermediate anchor stations.

runs: at the col between vasiliki and burgundy spires with scrambling to a rightward trending dihedral system below the south face
hits.text: Climbed by Fletch Taylor and Chris Dolejska on August 8, 1994 — the same day the pair also climbed Silver Star Mountain's northwest ridge, completing both routes within an 18-hour outing. Starting at the col between Vasiliki and Burgundy Spires with scrambling to a rightward-trending dihedral system below the south face, they instead stepped left onto fifth-class cracks: a single hand crack (5.7) leading to a finger crack (5.8+) and a belay. The second pitch climbs a 15-foot traverse left (5.9), then a widening finger crack (5.7) for about 50 feet to a large dihedral that leads to the summit. Described as a well-protected two- to three-pitch climb.

runs: short distance to the start of the winter commonwealth
hits.text:
The fast winter line does not start at Alpental. Park at Summit West and walk the short distance to the start of the winter Commonwealth ski and snowshoe trail, which is usually well compacted. Cross the log and head directly at the route.

Where the ground steepens, trend far left until you come up against huge cliffs, then go about 100 ft further left again and climb to the start of the gully. The whole approach is about a mile and takes roughly an hour on firm snow.

The adjacent Summit at Snoqualmie ski area does avalanche control on nearby slopes in season; check with the resort before a winter attempt.

runs: see the end of the gully it is possible to turn left before the
look for two large trees and follow the ramp up climbers left around the cliff
hits.text:
The cliffs are the marker, and the instruction is to overshoot them by 100 ft. Climbing the steepening slope you trend far left until you are stopped by huge cliffs. Those cliffs are not a wrong turn — they are the landmark. Go 100 ft further left past them and then up, and you are at the mouth of the South Gully. A published fix for the start is roughly 47.4395, -121.4070.

What confirms it once you are in: the gully begins at the cliffs that form it just above treeline, and after roughly 300 to 400 ft — about three 60 m pitches — you reach the first chockstone, sitting at a constriction in the canyon. That chockstone is the crux except in deep snow, and it can be passed either left or right. A second chockstone follows about 50 ft beyond. First chockstone at a constriction, second one 50 ft above: no other gully on this side gives you that pair.

The exit test for later: continue about 30 m past an ice or rock step of no more than 8 ft until you can see the end of the gully. It is possible to turn left before the gully ends — look for two large trees and follow the ramp up climbers' left around the cliff to the South Spur.

And one descent warning that parties get wrong: do not rappel from the south summit. Traverse the ridge to the middle summit first, until you are looking directly at the north summit, and rappel from the tree there. Rappelling early has tempted more than one party.

runs: just below the summit on the south side
hits.text: A moderate 4-5 pitch rock route up the steep (but not vertical) headwall visible just below the summit on the south side, topping out very near the true summit.

runs: the first major clearing west of ulrich's couloir
hits.text: Drop the steep, eroded boot path off the north side of the pass to Ingalls Creek, cross it, and follow the Ingalls Creek Trail west to the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir. Climb the clearing and the loose scree above it to the enclosed cirque at about 8,700 ft, then take about five pitches, none harder than 5.7, up the centre of the headwall, topping out just southwest of the true summit.

runs: onto a large ledge overlooking the west face
hits.text: Gain the upper South Rib and follow it back rightward. A chute leads onto a large ledge overlooking the west face, then a slab traverse leads toward the summit pyramid. Loose blocks sit on the ledges and rockfall is frequent, so keep the rope clear of them.

runs: the first major clearing west of ulrich's couloir
hits.text: Longs Pass to Ingalls Creek, then the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir

runs: the first major clearing west of ulrich's couloir
hits.text:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Longs Pass trail up open pine and sage switchbacks to Longs Pass at roughly 6,200 ft. Stop here — this is the one place on the whole day where you can see the entire south side of the mountain at once, and five minutes spent picking out the headwall from the pass is worth an hour of guessing later.

Drop off the north side of the pass on the steep, eroded boot path to Ingalls Creek, cross it, and join the Ingalls Creek trail.

Then the key move: from where the Longs Pass trail meets Ingalls Creek, go west along the creek trail and take the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir. That clearing is the line of ascent.

Above the clearing it is sustained scree and choss up to a cirque at about 8,700 ft. The technical climbing — five pitches, never harder than 5.7, plus a lot of fourth and easy fifth — starts up the centre of the headwall from there.

runs: the first major clearing west of ulrich's couloir
hits.text:
The cirque is the arrival, and it is unmistakable even in cloud because it closes around you. You climb loose ground for a long time and then the walls come up on three sides — very steep cliffs at about 8,700 ft with the summit directly above. That enclosure is the cue. Scree that keeps going with open ground on both sides means you are still below it.

Which clearing, which is the actual problem: from the Ingalls Creek trail, count west from where the Longs Pass trail came down to the creek. The correct line is the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir. Ulrich's is the big obvious gully; if you are ascending a defined gully rather than an open clearing, you are in Ulrich's itself and on a different route entirely. And if the clearing you picked is east of that point, you are heading for the Cascadian Couloir — the standard walk-up and the usual descent — which is easier ground and will not put you under a headwall.

Confirmation at the base: the technical pitches start up the centre of the headwall, and they top out very close to the true summit. Nothing on this route is harder than 5.7. If the ground in front of you looks harder than that, you have drifted to one side of the centre.

Preview it from Longs Pass. This is the rare approach where the whole objective is visible from a trail junction two thirds of the way through the day, and a party that identifies the headwall and the correct clearing from the pass essentially cannot get this wrong afterwards.

hits.text: Start at the Rainy Pass Picnic Area/Lake Ann trailhead on SR 20 (milepost ~157.5, elev. ~4,850 ft; 40-car lot with privy). Follow the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail (#740) about 1-1.5 miles to a signed junction and take the right fork toward Heather Pass (the left fork is the spur to Lake Ann). Climb through meadows to Heather Pass (~2.6 mi, ~6,100 ft), where the maintained trail ends. From the pass, pick up the unmarked climbers' path heading north, crossing two talus/boulder fields before dropping to Lewis Lake (~3.5-4 mi, ~5,700 ft; timbered campsites on the north side, water available) — this off-trail stretch is the main route-finding challenge of the approach, especially with cairns buried by early-season snow. From Lewis Lake, climb roughly 1,200 ft more of meadow and talus to Wing Lake (~5 mi, ~6,900 ft), the standard base camp, with sites in the trees on the right as you reach the lake and reliable water into late summer. From Wing Lake, go around the right (north) side of the lake and aim for the obvious talus/snow gully leading into the couloir just south of the summit; climb this gully, then angle climber's-right out of it to avoid cliff bands directly below the col, topping out at the south col on the crest of the south ridge — the true start of the climbing.

hits.text: The ridge is gained from either its north or south side via moderate scrambling between South Twin's true summit and a subpeak about a quarter mile northeast. Climbers moving between North and South Twin cross the Sisters Glacier southbound to a bergschrund below the ridge, then climb up (favoring snow over rock where possible) to the ridge crest and follow it, mostly Class 3, with some low-5th variations, to the summit. Arrowtip Tower, on the lower part of the ridge, offers good rock climbing for parties looking for extra pitches.

runs: the ruins of an old miner's log cabin
hits.text: Park at the gated bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River (~1,200 ft) at the end of FR 38, reached via Mosquito Lake Road off WA-542. From the gate, most parties mountain-bike the old quarry/logging road system for roughly 6-7 miles and well over 2,000 ft of gain, threading several forks and offshoots near Dailey Prairie (GPS/GPX tracking is recommended here since wrong turns are common) before the road becomes too rough or overgrown to ride, usually marked by a large culvert pipe at the timber-road terminus. Stash bikes in the woods and pick up the narrow climbers' path on foot — brushy, wet, and occasionally overgrown but not hard to follow. The path drops slightly, crosses a forested section, and fades out at a red talus slope, which often holds snow well into summer. From the talus, traverse rightward (south) up and across, over a timbered rib, passing the ruins of an old miner's log cabin, then continue up into Orsino Creek Basin — the last reliable water source before the climb. From the basin, pick a line up onto the West Ridge; the standard start is an obvious notch in the ridge crest around 5,200 ft. Total foot travel from the bike cache to the summit is roughly 4 miles with substantial additional gain (combined bike + foot gain for the full approach runs about 6,100 ft), taking most parties 4-5 hours one-way. Watch for loose rock on the climbers' path and lower talus, and for lingering snow on the talus slope and approach gullies in early/mid-season, which can require an ice axe.

an unpleasant slog up steep dirt scree and talus
hits.text:
The ruins of an old log cabin are the one man-made thing on this approach and they are the checkpoint. From the red talus slope where the climbers' path fades, traverse right — south — up and across, cross a timbered rib, and pass the cabin ruins. If you have not passed a collapsed cabin, you have not made the traverse and you are still below the basin.

Orsino Creek is the last water and the entry to the basin. Fill up. There is nothing above it.

The base is an obvious notch in the ridge crest at about 5,200 ft, and you get to it up a steep loose dirt gully. That combination — an unpleasant slog up steep dirt, scree and talus, then a defined notch in a crest — is the arrival, and it works in cloud because a notch is a thing you stand in with air on the far side. This is the standard start and it is where the West Ridge is gained down low.

The discriminator against the other route out of this basin, and it is a single number: the North Ridge route continues higher and further climber's left — north — up basin snow or talus to a saddle around 5,800 ft between North Twin's southeast ridge and South Twin's north ridge. So 5,200 ft and the obvious notch is the West Ridge; 5,800 ft and a saddle between two peaks is the North Ridge. Six hundred feet and a bearing separate two routes that share every step of the approach up to the basin.

The rock confirms the range: dunite, olivine-rich, exceptionally grippy, like coarse sandpaper. It is why parties choose to gain the ridge low rather than high — to maximise time on it.

Higher up, the false-summit bypass is worth carrying before you need it: leave the crest to the right — south — traverse ledges, and regain the crest about 200 yards short of the false summit, roughly 500 ft above where you left it. Staying exactly on the crest through that step is what forces parties into an improvised rappel.

runs: then traverse left to the base of the
hits.text:
Hike spire gully, which is cairned, to the last large tree. That tree is the turn. From it, traverse right across talus and snow to the gully leading to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire, then traverse left to the base of the east buttress.

So the sequence is three moves and a tree: up the cairned gully to the last large tree, right across talus, then left to the buttress base. The tree is the only thing in that sequence you can put a hand on, which is why it is the marker rather than the gully.

Why the notch matters even though you do not go to it: the gully you aim at is the one running to the gap between the two spires, the same continuous cleft that on the west side is the chockstone-filled chimney. It is the biggest feature on this side of the group. Aim at it, then step left before reaching it.

So the negative test is: if you have reached the notch itself you have gone up too far, and if you are on the far side of the cleft you are on North Early Winters Spire, where Flycatcher Buttress starts from a flat ledge.

What separates this route from the east buttress it shares a start with, and it is a decision made halfway up rather than at the base: Southern Man splits off around mid-height onto the south-facing headwall. Its own belays are described as vague and not yet fixed, which is itself a tell: do not expect a fully bolted rap line if you need to bail from the upper headwall. Natural anchors would be required there.

Descent: from the summit, the standard South Arete descent, downclimbing the arete with a short more exposed fifth-class section to the Rabbit Ears, then three single-rope 60 m rappels from bolted anchors and chains down the gully to the base.

runs: about 700 vertical feet below the marble creek mcallister pass
hits.text:
The base is the toe of the buttress at the foot of a prominent, often year-round snow gully, and the gully is located by descending — it starts about 700 vertical feet below the Marble Creek-McALLISTER Pass. If you have not lost roughly 700 ft from the pass, you are not at the gully yet.

At the top of that gully there is a fork, and it is the one thing on this peak most worth getting right. This route goes around to the right. The Direct Southwest Buttress instead goes straight up from the same point to three vertical cracks. Same gully, two routes, one turn.

The strongest negative test is published as a warning and it is worth carrying verbatim: do not climb directly below the ridge crest at the start. That variation leads into unwanted 5.10 overhanging terrain on loose rock. If the ground turns overhanging at 5.10 low on the route, you are on the wrong side of the crest and should reverse rather than push on — this route's own crux is 5.8 in a corner and it comes at pitch five, not at the start.

Confirm on pitch one: it is a full rope length, 55 to 57 m, up a corner and then slightly right, mostly 5.6 with one committing 5.7 or 5.8 move near the top, and the anchor is on cams to three inches in a crack. A short first pitch is not this route.

And confirm by which col you crossed: this line is reached over the Marble Creek-McAllister pass. The Northwest Ridge starts from a small col at the top of the McAllister's apron on the other side of the Needle and is only three short pitches; the East Ridge starts from the col between Point 8386 and the Needle.

The difference is at the top. Do not finish the gully to the pass. Break off to the north of it and climb the open books on the face above instead. runs: that begin north of the pineapple pass gully
hits.text:
The arrival test is a thing you do not do: do not go up to Pineapple Pass. Hike the stable talus toward the pass and then leave it, heading north of the gully that finishes at the pass. If you have stood in the notch at Pineapple Pass, you have overshot the start of this route and you are at the start of the South Face.

What you are looking for on the rock: open books. Pitches one and two climb open-book corners that begin north of the Pineapple Pass gully, and they lead to a left-facing slab. Corner, corner, then slab facing left. That sequence is the confirmation, and none of it requires seeing the summit.

And a third-pitch check if you are still unsure: pitch three finds three cracks running up to an overhang, and the route face-climbs to the left of those three cracks. Three cracks under a roof, and you go left of them. If you are climbing the cracks themselves you have drifted right.

How it differs from its two neighbours: The Tooth Fairy is further left again and goes at 5.9; the South Face starts from the notch at the top of the pass at 5.4. This route sits between them, both physically and in difficulty, at 5.5. If your first pitch feels like 5.9, you have gone too far left.

A warning that belongs with the finding: this face is loose, and it sits above the popular routes. Being on the correct start also means being above other people.

hits.text: A full-value, remote adventure alpine rock climb that is infrequently traveled and requires real route-finding rather than following an obvious line. Roughly 19 ropelengths (60m) wind up the rib and around towers: intermittent treed/sandy ledges, slabs, and short steep steps lead up an indistinct crest for about 500 vertical feet until it becomes a defined, knife-edged ridge (marked by a large open slab visible on climber's left from a distance); the rib then relaxes into low-angled, sometimes loose/sandy corners for another ~400 feet; the upper climb is steeper and more continuously exposed, featuring prominent gendarmes, a sharp ridge traverse, a left-trending ramp below a steep white headwall, and a final summit block on Crystal Lake Tower, then a notch and ridge crest that lead on to the westernmost Chessman.

runs: first ascent of the south peak was made
hits.text: A pair of pyramidal twin summits in the Entiat Mountains subrange of the North Cascades, within the Glacier Peak Wilderness on Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Wenatchee River Ranger District) land in Chelan County. The sharper south summit (8,392 ft) is the true high point; the north butte (8,080 ft) sits about a half-mile away across a connecting basin. The name comes from their twin-lensed profile as seen from the Entiat River valley. First ascent of the south peak was made August 20, 1953 by Rowland Tabor and Dwight Crowder. This route follows the southwest ridge/west-facing slopes — the standard line on South Spectacle Butte — reached via a long, mostly cross-country approach through Leroy Basin and the Ice Lakes basin. Traffic is light; most parties combine it with Ice Lakes camping or a Leroy-Carne loop.

hits.text: Drop north-east off the pass down talus into the Ice Lakes basin. Pass the north end of Upper Ice Lake and follow the dry stream bed down to the west shore of Lower Ice Lake, then pick up the faint remnants of the old Ice Lakes Trail on the north side. Both lakes are reliable water.

runs: to the west shore of lower ice lake
hits.text: The standard approach is a long, mostly cross-country line from the Phelps Creek Trailhead at the end of Phelps Creek Road (FR 6211), about 3,500 ft. Follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 up the east side of the valley — a gentle, well-graded grade of roughly 275 ft per mile — crossing into the Glacier Peak Wilderness at 2.6 miles and reaching the Leroy Creek ford at about 3.5 miles. Immediately across the ford, the unmaintained Leroy Creek high route (Trail #1512) branches steeply north-east; it is well trodden but climbs at roughly 1,200 ft per mile for about 1.5 miles into Leroy Basin, where established camps sit off a steep path above the creek crossing. This half is hot and exposed under an overnight pack, so carry several liters. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 ft anywhere in the wilderness, and a free self-issue wilderness permit is filled out at the trailhead. From camp, pick up the Carne Mountain high trail — an old sheepherder track — and follow it south-east, giving up a little elevation to cross the south fork of Leroy Creek before climbing to the 6,850 ft saddle at Leroy Pass; cairns mark the way but several paths braid apart in the basin, so stay on the lower and better-trodden line where they diverge. Continue east on faint footpaths through heather, then talus and scree, gaining about 750 ft over roughly a mile to Freezer Pass at 7,600 ft. There is no maintained tread here and the bootpaths come and go, so keep track of your line for the return; snow can linger on this stretch into early or mid July. Drop north-east off the pass down talus into the Ice Lakes basin, passing the north end of Upper Ice Lake and following the dry stream bed to the west shore of Lower Ice Lake. Both lakes are reliable water. Pick up the faint remnants of the historic Ice Lakes Trail on the north side and sidehill east at about 6,600 ft on slippery scrub and loose rock with no real tread — keep the party strung out in a line rather than stacked one above another, because almost everything here moves underfoot. Roughly a third of a mile brings you to the lip of a washed-out gully; downclimb the loose clay and scree into it and climb the far side back to about the same elevation, picking the crossing line carefully, since dropping too low can leave you cliffed out. This is the last reliable water before the summit. Beyond it the traverse eases into the open basin floor between the two Buttes at about 6,800 ft, where a scree-and-talus ramp gains the crest of the southwest ridge and the scrambling begins. A separate approach corridor exists on the west side of the peak: leaving Phelps Creek Trail #1511 at around 5,300 ft and climbing cross-country east through heather and talus benches to gain the peak's west-facing slopes. It is a shorter day from the trailhead and avoids the Freezer Pass crossing, but it is a different line from the one this route's waypoints and descent follow, and the north side of that ridge is cliffy and should not be entered.

runs: to the west shore of lower ice lake
hits.text: There is no rappelling on this route and no shortcut descent gully — it is a walk-off and downclimb by the line used on the ascent. From the 8,392 ft summit, reverse the ledges on the south-east corner of the summit block back onto the crest of the southwest ridge at about 8,100 ft; the cairns here blend into the surrounding rock and are easy to lose, so pick the line up deliberately rather than drifting down the first ledge system that goes. Downclimb the crest on Class 2-3 talus and broken rock, turning the gendarmes on climber's right as you did on the way up, and reverse the crux at around 7,700 ft — the Class 3 dike, the traverse on down-sloping rock, and the short chossy chute — facing in, one at a time, on rotten holds with real exposure. Below the gendarmes, descend the scree-and-talus ramp roughly 400 ft into the open basin floor between the two Buttes. From there retrace the traverse west: cross the washed-out gully at about 6,600 ft, keeping the party strung out in a line rather than stacked, and sidehill back across the loose scrub and rock to the west shore of Lower Ice Lake. Regain the faint remnants of the old Ice Lakes Trail, climb back up the talus to Freezer Pass at 7,600 ft, then follow the faint heather-and-scree footpaths west over Leroy Pass at 6,850 ft and down the Carne Mountain high trail into Leroy Basin camp. The bootpaths between the passes come and go, so the return is materially easier if you tracked your line on the way in. From camp, reverse the steep unmaintained Leroy Creek high route to the ford and follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 back down-valley to the trailhead. The hazards on the whole descent are rockfall, loose downsloping rock on the ridge, and losing the cairned or booted line in scree and talus — not rope work. An alternate exit some parties use drops west off the peak's west-facing slopes through heather and talus to rejoin Phelps Creek Trail #1511 directly at around 5,300 ft, avoiding the return over Freezer and Leroy Passes; it is a different line from the ascent, it leaves any camp at Ice Lakes or Leroy Basin behind you, and the north side of that ridge is cliffy and should not be entered, so treat it as a deliberate choice made in advance rather than a shortcut taken on the descent.

runs: to the west shore of lower ice lake
hits.text:
From the Phelps Creek Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, Phelps Creek Trail #1511 climbs the east side of the valley at roughly 275 ft per mile, crossing into the wilderness at 2.6 miles and reaching the Leroy Creek ford at about 3.5. Immediately across the ford the unmaintained Leroy Creek high route branches steeply north-east and climbs about 1.5 miles into Leroy Basin at about 6,100 ft, where the camps are. That half is hot and exposed under a pack.

From camp pick up the Carne Mountain high trail — an old sheepherder track — south-east; it gives up a little height to cross the south fork of Leroy Creek before climbing to Leroy Pass at 6,850 ft. Cairns mark the way but several paths braid apart in the basin: stay on the lower and better-trodden line where they diverge.

Continue east on faint footpaths through heather, then talus and scree, gaining about 750 ft over roughly a mile to Freezer Pass at 7,600 ft. There is no maintained tread here and the boot paths come and go, so track your own line for the return.

Drop north-east off the pass into the Ice Lakes basin, losing about 1,000 ft past the north end of Upper Ice Lake and down the dry stream bed to the west shore of Lower Ice Lake. Both lakes are reliable water.

runs: starts in the center of spectre's south face
hits.text: Established in August 2006 by Wayne Wallace and Mike Layton after a grueling approach, this route starts in the center of Spectre's south face and climbs about 800 feet of runout terrain into a 'deep, spooky' chimney that is completely enclosed inside the mountain at times, then continues on exposed face climbing past an offwidth section before a ridge traverse gains the summit. The route is noted for being largely devoid of crack protection through its runout sections.

runs: on the western slope of the northern pickets
hits.text: Spectre Peak (7,952'; a LIDAR-based figure gives 7,953') sits on the western slope of the Northern Pickets — it's grouped thematically with neighboring Ghost Peak and Phantom Peak near Swiss Peak and Mount Challenger, part of the Northern Pickets traverse line (Luna-Fury-Swiss-Spectre-Phantom-Crooked Thumb-Ghost-Challenger). It is one of the most remote and rarely climbed summits in the Pickets, with only two documented technical routes on record: Haunted Wall (IV 5.9+, 2,100', Wayne Wallace and Mike Layton, Aug 2006) and this South Ridge line.

hits.text: From the river, switchback steeply back up onto Easy Ridge and then follow the crest itself. This is a hot, dry, open, south-facing ridge with almost no shade; flowing water shows up relatively early along it, but the first-ascent party warned this stretch would be brutal later in the season and in dry years, so fill up while you can. Continue along and over Easy Peak to the established bivy beyond it, roughly a ten-hour day with a full pack from the trailhead.

runs: brutal later in the season and in dry years
hits.text: Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (elev. ~3,120 ft) at the end of Ruth Creek Road (FS-32). From the trailhead, follow the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail #674 gently up the Ruth Creek valley (views of Mt. Sefrit and Nooksack Ridge) for about 4 miles and roughly 2,000 ft of gain to 5,050 ft Hannegan Pass — this stretch is straightforward, well-graded, and has reliable water at Ruth Creek crossings for the first couple of miles. From the pass, stay on the maintained trail as it drops past Boundary Camp and Copper Creek Camp into the Chilliwack valley; roughly two miles beyond Copper Creek an easily missed side path leads down to the Chilliwack River ford (about 2,750 ft), and the Easy Ridge path climbs steeply from the far bank. From here it is sustained, largely cross-country travel: climb onto and follow Easy Ridge itself, a hot, dry, open, south-facing ridge crest with limited shade — flowing water is available relatively early on the ridge but the FA party warned it becomes brutal later in the season and in dry years. Continue along/over Easy Peak (a common first bivy, roughly a full day, ~10 hours, from the trailhead) and then descend/traverse past the notch known as Imperfect Impasse, before regaining elevation to Challenger Col on the flank of Mt. Challenger. From Challenger Col, traverse the southern Challenger cirque (glacial terrain — rope/crevasse-awareness recommended near the pocket glacier) toward the west ridge of Phantom Peak, a typical second bivy site, avoiding lingering snow at Pickle Pass. From this high camp it is a further, mostly straightforward cross-country traverse across the western slopes to the base of Spectre Peak's south ridge, reached around sunrise on what is effectively day three. In total this is roughly a 46-mile, ~17,500 ft round-trip approach-and-climb outing (74 km), typically broken into 2 or more travel days each way with route-finding, glacier travel, and off-trail ridge scrambling throughout — this is genuinely one of the longest, most remote approaches in the North Cascades, not a simple hike-in.

runs: to the western slope of the range from
hits.text: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.

runs: reach the fringe of the middle cascade glacier
hits.text: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (3,600 ft, at the end of the 23.1-mile Cascade River Road from Marblemount), hike the Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass (~5,400-5,560 ft). Continue on a climbers' path across talus to Cache Col (~6,900 ft), then descend steep snowfields (ice axe/crampons often needed) into the Kool-Aid Lake basin (~6,800 ft), a common base camp. From Kool-Aid Lake, cross talus/scree east toward Spider's south face, reach the fringe of the Middle Cascade Glacier (~6,500 ft) after a steep, narrow sidehill traverse, and cross the glacier (crevasses present; rope recommended) to Spider-Formidable Col (~7,320 ft), an alternate, higher base camp used by many climbing parties.

runs: eastward across a broad slope of dirt scree and talus
hits.text: One feature settles this: a prominent rock buttress bisects the peak's south face, and the gully you want is the one immediately to its right, to the east. Get there by dropping off the south side of the col — slither down the shallow moat beside the steep snow finger rather than fighting the snow itself — then traverse eastward across a broad slope of dirt, scree and talus cut by erosion runnels, angling up toward the face. The proof at the gully's foot is a deep, ugly erosion runnel spewing out of its mouth. Rather than crossing that runnel head-on, take the talus ramp beside it that leads up and into the gully. Inside, the gully is very narrow, quite steep and completely choked with loose rock: if the gully you are in is broad, clean or comfortable, it is the wrong one. If the big central buttress is on your right rather than your left, you have gone one gully too far west.

runs: to the col between point 5261 and spinnaker peak
hits.text: Two options exist to reach Spinnaker Peak's summit: the easier line climbs directly to the col between Point 5261 and Spinnaker Peak (steepest section of the trip, but low-exposure on the right line, and an ice axe isn't required if only Spinnaker is the objective); the harder option climbs Point 5261 first and follows the narrow, steeply-dropping ridge to Spinnaker's summit, which does require an ice axe and should be avoided in higher avalanche danger. The peak is seldom climbed despite its proximity to US Highway 2.

runs: divide between the east and west drainage basins
hits.text: Gap on the divide between the east and west drainage basins; gain Spinnaker's south ridge here and angle climber's-left up the final slopes to the summit.

runs: the col between point 5261 and spinnaker peak
hits.text: The base of the climb is the col between Point 5261 and Spinnaker Peak. Coming up out of the basin, Point 5261 is the nearer rocky sub-summit and Spinnaker the higher point beyond it; the col is the low saddle between the two, and the ground rising out of it is the steepest of the whole trip although on a well-chosen line it carries little exposure and needs no axe if Spinnaker is your only objective. Take the col directly. The alternative — climbing Point 5261 first and following the connecting ridge across — is a materially different proposition: that crest is narrow, drops steeply into a series of small notches, ices over when windblown, wants an ice axe, and should be left alone with any avalanche danger about. So the check is simple: if you find yourself on a knife-edged crest with cornices and notches, you have taken the harder variant rather than the standard one, and the col is below and to your side. On the way down, keep off the trail tread itself for winter travel, since it crosses several avalanche paths near here.

runs: one of the least often climbed of the everett pin peaks
hits.text: Spire Mountain (6,213-6,218 ft) is a three-summited peak — Northwest, Central, and Southeast Spires — in the Wild Sky Wilderness of the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, about 7 miles northeast of Index and 4 miles north-northeast of Gunn Peak. It rises directly above the North Fork Skykomish River, on the west side of the range, not near Sultan Basin or the Sauk drainage/Monte Cristo group. One of the least-often-climbed of the 'Everett Pin Peaks,' Spire is reached by a long, entirely off-trail approach through brush and cliff bands and finishes on an airy summit ridge with a genuine, exposed Class 5 step that trips up parties expecting an easy Class 3 walk-up.

runs: before the gully look on your left for
hits.text:
The marker at the base is dead trees. As the ground steepens toward the formation and before the gully, look on your left for tree snags — standing dead timber against the rock. The first pitch climbs cracks up from a snag. That is the start, and it is the only start on this formation with a landmark you can walk up and touch.

If you have entered the gully itself, you have gone too far right. The gully parallels this route and is used both as a descent and as a fast way to reach the bolted line beside it — it is not this climb.

Confirm on pitch two, which is the strongest check the route gives you: it traverses under a roof. If your second pitch runs sideways beneath an overhang rather than straight up, you are on line. Above that expect steepening ground with cracks and a good layback, then a wide ten-inch crack with finger and hand sections, then a corner crack to lieback, and a headwall finish.

Expect long scrambling sections between the pitches. That is this route's defining character and the main complaint about it — it is the reason a 5.7 with seven pitches takes a full day. Continuous roped climbing with no walking between would mean you are somewhere else.

Negative markers for the two neighbours. If you have traversed a long way rightward from the base on third and fourth-class ledges toward the middle of the face before starting, you are heading for the hard line that finishes on this route's last pitches. And if your first pitch is protected by bolts, you are on the partly bolted line — this route takes natural gear throughout.

Descent is most often a rappel of the line itself, and parties report it is slow and that ropes snag on flakes. The alternative is the third-class gully to climbers' right, faster but loose; stay high and skier's-right to limit what is above you.

runs: at the far west end of the pullout
hits.text:
Park in the highway turnout about two miles east of Washington Pass, near milepost 165. The climbers' trail starts at the far west end of the pullout, drops steeply through loose dirt and rock, crosses Early Winters Creek on logs, then traverses an avalanche path — the old line has two or three informal fixed rope sections here — toward the base of the formation. Around an hour and a half.

A newer variation of the path bears right just before the fixed lines and needs only a small amount of scrambling, which most parties now prefer.

There are two ways to reach this route once you are under the formation, and they are genuinely different days. The faster one takes the gully that parallels the arete beside it. The other climbs the first three pitches of that arete and then cuts across the gully, which is how parties who wanted a longer outing get here.

Take the left fork of NF-9070 and follow it until the road terminates in a large turnaround just below Silver Basin. From that turnaround, it's roughly a 20-30 minute approach on foot up into Silver Basin to reach the base of The Citadel's walls, including Sofa King Buttress on the NW side of the basin's east wall. The road is not plowed and is generally only clear of snow from around July through November.

hits.text: From Fish Creek Pass, gain the crest of Star Peak's northwest ridge directly rather than dropping to Star Lake. From the ledge, cross back through the right-most notch and descend the loose talus and scree slope to the cirque. From the base of the talus, traverse back to the basin below Goode and descend the cairned climbers' path and the burned ridge to the Park Creek trail just past the big washout, then continue via whichever of the three approach trails (Thunder Creek, McAlester Pass/Rainbow Creek, or Park Creek/Stehekin) matches your itinerary. hits.text:
Walk the Pete Lake trail #1323 up the Cooper River to a fork at about 3,120 ft, roughly five miles in. Turn right, continue about six tenths of a mile, and turn right again onto the Pacific Crest Trail at about 3,220 ft. Follow the PCT four and a half miles up a long series of switchbacks to about 5,500 ft.

The Vista Lakes tarns lie east of the trail at that height and hold the good bivy sites. Summit Chief is about two more miles from there. Reported times from the car to the upper lake run to most of a day with overnight loads, and every published account treats this as a two- or three-day trip.

This is also the last reliable water. The ground above is reported bone dry until you come back down to the lakes.

From camp, leave the PCT and traverse cross-country toward Summit Chief Pass, then follow the ridge north-west staying below the cliffs and gendarmes, into the upper basin south-east of the main summit. One party's hindsight on this traverse is worth having: they should have dropped to about 6,000 ft and taken the scree instead of holding height across steep sloping slabs.

hits.text:
There is a specific chain of features here and it ends at a piece of ground that is unmistakable once you know to look for it.

From the upper basin, find a small notch in the skyline ridge to the west. To reach it, head north-west toward a minor rock ridge that runs west-south-west to east-north-east across the base of the summit. That minor ridge is the base of the climb — arriving at it is arriving.

Gain it by the snow in the gap at its right, lower end, then walk along the top of the ridge to the notch at its west end. On the far side of the notch is a steep gully, usually icy in the morning, and beyond that a loose-rock gully; the exit is the gully on the right just below the summit.

Negative marker, learned the hard way and independently corroborated: from the snowfield below the south-east face, the first and left-most snow finger leading to the south ridge is a dead end. It runs into a deep notch and the party that took it had to retreat. Go instead to the upper right corner of the snowfield, exit onto steep dirt and scree, and pick up a left-slanting ramp to a higher notch. Two separate accounts arrive at the same instruction from opposite directions.

The moat is the gate and it has a date on it. Where the mountain rises in earnest at about 7,000 ft a moat forms, and it may be impassable after mid-July, perhaps earlier in a low-snow year. If it stops you, there may be Class 3 rock in the middle of the basin as an alternative, but plan the trip around the calendar rather than hoping.

Do not trust a single photograph for the crossing point on the south ridge; parties report the pictures circulating online do not match the ground.

The top five hundred feet is steep dirt and thoroughly untrustworthy rock — one climber said it had earned honorary Olympic Mountains status. That looseness is normal for this summit and is not a sign you have wandered onto harder ground.

runs: from the trailhead at the north end of cooper lake
hits.text: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.

runs: the trail begins as a rock lined gravel path
hits.text: From the Artist Point trailhead (elev. ~5,100 ft, at the end of Mt. Baker Highway/SR 542, GPS approx. 48.847, -121.693) walk to the northwest corner of the large paved parking lot — the signed Table Mountain Trail #681 starts opposite the vault toilets, on the side of the lot away from the highway. The trail begins as a rock-lined gravel path that climbs gently before reaching its first switchback within a few hundred feet. From there the route ascends a tight set of rocky switchbacks blasted directly into the cliff band on Table Mountain's southeast face — this is the crux of the approach: a narrow, exposed catwalk with steep drop-offs toward the Chain Lakes basin and Swift Creek drainage 400-800 ft below. Footing here is loose rock and gravel over hard-packed tread, and snow or verglas frequently lingers in this cliff section into July, making it the most hazardous stretch of the whole route; many parties turn back here in early season without traction devices. After roughly 400 ft of gain (about 0.4-0.5 mi from the car) the switchbacks top out on the broad, relatively flat summit plateau ("the table"). From here follow the well-trodden tread west/northwest along the south rim, which gives open views straight down onto the Chain Lakes Trail; numerous braided use-trails cross the plateau but the main route hugs the south side. At about 1.2 mi you reach the east side of the tabletop with views of Mount Baker and Ptarmigan Ridge, and by 1.3 mi you arrive at two small tarns that frame Mount Shuksan — a natural turnaround for most day hikers and the last easily identified landmark before the trail degrades into a sketchy, unmaintained scramble path descending toward the Table Mountain Glacier. There is no reliable water along the route: the summit tarns are shallow, silty, and not worth treating, so carry all water from the car. Overall to the high point is roughly 1.4-1.5 mi one-way with about 700-725 ft of gain from the trailhead.

runs: a broken chimney with a good jam crack
hits.text:
The col east of the summit block is the base, and the thing that confirms it is the wind. Parties who have stood there describe it as an incredibly windy notch below the east face — it is a gap on a ridge, so it funnels, and on a Cascade summit day you will feel it before you can see anything.

Getting there is a single bearing from camp: from Thunder Basin cross talus and snow toward the col that sits east of the summit block, near 8,000 ft. Crampons and an axe are normal for the snow, which stays firm in the morning. You are aiming for the gap beside the summit tower, not for the tower.

The positive test for the start of the climbing: from the col the route takes a loose gully on the left for about 85 ft to a ledge system. Loose first, ledge second. If the first thing above the col is clean solid rock, or if you are moving right rather than left, you are not on it.

The second confirmation is a crack. Above the ledge system the finish is a broken chimney with a good jam crack running up it, and that crack is the one genuinely positive hold-bearing feature on the summit block. Class 4 to easy fifth depending on conditions. If you are on a face with no chimney and no crack, you have drifted off the ledge system.

What it is not: this is a short summit block, not a wall. From the col to the top is roughly two rope lengths. If you have been climbing for hours above the col you are not on this route.

Rack and rock: everything from the col up is loose. Helmet, and space the party out — the gully drops what the leader pulls straight onto whoever is below.

runs: the crest of a semi open spur from
hits.text: From the Lena Lake Trailhead (Trail #810) off FS-25 at roughly 700 ft, hike the maintained Lena Lake Trail about 3 miles and ~1,100 ft of gain through second-growth and old-growth forest, crossing several creek drainages on the way, to Lena Lake (~1,800 ft) — a popular backpacking destination with a ranger station and established campsites, and the last easy, reliable water/camping before the climbers' route. Skirt the west side of the lake and pick up the unmaintained but well-trodden 'Brothers Trail' boot path, which continues up the East Fork Lena Creek drainage through the old-growth 'Valley of the Silent Men' for roughly another 2.5-3 miles to a climbers' camp (sometimes called Camp Brothers) at about 2,900 ft, marked by a fire ring — most parties treat this as their high camp for a two-day ascent. From camp, leave the tread and follow a climbers' path along the west fork of Lena Creek for about a mile; this crosses an avalanche debris field where slide alder and downed logs (some with hand-lines/notches cut in) obscure the route and creek fords may be required — go carefully, especially with a full pack. Beyond the debris field the path re-enters forest and climbs to the base of the South Couloir around 4,000-4,300 ft. Ascend the couloir (firm snow in early season, loose scree by mid/late summer) a few hundred feet, then exit onto its west side and continue up scree to about 5,000 ft, making an ascending rightward traverse below cliff bands to reach the crest of a semi-open spur. From the spur, work up and right to the base of 'the Hourglass,' a narrow rock/snow constriction that is the technical crux of the approach to the summit block (Class 3 scrambling, or a steep 35-45° snow climb in early season requiring an axe and solid self-arrest skills — watch for a moat opening at its base as the snow recedes). Above the Hourglass, continue on scree or snow toward the summit ridge and watch closely for a cairned, easy-to-miss notch on the right (climbers describe it as a 'dwarf door' — nearly invisible until you're directly in front of it); this notch is the route-finding key to the final gully leading to the true south summit, the last roughly 200 vertical feet of which is Class 4 with real exposure. Water is reliable at Lena Lake and along Lena Creek up to high camp; above camp, plan on snowmelt or carrying water, as there's nothing reliable once you're on the scree/couloir.

runs: on scree heather and lumpy basalt crossing many small ribs and gullies
hits.text:
The arrival test is a step in the ridge crest at about 6,100 ft, and the way you know it is the right one is the thing that happens if you go 100 ft higher. Working up and rightward from camp on scree, heather and lumpy basalt, crossing many small ribs and gullies, you meet the crest. There are two places you can meet it. The higher one, at about 6,200 ft, is a small notch whose far side is a 200-foot cliff — a party that tops out there has to back off and traverse out on exposed ledges with Class 3-4 slots between them. The one you want is the small step in the crest at about 6,100 ft, from which the ground drops steeply but climbably into the snow-filled Great Basin.

So the fog test is: top out, then look down. If the far side goes, you are at the step and on route. If the far side is a cliff, you are a hundred feet too high — do not try to force it, come back down and traverse.

Second test, once in the Great Basin: from it you climb a moderately steep snow couloir angling toward the North Brother, narrowing to a snow finger that reaches the summit ridge. If your couloir is running away from the north summit rather than toward it, you crossed the basin in the wrong direction.

What the traverse itself feels like, so nobody mistakes the connecting ridge for a mistake: the crest between the two Brothers is giant boulders forming a jagged run of horns and pinnacles, and traversing it is slow. Slow is correct here. The route is roughly seven roped pitches — fourth class to the notch, steep snow into the Great Basin, moderate snow on the east ridge, a sparsely protected rock traverse on the west side, mixed ground with moat belays, and a final steep couloir to the South Brother.

Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to a small meadow, then take the climbers' boot path breaking off just past a small stream, climbing through slabs, talus and meadow to the gully between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower. That gully is often snow-filled and icy into late June and carries high rockfall risk after snowmelt.

hits.text: Begins on the right side of the South Face and follows flakes, corners, and splitters up to a broad ledge roughly halfway up the face. From the ledge, walk leftward to start the upper half of the climb; the first pitch above the ledge heads up to the left side of the most prominent arete/pillar in the middle of the upper face. After two more pitches, the route trends rightward and reaches the summit via blocky ground just right of a prominent chimney.

hits.text: The Silver Horn is a sub-summit on the east ridge of Silver Star Mountain, east of the main summit, and both of its routes are on the clean white granite of its south face. That face is not reached from the Wine Spires pullout or Burgundy Col, which serve the other side of the crest. Instead, walk the Cedar Creek Trail from its trailhead at the end of FR 5310-200, off SR-20 about half a mile east of the Klipchuck Campground turnoff. After roughly five miles, turn off to the right below the old burn and follow a rough path up the right-hand side of the creek that drains the south side of the Silver Horn. Meadows at about 6,200 ft give good camping below the face.

hits.text:
The wall is clean white granite and it is visibly paler than what surrounds it, which is the first check that you are under the right formation. Follow the creek to the meadows and then up to the foot of it.

This route is the right-hand line. Start on the right side of the south face, on flakes, corners and splitters. Its neighbour begins with a layback off a large clean flake into a long left-facing corner system; if that is what is above you, walk right.

The defining feature is a broad ledge at half height, and it is the strongest thing this route has. Roughly halfway up the face the climbing arrives at a wide ledge that runs across the wall. That ledge is the route's hinge: from it you walk leftward before starting the upper half. A route that reaches a broad crossing ledge and then requires you to walk left along it is this one.

Confirm on the upper face. The first pitch above the ledge heads for the left side of the most prominent arete or pillar in the middle of the upper wall. That arete is the biggest feature up there and being on its left is the check. Two more pitches, then the line trends rightward to the summit.

The summit pitch separates the two routes absolutely. This one finishes on blocky ground just right of a prominent chimney. It does not go into the chimney. The neighbouring route tops out through a deep summit chimney. So: blocky ground beside a slot means this route; stemming up inside the slot means you have crossed onto the other line.

Negative marker lower down, since the two lines are close: if there was no broad crossing ledge and instead you moved rightward under a roof into a splitter to reach a smaller ledge, you are on the neighbour.

No descent has been described for this line itself. Because it shares the summit and the mid-face ledge with its neighbour, parties use that route's rappels down the south-east side: a seventy-metre rope, sparse fixed anchors, and enough webbing to build your own. Go up prepared to make anchors.

runs: in 1932 by bill degenhardt and h v strandberg
hits.text: Officially "Pinnacle Peak" on USGS maps, but almost universally called The Chopping Block for its distinctive squarish, blocky summit block. It sits at the south end of the Barrier Ridge in the Southern Pickets, North Cascades National Park, dividing Terror Creek Basin from Crescent Creek Basin, and is visible from the Newhalem visitor center on clear days. First climbed in 1932 by Bill Degenhardt and H. V. Strandberg — their summit cairn reportedly remained undisturbed for decades — it's now a common secondary objective for parties in the Southern Pickets for Mount Terror, Mount Degenhardt, or the Twin Needles.

hits.text: Stump Hollow is the open slabby heather ground at timberline between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block, and the first place after the forest where a tent actually goes down comfortably. Parties heading for the north side use it as the intermediate camp, because an easy rising traverse reaches the saddle northeast of the Chopping Block near 6,400 ft and drops into Crescent Creek Basin from there. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than the heather — this is thin alpine ground that shows every night somebody spends on it.
