runs: no sites are held as same day walk ups
hits.text: A wilderness permit is required and Flapjack Lakes is a named quota area, limited year round, so this is the one booking in the zone that will actually stop your trip. Permits are issued only through the federal recreation booking site; the online reservation window for this camp runs mid-June to mid-October, and the whole summer season releases in one drop on April 15 at 7 a.m. Pacific. No sites are held as same-day walk-ups — the old half-reserved, half-first-come arrangement is gone, and availability now updates live, so cancellations are the only late route in. For dates outside the online window you have to arrange it directly with the park's wilderness information office. Fees are a non-refundable per-permit reservation charge plus a per-person nightly charge for anyone sixteen and over, with an annual wilderness pass available that covers the nightly half. Parties of seven or more must take the group site. Bear canisters are required. Campfires are prohibited — the lakes are above the 3,500 ft parkwide fire line. Camping is in designated sites only. Stock is not allowed on the Flapjack trail, and dogs are not allowed on park wilderness trails. A park entrance pass is needed for the drive in, and the access road up Lake Cushman is unpaved for its last stretch and closes for snow and weather. Weekday permits here are usually gettable; summer weekends are not.

runs: near the right side of the lowest part of the
hits.text:
The objective is the small semi-detached tower at the lower right of the mountain's south wall, not the wall itself. Walk from camp toward the deep gully between the two and get onto the tower's own rock on the right side of that gully.

This line is the right-hand one on the tower's south face, and it has the only start on this face you can actually stand on and name: a large ledge low down, near the right side of the lowest part of the rock. Walk the base rightward until you can step up onto a ledge big enough to organise a rack on. That is the start. If you are standing on broken talus at the very bottom of the face with no ledge under you, keep walking right.

The route then confirms itself by behaviour rather than by a landmark: it zigzags. Five pitches that keep cutting back and forth across the right side of the face, which is why long slings are not optional here — rope drag is the thing people complain about, and drag is itself evidence you are on the correct line.

Negative markers. If you started at the lowest point of the face and went straight up the middle past a prominent roof, you are on the central line. If your first two pitches were a chimney or gully left of centre, you are on the three-pitch crack line further left. If you started at a pair of parallel cracks on the lower left and were off after two pitches, you are on the short cracks.

Also worth knowing: this route's descent is not the mountain's summit walk-off. It comes off the tower by the north-east gully in three rappels of about seventy-five feet, each covered by a doubled sixty-metre rope. If somebody has told you to walk west off the summit, they were describing the mountain, not the tower.

runs: hike up into the deep gully separating cathedral
hits.text: The drive itself is easy — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek Trailhead, about 23 miles total — but the climb to Cathedral Peak is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state. From the trailhead, the Andrews Creek Trail (#504) climbs roughly 12 miles to 6,680+ ft Andrews Pass, then descends into the Spanish Creek drainage before a side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lakes below the peak's southwest side, putting the one-way approach at around 18 miles with significant elevation gain and loss along the way. Most parties treat this as a 2-4 day backpack (roughly 40+ miles round trip), camping at or near Cathedral Lakes before making a summit push. A free self-issue wilderness permit is required at the trailhead, along with a trailhead parking pass; the first many miles are a hot, rocky, buggy uphill slog with little shade, so this is genuinely a remote, multi-day alpine objective rather than a day-approach crag. For this specific route: The Monk is a distinct, smaller detached tower/buttress leaning against Cathedral Peak's south/east flank, not part of the main South Face wall. From Cathedral Lakes camp, follow the same talus slope toward Cathedral Pass but hike up into the deep gully separating Cathedral Peak from The Monk, then start on The Monk's own faces (right side of the gully); most Monk routes descend via rappels down the NE gully.

hits.text:
From Glacier, WA, drive SR-542 east about 12 miles to the WSDOT Shuksan maintenance facility and turn onto Twin Lakes Road (FS-3065). The first 4.5 miles to the Yellow Aster Butte / Tomyhoi Lake trailhead are passenger-car friendly; beyond that the road narrows and is not maintained for passenger vehicles, and high-clearance is recommended for the final two miles to Twin Lakes. If the upper road is out, park at the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead and add roughly four miles round trip and 1,500 ft of gain.

From the isthmus between the Twin Lakes take the High Pass Trail — about two miles, losing roughly 300 ft as it skirts below Winchester Mountain before climbing to the pass.

From High Pass, ascend the scree or snow slope NNE to the col in Larrabee's South Arm; there is a trail here in summer. From the col descend slightly and traverse the basin.

The Pleiades are a series of jagged spires on Larrabee's east ridge, so this is not one summit but several.

runs: the scree or snow slope nne to the col in
hits.text: The climb starts at a gully leading to the notch between the first and second Pleiades, and finding it is a three-step sequence from High Pass. Up the scree or snow slope NNE to the col in Larrabee's south arm. Down slightly from the col. Across the basin. Then up the gully to the notch. The descent in the middle is the step people skip, and skipping it puts you on Larrabee's south ridge instead. The notch is between two spires and that is the confirmation. You are not aiming for a summit, you are aiming for the gap between the first and second towers of a jagged row. Arriving somewhere with rock on both sides of you and the basin below is the arrival. From the notch the two peaks are very different, and the choice matters. The second peak, to the east, is an easy scramble. The first peak, to the west, is third class in summer and has been reported as a snowy knife-edge with slabby, high-consequence exposure in winter conditions. Going the wrong way out of the notch is the difference between a walk and a serious ridge. What being on the wrong objective looks like: Larrabee's own South Ridge route leaves the same basin and its base is two parallel channels about 30 ft apart on a southwest spur at 6,900 ft — take the right-hand one for Larrabee. American Border Peak's route contours much further north around Larrabee's west flank to a col at 6,200-6,300 ft. All three leave High Pass. Only this one crosses the basin under Larrabee's east-side spires. The rock is loose and sandy throughout, which makes downclimbing as hazardous as the climb up. Keep the party close so nobody is under a falling stone.

runs: to the right of the west face and the tempest
one of the best 5.11 hand and finger cracks
hits.text: The Scoop follows a striking line of finger-and-hand cracks up to 1,000 ft to the right of the West Face and the Tempest, named for its crux pitch, which resembles a giant ice-cream scoop. Established by Matt Clifton, Evan Cabodi, and Stewart Matthiesen on August 9, 2010, after significant lichen-cleaning. It's considered one of the best 5.11 hand-and-finger cracks in the Pacific Northwest; a bypass exists via a 5.10+ hand crack ("Nectar") to the right for parties wanting to skip the 5.11c crux.

runs: to easier terrain belay below a small rotting tree
with a 5.10 hand crack to a nice belay ledge
up and left to the summit and the balanced rock
hits.text: P1 (5.9, ~100 ft): bouldery move off the ground to easier terrain, belay below a small rotting tree. P2 (5.10a, ~100 ft): move into a groove, tough moves out right where climbing eases. P3 (5.10a, ~100 ft): fun climbing into a dihedral crux, short slab to 'Launch Ledge'; move the belay left ~30 ft before P4. P4 (5.11c, ~195 ft, 'The Scoop'): nice crack into a corner, sustained finger/hand jams up and left, finishing with a 5.10 hand crack to a nice belay ledge (a 5.10+ variation, 'Nectar', skips the crux via a hand crack to the right). P5 (5.10b, ~100 ft): down and left on a small ledge into a slab dihedral (small cams/nuts useful, wet early season), out left of a roof to a belay ledge. P6 (5.10a, ~100 ft): right side up, back left to a rock tooth, a nice 5.9 dihedral to a small roof and final ledge (tree belay). P7-10: easy fifth-class climbing up and left to the summit and the balanced rock.

runs: right of the west face and the tempest
hits.text: Cross the outlet below the small dam at the lake's north end and follow the climbers' path up and across the timbered hillside into the west cirque, then boulder-hop talus to the wall. The Scoop starts right of the West Face and the Tempest, left of Rikki Tikki Tavi; climb three pitches to Launch Ledge, the Scoop corner above it, and on to the summit block.

runs: to the right of the west face and the tempest
hits.text: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601 off Icicle Creek Road; NW Forest Pass required) and follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) roughly 2.25 miles, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge near the 1.5-mile mark, to the junction where the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599A) branches left. Stay on #1599A across a second Mountaineer Creek log crossing and up steepening, rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake (about 4 miles and 2,280 ft of gain, roughly 1:45-2:00 hiking). From the lake, reach Colchuck Balanced Rock's west basin either via the shorter northern line — cross the lake's outlet below the small dam at the north end and follow a climbers' path across timbered hillside straight into the cirque (about an hour, plus ~20-25 minutes boulder-hopping the talus to the actual base) — or the longer southern/Aasgard line, following the lakeshore path counter-clockwise toward the Aasgard Pass slopes, cutting north through a slide-alder band (cairned) into the leftmost gully, climbing that ~1,000 ft to its top, then contouring east on an easy path into the basin (1.5-2 hours, more gain but no ford). The Scoop starts in the basin to the right of the West Face and the Tempest, left of Rikki Tikki Tavi — from the base of the wall, the first three pitches (up to 5.10a) lead to 'Launch Ledge,' the platform below the namesake Scoop corner pitch. Colchuck Lake is the last dependable water source; carry what you need for a long climbing day. Hazards mirror the West Face approach: slick/high log-bridge creek crossings early season, a real bushwhack through slide alder, loose gully talus, and lingering snow into early summer on the gully and basin.

hits.text: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road, ~8.5 miles from Leavenworth) and follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599). The first 1.5 miles climb gently through forest alongside Mountaineer Creek to a log-bridge crossing; about a mile past that, fork left at the signed junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599A). The final push switchbacks up a boulder moraine to the Colchuck Lake outlet — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft of gain, 2.5-3 hours at a steady pace. This is the last reliable water; fill up here. Work around toward the lake's south/east side and pick up the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, following it up steep talus/heather to roughly 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min; this slope holds snow into July and has a real slip-and-fall history). Break off climber's-left through a band of dense slide alder and heather — the brushy crux of the hike-in, 15-20 minutes — to the base of the gully system below Colchuck Balanced Rock's main wall. The Tempest begins at the center of the face, below the long bulge/roof, roughly mid-way along the base — a bit right of the West Face's gully start. Expect loose 3rd/4th-class rock in the final approach scramble; many parties rope up. Total trailhead-to-base time runs 3.5-4 hours.

hits.text: From the Snow Lakes Trailhead on Icicle Creek Road (about 4.2 mi from US-2, ~1,300 ft elevation), cross Icicle Creek on the trail bridge and begin the long, switchbacking climb up open, sun-baked slabs on Snow Lakes Trail No. 1553 — this lower stretch is notoriously hot with almost no shade, so carry more water than feels necessary for the first few miles. The grade eases as the trail enters the hanging valley and reaches Nada Lake at roughly 5.5-5.6 miles (~5,000 ft), banking most of the day's approach mileage but only a bit over half the total gain. Follow the trail/use path along the lake's west shore past scattered campsites to Nada Creek near the lake's upper end — a boulder-hop in normal summer flow, but a genuine ford in early-season high water. Immediately past the creek, leave the maintained trail: climb a cairned climbers' path staying along the south edge of a broad talus field toward the notch that opens into Temple Canyon. Where the talus narrows to roughly 75 ft, work right onto a class 2-3 ledge system that skirts a waterfall, then continue up slabs into scattered trees. A steep, loose dirt-and-rock climbers' path then leads into Temple Canyon proper, staying near the stream (the last reliable water before the summit block) as it steepens toward the canyon head. Near the top, scramble up and left onto the broad, larch-dotted plateau of Tamarack Meadows (~6,600 ft), cross another talus/boulder field above treeline, and follow a final sandy ramp under an overhang to the base of the South Ridge's technical section. Figure roughly 8 miles and ~7,000 ft one-way from the trailhead to the 8,295 ft summit — about 16-16.5 miles round trip, a very long car-to-car day if not camping at Nada Lake or in the canyon. Hazards: sustained sun exposure with no shade on the lower switchbacks, an unbridged Nada Creek crossing that gets serious with early-season snowmelt, faint cairn-dependent route-finding above Nada Lake, loose talus and scree throughout Temple Canyon, and lingering snow on north-facing ledges into early summer.

hits.text:
The base sits about 300 ft below the point where the top of Aasgard Pass meets the toe of Dragontail — so you are aiming under the junction of pass and mountain, not at it. Overshooting up the pass and then coming down is the common error.

The start is described as being in the middle of the protruding tower. On the ground the marker is above your head rather than at your feet: the first belay ledge is roughly 190 ft up and carries two bushes, and the route starts directly below the right-hand side of the right bush.

The first pitch also identifies itself by how it climbs. Fifty feet of easy ground leads to about ten feet of face moves around the right side of a recessed pod, and then back into the main crack system. If your first fifty feet is hard, or if there is no recessed pod to skirt, you are not on it.

The scree traverse in is the crux hazard of the approach — loose, exposed, and consequential given what is below.

runs: class 4 with one class 5 move in the chimney then easing to class 2 and 3 near the summit
hits.text: Parties typically combine this with the South Peak lookout climb in a single trip since both share the same long approach. From Camp Saddle/Tin Can Gap, descend onto the glacier and traverse to the base of the North Peak, then climb the West Couloir to the South Face. One party describes the climbing as Class 4 with one Class 5 move in the chimney, then easing to Class 2 and 3 near the summit — easier than it is sometimes described, with rock character compared to Chimney Rock.

runs: three fingers goat flats saddle lake trail 641
hits.text: FR 41 is closed to vehicles at the Canyon Creek bridge, so first walk or bike roughly 8-9 miles of road to the trailhead. The climb starts at the Tupso Pass trailhead on the Three Fingers-Goat Flats-Saddle Lake Trail #641. The trail climbs through forest, crossing a couple of small seasonal streams, to Saddle Lake at about 2.5 miles (last reliable, easy water before the alpine section; no camping within 200 ft of the lake and no fires from here on). From Saddle Lake continue roughly 2–2.5 more miles, gaining out of the timber into the open meadows of Goat Flats (~4.5 mi from the TH) — good camps and the last easy tentsites with views to Puget Sound. From Goat Flats the trail contours and climbs about 2 more miles to Tin Can Gap (~6.2 mi, roughly 3,500-3,800 ft of the day's gain done); this is the last maintained-trail point and the standard high camp/bivy for peak days. Tin Can Gap gives the first real view of the three summits and the Queest-Alb (Three Fingers) Glacier below. From the gap the route drops about 400 ft off-trail down snow/talus onto the glacier — early season this is a straightforward snow descent, but by late summer expect bare ice and a moat between rock and ice that requires care (crampons/axe recommended into at least July); crevasses open on the glacier by mid-summer so rope up if traveling as a team when covered. Cross the glacier and climb back up roughly 1,000 ft on the far side to the col between Middle and North Peak — this climb is on a mix of snow/scree and low-angle rock and is the route-finding crux of the approach. From the col, the North Peak route follows a ramp leading left then angling right into a shallow chimney, with sustained 4th-class and a few low-5th-class (5.0-5.4) exposed moves through loose-to-fair rock to the summit block; a harder 5.4 line exists on the upper west face but is avoided by most parties for rock quality. Carry a rope, a small rack, and glacier gear (axe/crampons, and a rope+harness for crevasse hazard) even in a scramble-grade season.

back to the north side of the ridge
hits.text:
Past Tin Can Gap you drop off-trail onto the Queest-Alb Glacier. Late in the season you can avoid the ice entirely by staying in the moat between the top edge of the glacier and the rock — and finding the entrance to that moat is the thing that goes wrong in bad weather. The trail crosses back to the north side of the ridge shortly before it and you meet the top of the glacier there; if you are on the south side of the ridge you have not crossed over yet.

The start of the actual climbing is not in doubt once you can see it: three wooden ladders, stacked in sequence and pinned into the rock with rebar and steel cable, run up the final rock band to the lookout deck. There is nothing else like them on the mountain. The transition between the second and third ladder is the hardest move and is awkward with a full pack, and the exposure is real.

The negative marker is which summit you are on. The lookout — and therefore the ladders — is on the south peak. If you have crossed the glacier and are scrambling rock toward a col with no ladders anywhere in view, you are heading for the Middle or North peak instead. Some parties also report a hand-line on a short exposed rock step just past Tin Can Gap before the glacier; treat any fixed rope there as unverified.

hits.text: This basin has its own rule and it is strictly enforced in spirit if not always in practice: no camping within one mile of the Yellow Aster Butte trail except at the tarns. Camp only on snow, rock or bare ground, never on the heather. No fires anywhere on the trail. Pack out all human waste; do not bury it. runs: 20 30 feet above the old p6 slung block anchor
hits.text: Two real options, and most parties take the walk-off. Option 1 (walk-off): from the East Shoulder, make an exposed, somewhat sketchy 4th-class traverse west (it borders on unprotected 5th-class slab in spots, so many parties stay roped) to gain the same descent gully used off the East Face. Downclimb the gully, then traverse north (right) to pick up the climbers'/cattle trail that runs up to Liberty Bell, which drops you onto the Blue Lake Trail; a faint climbers' path cuts off a final stretch of trail before the highway. Option 2 (rappel the route): from the top, the first anchor is a bolted station roughly 20-30 feet above the old P6 slung-block anchor. With double 70m ropes (a 70m lead line plus a 70m tag line) you can rappel from the very top of the route; doubled 60m ropes will not reach that first station. If you're bailing from above the P5 crux rather than finishing the route, two 60m ropes are workable using a fixed nut-and-sling anchor partway down P6 as an intermediate station — anything shorter risks coming up short between anchors. Lower down, the rappel stations are obvious, good-quality anchors on trees or bolts. Hardware is mixed vintage: some original 1989 5/16" bolts remain despite a post-2016 rebolting push, and at least one older fixed-nut/sling anchor is noted as aging — back up or inspect any anchor you didn't place yourself before weighting it.

runs: trapper lake and tributaries of the stehekin river
hits.text: Trapper Mountain (7,530 ft) rises on the crest of the North Cascades southeast of Cascade Pass, on the shared boundary of North Cascades National Park and the Glacier Peak Wilderness, about 0.7 mile east of Hurry-up Peak (7,821 ft) near the head of the Ptarmigan Traverse country. Runoff from the peak's basin and small glacial remnant feeds Trapper Lake and tributaries of the Stehekin River. It is a genuinely remote, seldom-visited scramble — access is a trail hike over Cascade Pass followed by a long off-trail bushwhack down to Trapper Lake — so parties can expect real solitude even in peak season. First climbed in 1949 by George Bell, Andrew Griscom, Harry King, and W. V. Graham Matthews.

hits.text: From the Lake Serene Trailhead, follow the maintained Lake Serene Trail #1068 roughly 4 miles and about 2,000 ft of gain to the lake basin. Traverse around the west side of the lake over talus and boulders to its south end, then climb steep brush and a gully system (snow-covered into early summer) toward the base of the North Peak's North Face. The standard North Face Route is a long, moderate alpine rock climb (Grade III, 5.6-5.7) on featured but sometimes rotten rock with significant brush; parties typically climb it car-to-car in a very long day (12-15+ hours) or with a bivy.

runs: 1.1 miles before the dingford creek trailhead at
hits.text: From North Bend take I-90 exit 34, then follow 468th Ave SE north about 0.6 mi to Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road (FS Road 56). The road is rough gravel/dirt for its upper miles; high-clearance is recommended. Continue roughly 16 miles up FS 56 (it bends right around the 12-mile mark) to an unsigned, easy-to-miss climbers'/fishermen's path on the north shoulder of the road about 1.1 miles before the Dingford Creek Trailhead, at roughly 1,350 ft elevation (approx. 47.526, -121.473). There is no trailhead sign or formal parking area — pull off where space allows. An older approach via the Taylor River trail system is now longer and rarely used, after the Taylor River bridge near Quartz Creek washed out — it now adds 6+ miles versus the standard Green Ridge line described above.

runs: 1.1 miles before the dingford creek trailhead at
hits.text: The trailhead is an unsigned climbers' and fishermen's path on the north shoulder of the Middle Fork road, roughly 1.1 miles before the Dingford Creek trailhead at about 1,350 ft — no sign, no formal parking, and easy to drive straight past. Climb Green Ridge steeply, staying left where a fork drops northeast to Green Ridge Lake, over the ridge high point near 4,840 ft, past a small tarn, then down about 800 ft into the Upper Garfield lake basin and north through steep forest to Charlie Brown Lake. That mid-route descent has to be re-climbed on the way out, so it costs far more than the raw mileage suggests.

runs: out onto the more south facing slopes of the mountain
hits.text: Charlie Brown Lake at about 4,390 ft is where the walking stops and the scramble begins, and it is the right place to stop because the whole remaining route is visible from its shore. From the outlet, work onto the peak's southeast slopes and thread up through broken cliff bands and duff to a broad talus field at roughly 4,850 ft — that talus field is the marker that you are on the correct line rather than one of the several plausible-looking weaknesses below it. From the top of the talus, angle left into an obvious gully with grassy slopes at its head. The gully is walled by rock on both sides and tops out near 5,400 ft at a notch beside a protruding rock on the south ridge, and it shoots you straight out onto the more south-facing slopes of the mountain. If you are traversing across the face rather than gaining height in a defined gully, you have gone past it. Above the notch the last few hundred feet are easy but steep heather to the summit ridge. Carry an axe and traction if snow is still sitting in that gully.

runs: to lucky pass the col between primus and tricouni
hits.text: Rope up and climb the Borealis Glacier, skirting the icefall in its middle. The glacier is split into a lower and an upper tier by slabs and cliffs; the upper tier leads to Lucky Pass, the col between Primus and Tricouni.

runs: split into upper and lower tiers separated by
hits.text: Start at Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20 (Diablo Lake, milepost 130, roughly 25 miles east of Marblemount) and park in the large lot above the boat ramp on the campground's south side — this is also the Thunder Creek Trailhead. Follow the maintained Thunder Creek Trail south about 6.5-6.7 miles to McAllister Camp (~1,900 ft), a backcountry stock camp where McAllister Creek meets Thunder Creek. The trail's original bridge over Thunder Creek near mile 6.6 washed out in fall 2017; parties now cross on logs a short way upstream of the old bridge site. Across the creek, pick up the unmaintained climbers' boot path at the first fork, climbing steeply through brush and around downed timber up the north ridge; a viewpoint near 4,600 ft gives the first look at Primus, Tricouni, and neighboring peaks. Continue through forest and heather to Borealis Lake (base camp), a flat bench below the Borealis Glacier. From camp, rope up for glacier travel and climb the Borealis Glacier, skirting the icefall in its middle — it has retreated significantly and split into upper and lower tiers separated by slabs and cliffs — navigating crevasses to Lucky Pass, the Primus-Tricouni col. From Lucky Pass, climb a steep snow finger roughly 200 ft up Tricouni's southwest side, then transition to rock ramps and ledges (class 3-4 scrambling) up the west ridge to the bouldery 8,102 ft summit. Hazards: crevasses on the Borealis Glacier (worse late season), a brushy and poorly marked boot path above McAllister Camp, and afternoon softening of the snow finger.

runs: begins in second growth forest and almost immediately
hits.text: Start at the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (Sunrise Mine Trail #707) off the Mountain Loop Highway near Big Four/Barlow Pass. The trail begins in second-growth forest and almost immediately crosses the South Fork Stillaguamish via a log crossing that can be a genuine obstacle during high runoff (early season/after rain). From there the trail climbs steadily through Wirtz Basin, breaks out of the trees into open talus and boulder fields marked by cairns, and reaches Headlee Pass at roughly 4,720 ft and 2.7 miles in — a narrow, rocky notch/couloir with loose rock underfoot where rockfall from parties above is a real hazard. Past the pass the trail drops briefly through trees, then crosses about a third of a mile of talus to Vesper Creek, which it follows up to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan, ~4,950 ft, ~3.5 mi/~2,700 ft gain from the trailhead) — the last reliable running water before the climb. From the lake, cross the outlet and follow the summit trail up talus and slabs to roughly 5,600-5,700 ft, then swing north across the slabs to the saddle/col between Vesper and Wolf Peak. From the saddle, a ledge system cuts across Vesper's north face at roughly 5,800 ft, reached by walking out steep, exposed heather benches that get slick when wet and hold a steep snow slope into early-to-mid summer (ice axe and possibly crampons recommended for that window). The ledge leads to a small notch overlooking the Vesper Glacier remnant, near where True Grit's start is found. Allow 3+ hours from the trailhead to the base of the route.

hits.text: Start from the large day-use lot on the north side of the highway at the pass, beside the ski area's substation and utility building, on the gated service road. Around a mile in, an easy-to-miss cairn-marked left fork leaves the road for Skyline Lake and the ridge — staying right on the road takes you to a cell tower instead. Past the lake the route crosses the low point in Skyline Ridge, drops into a creek drainage on the ridge's back side, and climbs back out to gain the Tye Ridge crest. There is no maintained trail; snow-free this is a stiff bushwhack, which is why most ascents are made on continuous snow.

runs: from skyline lake climb northwest through timber to
hits.text: The route's crux is at its start, and the start goes down rather than up. From Skyline Lake climb northwest through timber to the low point in the crest of Skyline Ridge at about 5,200 ft. The far side is not a walk-through: it is a drop of roughly 150 feet at close to fifty degrees, mossy loose rock and brush when snow-free and liable to cornice in winter. That drop-in is the confirmation you are in the right gap — a gap you can simply stroll over is the wrong one, and there are several plausible low points along that crest. It bottoms out at the head of a small creek near 4,800 ft, an early-season water source and the last one. From there a steep wooded slope opens into gentle meadows around 4,900 ft and thins through timber to the crest of Tye Ridge near 5,000 ft, which is where the brush finally clears and the going turns to open heather benches. Follow the crest north to the saddle between Sky Mountain and Tye Peak, then climb the ridgeline directly, staying on the highest ground to avoid cornices in winter and loose talus in summer.

From Burgundy Col, downclimb/scramble loose rock or steep snow around the north side of the spire to a twin-crack system marked by some obvious loose blocks about 60 ft up. hits.text: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on The Castle: from the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, continue about 1.2 miles further down the road (0.6 miles past where The Castle first becomes visible on the ridge) and park on the right (east) side where a dirt road from the Spangler Creek valley intersects the main road. Climb a long, very steep hillside to the base of the pinnacle.

Approach paths to individual crags (Megadike, Minidike, Weeping Wall, Joe's Rock) are unofficial, brushy, and easy to lose.

hits.text: Start at Barclay Lake trailhead (74920 NE Stevens Pass Hwy, Skykomish, WA 98288). Follow the pleasant level main trail for about 20 minutes to a bridge crossing a large creek (~1 mile). Before the bridge, break right into forest around a large boulder, then walk through relatively open forest or along the creek bed until reaching an open boulder field. Continue through the boulder field to reach steep gullies. Climb around the right side of a chossy waterfall (exposed scrambling). Continue up the wash to a ramp with hand lines, then up a 60–70° forested rib with fixed lines and natural protection, then approximately 800 feet of mostly roped-up slab via bolted sections and natural features. Total approach time: 2.5–3.5 hours for competent parties.

hits.text:
Start at the Barclay Lake trailhead (74920 NE Stevens Pass Hwy, Skykomish). Walk the pleasant, level main Barclay Creek trail for about 20 minutes and roughly a mile to a bridge crossing a large creek — often dry by mid-to-late summer.

Do not cross the bridge. Just before it, break right into the forest around a large boulder. Bushwhack through relatively open forest, or walk the creek bed, until you reach an open boulder field. Cross the boulder field to large trees and an open wash.

The wash leads to a steep, chossy, dirty waterfall; climb around its right side, staying out of the bushes — this stretch is exposed. Above that a ramp with hand lines, then a 60-70 degree forested rib with fixed lines and natural protection, including a low-fifth step in a gully protected by a fixed line, and a small rock face with a bolt. Then roughly 800 ft of mostly roped slab in 35-50 m pitches on bolts and natural gear. Competent parties with good beta take two and a half to four hours; the approach is technical and hard to get right even with information.

runs: unrope and scramble up and left to the base of the tower
hits.text: The end of the fixed and roped section is where you unrope and scramble up and left to the base of the tower. The test the first-ascent party wrote down is a negative one and it is the most useful thing on this approach: if what you are doing feels sketchy, you are off the line. The approach is unpleasant but it is protected the whole way — fixed lines, hand lines, bolts — so unprotected, committing ground means you have lost the route, not that the route has got harder. The base of the tower is the foot of a nearly 1,500 ft overhanging prow; there is no mistaking it once you are under it.

hits.text: Ares Tower is the highest of several named granite spires — Charon Tower, The Acropolis, Ares Tower, Vasiliki Tower, the Juno-Jupiter Towers, Aphrodite Tower, and Baccus Tower — strung along Vasiliki Ridge, which radiates north from the Wine Spires/Silver Star Mountain massif above Washington Pass. Fred Beckey and Herb Staley made the first ascent of the ridge on May 31, 1952; Beckey named it after Vasiliki Dwyer, a woman he met at Stevens Pass — the only Cascades feature he ever named after a woman. Despite its imposing look from the highway, Ares Tower itself is a moderate objective: essentially a 4th-class scramble to a notch just north of the true summit, finished by a short low-5th-class step (or an alternate direct low-5th variation up the west face).

Pick up the boot path skirting the bottom of the talus and follow the cairns carefully: this lower boulder and talus band is the trickiest route-finding on the whole approach, and it is considerably worse when snow covers the tread early in the season. runs: the large talus slope just south of spire gulch
hits.text: Park at the large paved turnout at the first hairpin turn on SR-20 (North Cascades Highway), about 1 mile east of the Washington Pass summit (roughly 5,160 ft elevation). There's no formal trailhead sign or numbered trail here — the route to Kangaroo Pass is an unmaintained but well-cairned climbers' path on Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest land along the edge of the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness. From the pullout, head south/southeast toward the base of the large talus slope just south of Spire Gulch (below the north side of Kangaroo Temple). Pick up the boot path skirting the bottom of the talus field and follow cairns carefully — this lower boulder/talus band is the trickiest route-finding on the approach, especially if snow-covered early in the season. The tread firms up into a distinct, easy-to-follow cairned trail once you're in the upper basin. Continue up mixed talus, boulders, and open slope to Kangaroo Pass (6,671 ft), gaining about 1,500 ft over roughly 1.5 miles — typically 1 to 1.5 hours. A small tarn just below the pass is the only water source on the approach and can be dry by late summer or fall; there is none higher, so carry enough from the car. Expect lingering snow from about 5,800 ft up to the pass into early-mid summer, depending on the year — an ice axe and/or microspikes are worth carrying into July. At Kangaroo Pass, leave the boot path and turn northeast onto Wallaby Peak's southwest ridge. A faint climbers' trail continues briefly then disappears on rock; stay on or near the ridge crest, weaving between its north and south sides across mixed rock, scree, and grassy benches. At about 7,400 ft, swing around onto the south flank into the south-facing summit gully. This gully is moderately steep with notable loose rock and scree — wear a helmet, especially with more than one person in the party, since climbers above can kick debris down onto those below; some parties pick a short Class 3 line on the gully's margins to avoid the worst of the scree. Near the top of the gully, exit left (northeast) for the short final scramble to the true summit. Total distance is about 3.0 miles one-way (6.0 mi / ~2,900 ft round trip, or 9.7 km); budget roughly 1 to 1.5 hours car-to-pass and another hour pass-to-summit.

hits.text: A striking twin-summit massif in the eastern Olympics, rising immediately north of Mount Constance (its nearest higher neighbor, 0.8 mi south-southeast) within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park. Warrior is the 11th-highest peak in the Olympic Range, built of Eocene-era pillow basalt uplifted with the range's obducted oceanic crust. Fred Beckey made the first ascent solo in 1945, climbing both the northwest and southeast (true, higher) summits in one push and naming the mountain; he's said to have carved his name into a rock at the saddle between the two summits, which some later parties report still finding.

runs: climb steep snow or a snow moat to
hits.text: This is the primary route to Warrior Peak's Southeast Summit. The route involves approximately 9-10 miles of approach hiking, making it a typical 2-day backpacking objective. From the cirque below the peak, ascend the obvious couloir between the SE and NW summits. If snow-filled (common early season), the couloir is steep and straightforward; if melted out, it's loose scree. Above the couloir, scramble to a saddle at approximately 7,000 feet, then climb steep snow or a snow moat to reach the exposed rock section. Some parties rope this short pitch; others solo it depending on conditions and skill.

runs: steep forest then steep open meadow then talus staying north of the
hits.text:
The first test is a creek you must not cross. Leave the trail before crossing the major stream that drains the Warrior / Inner Constance cirque. That stream is the last and largest of the several you meet going south from Boulder Shelter. Then climb east — steep forest, then steep open meadow, then talus — staying north of the streambed the whole way. The streambed is the handrail and it stays on your right. If you have crossed it and it is now on your left, you are on the wrong side of the drainage.

The arrival test is the cirque at about 5,900 ft, and it is unambiguous because it is a closed basin: the ground stops rising in front of you and the headwall closes round. From there, head north to the obvious couloir between the two peaks. Warrior has twin summits and the couloir runs up between them to a saddle at about 7,000 ft. There is one gully in that headwall with a summit on each side of it. If the gully you are in has a summit on only one side, it is not the one.

The test at the top of the couloir is which way to turn, and it is the single most useful sentence for this peak in fog: at the saddle, the higher peak is on your right. The southeast summit is the true top; the northwest summit at roughly 7,285 ft is the lower one. Coming up the couloir from the cirque, the true summit is to the right. Turn left and you will climb the wrong peak on ground just as loose.

Second test, on the summit block: above the saddle there is 20 to 50 feet of exposed, poor-quality rock rated Class 4 to low fifth on the block's northwest side, often gained over steep snow or a snow moat, and many parties fix a hand line on it. If your last obstacle before the top is a walk rather than a short difficult rock step, you are on the wrong summit.

What the season changes: the couloir is steep but straightforward when snow-filled, common early season; melted out it is a brutal scree slog to the same saddle. Both are the route.

runs: the prominent couloir north northeast to a saddle
hits.text: The working base for Warrior Peak, and the cheapest night in this zone by a wide margin because nothing has to be booked. It sits at about 4,950 ft and roughly 6.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead at 2,500 ft, past Camp Handy at 3,100 ft — an easy valley walk on maintained trail, which is why this and not the Dosewallips is how people actually get into this country. It is also 1.7 miles below Marmot Pass, so a Quilcene-side party can traverse in over the pass. For the Warrior Peak southeast summit the day runs south two-plus miles on the Dungeness trail, then up the prominent couloir north-northeast to a saddle near 7,000 ft; the couloir holds snow into late season and turns icy in cold weather, and the first twenty to fifty feet of rock above it is genuinely poor, low fifth class, and wants a rope. Camping higher in the cirque below the summit shortens that considerably and several parties recommend it, but it is a dry, unestablished bivy and you carry water for it. Best from July into September.

The line rambles up cracks and the ridge crest with sustained mid-fifth-class climbing throughout; the crux comes about halfway up, on pitch 4, on a short section of steep twin finger cracks, and the final pitch is an exposed, runout 5.8 face regarded by many parties as the route's real ("mental") crux. hits.text: West Twin Needle (7,936 ft) is the taller, western spire of the Twin Needles, a pair of rock pinnacles in the Southern Pickets immediately west of Mount Terror. Its slightly lower twin to the east (about 7,840+ ft) is the more technically serious of the pair; West Twin Needle carries easier class 2-3 flanks but this South Route tackles steeper 5.7 rock directly up its south/east side above Crescent Creek Basin. First climbed August 17, 1932 by William Degenhardt, James Martin, and Herb Strandberg, it sees very few ascents each year owing to the multi-day cross-country approach required to reach it.

runs: below the moraine to the head of crescent creek
hits.text: From the basin camp, the peak's south side shows two gullies separated by a dividing buttress, and picking the wrong one is the failure here. The right-hand gully is the trap: it cliffs out in a closed chimney and does not go. The line takes the minor rib on the climber's left of that rightmost gully. Get there by dropping about 300 ft below the moraine to the head of Crescent Creek and making a rising traverse beneath the gully system, past the adjacent buttress. The proof higher up is the chockstones: the gully leading up to the Eye Col is blocked by large jammed blocks, and pitching past them, including one narrow crack normally taken on a belay, is the crux of reaching the notch. If the gully you are in runs clean with no chockstones and narrows into a closed chimney above, back off — that is the right-hand gully. Above the notch, easy slabs and scrambling lead to the summit.

hits.text: Two trailheads serve this scramble, both off SR-20 between Rainy Pass and Washington Pass. Option A (PCT approach, most commonly used): park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass (~4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff). From the lot, leave the PCT almost immediately and strike out cross-country/climber's-path east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs — there is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT. Continue up through the trees (expect lingering snow patches into early summer) to about 6,100 ft, where the forest opens into a meadow basin below the west ridge/gully complex. From the basin, trend south/southeast on a rising traverse to gain the col/basin between Whistler and the southwest peak of Cutthroat, then work up the broad west ridge or the shallow gully just north of it to the summit shoulder; the final short section involves a rock gully with a visible ramp along the headwall over downsloping slabs and loose gravel — a helmet is recommended here for rockfall from parties above. Round trip via this line runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain (trailhead 4,850 ft to summit 7,790 ft). Option B (highway turnout approach, reaches the true south ridge): from the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass (0.7 mile before the Blue Lake trailhead, ~5,000 ft), walk back down/along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the west edge of a stand of trees. Follow the boot path up through a meadow, then rising-traverse to intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. From there, scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit; alternatively leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left (west) onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish to the summit that way. This line is also about 4 miles round trip with ~3,000 ft gain. Both approaches are trail-less above the first stretch of forest — expect route-finding, loose talus/scree in the gullies, and class 2-3 terrain with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest and summit gully; no reliable water source above the lower forest, so carry what you need from the car. No creek fords or avalanche paths of note on the standard summer line, but early-season snow lingers in the forest and basin and can make the gully sections firm or icy.

hits.text:
The trailhead is unmarked and the path start is a tree-line edge, so the find is at the road rather than on the mountain. The pullout is 0.7 mile before the Blue Lake Trailhead coming from Rainy Pass. If you have reached the Blue Lake Trailhead, you have driven 0.7 mile too far. From the pullout, walk the shoulder to where a stand of trees begins, and the boot path leaves from its west edge.

Follow the boot path up through a meadow, then rising-traverse to intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. A level section of ridge is the arrival, and a level stretch on a ridge is something you can feel underfoot without seeing anything.

From there, scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit. The alternative, which is also correct: leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left, west, onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish that way.

So the decision at 6,800 ft is a real fork and both branches work: stay on the crest for more exposure and directness, or cross two gullies west for easier ground.

The negative test against the other approach, which matters because both start within three miles of each other on the same highway: the PCT option leaves from the marked PCT North lot at Rainy Pass and gains a meadow basin at 6,100 ft below the west ridge. This one leaves from an unmarked turnout and gains the south ridge at 6,180 ft. Marked lot and west ridge, or unmarked turnout and south ridge.

runs: the second gully and follow it to the summit
hits.text: Everything starts from this lot. It is also the start of Whistler Mountain, which is unlike the rest: head east from the parking area into the second gully and follow it to the summit, about four miles round trip and three thousand feet of gain, and no camp helps in the slightest. There is a toilet and no water. Parties routinely sleep in the car here before a long PCT day. As with everything on this stretch of SR 20, access is governed by the winter closure — the highway shuts in late November or early December and normally reopens between mid April and early May, though a bad winter can push it very much later, so confirm before driving. Note also that this specific trailhead has been closed at times for roadwork in recent seasons, which strands the entire zone when it happens.

Follow it about 14 miles to the spur signed for Iron Gate, FR 3900-500, and drive that about 6 miles to the trailhead. FR 3900-500 is a rough high-clearance road, not for passenger cars or trailers. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is required to park, plus a free self-issue wilderness permit.

runs: about 5 miles south of the canadian border
hits.text: Windy Peak (8,335') is the easternmost of Washington's 100 highest peaks (the "Bulgers"), standing over the remote northeastern Pasayten Wilderness about 5 miles south of the Canadian border. Unlike most Bulgers, its standard route is a non-technical trail walk-up rather than a climb — it's cataloged here for peakbagging-list completeness, and the real challenge is logistical: a long, remote approach on gravel forest roads far from any town. A gabled-roof L-4 cab fire lookout was built on the summit in 1932 by E.W. Allen and Raymond Johnson, saw brief use in the WWII Aircraft Warning Service (Jul-Sep 1942), and was removed in 1963; remnants of its old telephone line are still visible on the northwest slope.

hits.text: From Tonasket, cross the Okanogan River and drive west on Loomis-Oroville Road to Loomis. Just north of town turn onto Toats Coulee Road, County Road 9425, which becomes 4066 and then FR-39, and follow it roughly 20 miles to the junction with FR-3900-300 at Long Swamp Campground, about 5,500 ft. That last stretch is a long dirt road and is often not reliably clear of snow and debris until late June. Park at the campground, fill out the self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk, and display a NW Forest Pass. Do not confuse this with the Windy Creek / Cathedral Driveway trailhead about 3 miles farther west on the same road system, which starts a different and brushier trail.

hits.text: From Tonasket, cross the Okanogan River and drive west on Loomis-Oroville Road to Loomis. Just north of town, turn onto Toats Coulee Road (County Rd #9425, becoming #4066 then FR-39) and follow it roughly 20 miles to the junction with FR-3900-300 at Long Swamp Campground — the standard trailhead for Windy Peak Trail #342. The Windy Creek/Cathedral Driveway trailhead is about 3 miles farther west on the same road system; the separate Iron Gate trailhead is reached via a rougher spur and has the roughest driving of the three approaches (last ~6 miles).

Below that, careful cramponing is needed through a rock defile where a narrow ribbon of snow winds between deep moats — described by one party as the most unnerving part of the descent. Continue down the northwest ridge's snow faces and benches to Tailgunner Pass, then down the Tailgunner Couloir and the bushwhack drainage back to Barclay Creek Trail and the trailhead.

hits.text: Witches Tower is the distinct granite pinnacle at the west end of the Enchantments, about 0.4 mi east-southeast of Dragontail Peak (its nearest higher neighbor) and dividing remnants of the Snow Creek Glacier between Little Annapurna and Dragontail. It's a compact, airy summit block commonly tacked on to an Aasgard Pass day, or linked with Colchuck Peak, Dragontail Peak, and Little Annapurna as part of the classic Enchantments traverse.

Protection placements on the crux can be tricky to find, so an experienced leader is recommended.

Stuart Lake trailhead to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, the boot path along the lake's west shore, Aasgard Pass at about 7,800 ft, then south across talus toward the tower and up snow or Class 2 rock to the col just southwest of it.

Published figures for the day put it at roughly six to eight hours and about 4,800 ft of gain from the trailhead to this point, which is a wide enough spread that it should be treated as a range rather than a plan.

From the col the climbing is short: about 100 ft up the sharp ridge, a few feet right onto the south face at Class 4, a 5.5 step-up, a short face, and a scramble to the summit slot.
